Name: spontaneous_vs_provoked_confabulation
Title: Two Types of Confabulation: Why LLMs Refuse When Asked but Fabricate When They Speak Freely
Short Hypothesis: Our novel unit of analysis is generation mode (directly queried vs. free-generating), not entity recognition itself. Primary falsifiable claim: for the SAME unknown entity that a model correctly refuses/hedges about under a direct query, the model's internal entity-recognition ('I don't know this') signal still fires when the entity appears mid free-generation, yet it fails to gate output there, so the model confidently fabricates attributes. The dissociation is thus causal, not a recognition failure: the self-knowledge probe reads 'unknown' equally in both modes, but the recognition direction causally disrupts downstream attribute-extraction only in the provoked mode and is decoupled from it in the spontaneous mode. Secondary analyses (not required for the primary claim): re-engaging the gate mid-generation restores hedging; fabrication scales with continuation pressure while the probe stays constant; and both effects transfer across entity types and models. The claim is refuted if fabrication rate is mode-independent, or if the probe fires substantially less in the spontaneous mode (a recognition failure rather than a gate bypass).
Related Work: Clinical neuropsychology (Kopelman 1987; Schnider et al. 1996) establishes a double dissociation between provoked confabulation (normal gap-filling when questioned) and spontaneous confabulation (unbidden fabrication from failed reality/temporal monitoring). In LLMs, 'Do I Know This Entity?' (2024) finds causal entity-recognition directions that gate knowledge refusal; answerability directions (2023) and factual self-awareness features (2025) recover similar self-knowledge signals; 'LLMs Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know' (2025) shows internal states track the recall process rather than truth. The exact setting limitation shared by all of these is that the self-knowledge/refusal signal is only ever measured in the PROVOKED regime, i.e., a question is explicitly posed and the very next token is the model's answer, so the gate is guaranteed the opportunity to act. None tests whether that same signal is engaged versus bypassed when the model itself introduces the entity during free generation under coherence/continuation pressure. Novelty here is primarily a new PHENOMENON (a provoked-vs-spontaneous behavioral dissociation in LLM fabrication) and a new MECHANISM (the recognition signal is present but causally decoupled from attribute-extraction specifically in free generation); the mid-generation re-gating is a secondary, more exploratory INTERVENTION contribution, not claimed as equally proven. This is not a provoked-query benchmark in a different wrapper: the object of study is the generation mode as a causal variable, tested on the identical entities the model already refuses under direct query, with matched-format controls to rule out prompt wording. It also differs from prior proposals of ours, which concern direct-query retrieval/expression rather than the queried-vs-free generation mode.
Abstract: Human neuropsychology distinguishes provoked confabulation (fabrication in response to a question) from spontaneous confabulation (unbidden fabrication reflecting failed reality monitoring). We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous dissociation and, if so, whether it is a causal gating failure rather than a recognition failure. LLMs carry an internal entity-recognition signal that gates refusal when they are asked about an unknown entity. Our primary, falsifiable hypothesis is that this gate is engaged when the model is provoked by a direct query but bypassed when the model spontaneously introduces the same unknown entity mid-generation, so a model that correctly refuses 'Who is <obscure name>?' will nonetheless fabricate a detailed biography for that name while free-generating a passage that mentions it. We pre-register a single primary dissociation metric (paired fabrication-rate lift, spontaneous minus provoked, on the identical entities) and a single primary causal metric (net fabrication suppression when the recognition representation is patched from a refusing provoked run into a fabricating spontaneous run). We isolate generation mode from prompt wording with matched-format controls, and we separate 'the probe fires' from 'the probe causally gates' with explicit ablations: a linear/SAE probe should read 'unknown' equally in both modes (present), while activation patching and attention analysis should show the recognition direction disrupts attribute-extraction heads only in the provoked mode (decoupled in the spontaneous mode). Secondary analyses test mid-generation re-gating, a continuation-pressure dose-response, and transfer across entity types and models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B). So what: if confirmed, direct questioning is not enough to characterize a model's fabrication risk during continuation, which matters for safety-eval designers (who must add free-generation probes, not just Q&A honesty benchmarks), refusal-training practitioners (who should supervise the gate under generation momentum, not only under queries), and mechanistic-interpretability researchers and model auditors (who gain a concrete present-but-decoupled failure mode and a candidate generation-time fix). Operationally, confirmation would push honesty evaluation and refusal training toward free-generation conditions and generation-time interventions; refutation (mode-independent fabrication, or a probe that simply weakens in free generation) would instead tell the field that a single self-knowledge signal governs fabrication regardless of mode, so query-time evaluation suffices and effort belongs on strengthening recognition itself. Either outcome is informative.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 - matched unknown/known entity dataset): Build entities the model demonstrably cannot recall (so any specific attribute is a fabrication) plus a matched known set. Data: constructed - ~250 clearly-unknown entities (nonexistent/fictional names generated to be plausible but absent from any corpus, plus ultra-long-tail real entities) and ~250 popularity-matched known entities; unknown status validated by direct probing and an entity-recognition probe; restrict the unknown set to entities the model refuses/hedges on under a direct query. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): fraction of candidate unknowns that (a) are refused/hedged under a direct query and (b) read as 'unknown' by the recognition probe (the eligible unknown set), and the matched known set answered assertively. Convincing: >= 200 eligible unknowns and >= 200 knowns. Indecision band: 120-200 eligible unknowns - reduced power, reported; below 120 the dissociation test is under-powered. Negative (model does not reliably refuse any unknowns under direct query) means there is no provoked-refusal baseline and H1/H2 cannot be posed on this model.

Experiment 2 (H0 - provoked vs spontaneous elicitation, matched-format controls, and fabrication scoring): Create matched provoked and spontaneous conditions per entity, plus format controls, and a fabrication scorer. Definitions (pre-registered): 'fabrication' = the model asserts >= 1 specific, checkable attribute (date, place, relation, quantity) about the entity as fact; 'hedge/refuse' = explicit uncertainty, refusal, or no specific attribute; a paraphrase of the prompt with no new attribute is NOT fabrication; for real long-tail entities, an asserted attribute that is verifiably TRUE is scored correct (not fabrication) and only unverifiable/false specifics count. Data: eligible entities. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Conditions: (a) provoked prompt ('Who is X? What did X do?'); (b) spontaneous prompt embedding X in a free-generation task with continuation pressure ('Write a short encyclopedia paragraph:' with X as topic, or a narrative introducing X); (c) matched-format controls - a provoked prompt wrapped in the SAME encyclopedia/narrative surface text but still ending in an explicit question, and a spontaneous prompt with identical lexical framing minus the question, so wording/task-surface is held constant and only queried-vs-free varies. Scoring: per-entity fabrication rate and asserted-attribute token probabilities, judged by GPT-4o plus attribute-level ground truth for fictional entities; human spot-check on 100 items for judge calibration (report kappa). Decisive metric (first): judge-human kappa on the calibration sample. Convincing: kappa >= 0.8. Indecision band: kappa 0.6-0.8 - noisy scorer; restrict to fictional entities where fabrication is unambiguous and report shrinkage. Negative (kappa < 0.6) means fabrication cannot be scored reliably and the design must change.

Experiment 3 (CORE; H1 - provoked/spontaneous dissociation exists; PRIMARY dissociation metric): Test that the same unknown entity is fabricated about more in the spontaneous than the provoked mode, holding prompt format constant. Data: eligible unknowns, both modes plus the matched-format controls from Experiment 2. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared: spontaneous vs provoked fabrication rate (paired, same entity); the matched-format control pair (isolates mode from wording); a single-signal null treating fabrication as one entity-difficulty signal independent of mode (logistic regression with mode x entity; paired McNemar); matched-known control (should assert in both modes). PRE-REGISTERED PRIMARY OUTCOME: fabrication-rate lift = P(fabricate | spontaneous) minus P(fabricate | provoked), paired, CI, measured on the matched-format pair. Convincing: lift >= 15 percentage points, CI excludes 0, while knowns assert in both modes and the format-only control shows no comparable lift. Indecision band: lift 5-15 points - weak mode effect; report as suggestive and lean on Experiment 5. Negative (lift CI includes 0, or the format-only control reproduces the lift) refutes H1: fabrication is mode-independent or a format artifact.

Experiment 4 (CORE; H2 - recognition signal is PRESENT in both regimes): Test that the 'unknown' self-knowledge signal fires equally under provoked and spontaneous modes, so any dissociation is not a recognition failure. This experiment establishes probe PRESENCE only; whether the probe causally gates is tested separately in Experiment 5 (the two are not treated as equivalent). Data: eligible unknowns, both modes. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; recover the entity-recognition direction via a linear probe on the entity-token residual stream (and SAE features where available), seeds {0,1,2}, label-shuffle null. Decisive metric (first): peak-layer unknown-vs-known probe AUROC at the entity position in the spontaneous mode, and its difference from the provoked mode. Convincing: spontaneous AUROC >= 0.75 and within 0.05 of provoked (signal present and mode-invariant). Indecision band: spontaneous AUROC 0.60-0.75 or 0.05-0.15 below provoked - partly weakened, a mix of bypass and recognition degradation; report as mixed. Negative (spontaneous AUROC << provoked, e.g., gap > 0.15) means the signal fails to fire in free generation - a recognition failure, not a bypass - refuting H2's core.

Experiment 5 (CORE; H2 - the gate is CAUSALLY disconnected in free generation; PRIMARY causal metric): Test that the recognition signal ceases to disrupt attribute-extraction in the spontaneous mode - i.e., 'probe fires' (Exp 4) does not imply 'probe gates'. Data: eligible unknowns, both modes. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) measure attention of attribute-extraction heads to the entity token in each mode; (b) activation-patch the entity-token recognition representation from a provoked (refusing) run into a spontaneous (fabricating) run and test whether fabrication is suppressed; (c) reverse control - patch spontaneous into provoked. Systems compared: recognition-patch vs random-position patch. PRE-REGISTERED PRIMARY OUTCOME: net fabrication-suppression rate from the provoked->spontaneous recognition patch, net of random-position patch. Convincing: net suppression >= 25 points AND attribute-head attention to the entity is measurably higher in the spontaneous mode despite equal recognition firing (Exp 4). Indecision band: net suppression 10-25 points - the gate is partly connected in free generation. Negative (< 10 points, or no attention difference) means the gate is not specifically disconnected, refuting H2's causal-disconnection claim.

Experiment 6 (CORE; secondary intervention - re-gating restores refusal in free generation): Test that restoring the recognition signal's effect converts spontaneous fabrication into hedging. This is the exploratory intervention contribution and is not required for the primary phenomenon/mechanism claims. Data: eligible unknowns, entity-disjoint train/test; amplify the 'unknown' direction (or restore its attention effect on attribute-extraction heads) at the entity position during free generation, seeds {0,1,2}, dose-controlled. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the injected effect. Systems compared: re-gating vs 'only state what you are sure of' system-prompt vs refusal fine-tuning vs random-direction. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = spontaneous-fabrication-to-hedge conversion rate divided by over-refusal rate on 200 known entities (which must stay assertive); secondary, accuracy on the 200 knowns, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: conversion >= 30% with < 5-point over-refusal on knowns, beating the system-prompt baseline on recovered-per-collateral. Indecision band: conversion 15-30% or over-refusal 5-10 points - partial; report parity with prompting. Negative (no better than system-prompt, or knowns get refused) refutes the re-gating claim but leaves H1/H2 intact.

Experiment 7 (AUXILIARY / appendix; H1 - continuation-pressure dose-response): Test that spontaneous fabrication scales with continuation pressure while the recognition signal stays constant (momentum overrides the gate). Data: eligible unknowns rendered at varied continuation pressure (entity position in the passage, how committed the prior text is to elaboration, sampling temperature 0.0-1.0). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Decisive metric (first): regression coefficient of fabrication rate on the continuation-pressure index, with the entity-position recognition-probe AUROC measured at each level. Convincing: fabrication-rate coefficient CI excludes 0 (rises with pressure) while recognition AUROC stays within 0.05 across levels. Indecision band: coefficient CI excludes 0 but recognition AUROC also drifts > 0.05 - pressure both raises fabrication and erodes recognition, confounding the override story; report as mixed. Negative (fabrication flat in pressure) refutes the continuation-pressure override account.

Experiment 8 (AUXILIARY / appendix; H1/H2 - transfer and architecture generality): Test that the dissociation and re-gating generalize across entity types and models. Data: eligible entities partitioned by type (fictional vs long-tail real); re-gating vector trained on one type, applied to the other. Models: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; re-run the primary metrics of Experiments 3-6, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-type re-gating conversion relative to within-type, plus replication of the provoked/spontaneous lift (Exp 3) per model. Convincing: cross-type conversion >= 50% of within-type AND the lift replicates (CI excludes 0) in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-type 30-50% - model/type-specific. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines H1-H2 to one model. Report whether larger models close the provoked-vs-spontaneous gap.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The provoked and spontaneous conditions differ in prompt format, so the dissociation could be a format artifact rather than a genuine mode effect; the matched-format controls (Exp 2/3), the single-signal null, and the constant-recognition-signal finding (Exp 4) are essential to attribute the effect to generation mode, and if the format-only control reproduces the lift the primary claim fails.

The recognition signal might in fact fire less in the spontaneous regime (a recognition failure, not a gate bypass); Exp 4 directly tests this and pre-commits that a large AUROC drop refutes the bypass claim - either outcome is informative but this is the main mechanistic risk.

'Probe fires' and 'probe causally gates' are distinct; we do not treat them as equivalent - Exp 5's patching and attention tests, not probe firing alone, are decisive for the causal-disconnection claim, and graded results remain informative.

Re-gating (Exp 6) is the most exploratory claim and could cause over-refusal on known entities or degrade fluency; the known-entity specificity control and over-refusal metric are central, and a negative here leaves the phenomenon and mechanism claims intact.

Scoring 'fabrication' during free generation is noisy for real long-tail entities (some asserted facts may be true); the pre-registered scoring rule counts verifiably-true specifics as correct and relies on fictional/nonexistent entities where any specific attribute is a fabrication, with reported coverage and a fictional-only fallback if kappa is low.
A single transferable re-gating vector may not exist if the bypass is entity-type-specific (Exp 8), limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B open models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: articulation_use_dissociation
Title: Say vs. Use: A Causal Double Dissociation Between the Knowledge LLMs Articulate and the Knowledge They Act On
Short Hypothesis: The novel scientific claim is a bidirectional, causal double dissociation between the knowledge an LLM can verbally articulate and the knowledge it actually uses in an implicit downstream decision. Concretely: (A) some facts are stated correctly but not used ('inert articulation') and (B) some facts are used correctly to drive a decision but cannot be stated ('tacit knowledge'), and these two directions are carried by partially distinct internal loci. 'Distinct loci' is the strong, testable version: steering an 'articulation' direction changes what the model says while leaving what it uses intact, and steering a 'use' direction does the reverse (a direction-specific double dissociation). This is stronger than mere probe separability and rules out the weaker alternatives that say/use share one representation or differ only by task-specific readout features on a single entangled subspace.
Related Work: Prior work establishes an acquisition-vs-utilization gap (Kandpal/Chen 2023; Physics of LMs 3.2, 2023), a 'know but don't tell' disconnect in long context (2024), missing-vs-unused knowledge in patents (2025), knowledge-reasoning dissociation in clinical NLI (2025), and comprehension-without-competence 'split-brain' framing (2025). Self-explanation-faithfulness work (NeuroFaith 2025) checks whether stated reasoning matches internal computation. What these measure: a unidirectional behavioral gap (the model has/states knowledge but fails to apply it), typically in one direction and without intervention. What they do not test: (i) the reverse, under-studied 'tacit knowledge' direction (used-but-unsayable), and (ii) whether articulation and use are *causally separable representations* rather than one signal read out two ways. Our novelty is primarily in the PHENOMENON (a bidirectional say/use double dissociation, elevating the tacit direction) and secondarily in the MECHANISM (direction-specific causal separability shown by intervention); the task construction is adapted from existing benchmarks and is not the main contribution. The delta to the closest family (utilization-gap / know-but-don't-tell / self-explanation faithfulness) is the move from a one-way behavioral mismatch to a causal double dissociation with targeted interventions. The tacit-knowledge direction is not reducible to a harder version of the usual gap: the usual gap is knowledge-present-but-unused (a use failure), whereas tacit knowledge is knowledge-used-but-unstatable (an articulation failure with successful use), the opposite off-diagonal cell that no amount of increasing use-task difficulty can produce. This is orthogonal to our prior proposals, which concern retrieval-to-output for direct factual queries; here the object is the mismatch between verbal articulation and implicit use of the same fact.
Abstract: Large language models are known to 'possess' knowledge they fail to 'use', but the relationship between what a model can say and what it actually acts on remains unclear. We propose that articulation and use draw on partially distinct internal representations, predicting a causal double dissociation. For a fixed fact f about a subject, we build two probes: an articulation query that asks the model to state f directly, and a use query that requires f only implicitly (e.g., choosing between two options where f is a hidden discriminator, or completing a task whose correct answer depends on f but never names it). We first document the behavioral double dissociation: inert-articulation facts (stated, not used) and tacit-knowledge facts (used, cannot be stated), quantifying their prevalence above a matched single-signal null. We then test the mechanistic claim that a separable 'say' locus and 'use' locus exist: linear probes identify residual-stream directions predicting articulation vs use success, and activation patching and steering test direction-specificity — amplifying the say-locus improves articulation without changing use, and amplifying the use-locus does the reverse. Crucially, we require steering/patching to beat merely correlational probes, distinguishing separate causal loci from task-specific readout on one entangled subspace. We further test whether tacit knowledge can be surfaced by patching from the use-pathway into the articulation-pathway. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA, T-REx, and comparison/classification tasks, with strict shortcut, specificity, and difficulty controls. So what: if confirmed, behavioral transparency is incomplete — a model may act on knowledge it never verbalizes, so an auditor who only asks a model what it knows (e.g., 'do you know an exploit for X?', or a clinical system queried for a contraindication) could clear a system that in fact uses that knowledge in its decisions; interpretability researchers, model auditors, and knowledge-editing practitioners would then need to measure use-pathways separately from verbal QA, and editing a fact's articulation would not guarantee editing its use. The claim is falsifiable: if false, the off-diagonal cells vanish under the single-signal null and steering cannot separate say from use, collapsing articulation and use to one signal; if true, direction-specific interventions produce the double dissociation.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — paired say/use task construction and validity): Build the measurement instrument and verify the use-query truly requires the fact, so downstream dissociation cannot be an artifact of an unsolvable or fact-independent task. Data: adapted from PopQA (14,282 QA pairs, 16 relations) and T-REx; for each fact f = (subject, relation, object) we build an articulation query ('What is X's {relation}?') and a use query where f is only an implicit discriminator (a comparison 'Which of A or B is larger in {attribute}?' or a classification 'Is X's {attribute} before 2000?'). Target ~2,000 facts spanning >=8 relations after filtering to single-token-first objects. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): use-query correctness when f is made indeterminate (matched query about an unknown subject) — must drop to chance (within +-5 points of the format's guessing rate). Convincing: >= 1,500 facts pass this validity gate. Indecision band: 1,000-1,500 facts pass — proceed with reduced power and report it; below 1,000 the use-query is contaminated by non-f cues and H1-H3 are not testable. Negative (use-queries solvable without f) means the format leaks and must be rebuilt before any dissociation claim.

Experiment 2 (H1 — behavioral double dissociation exists): Test that both off-diagonal cells (say-correct/use-wrong = inert articulation; use-correct/say-wrong = tacit knowledge) occur beyond what a single shared knowledge signal predicts. Data: validated facts from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; cross-tabulate per-fact articulation-success x use-success (2x2). Systems compared: observed off-diagonal mass vs a pre-registered single-signal null — a per-fact logistic model with one shared latent difficulty plus a fixed per-task bias, from which we test the residual say x use interaction; null distribution by permutation (1,000 permutations of the say/use labels within matched-difficulty strata). Decisive metric (first): residual say-use interaction coefficient (log-odds) with 95% CI, plus prevalence of each off-diagonal cell. Power: with ~2,000 facts an 8% off-diagonal cell is ~160 facts, giving >0.9 power to detect an interaction odds-ratio of 1.5 at alpha 0.05 (report realized power). Convincing: interaction CI excludes 0 AND each off-diagonal cell holds >= 8% of facts. Indecision band: interaction CI excludes 0 but one off-diagonal cell is 3-8% — a one-sided dissociation, weaker than the claimed double dissociation. Negative (interaction CI includes 0, off-diagonals explained by shared difficulty) refutes H1: say and use behave as one signal.

Experiment 3 (H1 — off-diagonal cells are genuine, not shortcuts; with error analysis): Test that tacit-knowledge cases genuinely use f and inert-articulation cases genuinely state f, and characterize the false cases. Data: the two off-diagonal cells from Experiment 2. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared: for tacit facts, (i) counterfactually flip f in an in-context statement and check the use-answer flips (necessity of f), (ii) confirm the use-query fails when f is indeterminate, (iii) an adversarially-matched control where surface cues (subject names, option format, lexical overlap) are preserved but f is made irrelevant to the correct answer — the model should NOT succeed above chance if it were truly using f; for inert facts, check articulation consistency across 4 paraphrases. Decisive metric (first): genuine-use rate (fraction of tacit facts whose use-answer flips with the counterfactual AND that fail the adversarial-cue control) and genuine-articulation rate (fraction of inert facts consistent across paraphrases). Convincing: both rates >= 70%. Indecision band: 50-70% — a substantial minority are shortcuts/guesses; retain only the passing subset and report shrinkage. Negative (< 50%) means the off-diagonal cells are largely artifacts and H1's interpretation fails. Error-analysis plan: for false 'tacit' cases, categorize by cause (surface-cue shortcut, lucky guess at chance, format leakage); for false 'inert' cases, categorize by cause (paraphrase-sensitive articulation, near-miss/format-parse failure); report category proportions.

Experiment 4 (H2 — separable internal loci by probing): Test that say-success and use-success are carried by partially distinct residual-stream information. Data: validated facts with say/use outcomes. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a say-probe and a use-probe (logistic regression, seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null) on subject-token and last-token residuals at each layer. Systems compared: each probe's own-task AUROC, and — after residualizing each probe's features against the other task's label — the unique per-task AUROC that survives. Decisive metric (first): unique (residualized) use-probe AUROC and say-probe AUROC at their best layers. Convincing: each retains AUROC >= 0.65 after residualization (task-specific information exists beyond shared signal). Indecision band: unique AUROC 0.55-0.65 — weak separability; the representations are mostly shared. Negative (unique AUROC <= 0.55, at shuffle level) means say and use share one representation and H2 is unsupported. Note: probe separability is necessary but not sufficient for distinct causal loci — it can reflect task-specific readout on a shared subspace; the causal test is Experiment 5.

Experiment 5 (H3 — direction-specific causal double dissociation; probing vs causation): Test that steering the say-locus changes what the model states without changing what it uses, and steering the use-locus does the reverse — the decisive evidence for separate causal loci beyond correlational probes. Data: matched say-correct/say-wrong and use-correct/use-wrong states; say-direction and use-direction = mean residual differences, seeds {0,1,2}. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the injected direction. Systems compared: amplify say-direction, amplify use-direction, opposite-direction control, random-direction control, and a correlational-probe baseline (steer along the raw probe weight vector rather than the causal mean-difference direction), on both articulation and use readouts. Decisive metric (first): specificity index = on-target task change minus off-target task change (percentage points), for each direction; plus the gap between causal-direction specificity and probe-vector specificity. Convincing: say-direction specificity >= 20 points and use-direction specificity >= 20 points, with random/opposite controls < 5 points AND causal directions exceeding the raw-probe baseline — a genuine causal double dissociation not reducible to probe correlation. Indecision band: specificity 8-20 points for one direction — partial, single-sided dissociation. Negative (both specificity indices < 8 points or match random/probe baseline) refutes H3: the two functions cannot be steered independently.

Experiment 6 (H3 — surfacing tacit knowledge by cross-pathway patching): Test the strong form of the use-locus claim — that information used but not stated can be routed into articulation. Data: tacit-knowledge facts (Experiment 3, genuine-use subset). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; patch the use-pathway residual (from the run where f is demonstrably used) into the articulation run at the probe-identified layers/positions. Systems compared: cross-pathway patch vs say-direction amplification vs ROME edit vs random-patch. Decisive metric (first): articulation-recovery rate (tacit facts now stated correctly) net of random-patch rate; secondary, specificity (accuracy on 200 unrelated held-out facts) and fluency (held-out perplexity delta). Convincing: net recovery >= 20 points with < 3-point unrelated-fact drop, beating say-direction amplification. Indecision band: net recovery 8-20 points or 3-6-point collateral — tacit content is partially routable; report as suggestive. Negative (< 8 points or ROME/say-direction do as well) means use-pathway content is not separately routable into articulation.

Experiment 7 (H2/H3 — transfer and architecture generality): Test that say/use directions are a general split, not relation- or model-specific. Data: facts partitioned by relation; directions estimated on a subset of relations, applied to held-out relations. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 2, 4, 5, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation steering specificity index relative to within-relation, plus replication of the behavioral interaction (Experiment 2) per model. Convincing: cross-relation specificity >= 50% of within-relation AND behavioral dissociation replicates in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in exactly 1 model or cross-relation specificity 30-50% — model/relation-dependent. Negative (no cross-relation transfer, no replication) confines H2-H3 to specific relations on one model. Also report whether the dissociation shrinks with model size.

Experiment 8 (H1 — task-format robustness): Test that the dissociation tracks say-vs-use rather than a particular use-query format or its difficulty. Data: each validated fact rendered in three use formats (comparison, classification, implicit completion), difficulty-matched by per-format chance rate. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Decisive metric (first): correlation of per-fact use-success across the three formats, and whether the say x use interaction (Experiment 2) survives within each format after controlling per-format difficulty. Convincing: interaction CI excludes 0 in >= 2 of 3 formats and per-fact use-success correlates r >= 0.5 across formats. Indecision band: interaction survives in exactly 1 format — format-specific, weakening generality. Negative (interaction vanishes once format/difficulty controlled) means the dissociation is a task-demand artifact, not a say/use representational split.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The dissociation could be an artifact of use-query difficulty (extra task demands) rather than a representational say/use split; the pre-registered single-signal null (Exp 2), format-robustness check (Exp 8), and counterfactual + adversarial-cue controls (Exp 3) are essential, and a residual interaction surviving these controls is the decisive behavioral evidence.

Say and use representations may be entangled on one subspace rather than cleanly separable; probe separability alone (Exp 4) is insufficient, so the direction-specific steering test that also beats a raw-probe-vector baseline (Exp 5) is the decisive causal evidence, and a graded/partial dissociation would weaken the strong claim while remaining informative.

Establishing that tacit-knowledge facts are genuinely 'used' (not solved by a shortcut) is hard; counterfactual flipping, indeterminacy checks, and the adversarially-matched control mitigate but may not fully eliminate confounds, and coverage will be limited; false 'tacit' and false 'inert' cases are catalogued in the Exp 3 error analysis.
Cross-pathway patching to surface tacit knowledge may induce confident confabulation on facts not actually held; strict specificity and fluency controls are required and utility may be capped.
A single transferable say/use direction may not exist if the split is fact-specific, limiting generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate probe/logit-lens readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: retrieval_gating_hypothesis
Title: The Retrieval Gate: Why LLMs Store Facts They Cannot Say, and How to Reopen Them
Short Hypothesis: Knowledge failures in LLMs are often not storage failures but *retrieval-gating* failures: the fact is encoded in intermediate representations but a query-dependent attention 'gate' fails to route it to the output. We hypothesize a small, identifiable set of attention heads acts as a query-conditioned router whose failure explains the internal-vs-external knowledge gap, and that intervening on this router recovers hidden knowledge without editing where the fact is stored. Primary falsifiable claim: a compact (k<=10), query-conditioned set of attention heads causally mediates whether an internally-recoverable fact is expressed, and reopening this gate recovers hidden facts more selectively than weight editing; the hidden-knowledge set and the reopening intervention are secondary supporting claims. We do not claim the gate is the sole determinant of expression, and if routing proves diffuse we report a distributed gate rather than abandon the account.
Related Work: Prior work localizes factual associations to mid-layer MLPs (ROME; Knowledge Neurons) and shows localization does not predict editability (Hase et al. 2023). Recent work shows retrieval is distributed, redundant, and non-contiguous (Hochman et al. 2026), that query-specific neuron selection depends on attention (Query Localization, 2024), and that LLMs harbor 'hidden knowledge' inaccessible to generation despite 1000 samples (Inside-Out, 2025). Fakepedia (2023) studies grounding vs. parametric recall. None of these isolate a *causal, query-conditioned routing mechanism* that gates whether stored knowledge reaches the output, nor demonstrate a targeted attention intervention that reopens hidden knowledge. We reframe the storage/retrieval debate: rather than asking *where* knowledge lives, we ask *what decides whether it is expressed on a given query*, and provide a mechanism-level causal account plus a lightweight intervention. Concretely, our delta is: Inside-Out documents hidden knowledge but offers no mechanism; ROME and Knowledge Neurons localize storage but not expression; query-localization shows attention selects neurons but does not isolate a compact, transferable set whose causal manipulation reopens hidden knowledge. The novelty center is the compact causal gate (claim 2); the matched hidden/expressed pair set and the non-destructive reopening intervention are supporting contributions, not the core delta.
Abstract: Large language models often 'know' a fact internally yet fail to produce it, a gap of up to 40% between internal and external knowledge. Existing explanations focus on where facts are stored (mid-layer MLPs) but leave open why storage sometimes fails to influence the answer. We propose the Retrieval Gate hypothesis: expression of stored knowledge is controlled by a small set of query-conditioned attention heads that route entity/attribute information to the final position, and knowledge failures are frequently *gating* failures rather than *storage* failures. We test this by (1) constructing paired 'hidden-knowledge' probes where linear readouts recover a fact from intermediate activations even when the model answers incorrectly; (2) using activation patching and attention-head causal tracing to identify which components differ between expressed and hidden cases across matched queries; (3) testing whether a compact, transferable set of 'gate' heads predicts expression across facts and query paraphrases; and (4) performing targeted interventions—amplifying gate-head attention to the subject token or patching gate-head outputs—to reopen hidden knowledge without editing MLP weights. We evaluate on GPT-J, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen3-8B using recovery rate of hidden facts, specificity (no collateral corruption of unrelated facts), and cross-query transfer. Confirming the hypothesis would unify puzzling findings (localization-editing mismatch, distributed redundant retrieval, hidden knowledge) under a single routing mechanism and yield a cheap, non-destructive alternative to weight editing for surfacing what models already know. Payoff by audience: interpretability researchers gain a routing-level account of why storage does not imply expression; knowledge-editing practitioners gain a reversible, seconds-per-fact, weight-preserving alternative to editing for surfacing latent facts, with a clear safety boundary since reopening is unsafe when a fact is not internally stored and can induce confident hallucination; reliability auditors gain a probe for stored-but-unexpressed knowledge. We keep the compact-gate claim defeasible: partial transfer still yields an informative distributed-gate result.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - hidden-knowledge set exists): Tests the premise that a non-trivial share of factual failures are retrieval-gating, not storage, failures - the fact is recoverable from intermediate representations though the model does not generate it. Data: three existing factual-QA sets used as-is and merged - PopQA (14,282 questions, 16 relations), the T-REx slice of LAMA (~34k subject-relation-object triples, 41 relations), and EntityQuestions (24 relations, ~176k questions); we sample 12,000 facts stratified by relation and by Wikidata-pageview popularity decile, fewer than the full pool because caching per-layer activations and training a probe at every layer is the compute bottleneck and 12k still gives >=300 facts per relation. Split 60/20/20 into probe-train / probe-val / test with no entity shared across splits. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B params, decoder-only), all base weights frozen; only a per-layer L2 logistic-regression content probe on the last-token residual stream is trainable, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: greedy-generation correctness vs. best-layer content probe, plus a random-label control probe and a probe trained on shuffled activations. Decisive metric: the hidden-set fraction = share of generation failures where the held-out content probe reaches top-1 accuracy >=0.7, reported first; supporting: per-layer probe AUROC, and control-probe accuracy (must sit near chance ~1/|answer-vocab|). Convincing: >=15% of failures are hidden while the control stays at chance. Undecidable band: a hidden fraction of 8-15% (control at chance) is real but possibly too small to carry the mechanism story - we would report it as a bounded phenomenon and run H2 only on the recoverable subset. Negative: <8% hidden, or the control probe matching the real probe, means apparent recovery is probe overfitting rather than stored-but-ungated knowledge, falsifying the retrieval-gating premise.

Experiment 2 (H2 - attention heads, not MLPs, carry the expressed/hidden gap): Tests that the component whose state differs between an expressed and a hidden run is attention (routing), not MLP (storage). Data: expressed-vs-hidden pairs matched on relation and popularity decile, drawn from the Experiment 1 test split; target 1,500 pairs (fewer than all hidden facts because activation patching costs one forward pass per component per pair; 1,500 gives ~90 pairs/relation). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; activation patching (no training) of the residual stream, per-layer MLP output, and per-head attention output from the expressed run into the hidden run at subject and last-token positions; 3 random re-pairings define a matched null. Systems compared: attention-head patches vs. MLP patches vs. full-residual patches vs. a random-source-run control. Decisive metric: fraction of patched components that flip the hidden run to the gold answer, reported separately for attention heads and MLPs (attention:MLP flip ratio first); supporting: total Delta log-prob of the gold token. Convincing: attention-head patches flip >=2x as many cases as MLP patches (e.g. >=30% vs <=15%), with a compact subset of heads accounting for most flips. Undecidable band: an attention:MLP flip ratio of 1.2-2.0x cannot separate routing-dominant from mixed - we would call gating partial and not claim attention dominance. Negative: MLP patches flip as many or more cases (ratio <=1.2x) means the gap lives in storage, not routing, falsifying H2.

Experiment 3 (H2 - a small, transferable, query-conditioned gate-head set): Tests that a small top-k head set (k<=10) predicts expression and generalizes across held-out facts and query paraphrases. Data: heads ranked by aggregated Experiment 2 causal contribution over probe-train pairs; evaluation on held-out test facts plus 5 paraphrases per fact (cloze, WH-question, indirect, templated, natural) from a template bank kept only when a natural-language-inference filter scores bidirectional entailment >=0.9, yielding ~6,000 (fact, paraphrase) items. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; gate-head features = attention mass the top-k heads place on subject/attribute tokens; a trainable linear classifier maps features to expression success, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: top-k gate-head features (k in {3,5,10,20}) vs. all-head features vs. an MLP-activation baseline vs. a random-head control. Decisive metric: AUROC of gate-head features predicting correct generation on held-out facts (first); supporting: AUROC across paraphrases and the k at which AUROC saturates. Convincing: k<=10 heads reach AUROC >=0.75 held-out and >=0.70 across paraphrases, within 0.03 of the all-head AUROC. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.60-0.75, or needing k>20 to reach it, means routing is real but diffuse - we would report a distributed gate and drop the 'small set' clause. Negative: AUROC <=0.60 or no better than the random-head control falsifies the compact-router claim.

Experiment 4 (H3 - reopening the gate recovers hidden facts without editing storage): Tests that intervening on gate heads recovers hidden facts more selectively than weight editing. Data: held-out hidden facts from the Experiment 1 test split, target 800 (fewer than all hidden facts because each is evaluated under a full specificity/fluency sweep). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME comparator; interventions are (a) scaling top-k gate-head attention toward subject tokens (scalar alpha swept 1-6), (b) patching gate-head outputs from a generic recall-prompting context, (c) a ROME MLP weight edit as the storage-editing comparator, (d) a random-head scaling control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: (a),(b) vs. ROME vs. random control vs. three simple baselines - logit-lens direct injection of the gold-answer direction, a generic recall-prompting/prompt-engineering baseline, and generic all-head (non-gate) attention scaling; a hallucination-risk arm additionally applies (a) to 200 facts with no internal probe support and reports the induced false-answer rate, so specificity is measured against knowledge the model does not store. Decisive metric: net recovered hidden facts per unit collateral = recovery rate / accuracy drop on 100 matched unrelated facts (first); supporting: raw recovery rate and held-out-text perplexity change. Convincing: gate-head interventions recover >=40% of hidden facts with <5% unrelated-accuracy drop and <2% perplexity rise, beating ROME on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, or a 1.0-1.5x advantage over ROME, is inconclusive on selectivity - we would report the intervention as viable but not clearly better than editing. Negative: recovery <20%, or collateral no better than ROME, means gate manipulation does not causally reopen storage-independent knowledge, falsifying H3.

Experiment 5 (H2 - expression is a function of the query-to-gate mapping): Tests that whether a fixed fact is expressed tracks gate-head activation across query phrasings, not MLP content. Data: 500 facts with mixed cross-format expression, each rendered in the 5 validated paraphrase formats from Experiment 3 (2,500 items). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; measure gate-head activation and MLP activation per (fact, format), seeds 0/1/2 for the regression splits. Systems compared: within-fact expression variance explained by gate-head features vs. by MLP activations, via nested logistic regression (Delta pseudo-R^2). Decisive metric: Delta pseudo-R^2 that gate-head features add over MLP features in explaining per-format expression (first); supporting: within-fact expression variance across formats. Convincing: gate-head features add Delta R^2 >=0.15 and account for the majority of within-fact cross-format expression variance. Undecidable band: Delta R^2 0.05-0.15 leaves query-conditioning weakly supported - report as suggestive only. Negative: Delta R^2 <0.05, or MLP features explaining expression as well as gate features, means expression is not governed by the query-to-gate mapping.

Experiment 6 (H1-H3 generality - architecture-general gating): Tests that the hidden set, attention dominance, compact gate, and reopening result hold beyond one model. Data: reuse the Experiment 1 sampling pipeline (12,000 facts) per model. Model: repeat Experiments 1-4 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen3-8B, all frozen, identical seeds and hyperparameters. Systems compared: Llama-3-8B vs. GPT-J-6B vs. Qwen3-8B on each decisive metric. Decisive metric: sign-consistency across models of the Experiment 2 attention:MLP flip ratio and the Experiment 4 recovered-per-collateral advantage (first); supporting: per-model hidden fraction and gate-head AUROC. Convincing: all three models show attention:MLP flip ratio >=1.5x and gate-head AUROC >=0.70. Undecidable band: the pattern holding in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - report scope limited to those architectures. Negative: the direction reversing in the majority of models means gating is model-specific, not general.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Linear-probe recovery may reflect probe overfitting rather than genuine hidden knowledge; mitigated by held-out probe evaluation and comparing to random-label control probes.

The set of gate heads may not be small or transferable; distributed/redundant retrieval (Hochman et al.) suggests routing could be diffuse, which would partially falsify the compact-gate claim but still yield an informative negative result.
Interventions that reopen hidden knowledge may also increase confident hallucination on facts the model does not actually store; specificity controls are essential and could limit practical utility.
Distinguishing gating failures from subtle storage differences is hard; matched-pair design and MLP-patching controls reduce but may not fully eliminate confounds.
Findings on 6-8B models may not scale to larger frontier models an academic lab cannot run.

Name: familiarity_before_retrieval
Title: Feeling of Knowing Before Knowing: A Dissociable Metacognitive Familiarity Estimate That Gates Retrieval Effort in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs compute a fast, early metacognitive 'familiarity' (feeling-of-knowing) estimate about a query that is largely driven by surface cues (entity/relation popularity, lexical familiarity) and is computed *before and independently of* actual content retrieval. This estimate gates how much retrieval effort is expended, so miscalibration of familiarity — not content storage — causes two symmetric failures: false-high familiarity yields confident confabulation with no retrieved content, and false-low familiarity suppresses retrieval of a fact that is actually stored (a 'give-up' failure appearing as abstention/hedging). We predict the familiarity estimate and the retrieved-content signal are linearly separable and causally dissociable, and that recalibrating familiarity alone (without touching stored facts) selectively fixes both failure modes. Primary falsifiable claim: a familiarity signal is linearly dissociable from retrieved content, becomes decodable at earlier layers, and causally gates retrieval effort - patching it changes whether an answer is attempted (Exp 5). Definitions: 'familiarity' = a predicted propensity to attempt a confident answer, regressed on surface popularity/lexical cues; 'content' = the specific correct answer decodable from the residual stream; 'retrieval effort' = answer-attempt rate and later-layer content-probe strength. Symmetric miscalibration is the mechanism for both confabulation (false-high) and give-up abstention (false-low); layer-onset alone is only suggestive, so the causal patch is the decisive test. Alternative hypotheses we explicitly falsify: a single confidence axis (Exp 4 must beat a scalar confidence probe) and probe-difficulty artifacts (Exp 5's causal patch must exceed a random-direction control).
Related Work: Prior knowledge-boundary work shows answerability/confidence is linearly readable in middle layers and can be steered (Slobodkin et al. 2023; (Un)answerability directions 2025; C3 2025; cross-lingual boundary 2025), that popularity predicts boundary perception (Knowledge Popularity 2025), that probabilistic 'belief' during generation diverges from parametric knowledge and causally drives retraction (When Do LLMs Admit Mistakes 2025), and that entropy/token-frequency neurons regulate confidence (Confidence Regulation Neurons 2024). All treat the boundary as a single confidence/answerability signal correlated with correctness. None decompose it into two dissociable computations — a *pre-retrieval familiarity/coverage estimate* versus the *actual retrieved content* — nor test whether familiarity is computed before content and causally *gates retrieval effort*, nor show that recalibrating familiarity alone (leaving stored facts untouched) fixes both over- and under-retrieval failures. This is also orthogonal to my prior proposals on expression gating, format-bound copies, candidate competition, and route arbitration: here the object of study is the model's *estimate of its own coverage* and its causal effect on whether retrieval is even attempted. In one paragraph of contrast: answerability/confidence-boundary work models a single boundary signal correlated with correctness and steerable; we claim two dissociable computations - a pre-retrieval familiarity estimate that is causally upstream of and separable from the retrieved content - and that recalibrating familiarity alone fixes both over- and under-retrieval. The central novelty is the layer-ordering plus causal-patch evidence, not popularity as a standalone predictor.
Abstract: Large language models sometimes confabulate confidently about things they do not know, and other times fail to produce facts they demonstrably store. We propose that both stem from a single overlooked mechanism: a fast metacognitive familiarity estimate — a 'feeling of knowing' about the query — that LLMs compute early, largely from surface cues, before and separately from actually retrieving content, and that this estimate gates how much retrieval effort is spent. When familiarity is falsely high, the model commits to answering with little retrieved content, producing fluent confabulation; when falsely low, it suppresses retrieval of a stored fact and abstains or hedges. We test three claims. (1) Dissociability: separate linear probes recover a familiarity signal (predictive of surface popularity and verbalized confidence) and a content signal (predictive of the specific correct answer), and these become decodable at different layers, with familiarity emerging earlier. (2) Miscalibration causes failures: by constructing mismatched items — high-familiarity/low-content (obscure facts phrased around popular entities) and low-familiarity/high-content (stored facts about rare entities) — we show confabulation concentrates in the former and give-up failures in the latter, at rates far above a single-confidence baseline. (3) Causal gating and recalibration: activation patching of the early familiarity direction changes downstream retrieval effort and answer attempts, and a low-rank recalibration steering vector that adjusts familiarity alone reduces confabulation and unlocks give-up failures with higher specificity than confidence-threshold abstention or ROME editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions, evaluating probe separability, layer-onset ordering, failure-mode prevalence, recovery/abstention accuracy, specificity, and fluency. User-facing framing: the target failures are confident hallucination, missed recall, and wrong abstention. Downstream, this offers a new control lever for reliability - adaptive retrieval, selective answering, and safer abstention policies driven by a metacognitive signal rather than a confidence threshold or weight edit - with an expected practical implication of fewer confident-wrong answers at a fixed answer rate. We pitch this as a reliability control lever, not a world-changing result, and anchor every claim to one central causal statement about familiarity gating retrieval.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1/H3 - familiarity is decodable early and separable from content): Tests that a familiarity signal becomes decodable at earlier layers than retrieved content and that the two are separable. Data: PopQA (14,282), T-REx/LAMA (~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); sample 10,000 single-token-first-entity facts stratified by relation and popularity, fewer than the pool for per-layer probe training and clean content readout. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; two trainable per-layer linear probes on the last-token residual - a familiarity probe (target: will the model attempt a confident answer; regressed on entity/relation popularity and verbalized confidence) and a content probe (target: the gold answer via tuned-lens); seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle controls. Systems compared: familiarity vs. content probe onset layers, with bootstrap CIs. Decisive metric: onset-layer difference (first-layer at AUROC>=0.7) between familiarity and content (first, familiarity should precede content); supporting: per-layer AUROC/accuracy of each. Convincing: familiarity onset precedes content onset by >=3 layers with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs, both probes above shuffle. Undecidable band: an onset gap of 1-3 layers, or overlapping CIs, cannot establish temporal precedence over probe-difficulty artifacts - defer the precedence claim to the causal test (Experiment 5). Negative: content onset at or before familiarity, or familiarity at shuffle level, falsifies the early-familiarity half of H1.

Experiment 2 (H3 - familiarity and content carry non-redundant information): Tests that the two directions are not collinear. Data: the residual activations from Experiment 1 (10,000 facts). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; measure cosine similarity and cross-linear-predictability of the familiarity and content directions, then residualize each on the other, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: familiarity predicting popularity/verbalized-confidence before vs. after removing content-predictive variance. Decisive metric: retained familiarity->popularity/confidence predictive AUROC after residualizing out content (first); supporting: direction cosine similarity. Convincing: familiarity still predicts popularity/confidence at AUROC >=0.70 after residualization and direction cosine <=0.5 - non-redundant signals. Undecidable band: post-residualization AUROC 0.55-0.70 or cosine 0.5-0.75 indicates partial entanglement - report a graded separability. Negative: post-residual AUROC <=0.55 or cosine >0.75 means the signals are effectively one direction, falsifying the separability half of H3.

Experiment 3 (H2 - familiarity x content mismatch dataset): Builds items that cross familiarity with content so the two failure modes can be isolated. Data: four cells - HF-LC (obscure attributes of popular entities the model does not store), LF-HC (stored facts about rare entities recoverable under strong prompting), plus HF-HC and LF-LC controls; target 1,500 items/cell (6,000), constructed by filtering the Experiment 1 pool with popularity statistics and content-probe/strong-prompt recovery, fewer per cell because each needs storage and familiarity validation. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; content availability validated by strong retrieval prompts + content probe, familiarity by verbalized confidence + popularity. Systems compared: the four cells. Decisive metric: cell purity = fraction of items meeting both their familiarity and content criteria (first); supporting: per-cell popularity and content-probe distributions. Convincing: >=70% purity in all four cells - a clean 2x2. Undecidable band: 50-70% purity means noisy cells - report with wider CIs. Negative: <50% purity in LF-HC (the hardest cell) means stored-but-rare facts cannot be reliably assembled, weakening the give-up-failure test.

Experiment 4 (H2 - the two symmetric failure modes localize to the predicted cells): Tests that confabulation concentrates in HF-LC and give-up failures in LF-HC. Data: the 6,000-item 2x2 from Experiment 3. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; per cell, rate of (a) confident confabulation (high-probability wrong attempt) and (b) give-up (abstain/hedge despite internally available content). Systems compared: cell-conditioned failure rates vs. a KEEN/answerability single-scalar-confidence baseline; chi-square and calibration curves. Decisive metric: difference in confabulation rate (HF-LC minus others) and give-up rate (LF-HC minus others), each above the confidence-probe baseline (first); supporting: calibration curves. Convincing: confabulation is >=20 points higher in HF-LC and give-up >=20 points higher in LF-HC, both beyond what the scalar confidence probe predicts (chi-square p<0.001). Undecidable band: 8-20 point concentrations, or gaps the scalar probe also captures, mean the two-factor account adds little over confidence - report as partial. Negative: <8 point concentration means failures do not localize by familiarity x content, falsifying H2.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 - familiarity causally precedes and gates retrieval): Tests that patching the early familiarity direction changes whether an answer is attempted and downstream content strength. Data: matched HF/LF paraphrase pairs of the same fact, target 1,500. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; patch the early familiarity direction from a high- into a low-familiarity run (and vice versa) at the Experiment 1 onset layer, query held fixed via matched paraphrases; random-direction control. Systems compared: familiarity patch vs. random-direction patch. Decisive metric: change in answer-attempt rate induced by the familiarity patch (first); supporting: change in later-layer content-probe strength and final-answer change. Convincing: raising familiarity increases attempt rate by >=25 points (and lowering it decreases attempts), vs <=5 points for random - familiarity causally gates retrieval effort. Undecidable band: a 10-25 point effect is weak causal control - report familiarity as contributory. Negative: <10 point effect, near control, means familiarity does not causally gate retrieval, falsifying the gating half of H1/H2.

Experiment 6 (H4 - recalibrating familiarity alone fixes both failure modes): Tests that a familiarity-only steering vector converts HF-LC confabulation to abstention and LF-HC give-ups to correct answers. Data: held-out HF-LC and LF-HC items, target 800 each. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME comparator; a rank<=8 vector moving familiarity toward its calibrated target (down for HF-LC, up for LF-HC), from mean differences of calibrated vs. miscalibrated matched states, alpha swept; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: familiarity recalibration vs. confidence-threshold abstention vs. an (un)answerability steering direction vs. ROME. Decisive metric: net-correct-behavior-per-unit-collateral = (confabulation->abstention rate on HF-LC + give-up->correct rate on LF-HC) / accuracy drop on 200 well-calibrated facts (first); supporting: per-cell conversion rates, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% appropriate conversion in each cell with <5% collateral, beating the baselines on net-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: 20-40% conversion or a 1.0-1.5x advantage means recalibration works but not clearly better than baselines - report parity. Negative: <20% conversion or no advantage falsifies H4.

Experiment 7 (H4 generality - one recalibration vector transfers across relations, directions, and models): Tests transfer of the recalibration and architecture-generality of the core results. Data: train one recalibration vector on a relation subset, apply to held-out relations and both failure directions; reuse the Experiment 1 pool per model. Model: single trained vector applied unchanged on Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 1, 4, 6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds. Systems compared: cross-relation/both-direction transfer vs. within-relation oracle; three models per decisive metric. Decisive metric: cross-relation conversion rate and cross-model sign-consistency of the Experiment 4 concentration and Experiment 6 advantage (first); supporting: per-model onset gaps. Convincing: cross-relation conversion >=25% in both directions and all three models show the failure-localization and a recalibration advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: transfer 10-25%, or the pattern in 2 of 3 models, is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: <10% transfer or majority model reversal means the mechanism is fact/model-specific.

Experiment 8 (H1 - familiarity is surface-driven): Tests that the familiarity estimate is mostly explained by surface cues rather than retrieved content. Data: the Experiment 1 familiarity-probe outputs over 10,000 facts. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; regress familiarity-probe output on entity popularity, relation co-occurrence frequency, and query lexical familiarity, with the content-probe strength as a competing regressor. Systems compared: surface-cue regressors vs. content-probe regressor. Decisive metric: share of familiarity variance explained by surface cues (partial R^2), reported first; supporting: content-probe partial R^2. Convincing: surface cues explain >=50% of familiarity variance and >=3x the content-probe share - familiarity is largely surface-driven. Undecidable band: surface share 30-50% or <2x content means familiarity is mixed - soften the 'surface-cue' claim to partial. Negative: surface cues explain <30% or less than content means familiarity is content-grounded, falsifying the surface-driven half of H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The familiarity and content signals may be entangled rather than cleanly separable; residualization and independent predictive targets mitigate this, but a graded/overlapping result would weaken the strong dissociation claim while remaining informative.

Layer-onset ordering (familiarity earlier than content) could be an artifact of probe difficulty rather than genuine computational timing; we use tuned-lens, matched probe capacities, and causal patching (Exp 5) as the decisive test rather than probe onset alone.

'Give-up' failures require confidently establishing that a fact is actually stored; strong-prompt recovery and content-probe evidence can overestimate storage, so we report coverage limits and use conservative thresholds.
Recalibration steering could induce new confabulation when raising familiarity, or over-abstain when lowering it; strict specificity and fluency controls are essential and may cap practical utility.
A single transferable recalibration vector may not exist if familiarity miscalibration is fact-specific, limiting generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate content-probe readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first entities with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: consistency_seams
Title: Consistency Seams: Predicting Ripple Failures from the Pre-Existing Geometry of an LLM's Knowledge, Before Any Edit
Short Hypothesis: Whether editing a fact ripples correctly to its logical consequences is largely predetermined by how the model *already* stores the related facts: logically-entailed fact pairs occupy shared, aligned representational subspaces when the model is internally consistent, and disconnected 'consistency seams' when it is not. We hypothesize that a purely observational, edit-free measure of representational coupling between two facts (shared-subspace alignment of their subject/relation representations) predicts ripple success at edit time better than gradient-based predictors, and that facts across a seam are causally the ones that fail to ripple. Primary falsifiable claim: a static, edit-free coupling score - the principal-subspace angle / CCA correlation between the residual-stream directions that read out fact A's and entailed fact B's answers, computed with no edit, no target answer, and no gradients - predicts per-pair ripple success at edit time with AUROC within 0.03 of, or above, GradSim, the closest predictor (which requires a specified edit). Minimum novelty claim if the lift is only modest: an edit-free, method-agnostic predictor that matches GradSim while removing the need for a specified edit is itself the contribution, alongside the causal 'consistency seam' account. Eligibility is restricted to linearly-decodable relations that admit a reliable readout direction; we report coverage.
Related Work: Ripple-effect work (RippleEdits 2023, MQuAKE 2023, ReCoE 2024, RippleBench 2025) benchmarks propagation failures of editing methods; ChainEdit/PropMEND/distillation propose fixes; GradSim (2024) explains failures via cosine similarity of the *gradients* of the original fact and its related knowledge, requiring an edit to be specified. All of these treat ripple as a property of the edit + method. Our proposal is distinct in three ways: (1) it is *observational and edit-free* — we ask whether the model's native, unedited representations of two logically-linked facts are coupled, independent of any editing method or target; (2) it introduces a static representational-geometry predictor (subspace alignment / coupling) rather than a gradient-based one that presupposes an edit direction; (3) it makes a causal claim that ripple failures concentrate at 'consistency seams' — pairs stored in misaligned subspaces — and tests this with subspace-targeted editing. Our seam measure requires no backprop through an edit, no target answer, and predicts across editing methods, which GradSim cannot. Relation to GradSim, stated exactly: same prediction task (will an edit to A ripple to B), but our score uses no edit, no target answer, and no gradients - only the model's native unedited geometry - and predicts across editing methods, which a gradient-of-the-edit predictor cannot. We separate the three claims - prediction (coupling forecasts ripple), explanation (seams reflect pre-existing inconsistency), and intervention (aligning subspaces enables ripple) - into distinct experiments, and ablate the CCA/subspace-angle metric against simpler representational-similarity baselines so the geometric measure is shown to matter.
Abstract: Editing a single fact in a large language model should ripple to its logical consequences (edit 'X's employer to Google' and 'X's boss' should follow), but existing methods propagate updates inconsistently. Prior explanations tie ripple failure to the edit itself — e.g., gradient similarity between the edited fact and its consequence. We propose that ripple success is largely determined *before any edit* by the geometry of how the model already stores the two facts. When the model is internally consistent about a logically-linked pair, their subject/relation representations occupy a shared, aligned subspace so an update to one is naturally read out by the other; when they are stored in misaligned, disconnected subspaces — a 'consistency seam' — updates cannot propagate. We introduce a static, edit-free coupling measure: for a fact pair (A, B) where B is entailed by A, we quantify the alignment between the subspaces that carry A's and B's answer-relevant information (via linear relational embeddings and CCA/subspace-angle between the residual-stream directions that read out each answer). We test three claims. (1) Predictiveness: pre-edit coupling predicts per-pair ripple success at edit time (ROME/MEMIT/in-context) with higher AUROC than GradSim, and does so without computing any edit. (2) Causality: ripple failures concentrate on low-coupling 'seam' pairs above frequency- and hop-matched baselines; injecting the missing coupling (aligning the subspaces) improves ripple. (3) Native inconsistency: even unedited, seam pairs already exhibit belief inconsistency (the model affirms A and B's rule but denies the entailed answer) more than coupled pairs. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on RippleEdits and MQuAKE, evaluating AUROC of ripple prediction, seam prevalence, causal recovery, and specificity. Downstream, an edit-free predictor supports concrete actions beyond diagnosis - routing edits away from seam-blocked facts, selecting models with fewer seams, and flagging brittle facts before editing - and is preferable to an edit-conditioned predictor because it needs no backprop, no target, and generalizes across methods, cutting benchmarking cost. We keep claims within the editing/reliability subfield and to linearly-decodable relations rather than overselling broad reach, and fix the seam threshold and falsifier (coupling no better than frequency/hop controls) in advance.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - edit-free coupling score between entailed fact pairs): Constructs logically-linked fact pairs and an observational coupling measure computed with no reference to any edit. Data: fact pairs (A, B) where B is a logical/compositional consequence of A (two-hop, sibling, inverse), extracted from RippleEdits (~5k edit instances with entailed-fact tests) and MQuAKE (multi-hop chains); target 4,000 pairs with single-token-first answers, fewer than the full benchmarks because both facts must admit a reliable readout direction. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; estimate each fact's answer-readout subspace via linear relational embeddings (LREs) and tuned-lens answer-token probes at subject and last positions; the pre-edit coupling score = principal-subspace angle / CCA correlation between A's and B's readout subspaces, computed with no edit and no target answer; seed 0. Systems compared: coupling for pairs later observed to ripple vs. not. Decisive metric: coverage = pairs with a reliable coupling score for both facts (first); supporting: coupling-score distribution. Convincing: >=2,500 pairs admit a reliable coupling score, spanning coupled and low-alignment cases. Undecidable band: 1,200-2,500 usable pairs is thin - report reduced power and restricted relations. Negative: <1,200 usable pairs means readout directions are too unreliable to build the coupling measure here.

Experiment 2 (H1 - edit-free coupling predicts ripple better than a gradient predictor): Tests the central claim that observational coupling forecasts ripple success without any edit. Data: the coupled pairs from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except during the edits being evaluated; apply ROME, MEMIT, and in-context editing to A and measure per-pair ripple success on B; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: pre-edit coupling (CCA/subspace-angle) vs. simpler representational-similarity baselines (mean cosine of readout directions, raw activation correlation) vs. GradSim (which requires the edit) vs. controls (entity/answer frequency, hop count, lexical overlap). Decisive metric: AUROC of coupling predicting ripple success, pooled and per-method (first); supporting: AUROC of GradSim and the controls it must match/beat. Convincing: coupling reaches AUROC >=0.70 and comes within 0.03 of, or beats, GradSim while using no edit-specific gradient - an edit-free predictor as good as the gradient one. Undecidable band: coupling AUROC 0.60-0.70, or trailing GradSim by 0.03-0.10, means coupling predicts but does not match the gradient predictor - report as a cheaper, weaker signal. Negative: AUROC <=0.60 or no better than the frequency/hop controls falsifies H1.

Experiment 3 (H1/H2 - ripple failures concentrate on seams): Tests that low-alignment 'seam' pairs fail to ripple above matched baselines and characterizes seams. Data: the pairs from Experiment 2, split into coupled vs. seam by a cross-validated coupling threshold. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen (edits as in Experiment 2). Systems compared: ripple-failure rate on seam vs. coupled pairs against a frequency-/hop-matched null (logistic regression / chi-square); seam predictors = relation type, entity-popularity asymmetry, co-occurrence proxy (on Pythia where feasible). Decisive metric: ripple-failure-rate difference between seam and coupled pairs, above the matched null (first); supporting: which features predict seams. Convincing: seam pairs fail to ripple at a rate >=20 points above coupled pairs beyond the matched null (p<0.001). Undecidable band: a 8-20 point gap is a real but modest concentration - report seams as a contributing, not dominant, factor. Negative: <8 points or null-indistinguishable means seams do not track ripple failure, falsifying the seam account of H2.

Experiment 4 (H2 - seams reflect pre-existing inconsistency, not edit artifacts): Tests that the model already holds inconsistent beliefs on seam pairs before any edit. Data: seam and coupled pairs from Experiment 3. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen, no editing; probe whether the model correctly answers A, affirms the connecting rule, yet fails/denies the entailed B; multiple rule phrasings for robustness. Systems compared: native-inconsistency rate on seam vs. coupled pairs. Decisive metric: difference in native (edit-free) inconsistency rate between seam and coupled groups (first); supporting: robustness across rule phrasings. Convincing: seam pairs show native inconsistency >=20 points above coupled pairs, stable across phrasings - seams are pre-existing organizational fractures. Undecidable band: an 8-20 point difference is a modest signal - report as partial support. Negative: <8 points, or a phrasing-dependent effect, means seams do not reflect pre-existing inconsistency, weakening H2's 'before any edit' framing.

Experiment 5 (H2 - restoring coupling causally enables ripple): Tests that aligning a seam pair's subspaces makes the edit propagate. Data: seam pairs from Experiment 3, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the evaluated edit; learn a low-rank alignment map that rotates B's readout subspace toward A's (estimated from coupled pairs of the same relation family), inject it, then edit A and re-measure ripple to B; controls: no alignment, a ChainEdit-style logical-chain in-context prompt, and a random-rotation control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: subspace-alignment vs. no-alignment vs. chain-prompt vs. random-rotation. Decisive metric: ripple-recovery rate on seam pairs under alignment, minus the no-alignment and random-rotation baselines (first); supporting: specificity (unrelated-fact accuracy and unrelated-pair ripple pre/post), held-out perplexity. Convincing: alignment recovers ripple on >=35% of seam pairs, >=20 points above no-alignment and random-rotation, with <5% collateral - restoring coupling causally enables propagation. Undecidable band: a 8-20 point recovery gain means partial causal support - report coupling as contributory. Negative: <8 point gain over controls, or collateral wiping out gains, means aligning subspaces does not enable ripple, falsifying the causal half of H2.

Experiment 6 (H1/H2 generality - coupling transfers across families and models): Tests cross-family predictive transfer and architecture-generality, including whether larger models have fewer seams. Data: compute coupling on one relation family, predict ripple on held-out families; reuse the Experiment 1 pipeline per model. Model: Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 1-4 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds/hyperparameters. Systems compared: cross-family coupling-AUROC vs. within-family; three models on seam prevalence and prediction. Decisive metric: cross-family AUROC of coupling predicting ripple (first); supporting: per-model seam fraction and whether it falls with model size. Convincing: cross-family AUROC >=0.65 and all three models show coupling predicting ripple above controls, with seam fraction not increasing with size. Undecidable band: cross-family AUROC 0.55-0.65 or the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: cross-family AUROC <=0.55 or majority model reversal means coupling is family/model-specific, limiting H1's reach.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The coupling/subspace-alignment measure is a modeling choice; LREs are linear for only ~half of relations, limiting coverage — we report which relations admit reliable readout directions and restrict primary analysis accordingly.

Coupling may correlate with simple confounds (co-occurrence, popularity, hop count); matched baselines and multivariate regression are essential, and the edit-free predictor's value rests on beating GradSim after controls.
