Repetition manipulations could act via verbatim in-context copying rather than genuine belief inflation; including both true and false repeated claims, using paraphrased (non-verbatim) repetitions, and comparing to a no-repetition-but-equal-length control separate copying from illusory-truth belief change.

Source-credibility framings may not be genuinely understood or may add confounding content; the manipulation-check (model can rate source reliability directly) and matched-length source framings mitigate this, and the neutral-source condition anchors the baseline.

The familiarity and credibility signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 4), not probe separability alone, are decisive, and a graded/partial dissociation would weaken the strong claim while remaining informative.

The gating intervention could over-suppress (making the model distrust trusted-source repeated claims) or degrade fluency; the trusted-source and aligned-condition specificity controls (Exp 4) are central and utility may be capped.
Verdicts are prompt-sensitive (true/false/uncertain framing, source phrasing); we use multiple paraphrases and report robustness, since framing itself may modulate the effect.
A single transferable credibility-gating vector may not exist if gating is source-type-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: homograph_entity_fusion
Title: Same Name, Merged Minds: How Shared-Name Entities Fuse Into One Representation and Bleed Attributes Across Each Other
Short Hypothesis: Primary claim (one falsifiable sentence): when two distinct real-world entities share a name (homograph entities, e.g. the basketball player and the statistician both named 'Michael Jordan'), an LLM builds a single fused subject representation keyed on the shared surface form, and this fusion causally produces attribute bleed — asserting for one entity an attribute that belongs to the name-sharing other — even when both facts are separately recoverable under disambiguation. 'Fusion' is defined operationally as reduced linear separability of the two namesakes' subject-token representations (probe AUC / subspace angle); it must predict per-item bleed and be causally necessary (patching/ablation), distinguishing it from a simpler popularity-default, lexical-similarity, or frequency-skew heuristic. Secondary predictions: (a) a distinct 'competing-namesake' signal is decodable at the subject position and causally drives the bleed; (b) injecting a low-rank disambiguation direction that separates the two entity representations recovers the correct attribute without editing any fact. The contribution is anchored as a mechanistic account (parametric representational fusion), not the behavioral observation of name confusion alone.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs merge information across same-name entities (AmbigDocs 2024; AmbER 2021; To Know or Not To Know 2024) but is largely in-context/multi-document, offers no internal mechanism, and no targeted fix. Entity-representation work shows entities form low-dimensional linearly-separable subspaces in early layers (On Entity Identification 2025; Entity Lens 2025) and that last-token subject representations undergo 'token erasure' as entity meaning is built (Token Erasure 2024)—but studies clean, unambiguous entities, not name-collisions. Co-occurrence/popularity work (Impact of Co-occurrence 2023; Information Anxiety 2024; AmbER popularity bias) shows recall is skewed toward frequent associations but does not isolate cross-entity attribute fusion under a shared name. My prior proposals use type-matched but differently-named distractors (retrieval_competition), incidental mentions of a different entity (context_priming_contamination), or a false aside about a different attribute of the same entity (presupposition_writeback); none concern two genuinely distinct entities forced to share one surface form, nor the parametric fusion of their subject representations. This transfers the human source-monitoring/name-collision confusion into parametric recall with a causal representational-fusion account and a non-destructive disambiguation fix. Primary novelty anchor (mechanistic interpretability): unlike AmbigDocs/AmbER-style in-context, multi-document ambiguity work, we study parametric recall from a bare-name prompt with no supporting documents, and the contribution is a causal representational-fusion mechanism plus a non-destructive disambiguation fix — with explicit controls separating fusion from popularity-prior, lexical-similarity, and frequency-skew accounts.
Abstract: User-facing consequence first: shared-name collisions (two Michael Jordans, many Springfields) can silently corrupt an LLM's factual answers — it reports the wrong namesake's attribute even though it stores both — a hidden failure mode for entity QA, retrieval-augmented generation, assistants, and knowledge editing, where ambiguous names are common. Many distinct real-world entities share a name: two people named Michael Jordan, several cities named Springfield, multiple films titled Crash. We ask whether large language models store such homograph entities as cleanly separate memories or fuse them into one representation keyed on the shared surface form, and whether that fusion causes a specific factual-recall failure. We propose homograph entity fusion: because the model builds a subject representation largely from the entity's name tokens, two entities sharing a name collapse toward a single fused representation, causing attribute bleed—the model asserts for one entity an attribute that actually belongs to the name-sharing other, even when it can produce both attributes when the entities are disambiguated. We test three claims. (1) Behavioral signature: for facts the model recalls correctly when the entity is uniquely specified (e.g. with a disambiguating descriptor), it produces cross-entity attribute bleed when the same query uses only the bare shared name, above popularity- and frequency-matched baselines, and the bleed is disproportionately toward the more popular namesake. (2) Representational fusion: a linear probe over the subject-token residual stream shows the two entities' representations are less separable for high-collision names, this fusion degree predicts attribute bleed, and a distinct 'competing-namesake' signal is decodable and causally drives the bleed (activation patching / ablation). (3) Disambiguation recovery: injecting a low-rank disambiguation direction that separates the two entity representations, or patching in a context-disambiguated subject representation, recovers the correct attribute with higher specificity and less collateral damage than fact editing or a 'be specific' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on Wikipedia-disambiguation-derived homograph sets, evaluating bleed prevalence, fusion-predicts-bleed geometry, causal recovery, and specificity. Because name ambiguity is pervasive in entity-linked tasks, this motivates homograph-aware factuality evaluation and representation-level disambiguation rather than only better prompting or fact editing. H1 (fusion causes bleed) is the primary claim; competing-namesake localization and disambiguation recovery are secondary. We state explicitly whether the low-rank disambiguation vector is a practical mitigation or mainly mechanistic evidence, alongside collateral and hedging controls.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — cross-entity attribute-bleed prevalence): Tests whether, for facts stored separately about two name-sharing entities, the model asserts one namesake's attribute for the other under a bare-name query. Data: Wikipedia disambiguation pages (tens of thousands) mined (AmbigDocs/AmbER-style) into homograph sets of >=2 distinct entities sharing an exact name (people/places/works), each with distinct attributes under matched relations and Wikipedia-pageview popularity; target ~1,000 (entity, attribute) items per model, restricted to items the model recalls correctly under a DISAMBIGUATED query (so both facts are demonstrably stored); report coverage. Paired BARE-NAME vs DISAMBIGUATED queries; single-token-first answers. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, all weights frozen, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: bleed rate under BARE-NAME vs a popularity- and frequency-matched unique-name control (logistic regression); directionality tested toward the more-popular namesake. Decisive metric: cross-entity bleed rate = fraction of disambiguated-correct items on which the bare-name query returns the OTHER namesake's attribute; secondary: bleed-vs-popularity-gap slope. Convincing: bleed rate >=15 pp above the matched unique-name control in >=2 of 3 models, rising with the popularity gap. Undecidable band: 5-15 pp above control -> bleed present but weak, partial support. Negative (<5 pp above control) means shared names do not induce cross-entity bleed beyond baseline error, refuting the behavioral signature.

Experiment 2 (H1 — fusion degree predicts bleed): Tests the claim that the degree of representational fusion of the two namesakes predicts per-item attribute bleed. Data: the homograph pairs and unique-name controls from Exp 1; residual stream cached at the subject-token positions across layers. Model: frozen models; fitted objects are per-layer L2-logistic probes that (a) decode which namesake is intended and (b) decode each namesake's attribute, trained on 70% / tested on 30% of pairs over 3 seeds (0/1/2), with label-shuffle nulls. A per-pair fusion score = 1 minus namesake separability (probe AUC / subspace angle between the two namesakes' subject representations). Systems compared: fusion score of high-collision homograph pairs vs unique-name entities (should be cleanly separable); fusion score as a predictor of the Exp-1 per-item bleed rate. Decisive metric: correlation / AUROC of fusion score predicting per-item bleed; secondary: homograph-vs-unique separability gap. Convincing: fusion predicts bleed with AUROC >=0.70 (>> shuffle) and homograph pairs are measurably less separable than matched unique-name entities in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.58-0.70 -> weak geometric link, partial support. Negative (AUROC <=0.58, or no separability gap) means bleed is not explained by representational fusion — the geometry claim fails even if the Exp-1 behavior holds.

Experiment 3 (H2 — competing-namesake signal localization): Tests that a distinct, content-separable 'competing-namesake' signal exists at the subject position. Data: matched BARE-NAME (fused) vs DISAMBIGUATED (separated) runs for the Exp-1 items; subject-position residual stream cached across layers. Model: frozen; a per-layer L2-logistic probe targets the presence of a name collision and the popular namesake's identity, trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds; the correct-attribute content signal is probed separately and residualized out; shuffle null. Systems compared: the competing-namesake probe before vs after residualizing out the content signal; its layer profile relative to the early-layer entity-formation window. Decisive metric: per-layer AUROC of the competing-namesake signal predicting bleed, after residualizing out content; secondary: onset layer (should be in the early entity-formation window and precede the answer). Convincing: post-residualization AUROC >=0.72 with a clear early-layer onset in >=2 of 3 models, and the signal tracks the collision/popular-namesake rather than the queried attribute. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.60-0.72 -> signal present but entangled with content, partial. Negative (AUROC at shuffle after residualization) means there is no separable competing-namesake signal; the localization claim fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 — competing-namesake signal is causal): Tests that the competing-namesake signal causally drives the bleed. Data: 300 bleed cases and 300 unique-name items per model, held out from Exp-3 probe training. Method: patch the subject-token representation from a DISAMBIGUATED (correct) run into a BARE-NAME bleed run; suppress the competing-namesake direction (low-rank difference between fused and separated states); inject the popular-namesake representation into a unique-name query. Model: frozen; interventions at the Exp-3 layers, dose swept in {0.5,1,2,4}x, 3 seeds. Systems compared: (a) disambiguated->bleed patch (restore), (b) namesake-direction suppression (reduce bleed), (c) popular-namesake injection into a unique-name query (induce bleed), (d) content-only patch and random-direction controls. Decisive metric: correct-attribute recovery rate from patching vs the content-only/random controls; secondary: induced-bleed rate from injection with dose-response. Convincing: patching recovers >=50% of bleed cases and suppression cuts bleed >=40%, while injection induces >=15 pp bleed over random-direction with monotone dose-response, and the content-only patch does neither, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: recovery 25-50%, or induced-bleed 5-15 pp over control -> partial causal role, suggestive. Negative (recovery <=25% and induced-bleed <=5 pp over control, or content-patch matches) means the signal is correlational, not the cause of bleed.

Experiment 5 (H3 — disambiguation-recovery intervention with specificity): Tests that injecting a disambiguation direction recovers the correct attribute without editing any fact, and does so specifically. Data: held-out bleed cases (>=400 per model); specificity sets = the OTHER namesake's own queries, unique-name facts, and already-correct bare-name facts; a genuinely-ambiguous subset where the model should hedge. Model: frozen; a low-rank disambiguation steering vector = mean subject-token difference between the intended namesake's disambiguated state and the fused bare-name state, fitted on a subset of homograph pairs and applied to held-out pairs and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: disambiguation steering vs a 'which one do you mean / be specific' re-prompt, providing the disambiguating descriptor (upper bound), a simple name-frequency reranker baseline (always answer the more-popular namesake), ROME editing (expected null since both facts are stored), and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: correct-attribute recovery rate, reported jointly with collateral change on the other-namesake, unique-name, and already-correct sets, and with preserved hedging on the ambiguous subset; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: recovery >=40% with <=2 pp collateral drop on all specificity sets, hedging preserved, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, and >=60% transfer across held-out pairs and models. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, collateral 2-5 pp, or transfer 40-60% -> capped/partial generality. Negative (recovery <=20%, collateral >5 pp, or corrupts the other namesake) means no clean non-destructive fix; the disambiguation claim fails.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Bleed could reflect genuine ambiguity resolution (the bare name really is ambiguous, and defaulting to the popular namesake is reasonable) rather than a fusion failure; the key test is that the model recovers the correct attribute under DISAMBIGUATED queries (so the knowledge is separable-in-principle) and the specificity control that it should hedge when truly ambiguous—distinguishing unwanted fusion from rational defaulting.
The fusion and correct-attribute-content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 4), not probe separability alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Disambiguation steering could over-correct—forcing a namesake reading where the query is genuinely ambiguous, or corrupting the popular namesake's own recall; the other-namesake and hedging-appropriate specificity controls (Exp 5) are central and utility may be capped.

Bleed may be rare for low-collision names or when the less-popular namesake is very obscure (genuine ignorance rather than fusion); the disambiguated-recall gating and popularity-matched baselines separate these, and coverage is reported.

Shared names are often multi-token; subject-representation readout is cleanest for names with a stable last-token representation (per token-erasure work)—we report coverage and restrict primary analysis accordingly.
A single transferable disambiguation vector may not exist if fusion is name-pair-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: granularity_overcommitment
Title: Too Precise to Be Right: A Largely Query-Independent Precision Prior That Makes LLMs Overcommit to a Granularity and Hide Coarser Correct Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: Primary claim: when a factual query admits answers at multiple granularities (e.g., 'August 4, 1961' vs '1961' vs 'the 1960s' for a birth date), an LLM sets the answer's *specificity level* via an internal 'precision prior' that is at least partly separable from retrieval of the specific value, and this axis can be causally steered — without editing any fact — to recover a coarser correct answer. Granularity overcommitment (emitting a confident, wrong fine-grained value while the coarser correct value is internally available) is thus a systematic, mechanistically localizable failure, not mere ignorance. Secondary/auxiliary claims: (a) the chosen granularity is linearly decodable from intermediate activations before the fine value resolves; (b) the precision prior is *largely query-independent* — operationalized (the weaker, testable version we commit to; full independence is NOT assumed) as: generic format/precision cues (relation type, prompt phrasing, entity popularity) explain a strictly larger share of variance in the chosen granularity than the model's internal confidence in the fine value; (c) overcommitment concentrates on long-tail entities where the fine value is uncertain but a coarse value is stored. We do not assume a single clean precision-prior direction exists; whether a low-rank, transferable direction suffices is itself a tested question. The contribution is BOTH a mechanistic account of granularity selection AND a causal intervention on it — distinct from prior purely behavioral or decoding-time treatments.
Related Work: GRANOLA QA (Yona et al. 2024) behaviorally shows LLMs default to overly specific answers that are often wrong, and that scoring against multi-granularity answers reveals ~20 points of otherwise hidden knowledge (larger for rare entities); their fix, DRAG, is a decoding heuristic tied to output uncertainty, with no mechanistic account and no internal intervention. Inside-Out (2025) and 'Empty Shelves or Lost Keys?' (2026) show a large recall/access gap between encoded and expressed knowledge but do not treat *answer granularity* as the axis of failure. Concept Depth (2024) and layer-wise knowledge-encoding studies characterize where concepts of varying complexity emerge, not a granularity-selection decision. Knowledge-editing granularity work (DiKE 2025, FiNE 2025) concerns editing precision at the fact level, not the model's own choice of answer specificity. Positioning as a table (axis: phenomenon / mechanism / intervention): GRANOLA+DRAG = phenomenon + decoding-time patch, no mechanism, no internal intervention; Inside-Out / access-gap = phenomenon (encoded-vs-expressed gap), partial mechanism, no granularity axis, no intervention; this work = same phenomenon BUT new mechanism (a separable, largely query-independent precision prior that sets granularity before content resolves) AND new causal intervention (steering that recovers coarse-correct answers without fact editing). Novelty therefore lives in the MECHANISM and the INTERVENTION, not the phenomenon (which GRANOLA established) and not the setting (standard multi-granularity factual QA). This is orthogonal to my prior proposals on single-granularity retrieval, competition, arbitration, or enumeration closure; here the object is the *specificity level* of the answer.
Abstract: Large language models often answer factual questions with a confidently wrong, overly specific value even when they reliably know a coarser, correct one — stating an exact but wrong date when they know the correct decade. GRANOLA QA shows this behaviorally and that multi-granularity scoring surfaces ~20 points of hidden knowledge (more for rare entities), but why models commit to a granularity — and whether that commitment can be steered from inside the model — is unknown. We propose that answer specificity is set by a distinct, largely query-independent precision prior computed in intermediate layers before the specific content is resolved, and that granularity overcommitment is a mechanistically localizable failure. Falsifiable framing: if content-only patching shifts granularity as much as our precision-prior intervention, if fine-value confidence explains more granularity variance than format cues, or if suppressing the precision prior fails to recover coarse-correct answers above a re-prompt baseline, the theory is refuted. We test three claims on multi-granularity factual queries (dates, locations, quantities, taxonomic categories). (1) Dissociability and locus: a linear granularity probe predicts the specificity level before the answer is written, is separable (via residualization and random-subspace nulls) from a content probe, and — by regression — tracks generic format/precision cues more than internal fine-value confidence. (2) Overcommitment geometry: overcommitment errors concentrate on long-tail entities where the fine value is uncertain but a coarse value is verifiably stored, above frequency-matched baselines. (3) Causal recovery: suppressing or patching the precision-prior direction (causal mediation, not just probing) shifts the model to the correct coarser answer while preserving correct fine answers, beating a 'be less specific' re-prompt, DRAG-style decoding, and fact editing. So what: scientifically, this reframes a class of factual errors as a granularity-selection decision separable from retrieval, telling the interpretability and knowledge-evaluation communities to score and probe answer specificity as its own axis — this holds even if no steering method is deployed. Practically, evaluation authors gain motivation for multi-granularity scoring and coarse-correct credit, calibration researchers a new locus for over-specificity, and factual-QA practitioners a route to safer systems that prefer a coarse-correct answer over a confident fine error (e.g., abstention/back-off policies). Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on GRANOLA-EQ and multi-granularity T-REx/PopQA, evaluating probe separability, driver regression, overcommitment prevalence, causal recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — multi-granularity dataset): Build items with an ordered set of correct answers at increasing coarseness so granularity choice and correctness are scored independently. Operational definitions: a 'granularity ladder' is an ordered set of >= 2 answers each verifiably correct, strictly nested in coarseness; the model's 'granularity level' is the coarsest ladder rung its free-form answer entails (parsed by rule + string match). Data: GRANOLA-EQ (multi-granularity EntityQuestions) as-is, augmented with items built from T-REx/PopQA for four answer types — dates (day/month/year/decade), locations (city/region/country), quantities (exact/rounded/order-of-magnitude), taxonomic categories (species/genus/family). Target ~2,500 items; per item record the ordered correct answers, the model's answer, and its granularity level; restrict readout to single-token-first coarse answers where needed; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; temperature 0. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items with a well-formed ladder (>= 2 distinct correct coarseness levels) and a parseable model granularity level. Convincing: >= 1,500 usable items, >= 300 per answer type. Indecision band: 1,000-1,500 — reduced per-type power, reported; below 1,000 the ladders are too sparse. Negative (few items admit multiple granularities) means the phenomenon is not well-posed for these types and the type set must be revised.

Experiment 2 (H0 — coarse-value storage verification, leakage-controlled): Establish, per wrong-fine item, that the coarser correct value is stored, so overcommitment ('overcommitment-candidate' = fine answer wrong AND coarse value both directly answered AND probe-decodable) is separable from ignorance. Data: usable items whose fine answer is wrong. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; verify the coarse value via (a) a direct coarse-question prompt ('In what decade was X born?') and (b) a logistic-regression content probe decoding the coarse value from the residual stream (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null). Leakage controls: the coarse-question prompt never contains the fine value; probe train/test entities are disjoint from readout entities; a paraphrase held-out set checks phrasing does not leak the label; report the false-positive rate of the storage test on frequency-matched entities the model verifiably does NOT know. Decisive metric (first): fraction of wrong-fine items in the overcommitment-candidate set. Convincing: >= 600 candidates with storage-test false-positive rate < 10%. Indecision band: 350-600 candidates — reduced power, reported; below 350 overcommitment cannot be reliably separated from missing knowledge. Negative (coarse value rarely stored on wrong-fine items) means fine errors are genuine ignorance, refuting the premise.

Experiment 3 (H1 — granularity decodable before content, with representational controls): Test that the answer's specificity level is decodable from intermediate activations before the fine value resolves. Data: usable items. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a granularity probe (ordinal fine/mid/coarse) and a content probe (fine value) at every layer via logistic/ordinal regression (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold). Controls beyond linear probing: label-shuffle null, tuned-lens capacity control, and a random-subspace baseline (probe restricted to a random directions-matched subspace) to guard against over-reading linear decodability. Decisive metric (first): onset-layer difference = (layer where content probe first resolves the fine value at >= 0.7) minus (layer where granularity probe first reaches >= 0.7), bootstrap CI; secondary, residualized unique granularity AUROC after partialling out content, tested against the random-subspace baseline. Convincing: onset difference >= 3 layers (granularity earlier), CI excludes 0, unique granularity AUROC >= 0.65 and above the random-subspace null. Indecision band: onset difference 1-3 layers — weak ordering; H1's 'before content' then rests on the causal test (Exp 6). Negative (difference CI includes 0, or granularity not uniquely decodable above the random-subspace null) refutes the pre-content precision-prior claim.

Experiment 4 (H1 — precision prior driven by format cues, not fine-value confidence): Test the operational 'largely query-independent' claim: granularity is dominated by generic precision cues over confidence in the fine value. Data: usable items with granularity-probe output. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Decisive metric (first): partial variance in the granularity-probe output explained by the format block (relation type, prompt phrasing open/'be brief'/'be precise', fixed per-relation default granularity) versus the fine-confidence block (content-probe strength, top-fine logit margin), with CIs. Convincing: the format block explains a strictly larger variance share than the fine-confidence block, both CI-excluding 0 — this satisfies the committed weaker version of query-independence. Indecision band: the two blocks' shares within 5 points of each other — granularity reflects both; report as mixed (partial query-dependence). Negative (fine-confidence dominates) refutes even the weaker query-independence clause.

Experiment 5 (H2 — overcommitment concentrates on long-tail entities): Test that overcommitment errors concentrate where the entity is rare (fine value uncertain) but a coarse value is stored. Data: overcommitment-candidate set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared: overcommitment rate as a function of entity popularity and per-relation default precision vs a null controlling answer frequency and lexical similarity (logistic regression; permutation CI). Decisive metric (first): partial coefficient of (low) entity popularity on overcommitment probability, and of default precision, with CIs. Convincing: both coefficients CI-exclude 0, with monotone concentration on long-tail entities and high-precision relations. Indecision band: exactly one coefficient CI-excludes 0 — partial concentration; report which factor drives it. Negative (neither significant) refutes H2.

Experiment 6 (PRIMARY — causal test of the precision-prior direction via mediation): Decisively test that granularity is causally set by a (partly) separable direction, not by content. Data: overcommitment-candidate items and matched coarse-answer runs (elicited by a 'be approximate' prompt). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) subtract the learned low-rank granularity vector (mean coarse-answer minus fine-answer residual difference) at the identified layers and test a shift to the correct coarse answer; (b) activation-patch (causal mediation) the granularity representation from a coarse run into an overcommitment run; (c) reverse control — inject the fine-precision direction to force overcommitment; (d) content control — patch only the content direction and confirm granularity is unchanged; (e) random-direction / random-subspace control matched for norm and rank. We do NOT assume a single clean direction exists; the rank needed for the effect is reported. Decisive metric (first): coarse-correct recovery rate = fraction of overcommitment items shifted to the correct coarse value (not a new wrong fine value), net of random. Convincing: net recovery >= 25 points, content-only patch < 5 points, reverse injection induces overcommitment >= 25 points. Indecision band: net recovery 10-25 points — granularity partly separable; report. Negative (< 10 points, or content-patch shifts granularity as much as the precision-prior intervention) refutes the separable-precision-prior mechanism — this is the load-bearing falsifier for the primary claim.

Experiment 7 (H3 — recovery beats re-prompting and DRAG, with specificity): Test that suppressing the precision prior recovers the coarse-correct answer more cleanly than asking for less specificity or decoding heuristics. Data: candidate set, item-disjoint train/test; dose-controlled suppression. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the subtracted direction. Systems compared: granularity suppression vs 'be less specific / give the decade' re-prompt vs DRAG-style uncertainty decoding vs ROME edit (expected not to help) vs random-direction. Interpretation of the causal gain: the re-prompt and DRAG act on outputs/decoding; our intervention acts on the internal precision axis — a gain over both isolates an internal, content-independent locus. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = coarse-correct recovery rate divided by the coarsening rate on 200 items the model answers correctly at fine granularity (the over-coarsening control); secondary, accuracy on 200 unrelated facts, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: recovery >= 30% with < 3-point coarsening of correct-fine items, beating both the re-prompt and DRAG baselines on recovered-per-collateral. Indecision band: recovery 15-30% or coarsening 3-6 points — partial; report parity with re-prompting/DRAG. Negative (no advantage over re-prompt or DRAG, or correct-fine answers get coarsened) refutes H3.

Experiment 8 (auxiliary — cross-model replication, transfer, and source): A deliberately smaller, cleaner cross-model check to reduce single-family dependence, plus transfer and precision-prior source quantification. Data: candidate items partitioned by relation/answer type; suppression vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen (plus Pythia 1.4B/2.8B/6.9B for scale); re-run the core tests (Exp 2, 5, 6, 7), seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation coarse-correct recovery relative to within-relation, replication of overcommitment concentration (Exp 5) per model, and partial regression coefficients of overcommitment rate on (entity popularity, per-relation default granularity, fine-value uncertainty). Convincing: cross-relation recovery >= 50% of within-relation, concentration replicates in >= 2 of 3 models, popularity/uncertainty coefficients CI-exclude 0, and overcommitment falls across Pythia scale. Indecision band: replication in 1 model, cross-relation 30-50%, or source coefficients CI half-width overlapping 0 by < 0.02 — model-specific or entangled; report inconclusive. Negative (no transfer, no source signal) confines H1-H3 to one model and one relation family.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Granularity and content signals may be entangled rather than cleanly separable; the causal patching/mediation tests (Exp 6), not probe onset alone, are decisive, and a graded result would weaken the strong dissociation while remaining informative.

A single clean, low-rank precision-prior direction is a hypothesis, not an assumption; Exp 6 reports the rank needed for the effect and treats failure to find a low-rank transferable direction as an informative (partly negative) result.

Verifying the coarse value is 'stored' risks overestimation from prompt/label leakage; conservative content-probe thresholds, entity-disjoint probes, paraphrase held-outs, and a reported false-positive rate on known-unknown entities (Exp 2) mitigate this.
Linear probes can over-read decodability as mechanism; random-subspace nulls, tuned-lens capacity controls, and causal mediation (not probing alone) back every representational claim.
Granularity is naturally ordinal/graded, not discrete; we model it ordinally and report continuous granularity scores rather than forcing clean levels.

Granularity suppression could over-coarsen — making the model vague even when it knows the precise answer; the correctly-answered-fine specificity control (Exp 7) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.

The precision prior may be partly query-dependent (some phrasings legitimately demand specificity); we commit only to the weaker, operationalized query-independence (format cues > fine-value confidence in variance explained), not full independence.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if granularity control is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token coarse answers (e.g., month names, region names) complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B open models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: enumeration_closure_gate
Title: Knowing More Than It Lists: A Closure Signal That Terminates LLM Enumeration Before Its Knowledge Is Exhausted
Short Hypothesis: Our one novel claim is mechanistic: when an LLM enumerates the members of a set (e.g., 'list the countries bordering France'), termination is governed by a decodable 'closure' signal in the residual stream that crosses a threshold and halts listing before the model's stored member set is exhausted. Concretely: (1) Completeness gap - at the position where the model emits its stop token, at least one additional valid member is still internally recoverable and single-item-verifiable, so the stop is premature relative to stored knowledge; (2) Closure axis - a linear closure direction, decodable at intermediate layers before the stop, predicts termination and is driven more by generic count/list-length priors than by actual member-set exhaustion; (3) Causal control - suppressing this direction extends enumeration and recovers additional true members with high specificity, outperforming a 'keep listing' re-prompt. We treat the closure direction as a partly shared axis across relations and models, not a single query-independent vector, unless cross-relation/cross-model transfer is demonstrated.
Related Work: The novelty of this work is mechanistic and lies in isolating and intervening on the termination decision; the behavioral fact that LLMs truncate enumerations is already known, so we do not claim it. Prior mechanistic work explains the promote-then-suppress dynamics that generate *distinct* successive answers (Promote-Suppress-Iterate 2025) and how counting is computed layerwise (CountScope 2025; When Can Transformers Count to n 2024). These explain how the next distinct member is produced and how a running count is maintained, but not *why the model decides to stop*: termination is a separate causal object - a gate that halts the promote-suppress loop - rather than a step within it, and none of these works localize or intervene on it. Benchmarks show LLMs cannot enumerate completely (Can LMs Store/Retrieve 1-to-N 2023; Do LLMs Know How Much They Know 2024; Olympic Rankings 2024), are brittle on set membership (Brittleness of Set Membership 2025), and cannot detect omissions (AbsenceBench 2025); these are behavioral characterizations of omission - they measure that outputs are incomplete but do not test whether unlisted members remain internally recoverable, nor identify a residual-stream signal that causes the stop. Our delta over them is that we isolate a residual-stream closure gate and causally suppress it to recover true members. Aggregation/completeness is otherwise studied at the systems level (AGGBench 2026; GraphRAG). To be explicit about where novelty lives: the phenomenon (premature enumeration closure) is established behaviorally; our contributions are (i) the completeness-gap measurement tying the stop to still-recoverable stored members, (ii) the decodable closure axis separable from an exhaustion signal, and (iii) the causal steering method that recovers members - with (ii) and (iii) as the core mechanistic novelty. This is orthogonal to our prior single-answer recall/gating proposals: here the object is the decision to *stop enumerating* and the completeness gap it causes.
Abstract: Large language models routinely stop listing set members before exhausting what they know: asked to list films of a director or countries bordering a nation, they produce a plausible-length answer and stop, omitting members they can produce when prompted individually. Prior work explains how models generate distinct successive answers and how they count, but not why they decide to stop. We propose that enumeration termination is governed by a decodable closure signal in the residual stream that crosses a threshold and halts listing - often before the model's stored member set is exhausted, producing a completeness gap. Falsifiable framing: if, at the stop token, no additional true member is both linearly recoverable and confirmed by a conservative single-item verification prompt, or if suppressing the closure direction yields no net true-member gain over random-direction suppression, the mechanistic hypothesis is refuted. We test three claims on one-to-many factual queries. (1) Completeness gap: at the stop position, additional valid members are still internally recoverable, showing the stop is premature relative to stored knowledge. (2) Closure locus and drivers: a linear closure direction, decodable before the stop token, predicts termination and, in a pre-registered regression with leakage controls, tracks generic list-length/count priors more than actual set exhaustion. (3) Causal intervention: suppressing the closure direction (or ablating the attention that reads it) extends enumeration and recovers additional true members, with specificity controls and negative controls (already-complete small sets; synthetic fixed-size sets) ensuring the model does not fabricate, and outperforming re-prompting, iterative self-asking, and constrained-decoding baselines. So what: this reframes many enumeration omissions as a stopping-prior artifact rather than missing knowledge, which matters for (a) interpretability - a concrete, steerable termination gate; (b) factual-recall and knowledge-coverage evaluation - probes that under-list may under-estimate stored knowledge, so completeness benchmarks should separate 'not known' from 'not listed'; (c) retrieval/aggregation - closure suppression is a cheaper knob than repeated re-prompting; and (d) omission detection - the closure signal is a candidate internal detector for premature stops. A developer would prefer suppression over re-prompting when re-prompts re-list duplicates or drift off-type and when an internal, dose-controllable knob that raises recall at matched false-member rate is available. We emphasize this advances diagnosis and a controllable intervention rather than a deployed system. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on curated one-to-many relations, evaluating completeness-gap prevalence, closure-prediction AUROC, recovered-member yield, precision, and fluency.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 - one-to-many dataset with complete ground truth): Build set-valued queries with authoritative complete membership so a completeness gap can be measured. Data: constructed from Wikidata for five set-valued relations (countries bordering X; films directed by X; children of X; member states of an organization; elements in a chemical group), sampled to cover small (3-8) and large (15-40) true set sizes; target ~600 queries (>=100 per relation, balanced across size bins). For each, record the model's free enumeration and the ground-truth member set; restrict to single-token-first members where readout requires it; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; temperature 0, 3 prompt seeds. Decisive metric (first): fraction of queries with complete, verifiable Wikidata ground truth and a well-defined stop token in the model's output (the eligible set). Convincing: >= 400 eligible across both size bins. Indecision band: 250-400 eligible - reduced power, reported; below 250 the ground-truth coverage is too thin to estimate gaps. Negative (few relations have clean complete membership) means the phenomenon cannot be measured with authoritative labels and the relation set must be revised.

Experiment 2 (H1 - completeness gap at the stop, with a conservative verification protocol): Operational definition: a query has a completeness gap iff, at the list-ending token, there exists at least one true member NOT already listed that is BOTH (a) lens-recoverable (ranked above a held-out precision-calibrated threshold by tuned-lens over member-typed candidate tokens, restricted to the relation's answer type and excluding already-listed members) AND (b) confirmed by a single-item verification prompt ('Is Y a member of {set}?') under a conservative decision threshold. Data: eligible set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Probe-leakage controls (address false positives): calibrate the lens threshold on random-candidate sets and on adversarially matched unlisted FALSE candidates (same type, matched frequency), and report the lens's precision/recall so the reported gap rate is net of the false-candidate false-positive rate. Systems compared: observed recoverability vs a null where stopping coincides with exhaustion. Decisive metric (first): completeness-gap rate = fraction of stops meeting BOTH conditions above, net of the false-candidate false-positive rate. Convincing: gap rate >= 30%, concentrated on large sets. Indecision band: 15-30% - a real but modest gap; report and rely on the causal test for interpretation. Negative (gap rate < 15%, stops coincide with exhaustion) refutes H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 - a decodable closure direction separable from exhaustion, decodable != causal): Test that termination is *predicted* by a closure signal distinct from a remaining-members signal; we treat this as evidence of decodability only, reserving causal claims for Experiment 5. Data: pre-stop steps from eligible enumerations. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a stop-prediction probe (will the next step be a stop?) and a remaining-members probe (does the residual still encode unlisted members?) via logistic regression at each layer (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null). Label-leakage controls: partial out / stratify by prompt template, relation frequency, and items-already-emitted (answer-length prior) so the stop probe cannot exploit these surface cues; report AUROC before and after removing each. Decisive metric (first): stop-prediction peak-layer AUROC, and the residualized unique AUROC of each probe after partialling out the other. Convincing: stop AUROC >= 0.75 (after leakage controls) and each probe retains unique AUROC >= 0.65 after residualization. Indecision band: unique AUROC 0.55-0.65 - the two signals are largely entangled; H2's 'distinct direction' is weak. Negative (stop AUROC <= 0.6, or no unique closure signal) refutes the closure-direction claim.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 - one pre-registered causal-model regression: closure and the gap are driven by length priors, not storage): A single pre-registered regression (merging the prior separate driver/source analyses) with declared confounds and two outcomes. Data: pre-stop steps and per-query gap rates from the eligible set. Models: Llama-3-8B frozen (plus Pythia 1.4B/2.8B/6.9B for a scale axis). Predictors, grouped into blocks: (a) length priors - items already emitted, typical set-size for the relation from other subjects; (b) exhaustion signals - true members remaining, recoverability from Experiment 2; (c) tail obscurity / member-popularity distribution and relation frequency; (d) surface cues - self-attention/repetition. Outcomes: (1) closure-probe output; (2) completeness-gap rate. Decisive metric (first): partial coefficients and relative variance explained per block, with CIs, for each outcome. Convincing: for both outcomes the length-prior + tail-obscurity blocks explain a strictly larger share than the exhaustion block (CI-excluding 0), gap increasing with set size and tail obscurity and decreasing across Pythia scale. Indecision band: competing blocks' variance shares within 5 points - closure reflects both roughly equally; report as mixed. Negative (exhaustion dominates, or gap unrelated to size/obscurity) refutes H2's 'driven by priors' clause: closure tracks real exhaustion.

Experiment 5 (H3 - closure suppression causally extends valid enumeration; the decisive causal test): Test that removing the closure signal continues true enumeration and that injecting it forces premature stops. Data: eligible queries with a completeness gap. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) subtract the learned low-rank closure vector at the identified layers when a stop is imminent; (b) ablate attention heads reading the closure signal; (c) reverse control - inject the closure direction early to force premature stopping. Systems compared: closure suppression vs random-direction suppression vs head-ablation vs random-head ablation. Decisive metric (first): additional true members recovered per query (net of random suppression), with precision of newly emitted tokens (fraction that are ground-truth members, not repeats/fabrications). Convincing: >= 1.0 additional true member per large-set query at precision >= 0.7, and reverse injection shortens lists >= 25%. Indecision band: 0.3-1.0 additional true members or precision 0.5-0.7 - extends lists but with rising fabrication; report the completeness-precision trade. Negative (no net gain over random suppression, or precision at chance) refutes H3's causal core.

Experiment 6 (H3 - closure-suppression recovery beats stronger baselines, with specificity and negative controls): Test that suppression recovers members more cleanly than prompting-based alternatives. Data: eligible set, query-disjoint train/test; dose-controlled suppression. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the subtracted direction. Systems compared: closure suppression vs (i) 'are there more? continue listing' re-prompt, (ii) iterative self-asking, (iii) constrained decoding over member-typed candidates, (iv) forced continuation (suppress stop token) without intervention, (v) temperature increase / beam widening. Negative controls where suppression should NOT help: on small sets the model already completes, and on a synthetic task with a known fixed set size, the false-member rate must not rise. Decisive metric (first): recovered-true-member yield at matched false-member rate; secondary specificity - false-member rate on already-complete small and synthetic-fixed sets (measured pre/post), and fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: suppression recovers >= 50% more true members than the best baseline at equal or lower false-member rate, with < 3-point false-member increase on the negative-control sets. Indecision band: 20-50% more, or a 3-6-point false-member increase - partial advantage; report parity with baselines. Negative (no advantage over the stronger baselines, or fabrication explodes) refutes H3's specificity and its distinction from prompting.

Experiment 7 (H1/H3 - transfer and architecture generality; tests the 'partly shared axis' claim): Test whether the closure signal and its suppression generalize across relations/sizes and models, and quantify how shared the axis is. Data: eligible queries partitioned by relation; closure vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out relations. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 2, 5, 6, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation and cross-model recovered-member yield relative to within-relation, plus replication of the completeness gap (Experiment 2) per model. Convincing: cross-relation yield >= 50% of within-relation AND completeness gap replicates in >= 2 of 3 models (supports a partly shared closure axis). Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-relation 30-50% - relation/model-specific. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines the closure axis to one relation/model. Report whether larger models have smaller completeness gaps.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The completeness gap could reflect that unlisted members are not truly stored (probe/logit-lens false positives); the single-item verification control (Exp 2b), the random and adversarially-matched false-candidate calibration, and reported lens precision/recall are essential, and the gap rate is reported net of the false-candidate false-positive rate.

Closure and exhaustion signals may be entangled rather than separable directions; decodability (Exp 3 AUROC) alone is not treated as mechanism - the causal suppression/injection tests (Exp 5) are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Closure suppression could induce fabrication or repetition (the model keeps listing false members); precision, false-member specificity, and the negative controls (already-complete small sets, synthetic fixed-size sets) in Exp 6 are central, and utility may be capped if suppression trades completeness for hallucination.

Stop-prediction probes can exploit surface cues (prompt template, relation frequency, answer-length prior); Exp 3 partials these out and reports AUROC before/after, but residual leakage would weaken the decodability claim.
Ground-truth set completeness is hard for open-ended relations; we restrict to relations with authoritative complete membership (Wikidata-verifiable) and report coverage limits.

A single fully query-independent closure vector may not exist if termination is relation-specific; we therefore claim only a partly shared axis and test transfer directly (Exp 7), which if it fails confines the finding without invalidating the per-relation mechanism.
Multi-token members and stop-token detection vary across tokenizers; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first members and canonical stop conditions with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget; results advance diagnosis and a controllable intervention rather than a deployed system.

Name: difficulty_effort_gate
Title: Fooled by Hard-Looking Questions: A Perceived-Difficulty Signal That Gates Retrieval Effort and Hides Easy Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: LLMs compute an early, linearly-encoded 'perceived difficulty' signal about a factual query that is driven substantially by surface complexity (query length, syntactic nesting, rare/technical vocabulary, hedge words) rather than the actual knowledge state, and this signal causally gates retrieval effort/processing depth. We state the novelty as an explicit causal bridge between two things that are each already known: (i) difficulty is linearly represented with causal heads (known), and (ii) factual QA is brittle to paraphrase (known); NEW is that surface-driven perceived difficulty CAUSALLY gates retrieval depth so that a stored, otherwise-answerable fact is under-retrieved on hard-looking-but-easy queries, that the missed fact stays internally decodable, and - the strongest and most distinctive claim - that suppressing the difficulty direction restores the answer SELECTIVELY, preserving appropriate hedging on genuinely hard items rather than globally boosting confidence. The alternative to rule out is ordinary paraphrase brittleness / semantic interference; the cleanest evidence uses meaning-preserving, minimal-content manipulations (hedging, technical vocabulary, syntactic wrapping) varying one factor at a time. We predict (1) the difficulty signal is decodable before retrieval and tracks surface complexity more than true fact difficulty; (2) inflating surface complexity while holding the fact fixed causes under-retrieval of stored facts, with the answer remaining recoverable; and (3) suppressing the difficulty direction restores the answer while sparing hedging on genuinely hard items, beating simple prompt-simplification baselines.
Related Work: Recent work shows LLMs linearly encode problem difficulty with identifiable causal attention heads (Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism, 2025) and that difficulty perception diverges from entropy; Concept Depth (2024) and Demystifying LLM Layers (2025) show complex concepts/reasoning recruit deeper layers while retrieval is shallow; 'know but don't tell' (2024) documents a probe-vs-generation gap; Information Anxiety (2024) shows popularity reduces attention to constraint tokens. The main alternative explanation - which we name and target directly - is the paraphrase-brittleness / robustness literature showing factual QA changes under surface rephrasing; prior work there treats brittleness as a benchmarking phenomenon without a mechanism. The delta, stated against that baseline: brittleness work shows accuracy varies with phrasing but does not show that surface complexity acts THROUGH an internal perceived-difficulty signal that gates retrieval depth, that the fact stays decodable during the failure, or that a targeted suppression of the difficulty direction recovers it WITHOUT indiscriminately reducing abstention. Ruling the alternative out requires that surface complexity (not added semantic content) predict under-retrieval, that patching the difficulty representation alone recover the answer, and that the recovery be selective. This differs from the familiarity_before_retrieval proposal (a scalar coverage/feeling-of-knowing estimate): here the gating variable is the perceived hardness of the query, driven by surface cues.
Abstract: Large language models internally represent how difficult a problem is, encoded linearly with identifiable attention heads. We ask whether this perceived-difficulty signal causally shapes factual recall: does judging a query 'hard' make the model allocate less retrieval effort, so a stored fact goes unretrieved simply because the question LOOKS difficult? Both endpoints are prior art - difficulty is causally represented, and factual QA is paraphrase-brittle; our contribution is the causal bridge between them, and its practical consequence: models may hide easy, already-stored knowledge when a question merely looks hard, so this is not just another robustness patch but a mechanistic, actionable diagnosis relevant to benchmark design, deployment prompting under diverse user phrasing, calibration/abstention, and interpretability tooling. We propose the difficulty-effort gate: perceived difficulty is computed early, driven substantially by surface complexity (length, nesting, technical vocabulary, hedging) rather than the true knowledge state, and gates processing depth spent on retrieval. The signature failure is difficulty-driven under-retrieval: a fact answered under a plain phrasing is missed when a semantically-equivalent query is dressed up to look hard. We articulate the causal DAG (surface complexity -> perceived difficulty -> retrieval depth -> failure) against alternatives (semantic interference, ambiguity, generic long-context degradation), validate paraphrase meaning-preservation with GPT-4o plus human spot-checks and a fact-target check, and vary one complexity factor at a time. We test three claims. (1) Localization and drivers: a linear difficulty probe is decodable before the answer, tracks surface-complexity cues more than actual fact difficulty, and is residualized-separable from fact-content. (2) Causal gating: inflating surface complexity while holding the fact fixed raises the difficulty signal and reduces retrieval, patching the difficulty representation from a plain-phrasing run restores the answer, and the missed answer remains available (probe plus answer-token rank / forced-choice readout). (3) Selective suppression: subtracting the difficulty direction recovers stored facts while preserving appropriate hedging on genuinely hard items - the claim that separates this from generic confidence boosting - and beats prompt-simplification, entropy/confidence, and generic-patching baselines; we report a downstream reliability metric under paraphrase diversity. We prioritize the cleanest manipulations and strongest interventions over breadth. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Surface-complexity paraphrase dataset and difficulty-probe drivers): Tests H1, that a difficulty signal is decodable before retrieval and tracks surface complexity more than true fact difficulty. Data: constructed from PopQA (~14k), T-REx (LAMA subset ~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); select 2,500 facts the model answers correctly under a plain phrasing; generate five semantically-equivalent variants per fact (plain, length-inflated, syntactically nested, technical/rare-vocabulary, hedge-laden), validated for meaning-preservation by GPT-4o + human spot-check with the fact target confirmed unchanged; single-token-first answers; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Trainable: a linear difficulty probe on subject-token/last-token residual stream per layer (targets: ordinal surface-complexity level, and separately the model's own elicited difficulty rating), L2-regularized, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV; a fact-content probe for residualization. Systems compared: difficulty-probe output regressed on surface-complexity features vs on true fact difficulty (plain-phrasing accuracy / entity popularity). Decisive metric (before data), first: standardized regression coefficient of the difficulty signal on surface complexity MINUS its coefficient on true fact difficulty, plus onset layer (decodable before the answer token) and residual AUROC after removing content. Convincing = surface-complexity coefficient >=2x the fact-difficulty coefficient AND residual AUROC >=0.70 AND onset precedes the answer token. Negative = fact-difficulty coefficient >= surface coefficient, or residual AUROC <=0.55 (signal not surface-driven or not separable; H1 fails). Indecision band residual AUROC 0.55-0.70: report an entangled, graded difficulty signal.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Difficulty-driven under-retrieval prevalence and storage): Tests the behavioral half of H2, that inflating surface complexity while holding the fact fixed reduces correct retrieval of a stored fact. Data: Exp 1 variants. Model: same three frozen; a content probe (seeds {0,1,2}) to verify storage during failures. Systems compared: per-fact accuracy across complexity variants vs a null where paraphrasing only adds output noise (paired McNemar; mixed-effects logistic with complexity x fact), controlling for query length and answer frequency; content-probe recovery on failures. Decisive metric (before data), first: accuracy drop from plain to a semantically-equivalent surface-complex phrasing for the SAME fact, per complexity type. Convincing = drop >=10pp for >=2 complexity types (CI excluding 0), and on those failures the content probe recovers the correct answer at >=40pp above verbalized (hidden, not absent). Negative = drop <=2pp (surface complexity does not suppress retrieval; H2 fails). Indecision band 2-10pp: report weak under-retrieval; the technical-vocabulary and hedging conditions (minimal added content) are the cleanest.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal gating via patching and head ablation): Tests H2's causal claim, that the difficulty representation gates retrieval. Data: 1,000 held-out under-retrieval failures (Exp 2). Model: same three frozen; activation edits at the difficulty-onset layers (Exp 1) and ablation of the difficulty attention heads identified by prior difficulty-perception work; dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) patch the difficulty representation from a plain-phrasing run into the complex-phrasing failure; (b) reverse control injecting the high-difficulty direction into a plain-phrasing run; (c) ablate the difficulty heads; (d) content control (patch content alone -> should not change gating); random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-fact recovery rate (matches the plain-phrasing answer) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp over random at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=15pp under-retrieval in plain runs. Negative = <=5pp recovery (difficulty not causal; H2 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Depth-of-processing analysis): Tests the mechanism linking H2's difficulty signal to retrieval effort/processing depth. Data: Exp 1 plain vs complex variants for matched facts. Model: same three frozen; logit-lens/tuned-lens over the answer tokens; no weight training. Systems compared: the layer at which the correct answer first becomes the top candidate under plain vs complex phrasing. Decisive metric (before data): shift in answer-onset layer (complex minus plain) and its correlation with the difficulty-probe magnitude. Convincing = answer onset is delayed by >=2 layers under complex phrasing (or never reached) with the delay correlating with difficulty-probe magnitude (rho >=0.3, CI excluding 0). Negative = onset-layer shift CI includes 0 (difficulty unrelated to processing depth; the effort-gating mechanism is unsupported, though behavioral H2 may stand). Indecision band 0-2 layer shift: report a weak depth effect.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Suppression recovery preserving appropriate hedging): Tests H3, that subtracting the difficulty direction recovers stored facts WITHOUT destroying appropriate hedging on genuinely hard items. Data: 1,000 held-out under-retrieval failures; a genuinely-hard set the model does NOT store plus legitimately complex questions (600 items) where hedging/abstention is correct; 200 unrelated facts. Model: same three frozen; a low-rank difficulty steering vector (mean high-minus-low-difficulty activation difference) subtracted; best dose. Systems compared: our suppression vs a 'take your time / this is simple, just answer' re-prompt, the difficulty-head ablation, ROME editing (existing, expected null), random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: under-retrieval recovery rate MINUS the increase in confident wrong answers on genuinely-hard items (recovered-per-unit-overconfidence). Convincing = recovery >=25pp while genuinely-hard false-answer/over-confidence rate rises <=5pp, unrelated accuracy drops <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = genuinely-hard false-answer rate rises >=20pp (we converted appropriate hedging into hallucination) or no recovery. Indecision band 5-20pp overconfidence: utility capped; report the trade-off curve.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Cross-relation and cross-model transfer): Tests whether a single difficulty-suppression vector generalizes. Data: vector fit on a subset of relations/complexity types (Exp 5) applied unchanged to held-out relations and complexity types (800 failures). Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction. Decisive metric (before data): transferred recovery as a fraction of in-domain-refit. Convincing = >=60% of in-domain on >=2 complexity types and >=2 models. Negative = <=20% (relation/complexity-specific; generality fails). Indecision band 20-60%: partial transfer. Report Spearman rho between model scale and surface-complexity-driven under-retrieval rate (rho <=-0.3 suggestive that larger models are more robust; N=3 caveat).

Experiment 7 (H1 — Source analysis of surface-complexity drivers): Tests H1's mechanistic source, quantifying how much the gate is driven by superficial query complexity rather than genuine hardness. Data: all Exp 2 under-retrieval outcomes with per-query features (length, syntactic-nesting depth, rare-vocabulary count, hedge presence) and true fact difficulty (plain-phrasing accuracy / popularity). Model: same three frozen; no new training. Systems compared: nested regression predicting under-retrieval from surface-complexity features vs from true fact difficulty. Decisive metric (before data): incremental variance (Delta R^2) explained by surface-complexity features over true-fact-difficulty-only. Convincing = Delta R^2 >=0.10 with positive coefficients on nesting/rare-vocabulary/hedging across >=2 models. Negative = Delta R^2 <=0.02 (under-retrieval is genuine difficulty, not surface-driven; the core mechanistic claim fails). Indecision band 0.02-0.10: report surface complexity as a partial driver alongside genuine hardness.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Surface-complex paraphrases may not be perfectly meaning-preserving; added clauses could introduce genuine ambiguity or distractor content rather than pure difficulty inflation, confounding under-retrieval with interference. Strict semantic-equivalence validation, the fact-target check, and length controls are essential, and the technical-vocabulary/hedging conditions (which add minimal new content) are the cleanest tests.

The difficulty signal and fact-content signal may be entangled; the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 4), not probe onset alone, are decisive, and a graded result would weaken the strong gating claim while remaining informative.

Suppression could over-correct on genuinely hard/unknown items, converting appropriate hedging into confident hallucination; the genuinely-hard specificity control (Exp 6) is central and practical utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.

Perceived difficulty may be partly legitimate (some complex phrasings truly are harder to parse); the driver regression separates surface-complexity from true fact difficulty rather than claiming difficulty perception is entirely spurious.

Verifying a fact is 'stored' during under-retrieval risks overestimation from probe overfitting; held-out probes, conservative thresholds, and plain-phrasing recall as an additional check with reported coverage mitigate this.
A single transferable difficulty-suppression vector may not exist if the gate is relation- or complexity-type-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: fluency_as_truth_heuristic
Title: Easy to Read, Easy to Believe: An Internal Retrieval-Fluency Signal LLMs Misuse as a Truth Cue
Short Hypothesis: Primary claim (one falsifiable sentence): in factual verification an LLM causally MISUSES its own processing/retrieval fluency as evidence for truth — holding truth value and propositional content fixed, a decodable fluency representation (not the statement's actual validity) shifts the verdict, so fluently-processed FALSE statements are over-accepted and disfluently-processed TRUE statements are over-rejected. 'Fluency' is operationalized via several independent surface/processing-ease cues (rhyme/phonetic ease, high-frequency phrasing, prior in-context repetition, lexical simplicity), each truth- and meaning-preserving, so a shared effect isolates fluency rather than any single confound, and it is distinguished from confidence, memorization, verbosity, and repetition-copying. This is explicitly a causal-misuse claim ('truth fixed, fluency varied'), not 'LLMs like fluent text'. Secondary predictions: (a) the fluency signal is decodable before the verdict and separable from a content/truth signal; (b) suppressing it selectively removes the two directional errors while preserving correct verdicts and appropriate uncertainty.
Related Work: Human cognitive science robustly establishes that processing fluency and retrieval fluency are used as cues for truth and confidence, independent of actual validity (Epistemic Status of Processing Fluency 2010; Illusory Certainty / repetition-fluency 2024; Processing Fluency and Judgment 2016; Retrieval Fluency contributes to JoLs 2019). In LLMs, prior interpretability work encodes only truth/correctness-correlated signals: attention-to-constraint predicts factual accuracy (SAT Probe 2023), attention-head entropy predicts correctness (HEADENTROPY 2026), local intrinsic dimension separates truthful from untruthful generations (2024), and entropy/token-frequency neurons regulate confidence (Confidence Regulation Neurons 2024); Information Anxiety (2024) shows popular queries converge early internally. Idiom-recall work (2023) shows memorized content is promoted early (a fluency proxy). Crucially, all of these treat internal ease/confidence signals as (imperfect) indicators of truth; none test the reverse causal misuse — that an LLM treats its own retrieval fluency as EVIDENCE for truth, causing it to accept fluently-processed falsehoods and reject disfluently-processed truths in a verification task. This transfers the human fluency-as-truth heuristic into LLM verification with a causal fluency-signal locus and a non-destructive fix, and is orthogonal to my prior proposals, which all concern retrieval/expression of a target answer rather than verification of a presented statement. Primary novelty anchor (mechanistic interpretability): prior interpretability work reads internal ease/confidence signals as (imperfect) indicators of truth; our contribution is the reverse causal misuse — holding truth fixed and showing a separable fluency representation causally drives verification verdicts — instantiated with a controlled verification task and a suppression fix, not a new general mechanism.
Abstract: User-facing consequence first: an LLM used as a fact-checker or LLM-as-judge may believe fluent falsehoods and doubt disfluent truths because it treats how easily it processes a statement as evidence that the statement is true — a directional bias that can flip verdicts on otherwise easy claims. Humans judge statements they process fluently as more likely true — a fluency-as-truth heuristic that operates independently of the statement's actual validity. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous, mechanistically-localizable bias in factual verification. Existing interpretability work reads internal ease/confidence signals as indicators of truth; we test the reverse causal misuse: that an LLM treats how fluently it can process a statement as evidence for that statement's truth, causing it to over-accept fluently-processed falsehoods and over-reject disfluently-processed truths. We test three claims. (1) Behavioral signature: on true/false verification of factual statements, holding truth value fixed, manipulating processing fluency (via surface cues — rhyme/phonetic ease, high-frequency phrasing, prior in-context repetition, and lexical simplicity) shifts verdicts toward 'true' for fluent framings and 'false' for disfluent ones, producing directional errors above content-matched baselines. (2) Localization and drivers: a linear retrieval-fluency signal is decodable before the verdict, tracks surface/processing-ease cues more than the statement's actual truth (measured by plain-phrasing verification accuracy), and is separable (via residualization) from a content/truth signal. (3) Causal control: activation-patching the fluency representation from a disfluent-but-true (or fluent-but-false) matched run, and suppressing the fluency direction, remove the fluency-induced verdict bias with high specificity — preserving correct verdicts and appropriate uncertainty — whereas a 'ignore how it sounds, judge only the facts' re-prompt does not. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on FEVER-style and curated true/false factual sets, evaluating fluency dose-response, verdict-bias geometry, causal removal, and specificity. This is directly relevant to model-as-judge pipelines, automated fact-checking, benchmark grading, and safety filtering; we separate phenomenon value from method value and test whether the effect persists on naturally occurring claims, not only engineered manipulations. H1 (causal fluency-as-truth misuse) is primary; localization and debiasing are secondary analyses.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — fluency-induced directional verdict bias): Tests that, holding truth value and propositional content fixed, fluent framings push verification verdicts toward 'true' and disfluent framings toward 'false'. Data: factual statements with known truth labels from FEVER (~185k claims) and curated true/false sets over PopQA/T-REx facts; target ~1,200 statements per model (capped for the framing x caching cost; report coverage), each rendered in 5 meaning- and truth-preserving framings (plain; rhyming/phonetically easy; high-frequency lexical; rare/technical; prior in-context repetition vs first-exposure), validated by a GPT-4o judge plus a 100-item human spot-check (>=90% agreement, truth unchanged). Verdicts via a fixed true/false/uncertain template plus 3 paraphrases. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: each fluency framing vs the plain baseline and a content-matched null (framing that adds equal length but no fluency manipulation); paired McNemar. Decisive metric: signed verdict shift toward 'true' for fluent and toward 'false' for disfluent framings, holding truth fixed (fluency x truth-value interaction), yielding the two diagnostic error types (fluent-false over-acceptance, disfluent-true over-rejection). Convincing: >=8 pp acceptance lift for fluent-false and >=8 pp rejection lift for disfluent-true over the content-matched null, consistent in sign across >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: 3-8 pp -> bias present but weak, partial support. Negative (<3 pp, or no consistent sign) refutes the fluency-as-truth transfer — an informative cross-species divergence.

Experiment 2 (H2 — retrieval-fluency signal decodable before the verdict and driven by ease not truth): Tests that a linear fluency signal is decodable before the verdict, tracks processing-ease cues more than actual truth, and is separable from a content/truth signal. Data: the Exp-1 items with residual stream cached at the statement/last-token positions across layers. Model: frozen; per-layer L2-logistic probes — a fluency probe (target = ordinal fluency level; plus, as robustness, self-rated ease and the content-promotion layer) and a content/truth probe — trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds with shuffle nulls. Systems compared: fluency-probe output regressed on surface fluency cues vs actual truth / plain-phrasing verification accuracy (standardized betas); fluency probe residualized on the content probe. Decisive metric: fluency-cue beta vs truth beta in predicting the fluency signal; secondary: fluency-probe peak AUROC and onset layer (before the verdict token), and residual separability. Convincing: fluency-cue beta at least 2x the truth beta, fluency-probe AUROC >=0.75 peaking before the verdict, and residual AUROC (after removing content) >=0.70, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: cue-to-truth beta ratio 1-2x, or AUROC 0.60-0.75 -> signal partly a truth proxy, partial support. Negative (fluency signal tracks truth more than cues, or is not separable from content) means there is no distinct retrieval-fluency signal; the locus claim fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — the fluency signal causally drives the verdict): Tests that manipulating the fluency representation flips verdicts in the predicted direction, independent of content. Data: 300 matched fluent-but-false and disfluent-but-true trials per model, held out from Exp-2 probe training. Method: patch the fluency representation from a disfluent-but-true run into a fluent-but-false run (and vice versa) at the Exp-2 onset layers; suppress or inject the fluency direction (low-rank high-minus-low-fluency difference); a content/truth-only patch control. Model: frozen; dose swept in {0.5,1,2,4}x, 3 seeds. Systems compared: fluency-patch/inject vs content-only patch vs random-direction control. Decisive metric: per-item verdict-flip rate in the fluency-predicted direction from the fluency intervention vs the random-direction control; secondary: dose-response monotonicity, and that the content-only patch changes the verdict via truth without reproducing the fluency-bias pattern. Convincing: fluency injection flips >=25% of verdicts toward the bias with monotone dose-response (>> random-direction), while the content-only patch shows a different (truth-driven) pattern, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: flip 10-25% -> partial causal role, suggestive. Negative (flip <=10% over control, or indistinguishable from the content patch) means the fluency signal is correlational, not causal.

Experiment 4 (H3 — fluency-debiasing intervention with specificity and generality): Tests that suppressing the fluency direction selectively removes the two directional errors while preserving correct verdicts, and generalizes. Data: held-out fluency-biased verification items (>=400 per model); specificity sets = items where fluency and truth already agree, genuinely-ambiguous statements that warrant 'uncertain', and 200 unrelated verification items. Model: frozen; a low-rank fluency steering vector fitted on a subset of cues/relations and applied to held-out cues/relations and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: fluency-subtraction vs an 'ignore how it sounds, judge only the facts' re-prompt, chain-of-thought verification, and a random-direction control.
