Decisive metric: reduction in fluent-false over-acceptance and disfluent-true over-rejection (verdict accuracy moving toward the plain baseline), reported jointly with collateral change on the fluency-truth-agree, uncertainty, and 200-unrelated sets; secondary: output perplexity. Convincing: >=40% of the fluency-induced error removed with <=2 pp collateral drop and preserved 'uncertain' behavior, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, transferring across cues and models. Undecidable band: 20-40% removed, or collateral 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (<=20% removed, collateral >5 pp, or flips fluent-but-true items) means no clean debiasing; the fix claim fails.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Fluency manipulations (rhyme, rare vocabulary, repetition) risk altering meaning or introducing genuine ambiguity rather than pure processing ease; strict truth-value and semantic-equivalence validation, content-matched baselines, and using multiple independent fluency cues (so any shared effect isolates fluency, not one confound) are essential.

LLMs might not reproduce the human directional bias (e.g., verdicts could be insensitive to surface fluency, or the effect could be pure repetition-copying); a null or divergent pattern would refute the transfer but is itself an informative cross-species finding, and the repetition cue is distinguished from verbatim copying by including both true and false repeated items.

The fluency and content/truth signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 3), not probe onset alone, are decisive, and a graded/partial dissociation would weaken the strong claim while remaining informative.

Debiasing could over-correct — making the model reject fluent-but-true statements or lose appropriate confidence; the fluency-truth-agree and genuine-uncertainty specificity controls (Exp 4) are central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
The fluency probe target (ordinal cue level / promotion layer / self-rated ease) is a proxy for internal retrieval fluency; we report multiple operationalizations and their consistency.
A single transferable fluency-suppression vector may not exist if the bias is cue- or relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Verification verdicts are prompt-sensitive (true/false/uncertain framing); we use multiple paraphrases and report robustness, since framing itself may modulate the bias.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

The engineered fluency cues may not reflect naturally occurring fluency; we include a held-out set of naturally fluent-vs-disfluent real claims and report whether the verdict bias persists there, so the effect is not an artifact of construction.

Name: abstention_momentum
Title: Abstention Is Contagious: How One 'I Don't Know' Suppresses Knowledge on the Next Question
Short Hypothesis: Primary claim (one falsifiable sentence): abstention carries session-level momentum — the ACT of abstaining ('I don't know') on one query causally raises the probability of abstaining on a later, unrelated, easily-answerable query in the same conversation, hiding knowledge the model demonstrably holds (abstention hysteresis). This is distinguished from generic conversational degradation, sycophancy, and refusal over-triggering by an answer-first control (same prior-turn structure, no abstention) and an equal-length filler control, and the effect must scale with the number and recency of prior abstentions. Secondary predictions: (a) on contaminated failures the correct answer stays internally decodable (hidden, not rationally discarded); (b) a transient, content-separable 'abstention-mode' signal imprinted by the prior abstention is decodable at the later query and causally drives contamination — 'transient/query-independent' meaning it tracks prior-abstention presence/recency rather than the current fact and decays with intervening answered turns; (c) suppressing it restores correct answers while preserving genuinely appropriate abstention on unanswerable follow-ups.
Related Work: Prior work treats each query's abstention/refusal decision as independent: entity-recognition directions gate knowledge refusal on the current entity (Do I Know This Entity, 2024), sparse ambiguity-encoding neurons control answer-vs-abstain for the current question (AENs, 2025), over-refusal benchmarks measure per-prompt refusal rates (OR-Bench, 2024; Do RALMs Know When They Don't Know, 2025), and abstention frameworks estimate per-query knowledge boundaries (ABCA, 2025; Know Your Limits survey, 2024). None test whether the *act of abstaining on one query causally biases the abstention decision on a later, independent query* within a session, whether this hides knowledge the model would otherwise express, or whether a transient abstention-mode signal carries this contamination. This transfers the human response-set perseveration / decision-hysteresis phenomenon into LLM knowledge expression, and is orthogonal to my prior single-turn gating proposals (familiarity, difficulty, stress, persona) which all manipulate the *current* query rather than a *prior abstention act*. Primary novelty anchor: the new phenomenon is abstention-specific momentum across independent queries (not generic multi-turn drift), and the mechanistic contribution is a separable, causally-testable abstention-mode signal; the behavioral finding is designed to stand alone even if the causal mechanism does not.
Abstract: User-facing consequence first: a single earlier 'I don't know' can make a model refuse the next easy, unrelated question it actually knows — so abstention behaves as a contagious conversational STATE, not a per-query decision, causing systematic under-answering in real chat systems. Large language models increasingly operate over multi-turn conversations, deciding on each turn whether to answer or abstain. Existing work treats these abstention decisions as independent per-query events. We ask whether abstention is instead contagious: does the act of saying 'I don't know' on one query causally increase the model's propensity to abstain on a subsequent, unrelated, easily-answerable query in the same session—thereby hiding knowledge the model demonstrably holds? We call this abstention hysteresis. We first document the behavior: for facts a model answers correctly in a fresh context, we compare later-query abstention rates between a condition where the model first genuinely abstained (on an unanswerable prior query) and matched controls where it first answered a question or saw equal-length filler. We predict elevated abstention (and reduced accuracy) after a prior abstention, above baselines, scaling with how many prior abstentions occurred and their recency. We then test the mechanism with a Location plus Causal Intervention strategy: a transient 'abstention-mode' signal imprinted by the prior abstention should be linearly decodable, separable (via residualization) from the current-query content signal, and—during a contaminated failure—the correct answer should remain internally decodable (hidden, not lost); activation patching from an answer-first run and suppression of the abstention-mode direction should restore correct answers with high specificity, while preserving genuinely appropriate abstention on truly unanswerable follow-ups. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA/T-REx plus a medical subset, evaluating hysteresis prevalence, dose-response, hidden-knowledge recovery, causal recovery, and specificity. This reframes abstention as a stateful failure mode with concrete deployment consequences (session resets, refusal auditing, chat UX), not just another degradation metric. H1 (hysteresis) is primary and publishable on its own; hidden-knowledge, localization, and the suppression fix are secondary; we also test whether the effect depends on the literal phrase 'I don't know' or on any abstention/uncertainty expression.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — abstention hysteresis prevalence and dose-response): Tests that abstaining on one query raises abstention on a later unrelated, answerable query, beyond conversational drift. Data: PopQA (14,267), T-REx, EntityQuestions; per model select target facts answered correctly in isolation; target ~1,200 facts (capped; report coverage). Two-stage sessions holding total length equal: ABSTENTION-FIRST (a genuinely unanswerable prior query on which the model abstains, verified), ANSWER-FIRST (an answerable prior it answers), and FILLER (equal-length neutral text). Dose variants: 1/2/3 consecutive prior abstentions and varied recency (turns to target); plus a phrasing ablation contrasting the literal 'I don't know' against other abstention/uncertainty expressions (e.g., 'I'm not sure', a hedge) to test whether momentum is tied to the specific phrase or to abstention behavior generally. Single-token-first targets. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: target abstention rate / accuracy across the three conditions (paired McNemar; mixed-effects logistic), and across dose. Decisive metric: target-query abstention-rate increase (and accuracy drop) in ABSTENTION-FIRST vs the ANSWER-FIRST and FILLER controls; secondary: dose-response with number and recency of prior abstentions. Convincing: >=10 pp higher abstention (or >=8 pp lower accuracy) in ABSTENTION-FIRST than both controls, rising with dose, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: 3-10 pp -> hysteresis weak, partial support. Negative (<3 pp, or a protective/opposite effect) refutes the hysteresis transfer — an informative behavioral finding either way.

Experiment 2 (H1 — hidden knowledge under contaminated abstention): Tests that on contaminated failures the correct answer remains internally decodable (hidden, not rationally discarded). Data: contaminated failures from Exp 1 (target abstained/wrong in ABSTENTION-FIRST but correct in isolation), with their ANSWER-FIRST counterparts; residual stream cached at the target-query positions. Model: frozen; a per-layer L2-logistic content probe (target = correct answer) trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds with a shuffle null. Systems compared: content-probe recovery on contaminated failures vs the verbalized accuracy (~0) and vs the ANSWER-FIRST run. Decisive metric: content-probe recovery of the correct answer on contaminated failures; secondary: comparability to the ANSWER-FIRST recovery. Convincing: recovery >=60% (>> verbalized and >> shuffle), comparable to ANSWER-FIRST, in >=2 of 3 models — the knowledge is hidden, not lost. Undecidable band: recovery 40-60% -> partly hidden, partly a genuine competence downgrade, partial support. Negative (recovery near verbalized/chance) means the contaminated abstention reflects rational recalibration or loss, not hidden-knowledge suppression.

Experiment 3 (H2 — abstention-mode signal localization): Tests that a transient, content-separable 'abstention-mode' signal imprinted by the prior abstention is decodable at the later query. Data: matched ABSTENTION-FIRST vs ANSWER-FIRST runs at the target query for the Exp-1 facts; residual stream cached across layers. Model: frozen; a per-layer L2-logistic probe targets the presence/recency of a prior abstention, trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds; residualized against the current-query content probe; shuffle null. Systems compared: the abstention-mode probe before vs after residualizing out content; its layer/position profile and attention over the prior-abstention tokens. Decisive metric: per-layer AUROC of the abstention-mode signal predicting target abstention, after residualizing out content; secondary: onset before the answer, and tracking of prior-abstention presence/recency rather than the specific fact. Convincing: post-residualization AUROC >=0.72 with a clear onset before the answer, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.60-0.72 -> signal entangled with content, partial. Negative (AUROC at shuffle after residualization) means there is no separable abstention-mode signal; the locus claim fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 — abstention-mode signal is causal): Tests that the abstention-mode signal causally contaminates later recall. Data: 300 contaminated failures and 300 answer-first facts per model, held out from Exp-3 probe training. Method: patch the target-query residual stream from an ANSWER-FIRST run into a contaminated ABSTENTION-FIRST run; suppress the abstention-mode direction; inject the abstention-mode direction into an ANSWER-FIRST run to induce contamination; a content-only patch control. Model: frozen; interventions at Exp-3 layers, dose swept {0.5,1,2,4}x, 3 seeds. Systems compared: patch-restore, suppression, injection-induce, content-only patch, random-direction control. Decisive metric: induced-abstention increase from injection vs the random-direction control (dose-response); secondary: recovery rate of the correct answer from patch/suppression vs the content-only patch. Convincing: injection induces >=15 pp abstention over random-direction with monotone dose-response, and patch/suppression recovers >=50% of correct answers while the content-only patch does not, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: induced 5-15 pp, or recovery 25-50% -> partial causal role. Negative (induced <=5 pp over control, or content patch matches) means the abstention-mode signal is correlational.

Experiment 5 (H3 — recovery with appropriate-abstention specificity and generality): Tests that suppressing the abstention-mode signal restores correct answers without forcing hallucination on genuinely unanswerable follow-ups, and generalizes. Data: held-out contaminated failures (>=400 per model); specificity sets = truly-unanswerable follow-ups (must still be abstained, not hallucinated) and 200 unrelated answerable facts. Model: frozen; a low-rank abstention-mode suppression vector fitted on a subset of relations and applied to held-out relations and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: suppression vs a 'treat each question independently' re-prompt, re-querying the target in a fresh context (upper bound), refusal-tuning, and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: recovery rate on contaminated failures, reported jointly with the false-answer rate on truly-unanswerable items (must not rise) and collateral on the 200 unrelated facts; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: recovery >=40% with <=2 pp rise in false answers on unanswerable items and <=2 pp collateral drop, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, transferring across relations and models. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, or unanswerable false-answer rise 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (recovery <=20%, or induces hallucination on unanswerable items >5 pp) means suppression cannot separate contamination from appropriate abstention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The effect could be generic conversational drift or output-format entrainment rather than an abstention-specific momentum; the answer-first control (same prior-turn structure, no abstention) and equal-length filler control (Exp 1), plus the induce-on-demand test (Exp 4), are the decisive separators.

LLMs might not reproduce the hysteresis effect (per-query independence, or prior abstention could even prime helpfulness); a null or opposite result refutes the transfer but is an informative cross-species / behavioral finding.

Contaminated abstention could reflect rational recalibration (the model updates downward on its own competence) rather than hidden-knowledge suppression; the content probe (Exp 2) and fresh-context recovery separate hidden from lost knowledge.
The abstention-mode and content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 4), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Suppression could break genuinely-appropriate abstention on unanswerable follow-ups (inducing hallucination); the unanswerable-item false-answer specificity control (Exp 5) is central and utility may be capped.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if hysteresis is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: strategy_arbitration
Title: Retrieve or Assemble? How LLMs Arbitrate Between Memorized Shortcuts and Compositional Computation, and Why Choosing Wrong Hides Known Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: For many derivable facts an LLM has two internal pathways to the answer: a memorized 'shortcut' that recalls the answer atomically, and a 'compositional' pathway that assembles it from intermediate sub-facts. We hypothesize an internal, query-conditioned arbiter selects which pathway drives the output; a distinct and common failure mode is misarbitration — the model commits to whichever pathway is weaker for that query even though the other pathway holds the correct answer. We predict (1) which pathway is selected is linearly decodable at intermediate layers before the answer is written, (2) misarbitration accounts for a substantial fraction of failures on facts the model can otherwise produce via the alternate pathway, and (3) a lightweight steering intervention that biases the arbiter toward the stronger pathway recovers these hidden answers more selectively than weight editing. Primary falsifiable claim: there exists a pre-answer internal state that predicts route choice (compositional vs. shortcut) and on which intervention changes answer selection without changing route competence; misarbitration - selecting the weaker route while the alternate route is internally viable - is a substantial, recoverable share of errors. Definitions: 'route availability' = the route's answer/bridge is internally decodable or its shortcut fires; 'route selection' = which route causally drives the output (established by single-route ablation, Exp 4); 'misarbitration' = an error where the non-selected route was available; 'selective recovery' = gold becomes top-1 under arbiter steering with <5% collateral. We separate the descriptive (decodability), causal (arbiter state), and intervention (steering) claims and do not overclaim broad deployment impact - the contribution is diagnosis and targeted correction on derivable facts.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs solve two-hop tasks either compositionally (with detectable intermediate variables) or 'directly'/idiomatically, and that mechanism choice is only weakly correlated with accuracy and tracks embedding-space linearity (How Do LLMs Compose Functions?, 2025); probabilistic recall-and-extract and distributional parallel-reasoning accounts describe internal multi-hop dynamics (Layer-Order Inversion, 2026; Distributional Reasoning, 2024); co-occurrence shortcuts are distinguished from true factual associations by layer (Co-occurrence is not Factual Association, 2024); grokking integrates memorized facts into reasoning circuits (Grokked Transformers, 2024). All of these characterize that two mechanisms exist or describe multi-hop dynamics, but none ask whether the model actively *arbitrates* between an atomic-shortcut pathway and a compositional pathway on a per-query basis, whether that arbitration is predictable/steerable before the answer, or whether *misarbitration* is a recoverable failure mode. My prior proposals concern single-fact routing gates, format-bound duplicate copies, and interference among competing candidate facts; this proposal is orthogonal: it concerns selection between two *procedurally distinct* routes to the same answer. Delta over bridge-patching and latent-reasoning work: they show two routes exist and that a bridge entity is decodable, but do not test whether a pre-answer, query-conditioned arbiter state causally selects the route independent of route competence - the signal Experiment 4 isolates by changing route choice while holding both routes' competence fixed. User-visible framing: this asks why a model misses an answer it could internally assemble or recall, and gives evaluation/debugging a way to separate genuine ignorance from arbitration failure; interpretability, editing, and reliability researchers would use it to decide when to steer routing rather than edit weights.
Abstract: Large language models can reach the same fact by different internal routes: recalling it as a memorized association, or assembling it from constituent sub-facts. We hypothesize that the model arbitrates between these routes on a per-query basis, and that a common, overlooked failure mode is misarbitration — committing to whichever route is weaker for the current query even though the alternate route encodes the correct answer. We study this on derivable facts (e.g., 'the capital of the country where X was born') for which both a memorized shortcut and a two-hop compositional path can in principle yield the answer. We first build, per fact, evidence for which routes are viable: probing whether the compositional intermediate (bridge entity) is decodable in the residual stream, and whether the atomic shortcut fires (via co-occurrence-based and single-hop-recall diagnostics). We then test three claims: (1) which route drives the output is linearly decodable from intermediate activations before the answer token is written; (2) using activation patching to isolate the pathways, misarbitration failures — where the model outputs the wrong answer despite the alternate route being internally viable — form a substantial and identifiable fraction of errors; and (3) a low-rank steering vector that biases the arbiter toward the viable route recovers correct answers with higher specificity and lower collateral damage than ROME/MEMIT editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on SOCRATES, PopQA, and T-REx-derived two-hop sets, evaluating route-prediction AUROC, misarbitration prevalence, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency. Confirming these claims reframes many knowledge failures as strategy-selection errors and yields a cheap, non-destructive way to surface answers the model could compute but does not. Concretely, a correctly-computable fact the model gets wrong becomes fixable by a training-free steering nudge rather than a weight edit - useful when edits are costly or collateral-prone. Causal controls include random-direction steering, matched-logit/entropy comparisons, and a route-availability-only baseline, so the arbiter claim is not confounded with route weakness; we keep the experimental package minimal and decisive rather than broad.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 - dual-route facts with measured route availability): Builds two-hop facts g(f(x)) with a compositional route and a possible atomic shortcut, and measures per-model route competence - the substrate for the misarbitration-prevalence test. Data: two-hop items from SOCRATES (a two-hop latent-recall benchmark), plus compositions assembled from PopQA and T-REx/LAMA single-hop relations; we build 6,000 g(f(x)) facts (e.g. capital-of-birth-country) where both single hops f(x) and g(z) are individually answerable by the model, fewer than all possible compositions because each needs single-hop verification on every model. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; measure single-hop accuracy on f(x) and g(z), direct-composition accuracy on g(f(x)), and shortcut viability via co-occurrence diagnostics (does x co-appear with the answer); seed 0. Systems compared: single-hop vs. composed accuracy per fact. Decisive metric: coverage = fraction of facts where at least one route is viable (both single hops answerable, or shortcut co-occurrence present) (first); supporting: per-relation route-availability breakdown. Convincing: >=60% of facts have >=1 viable route and >=25% have both, giving a usable arbitration substrate. Undecidable band: 40-60% coverage is a thin substrate - proceed but flag power. Negative: <40% coverage means too few facts admit an alternate route, so misarbitration cannot be studied at scale here.

Experiment 2 (H1 - per-fact route viability labeling): Labels, per fact, whether the compositional route (bridge f(x) decodable) and the shortcut route (answer decodable without a bridge signature) are internally available. Data: the 6,000 dual-route facts from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; a tuned-lens (trained once, frozen) reads the bridge entity f(x) from intermediate-layer residuals at the last-subject position, and reads the answer directly for shortcut viability; label-shuffle control. Systems compared: tuned-lens vs. raw logit-lens bridge decoding. Decisive metric: bridge-decoding accuracy at the best intermediate layer (first); supporting: fraction of facts with each route labeled viable. Convincing: bridge decoding reaches >=0.7 accuracy on facts the model composes correctly (validating the lens signal) and yields clear per-fact route labels for >=70% of facts. Undecidable band: bridge decoding 0.5-0.7 makes route labels noisy - restrict downstream analysis to high-confidence labels and report coverage. Negative: <0.5 bridge decoding, near shuffle, means route viability cannot be read, blocking the decoding and prevalence tests.

Experiment 3 (H1 - route choice is linearly decodable before the answer): Tests that which route drives the output is decodable from intermediate residuals before the answer token, using patching-derived ground truth. Data: facts with a patching-established route label from Experiment 4; target 3,000 with clean labels. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; a trainable linear probe on pre-answer intermediate-layer residuals predicts compositional-vs-shortcut route, seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle control. Systems compared: route probe vs. shuffled-label control; probe AUROC across layers. Decisive metric: cross-validated AUROC of route prediction (first); supporting: earliest layer at which AUROC exceeds 0.7. Convincing: AUROC >=0.75 at a layer preceding answer commitment - route choice is decodable in advance. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.60-0.75 means route choice is partially anticipable - report weak decodability. Negative: AUROC <=0.60 or no better than shuffle means route selection is not linearly pre-decodable, falsifying H1.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 - causal pathway isolation and ground truth): Causally separates the two routes and defines the route-usage ground truth used by Experiment 3. Data: 2,000 correctly-answered dual-route facts. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch/ablate the bridge-entity representation at the last-subject position to knock out composition and see if output survives via shortcut; (b) suppress the early atomic-shortcut signal and see if output survives via composition; random-direction control. Systems compared: bridge-ablation vs. shortcut-suppression vs. random control. Decisive metric: fraction of facts where exactly one manipulation changes the output, giving a clean route label (first); supporting: per-route causal contribution. Convincing: >=50% of facts yield a single-route causal label (one manipulation flips, the other does not) vs <=10% for the random control. Undecidable band: 25-50% clean-label rate means routes are partly entangled - report coverage limits and treat ambiguous facts separately. Negative: <25%, near control, means the two routes are not causally separable, undermining the arbiter framing.

Experiment 5 (H2 - misarbitration is a substantial share of failures): Tests that many errors occur despite a viable alternate route. Data: all errors on dual-route facts across the datasets and the three models; target 5,000 errors on Llama-3-8B for the primary count. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify each error as misarbitration (alternate route viable per Experiments 2/4) vs. genuine ignorance (neither route viable). Systems compared: misarbitration rate vs. a frequency/similarity-matched null estimating chance co-viability. Decisive metric: fraction of errors that are misarbitration, above the matched null (first); supporting: per-relation breakdown. Convincing: >=25% of errors are misarbitration, >=10 points above the matched null - a common, distinct failure mode. Undecidable band: 10-25% above null of <10 points means misarbitration is real but minor - report as a secondary failure mode, narrowing H2. Negative: <10% misarbitration or indistinguishable from the null means errors are dominated by genuine ignorance, falsifying H2.

Experiment 6 (H3 - arbiter steering recovers hidden answers more selectively than editing): Tests that biasing the arbiter toward the viable route recovers misarbitration failures. Data: held-out misarbitration failures from Experiment 5, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; a rank<=8 steering vector = mean activation difference between correct compositional runs and matched misarbitrated failures (and a symmetric shortcut-biasing vector), added at the Experiment 3 route-decodable layer, alpha swept; random-direction control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: arbiter steering vs. ROME vs. MEMIT vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-facts-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated facts (first); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity change. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% unrelated-accuracy drop, beating ROME/MEMIT on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage over editing is parity - report as comparable. Negative: recovery <20% or no advantage over editing falsifies the selectivity half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 - one arbiter vector generalizes across relations): Tests whether a single steering vector transfers rather than being fact-specific. Data: train the vector on one relation subset (target 20 relations), apply to held-out relations (target 10), on their misarbitration failures. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; single trained vector applied unchanged, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: cross-relation transfer vs. within-relation (oracle) steering. Decisive metric: cross-relation recovery rate (first); supporting: gap to the within-relation oracle. Convincing: cross-relation recovery >=25% and within 0.5x of the oracle - a general arbitration signal. Undecidable band: recovery 10-25% or below 0.3x of oracle means the signal is largely relation-specific - report limited transfer. Negative: <10% cross-relation recovery means no general arbiter vector exists, limiting H3's generality.

Experiment 8 (H1-H3 generality - architecture-general arbitration): Tests that route decodability, misarbitration prevalence, and steering hold beyond one model. Data: reuse the Experiment 1 dual-route set (6,000 facts) per model. Model: repeat Experiments 2-6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds/hyperparameters. Systems compared: Llama-3-8B vs. GPT-J-6B vs. Qwen2.5-7B on each decisive metric. Decisive metric: sign-consistency of route-probe AUROC, misarbitration-vs-null gap, and steering advantage across models (first); supporting: per-model coverage. Convincing: all three show route AUROC >=0.70, positive misarbitration gap, and steering advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: reversal in the majority means arbitration is model-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Shortcut vs compositional 'routes' may not be cleanly separable when representations are entangled (superposition); patching-based dissociation may leave ambiguous cases, which we report as coverage limits rather than force into the dichotomy.
Logit-lens/tuned-lens decoding of the bridge entity is noisy; we mitigate with tuned-lens, answer-type filtering, and causal patching as the decisive test rather than lens readouts alone.

Route choice may be graded/mixed (both pathways contribute) rather than a discrete arbiter; a graded result would weaken the clean arbitration framing but remains informative, and we report continuous route-contribution measures.

Steering toward a 'viable' route could induce confident hallucination on facts where the route only appears viable; strict specificity and perplexity controls are essential and may cap practical utility.
A single transferable arbiter vector may not exist if arbitration is fact-specific, limiting the intervention's generality though still scientifically informative.
Distinguishing misarbitration from subtle storage weakness is hard; matched-pair design and route-availability controls reduce but may not fully eliminate confounds.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: context_priming_contamination
Title: Primed to Err: How Irrelevant Contextual Mentions Contaminate an LLM's Factual Recall
Short Hypothesis: One falsifiable claim: merely mentioning a related but irrelevant entity B earlier in the prompt causes an LLM to answer an unrelated target A's question with B's attribute b, even though b never appears anywhere in the context. We call this context-priming contamination and hypothesize it (1) is a gradable behavioral phenomenon whose rate rises with the semantic similarity between B and A and with the recency/salience of B's mention, distinct from generic distraction (a same-length unrelated mention) and from contextual entrainment/copying (b is absent, so any b in the answer must come from parametric recall); (2) is carried by a residual-stream 'primed-entity' direction that attention over the distractor-mention tokens injects into A's answer readout; and (3) can be causally suppressed by ablating the distractor-token attention or subtracting the primed-entity direction, restoring correct recall without editing the fact.
Related Work: The closest prior work, positioned as a same-behavior / same-mechanism / same-setting table: (1) Shi et al. 2023 ('LLMs Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context') — same coarse behavior (irrelevant text hurts accuracy), NOT same mechanism (no residual-stream locus), NOT same setting (math word problems, irrelevant sentences need not name a semantically related entity, and no attribute-bleed readout). (2) Contextual entrainment / in-context knowledge conflict (Fakepedia 2023; DynamicQA 2024) — related behavior but the injected context explicitly contains or contradicts the fact; NOT same setting, because we forbid the contaminating attribute b from appearing in the prompt, so the effect cannot be copying/entrainment. (3) Induction-head / copy-mechanism work — same mechanistic vocabulary (attention-mediated) but explains verbatim copying of tokens present in context, NOT attribute contamination of parametric recall where the answer token is absent from context. (4) Retrieval-competition / knowledge-conflict work (including my retrieval_competition proposal) — distractors are co-activated by the query itself or by logically-linked context, NOT by an incidental, non-contradictory neighbor mention. The novelty lives primarily in the SETTING (source-monitoring-style attribute bleed with b absent from context) and secondarily in the MECHANISM (a localizable primed-entity direction with a non-destructive suppression fix); the behavior is a sharpened, controlled special case of known distraction rather than an entirely new phenomenon. We transfer the classic human semantic-priming / source-monitoring error into parametric factual recall and give it a causal account.
Abstract: Human memory retrieval is famously contaminated by recently activated but irrelevant material—semantic priming and source-monitoring errors. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous phenomenon in parametric factual recall: does merely mentioning a related but irrelevant entity earlier in the prompt corrupt the model's answer about an unrelated target? We call this context-priming contamination, and we state it as one falsifiable claim: an incidental mention of B makes the model answer target A's question with B's attribute b, even though b never appears in the prompt. The strongest alternative explanations are generic distraction (any prepended sentence adds attention load) and contextual entrainment/copying (the answer is lifted from context); we pre-register the controls that kill each—a matched-length unrelated-entity prime for the former, and the requirement that b be absent from the prompt for the latter—so the novelty rests on a falsifiable delta, not a vague priming story. We first document the behavior: for a target fact (e.g., the capital of country A), we prepend a neutral, non-contradictory sentence mentioning a semantically related distractor entity (e.g., neighboring country B) and measure how often the model answers with B's attribute (B's capital) instead of A's, above a matched neutral-prime baseline and stratified by target popularity, answer prior, entity type, and prompt length. We predict contamination is gradable—rising with distractor-target similarity and with the recency/salience of the mention—and concentrated on low-frequency targets. We then test a candidate mechanism (framed as candidate until the causal intervention succeeds) with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy: a linear probe should recover a 'primed-entity' signal in the residual stream at A's answer position that is absent under neutral primes; activation patching, attention-head analysis, and a mediation test should show that attention over the distractor-mention tokens injects this signal beyond mere residual correlation; and ablating that attention or subtracting the out-of-sample primed-entity direction should restore correct recall with high specificity (unrelated facts and un-primed recall unchanged), whereas ROME-editing the fact does not address the cause. Why practitioners should care: RAG pipelines and multi-turn prompts routinely place semantically neighboring entities near a query, so if an irrelevant mention can silently flip a factual answer, this is a concrete, previously underappreciated failure mode for prompt hygiene, retrieval, and higher-stakes medical QA, and it yields a cheap suppression fix and a new context-sensitivity evaluation. So-what if negative: if the effect vanishes under our controls, that is itself a useful result—it bounds prompt-distractor risk and shows current distraction concerns do not extend to attribute bleed; if positive, it motivates new robustness tests and suppression baselines. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions, evaluating contamination rate, similarity/recency dose-response, probe recovery, causal recovery with mediation, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — priming dataset construction, ablation matrix, and copying control): Build primed prompts where any contaminated answer must come from parametric recall, not surface copying, so H2 cannot be explained by induction. Data: adapted from PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions; for each target fact (subject A, relation r, answer a) select a same-type distractor B with a different attribute value b != a, and record A-B semantic similarity (entity-embedding cosine, taxonomic/geographic distance). Construct the full ablation matrix per item: (i) no-prime control, (ii) matched-length neutral-prime (dissimilar unrelated entity), (iii) related-prime ('I was reading about {B} yesterday. What is the {relation} of {A}?'), (iv) same-entity-but-irrelevant prime (mentions B in a way unrelated to relation r), (v) shuffled-entity-name control, and (vi) a random-answer sanity control; crucially b never appears in any prompt. Record per-item confounds: target popularity, answer prior frequency, entity type, prompt length, lexical overlap. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items where the model answers the no-prime query correctly (the eligible set — contamination is only meaningful where baseline recall works) AND b is absent from the prompt. Convincing: >= 1,500 eligible across >=8 relations after filtering to single-token-first answers; report coverage. Indecision band: 1,000-1,500 — reduced power; below 1,000 baseline recall is too weak to detect contamination. Negative (baseline recall at chance) means the model cannot recall these facts and priming cannot be studied.

Experiment 2 (H1 — context-priming contamination exists, vs two named nulls): Test that merely mentioning B specifically raises the rate of answering b, ruling out generic distraction and entrainment. Data: eligible set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared (ablation matrix from Exp 1): related-prime vs matched-length neutral-prime vs same-entity-but-irrelevant prime vs shuffled-name vs no-prime. Decisive metric (first): contamination-rate lift = P(answer = b | related-prime) minus P(answer = b | neutral-prime), tested against a null controlling answer frequency, popularity, entity type, prompt length, and lexical overlap (stratified/matched logistic regression; permutation CI). Practical-failure quantification: also report the absolute rate at which a nearby irrelevant entity changes the answer under the realistic related-prime template. Convincing: lift >= 8 percentage points with 95% CI excluding 0, neutral-prime not above no-prime by more than 2 points (kills generic distraction), and shuffled-name prime not raising b (kills lexical artifact). Indecision band: lift 3-8 points — a weak effect that may be generic load; report as suggestive. Negative (lift CI includes 0, or neutral-prime equally raises b) refutes H1.

Experiment 3 (H1 — dose-response on similarity and recency): Test that contamination scales with distractor-target similarity and mention recency/salience. Data: eligible set, crossed over similarity bins and recency (token distance to query, number of mentions, syntactic prominence), stratified by target popularity. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Decisive metric (first): regression coefficients of contamination rate on similarity and on recency, with CIs; secondary, similarity x target-popularity interaction. Convincing: both similarity and recency coefficients CI-exclude 0 with monotone per-bin curves, and low-popularity targets more contaminated. Indecision band: exactly one of the two coefficients CI-excludes 0 — partial dose-response; report which factor drives it. Negative (neither coefficient significant) means contamination does not scale as claimed, refuting H1's gradable-scaling clause.

Experiment 4 (H2 — primed-entity signal in the residual stream): Test that a decodable primed-entity signal is present at A's answer position and aligned with b's readout. Data: eligible set across related/neutral/no-prime runs, with item-disjoint train/test folds to keep the direction out-of-sample. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a logistic-regression probe (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null) to decode presence/identity of distractor B from the answer-position residual stream at each layer. Decisive metric (first): peak-layer AUROC for detecting the primed signal in related-prime vs neutral-prime, and cosine alignment of the primed-entity direction with b's unembedding vector. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 and alignment significantly above a random-direction null. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.75 — a weak/partial signal; the causal test (Experiment 5) is then decisive. Negative (AUROC <= 0.60 or no unembedding alignment) means no primed-entity signal, undercutting H2. Note: probe success alone is correlational; the mechanism is treated as candidate until Experiment 5.

Experiment 5 (H2/H3 — attention injects the contaminating signal, causally, with mediation): Test that distractor-token attention is the injection route, beyond correlation. Data: contaminated related-prime items. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) identify query/answer-position heads attending to distractor-mention tokens and ablate that attention; (b) activation-patch the answer-position residual from a no-prime run into a contaminated run and measure recovery of a; (c) reverse control — inject the primed-entity signal into a no-prime run to induce contamination on demand; (d) mediation analysis — quantify the fraction of the contamination effect explained by the distractor-attention pathway (indirect effect via path patching) versus the direct residual correlation, to show attention mediates rather than merely correlates. Systems compared: distractor-attention ablation vs random-head attention ablation vs no-prime patch vs random-position patch. Decisive metric (first): contamination-reduction from distractor-attention ablation, net of random-head ablation. Convincing: distractor-attention ablation cuts contamination by >= 50% relative, no-prime patch recovers a in >= 25 points net, reverse injection induces contamination >= 25 points, mediation attributes >= 50% of the effect to the attention pathway; random controls < 5 points. Indecision band: attention-ablation reduction 20-50% relative or mediated fraction 30-50% — attention is one of several routes; frame mechanism as partial. Negative (ablation ~ random, or near-zero mediated fraction) means attention over the mention is not the causal route, refuting H2's mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H3 — suppression restores recall without editing the fact): Test that subtracting the out-of-sample primed-entity direction fixes contamination cleanly. Data: eligible set, item-disjoint train/test; steering vector = mean residual difference (contaminated minus neutral-prime matched states) computed on the train split only, seeds {0,1,2}, rank<=4, subtracted at the identified layers; the direction is thus defined out-of-sample to avoid circularity with the probe/intervention. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the subtracted direction. Systems compared: primed-entity subtraction, distractor-attention ablation (Experiment 5a), ROME edit of the target fact (expected not to help), random-direction control. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = contamination-recovery rate divided by accuracy drop on correctly-answered primed facts (over-correction control); secondary, accuracy on 200 unrelated un-primed facts, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: recovery >= 30% with < 3-point drop on correctly-answered primed facts and on the 200 facts, beating ROME. Indecision band: recovery 15-30% or collateral 3-6 points — partial; report parity. Negative (no better than random, or harms correct cases) refutes H3.

Experiment 7 (H1/H3 — transfer and architecture generality): Test generality across relations, distractor types, and models. Data: eligible items partitioned by relation; suppression vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out relations. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 2-6, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation contamination-recovery relative to within-relation, plus replication of the contamination lift (Experiment 2) per model. Convincing: cross-relation recovery >= 50% of within-relation AND lift replicates (CI excludes 0) in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-relation 30-50% — model/relation-specific. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines H1-H3 to one model. Report whether larger models contaminate less.

Experiment 8 (H1 — safety-domain transfer, auxiliary): Test that context-priming contamination produces higher-stakes errors. Data: constructed from a curated safe subset of medical facts (drug-indication or symptom-disease), with a benign related-drug/disease mention as the distractor; ~400 items, held to publicly documented, non-actionable facts. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; replicate Experiments 2-3. Decisive metric (first): contamination-rate lift in the medical setting versus the general-knowledge lift. Convincing: medical lift CI excludes 0 and is at least as large as the general lift. Indecision band: medical lift 3-8 points — present but modest; report the elevated-stakes framing cautiously. Negative (no lift in medical domain) means the phenomenon does not transfer to this higher-stakes setting, bounding the practical claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The neutral prime may not be truly neutral (any prepended sentence adds tokens/attention load); the matched-length neutral-prime, same-entity-but-irrelevant, and shuffled-name controls in the Experiment 1 ablation matrix are essential to attribute the effect to semantic priming rather than generic distraction.

Contamination could be driven by verbatim copying (induction/contextual entrainment) rather than parametric-recall corruption; we require the distractor's attribute b to NOT appear anywhere in the prompt, so any b in the answer must come from parametric recall, and the attention/mediation analysis distinguishes copying from attribute injection.

The primed-entity signal and target recall may be entangled, and probe success is only correlational; the causal patching/ablation and mediation tests (Exp 5)—not probe AUROC alone—are decisive, and we frame the mechanism as a candidate until they succeed. Graded results remain informative.
The primed-entity direction could be defined circularly with the intervention; we compute the direction on an item-disjoint train split and evaluate suppression out-of-sample to avoid this.

Suppression could over-correct (harm cases where a contextual mention is legitimately relevant) or degrade fluency; the correctly-answered-primed and unrelated-fact specificity controls are central and utility may be capped.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if contamination is relation- or distractor-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget; Experiment 7 tests only three open models.

Name: presupposition_writeback
Title: Presupposition Writeback: How a False Aside About One Attribute of an Entity Silently Corrupts an Unrelated Fact the Model Knows
Short Hypothesis: PRIMARY (behavioral): When a query embeds a false presupposition about one attribute A of a subject as an incidental aside, and asks only about a *different, unrelated* attribute B that the model otherwise recalls correctly, LLMs answer B wrong more often than under a matched true-presupposition aside; this cross-attribute, same-subject spillover is gradable, scaling with the false aside's plausibility and the semantic relatedness of A to B. This behavioral claim is the primary, most-established contribution. SECONDARY (mechanistic, treated as hypotheses to be tested, not assumed): (H2) the false attribute a_false is 'written back' into the subject's early residual-stream representation via early attention over the presupposed-attribute tokens, decodable at the subject position even though A was never queried; (H3) suppressing that route -- ablating the writeback attention or subtracting the writeback direction -- restores correct recall of B without editing any stored fact. Falsifiable core: if a false aside about A degrades B no more than a matched true aside (or than an unrelated-content aside of equal length), the phenomenon does not exist.
Related Work: Prior false-premise work studies models answering, rejecting, or hallucinating about the false premise *itself*. FAITH (2024) localizes 'false-premise heads' that disturb extraction of the *presupposed* object; DecoPrompt (2024) decodes prompts to cut hallucination *on the false premise*; FalseQA/CREPE (2022-2023) and 'LLMs Struggle to Reject False Presuppositions when Stakes are High' (2025) benchmark rebuttal/abstention *of the premise*. In all of these the asked attribute and the presupposed attribute coincide. This proposal varies them independently. Comparison of what each work varies -- Asked attribute / Presupposed attribute / Subject overlap: FAITH: presupposed object / presupposed object / same (asked == presupposed); DecoPrompt: presupposed object / presupposed object / same; FalseQA/CREPE: the premise / the premise / same; my prior context_priming_contamination proposal: attribute of entity X / content about a *different* distractor entity Y / different subjects (cross-entity bleed); THIS work: attribute B / a *different* attribute A of the *same* subject / same subject, and the query never asks about A. The novelty is thus primarily (i) a PHENOMENON/SETTING novelty -- cross-attribute, same-subject spillover onto an otherwise-correct fact, a configuration no prior work isolates -- and secondarily (ii) a MECHANISM hypothesis (subject-position writeback + non-destructive suppression). We do not claim the mechanism is established a priori; it is what the causal experiments test. The strongest alternative -- that any added clause causes generic distraction/attentional load -- is pre-registered and addressed by the matched true-presupposition baseline, an unrelated-content aside of equal length, and the relatedness dose-response (a generic-distraction account predicts no dependence on A-B relatedness).
Abstract: Large language models are known to be misled when a question's premise is false and the question asks about that very premise. We isolate a subtler failure: a false presupposition slipped in as an incidental aside about one attribute of a subject silently corrupts the model's recall of a *different, unrelated* attribute it otherwise knows. For example, asking 'Given that Marie Curie was born in Germany, what field did she win her Nobel Prize in?' can degrade the otherwise-correct 'Physics/Chemistry' answer even though nationality is irrelevant to the prize field. We call this presupposition writeback. The practitioner consequence is direct: in retrieval-augmented and multi-turn pipelines, chat history, tool outputs, or user asides routinely carry incidental false attributes about an entity; if those silently corrupt *unrelated* facts the model actually knows, a system can produce a confidently wrong answer to a question whose retrieved evidence was never even about the corrupted field -- a failure mode current false-premise defenses (which watch the asked attribute) do not catch. We motivate the stakes with a curated safe clinical-QA slice (a false aside about a drug's route while asking its correct indication). Our primary contribution is behavioral and falsifiable: across relation pairs we measure how often a false aside about attribute A flips a correct answer on an unrelated attribute B, against a matched TRUE-presupposition control and an unrelated-content aside of equal length, so any extra error is attributable to falseness and not to adding a clause or to attentional load; the effect must be gradable in the aside's plausibility and in A-B relatedness (a generic-distraction account predicts no relatedness dependence). We then test -- not assume -- a mechanistic account with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy: a probe should recover a writeback signal for a_false at the subject position though A was never queried; activation patching and attention ablation should show early attention over the presupposed-attribute tokens injects it; and suppressing that route should restore B without editing any stored fact. Probes alone are treated as suggestive; the causal patching/ablation/reverse-injection tests are decisive. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA/T-REx, reporting how prevalent and robust the effect is across models and relation pairs.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (PRIMARY-behavioral, H0 -- cross-attribute presupposition dataset and eligibility): Build items where a false aside about attribute A can corrupt recall of an unrelated attribute B the model otherwise answers, with a matched true-presupposition baseline so any effect is attributable to falseness, not to adding a clause. Data: adapted from PopQA/T-REx, selecting subjects with >=2 known attributes under distinct relations; per subject a queried attribute B (relation r_B, correct b) and a presupposed attribute A (relation r_A, true a_true, plausible false a_false). Four conditions per item, all asking ONLY about B: no-presupposition; true-presupposition (aside states a_true); false-presupposition (aside states a_false); unrelated-content aside (a length/structure-matched clause about a third, off-topic entity, to control generic attentional load). Confound controls: match a_false and a_true on token length and match the false/true/unrelated asides on total prompt length; log per-item lexical overlap with the B-answer and clause surprisal for use as regression covariates; restrict primary analysis to single-token-first B; target ~2,000 subjects across >=6 relation pairs; report coverage. Matched-item procedure: a_false is drawn from the same relation r_A and type as a_true (e.g. a real but incorrect country for a nationality aside) so false and true asides are semantically parallel; report the fraction of pairs a human spot-check rates as parallel. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items answered correctly on B under BOTH no-presupposition AND true-presupposition (the eligible set -- writeback is only defined where recall is otherwise robust). Convincing: >= 1,200 eligible. Indecision band: 800-1,200 -- reduced power; below 800 baseline B recall is too weak to detect corruption. Negative (B recall collapses under the true aside) means adding any clause breaks recall, so falseness cannot be isolated.

Experiment 2 (PRIMARY-behavioral, H1 -- a false aside corrupts an unrelated attribute beyond true and unrelated-content asides): Data: eligible set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; writeback error = B correct under no- and true-presupposition but wrong under false-presupposition. Systems compared (the controls are the point): false-presupposition vs the matched true-presupposition (key paired baseline) vs the unrelated-content aside (generic-load control) vs no-presupposition. Decisive metric (first): writeback error-rate lift = P(B wrong | false) minus P(B wrong | true), paired McNemar test, with a logistic mixed model including prompt length, lexical overlap, clause surprisal, subject popularity, and b frequency as covariates and subject as random effect. Convincing: adjusted lift >= 6 percentage points, CI excludes 0, AND the false-vs-unrelated-content contrast is also >= 6 points (so the effect is falseness-specific, not generic distraction), with true- and unrelated-content asides each within 2 points of no-presupposition. Indecision band: lift 2-6 points -- weak effect possibly from residual mismatch; report as suggestive. Negative (lift CI includes 0, or false approx unrelated-content) refutes H1: a false aside does not selectively corrupt the unrelated attribute.

Experiment 3 (PRIMARY-behavioral, H1 -- dose-response on plausibility and relatedness): Test that writeback error scales with a_false plausibility and r_A-r_B relatedness -- the signature that separates targeted writeback from generic distraction, which predicts NO relatedness dependence. Data: eligible set crossed over a_false plausibility bins (prior likelihood / type-match) and r_A-r_B relatedness (relation-embedding similarity, same- vs cross-domain). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Decisive metric (first): regression coefficients of writeback error on plausibility and on relatedness, with CIs, in the same mixed model (length/overlap/surprisal/popularity covariates); secondary, interaction with subject popularity. Convincing: both coefficients CI-exclude 0 with monotone per-bin curves, larger error for low-popularity subjects. Indecision band: exactly one coefficient CI-excludes 0 -- partial dose-response; report which factor drives it (a significant relatedness slope specifically rules out generic distraction). Negative (neither significant) refutes the gradable-scaling clause of H1.

Experiment 4 (SECONDARY-representation, H2 -- probe evidence that the false attribute enters the subject representation; suggestive, not decisive): Test that a_false becomes decodable in the subject-token residual stream even though A was never queried, and that the correct-b signal weakens. Data: eligible set across the four conditions. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a logistic-regression probe (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null) to decode a_false from the subject-token residual at each layer, comparing false- vs true- vs no-presupposition vs unrelated-content. Decisive metric (first): peak-layer AUROC for detecting a_false in the subject representation under false-presupposition, its cosine alignment with a_false's unembedding, and the gap over the true-presupposition run; secondary, drop in a decodable-b signal at the query position. Convincing: a_false AUROC >= 0.75 (above the true-presupposition run) with unembedding alignment above a random-direction null, and a measurable b-signal drop. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.75 -- weak/partial writeback signal. Per the causal-primacy rule, probe results are reported as suggestive only and never as standalone evidence of writeback; Experiment 5 is the decisive test. Negative (AUROC <= 0.60, no b-signal drop) undercuts H2's representational claim.

Experiment 5 (SECONDARY-causal, H2/H3 -- THE decisive causal test: early attention writes back the false attribute): Test that early subject-position attention over the a_false tokens is the injection route. This experiment, not the probe, is the decisive evidence for writeback. Data: writeback-error items. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) identify early subject-position heads attending to the presupposed-attribute tokens and ablate that attention; (b) activation-patch the subject-token residual from a no-presupposition run into a false-presupposition run and measure recovery of b; (c) reverse control -- inject the a_false direction into a no-presupposition run to induce B errors on demand. Systems compared: presupposition-attention ablation vs random-head ablation vs no-presupposition patch vs random-position patch. Decisive metric (first): writeback-error reduction from presupposition-attention ablation, net of random-head ablation. Convincing (conservative, all three must hold): ablation cuts writeback error >= 50% relative, no-presupposition patch recovers b >= 25 points net, AND reverse injection induces errors >= 25 points; random controls < 5 points. Indecision band: ablation reduction 20-50% relative, or only two of the three convergent signals hold -- attention is one route among several; report as partial causal support. Negative (ablation approx random, or patch/injection null) refutes H2's early-attention mechanism regardless of the probe result.

Experiment 6 (SECONDARY-causal, H3 -- suppression restores unrelated-attribute recall without editing any fact): Test that subtracting the writeback direction fixes B cleanly. Data: eligible set, item-disjoint train/test; steering vector = mean subject-token difference (false-presupposition writeback-error minus matched true-presupposition states), seeds {0,1,2}, rank<=4, subtracted at the identified layers. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the subtracted direction. Systems compared: writeback subtraction, presupposition-attention ablation (Exp 5a), ROME edit (expected not to help -- no stored fact is wrong), FAITH false-premise-head constraint, random-direction control. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = B-recovery rate divided by accuracy drop on true-presupposition items (over-correction control); secondary, accuracy on 200 unrelated no-presupposition facts, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: recovery >= 30% with < 3-point drop on true-presupposition items and on the 200 facts, beating ROME and FAITH. Indecision band: recovery 15-30% or collateral 3-6 points -- partial; report parity. Necessity note: Exp 5's ablation/patching is the decisive existence proof of the writeback route; Exp 6's steering is an auxiliary practicality test of a portable fix and is not required for the causal claim. Negative (no better than random, or harms true-presupposition cases) refutes the practical clause of H3.

Experiment 7 (PRIMARY-behavioral + SECONDARY, H1/H3 -- transfer, architecture generality, and prevalence): Test generality across relation pairs, subject types, and models, and report how prevalent the effect is. Data: eligible items partitioned by relation pair; suppression vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out relation pairs. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 2-6, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): replication of the writeback lift (Exp 2) per model, and cross-relation-pair B-recovery relative to within-pair; secondary, absolute writeback error rate per model to quantify prevalence. Convincing: lift replicates (CI excludes 0) in >= 2 of 3 models AND cross-pair recovery >= 50% of within-pair. Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-pair 30-50% -- model/relation-specific. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines the phenomenon to one model. Report whether larger models show lower writeback error and the mean per-model prevalence, so readers can judge real-world frequency.

Experiment 8 (PRIMARY-behavioral, H1 -- elevated-stakes domain transfer): Test whether presupposition writeback produces higher-stakes cross-attribute errors, making the practitioner consequence concrete. Data: constructed from a curated safe subset of clinical facts -- a false aside about a drug's route-of-administration while asking its correct indication; ~400 items, restricted to publicly documented, non-actionable facts, with the same four conditions and matching controls as Exp 1. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; replicate Experiments 2-3. Decisive metric (first): writeback error-rate lift in the clinical setting versus the general-knowledge lift. Convincing: clinical lift CI excludes 0 and is at least as large as the general lift. Indecision band: clinical lift 2-6 points -- present but modest; frame the elevated-stakes claim cautiously. Negative (no clinical lift) bounds the practical safety claim to general knowledge.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The main alternative account is generic distraction / attentional load rather than attribute-specific writeback. This is pre-registered and attacked three ways: the matched true-presupposition baseline (Exp 2), an unrelated-content aside of equal length (Exp 2), and the relatedness dose-response (Exp 3), which a generic-distraction account predicts to be flat. If the false-vs-unrelated-content contrast is null or relatedness has no slope, we report the phenomenon as unsupported.

The true-presupposition control may not perfectly match the false one (a_false could be rarer/higher-surprisal than a_true); we match token length, draw a_false from the same relation and type as a_true, include lexical overlap and surprisal as regression covariates, and report the fraction of pairs judged semantically parallel.

The writeback signal and correct-b recall may be entangled, so probe AUROC alone cannot establish writeback; per the causal-primacy rule the patching/ablation/reverse-injection tests (Exp 5) are treated as decisive and probes (Exp 4) as suggestive only.

Suppression (Exp 6) could over-correct when the presupposition is legitimately relevant, or degrade fluency; the true-presupposition and unrelated-fact specificity controls are central, utility may be capped, and the steering fix is auxiliary to the causal claim.

Writeback errors may be rare relative to genuine ignorance, limiting downstream harm; the paired within-subject design maximizes power, Exp 7 reports absolute prevalence per model, and a modest but significant lift is still scientifically informative even if practically bounded.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if writeback is relation-pair-specific (tested in Exp 7), limiting practical generality though still informative about mechanism.

Multi-token B answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage, and relation asymmetry and subject popularity are handled as covariates/random effects in the mixed model.
Findings on 6-8B open models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget; we scope claims to the tested models and report scale trends across the three.

Name: hindsight_contamination
Title: Cursed by Its Own Knowledge: A Hindsight-Bias Signal That Contaminates LLM Self-Assessment of What It Would Have Known
Short Hypothesis: Primary claim (operational, one falsifiable sentence): once the answer to a factual question is present in an LLM's context, the model's counterfactual self-estimate is contaminated — for facts it demonstrably does NOT store, revealing the answer inflates its rated 'would I have known this without being told?' / 'how foreseeable was this?' judgment relative to a matched outcome-blind condition, and this inflation SCALES WITH the revealed answer's plausibility (the human hindsight signature), distinguishing genuine contamination from uniform prompt compliance or rational updating. We keep three counterfactual targets distinct — 'would I have answered correctly?', 'was the answer foreseeable?', and 'would I have known the fact?' — and measure them separately (replacing the stronger 'unable to represent the answer-naive state' framing with these operational proxies). Secondary predictions: (a) an 'outcome-knowledge' signal imprinted by the revealed answer is decodable and separable from the model's genuine answer-naive knowledge signal; (b) it causally drives the inflated estimate; (c) suppressing it restores calibrated self-assessment (correctly saying it would NOT have known facts it does not store) without lowering confidence on genuinely-known facts. We claim restoration of calibration, not universal bias suppression.
Related Work: Human cognitive science robustly establishes hindsight bias and the curse of knowledge: knowing an outcome inflates judged prior-likelihood and impairs perspective-taking toward a less-informed self/other (Curse of Knowledge in false-belief reasoning, 2014; Rational Account of Anchor Effects in Hindsight Bias, 2021, which ties the effect to outcome plausibility; false-belief/curse-of-knowledge developmental work, 2021). In LLMs, knowledge-conflict and fact-vs-counterfactual competition work (Ortu et al. 2024 Competition of Mechanisms; reproductions 2025; Fakepedia) studies how a context-provided answer competes with parametric recall for the *object-level output*, and self-knowledge/answerability probes (Do I Know This Entity 2024; in-advance-correctness directions 2025) estimate whether the model knows a fact. Crucially, none study the *metacognitive/counterfactual* judgment: whether revealing the answer contaminates the model's estimate of what it *would have* known or how foreseeable the answer was, none test the human hindsight-bias signatures (inflation scaling with answer plausibility; failure of the answer-naive-self perspective), and none isolate an outcome-knowledge contamination signal separable from genuine knowledge. This is orthogonal to all my prior proposals, which concern object-level retrieval/expression rather than contaminated self-assessment, and to competition-of-mechanisms work, which concerns the output token rather than a counterfactual metacognitive estimate. Primary novelty anchor: prior work studies whether provided answers bias judgments of EXTERNAL outputs or whether a model knows a fact; our target is a different metacognitive object — the counterfactual self-estimate of what the model WOULD have known — plus the plausibility-scaling hindsight law and a separable, causally-testable outcome-knowledge signal, not reducible to ordinary answer contamination or prompt compliance.
Abstract: User-facing consequence first: an LLM shown an answer may then over-claim it 'would have known' a fact it actually does not store — a human-like hindsight bias that corrupts self-knowledge, not just answers, and undermines any setting that relies on the model to report uncertainty, explain its ignorance, or justify confidence (tool-use decisions, refusal, calibration). Humans who learn an outcome cannot un-know it: they overestimate how predictable it was and how likely they (or a less-informed other) would have guessed it—the hindsight bias and curse of knowledge. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous, mechanistically-localizable metacognitive contamination. When an LLM is shown the answer to a factual question and then asked to judge, from an answer-naive standpoint, whether it would have known the answer or how obvious the answer is, does the revealed answer inflate that judgment beyond the model's genuine knowledge? We first document the behavior: for facts we can independently verify the model does or does not store (via clean, answer-naive querying), we compare the model's self-estimated 'would-I-have-known' / foreseeability judgment in an outcome-revealed condition versus an outcome-blind condition, testing for systematic overestimation, and for the human signature that inflation scales with the revealed answer's plausibility. We then test a Location + Causal Intervention hypothesis: an 'outcome-knowledge' signal imprinted by the revealed answer is linearly decodable, is separable (via residualization) from the model's genuine answer-naive knowledge signal, and causally drives the inflated self-estimate. Activation patching from an outcome-blind run, and suppression of the outcome-knowledge direction, should restore calibrated self-assessment (the model correctly says it would NOT have known facts it does not store) with high specificity—preserving accurate self-assessment on facts it genuinely knows—whereas a 'judge as if you hadn't seen the answer' re-prompt does not. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA/T-REx-derived facts, evaluating overestimation prevalence, plausibility dose-response, signal separability, causal recovery, and specificity. This ties directly to trust calibration and safety/honesty. H1 (plausibility-scaled would-have-known inflation on UNKNOWN facts) is primary; the outcome-knowledge signal, its causal role, and the debiasing fix are secondary. Plausibility is manipulated while controlling revealed-answer length and frequency, and within-fact paired (revealed vs blind) comparisons are the primary measure to avoid absolute-calibration confounds.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — hindsight overestimation of would-have-known): Tests that revealing the answer inflates the model's answer-naive self-estimate, especially for facts it does not store, and that the inflation is genuine hindsight contamination (scales with answer plausibility) not uniform compliance. Data: PopQA (14,267), T-REx, EntityQuestions; per model split facts into a KNOWN set (reliably answered across paraphrases + content probe) and an UNKNOWN set (reliably failed); target ~800 UNKNOWN + ~800 KNOWN per model (capped; report coverage). Two conditions per fact: OUTCOME-REVEALED (answer shown, then 'Would you have known this without being told? 0-100' and 'How obvious/foreseeable is this? 0-100') and OUTCOME-BLIND (same self-estimate, answer withheld). Plausibility variant: revealed answer is the true (plausible) vs a less-plausible presented answer, matched for token length and lexical frequency so plausibility is not confounded by surface familiarity. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0; within-fact paired comparisons (revealed vs blind) as the primary measure. Systems compared: revealed vs blind estimates on the UNKNOWN set (where correct self-assessment is 'no'), with the KNOWN set as an appropriateness anchor; plausible vs less-plausible revealed answers. Decisive metric: would-have-known inflation = revealed-minus-blind estimate on the UNKNOWN set (points, 0-100); secondary: whether inflation grows with revealed-answer plausibility (distinguishing contamination from uniform compliance). Convincing: >=15-point inflation on UNKNOWN facts (>> the KNOWN-set change) that scales with plausibility, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: 5-15-point inflation, or no plausibility scaling -> effect weak or possibly uniform compliance, partial support. Negative (<5-point inflation, or equal for plausible/implausible) refutes hindsight contamination — the model is calibrated about its ignorance.

Experiment 2 (H2 — outcome-knowledge signal separable from genuine knowledge): Tests that an 'outcome-knowledge' signal imprinted by the revealed answer is decodable and separable from the model's genuine answer-naive knowledge signal. Data: OUTCOME-REVEALED vs OUTCOME-BLIND runs at the self-estimate position for the Exp-1 facts; residual stream cached across layers. Model: frozen; a per-layer L2-logistic probe targets the presence/plausibility of the revealed answer, trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds; residualized against a genuine-knowledge/self-knowledge probe (target = true stored/not-stored status); shuffle null. Systems compared: the outcome-knowledge probe before vs after residualizing out genuine knowledge; its prediction of inflated estimates on the UNKNOWN set. Decisive metric: per-layer AUROC of the outcome-knowledge signal predicting inflated UNKNOWN-set self-estimates, after residualizing out genuine knowledge; secondary: that the signal tracks revealed-answer presence/plausibility, not true stored status. Convincing: post-residualization AUROC >=0.72 and the signal tracks the revealed answer rather than stored status, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.60-0.72 -> signal entangled with genuine knowledge, partial. Negative (AUROC at shuffle after residualization) means there is no separable outcome-knowledge signal; the contamination-locus claim fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — the outcome-knowledge signal causally inflates the self-estimate): Tests causal override of the counterfactual self-estimate. Data: 300 UNKNOWN-set revealed/blind matched pairs per model, held out from Exp-2 probe training. Method: patch the self-estimate residual stream from an OUTCOME-BLIND run into an OUTCOME-REVEALED run; suppress the outcome-knowledge direction; inject it into an OUTCOME-BLIND run to induce inflation (dose-response with plausibility); a content control on object-level facts. Model: frozen; interventions at Exp-2 layers, dose swept {0.5,1,2,4}x, 3 seeds. Systems compared: patch-restore, suppression, injection-induce, content control, random-direction control. Decisive metric: estimate movement toward the calibrated answer-naive value from patch/suppression vs the random-direction control (points); secondary: induced inflation from injection with plausibility dose-response, and that the content control leaves object-level answers unchanged. Convincing: patch/suppression moves UNKNOWN-set estimates >=10 points toward calibrated and injection induces >=10 points of inflation over random-direction with dose-response, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: 4-10 points -> partial causal role. Negative (<4 points over control, or content control also moves estimates) means the signal is correlational, not the cause.

Experiment 4 (H3 — debiasing self-assessment with KNOWN-set specificity and generality): Tests that suppressing the outcome-knowledge direction restores calibrated self-assessment without suppressing confidence on genuinely-known facts, and generalizes. Data: held-out OUTCOME-REVEALED items (>=400 per model); specificity sets = KNOWN facts (high self-estimate is correct) and 200 unrelated object-level facts.
