Model: frozen; a low-rank outcome-knowledge steering vector fitted on a subset of relations and applied to held-out relations and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: outcome-knowledge subtraction vs a 'judge as if you had not seen the answer / take an uninformed model's perspective' re-prompt, chain-of-thought, and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: reduction in UNKNOWN-set would-have-known calibration error (estimate vs true stored status), reported jointly with the change in KNOWN-set estimates (must stay high) and object-level accuracy on the 200 unrelated facts; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% reduction in UNKNOWN-set calibration error with <=5-point drop in KNOWN-set estimates and <=2 pp object-level collateral, beating the re-prompt by >=15%, transferring across relations and models. Undecidable band: 20-40% reduction, or 5-10-point KNOWN-set drop -> capped utility. Negative (<=20% reduction, or KNOWN-set estimates collapse) means self-assessment cannot be debiased non-destructively.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The inflated would-have-known estimate could reflect the model rationally updating (once told the answer, it genuinely could produce it on a re-query) rather than a contaminated counterfactual judgment; the design targets the UNKNOWN set and explicitly asks for the answer-naive counterfactual, and the ground-truth knowledge status (Exp 1) is the anchor—claiming it would have known a fact it demonstrably fails on clean querying is the diagnostic error, but framing the counterfactual clearly is essential and prompt-sensitive.

LLMs might not exhibit the effect (they could be well-calibrated about their own ignorance, or comply uniformly with any revealed token); a null or uniform-compliance result would refute the transfer but is itself informative, and the plausibility dose-response (Exp 1) distinguishes genuine hindsight contamination from uniform compliance.
The outcome-knowledge and genuine-knowledge signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 3), not probe separability alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Debiasing could over-suppress—making the model underestimate its knowledge on KNOWN facts, or degrade fluency; the KNOWN-set specificity control (Exp 4) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
Establishing UNKNOWN status risks false negatives (the model may store a fact it fails to express); conservative multi-paraphrase + content-probe thresholds and reported coverage mitigate this.

Self-estimate elicitation (0-100 ratings) is prompt-sensitive and models may be poorly calibrated in absolute terms; we use within-fact paired comparisons (revealed vs blind) rather than absolute calibration as the primary measure, and report robustness across phrasings.
A single transferable debiasing vector may not exist if contamination is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: fragmentary_recall
Title: On the Tip of the Model's Tongue: Structured Partial Knowledge of Unproducible Answers in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM fails to produce a specific factual answer, it is not in a binary known/unknown state: like humans in a tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, it internally holds structured partial knowledge of the specific unproduced target - its semantic category, its first letter/subword, its length, and its lexical neighbors. We separate genuinely target-specific fragments from query-predictable ones: category and length may be partly implied by the relation/query, so we credit as evidence only decoding that exceeds a relation- and frequency-matched chance baseline on held-out entities, and we pre-register which attributes count as success versus leakage. The novelty over full-answer hidden-recovery work (e.g., Inside-Out) is that the claim is not that the whole answer is latent, but that MULTI-ATTRIBUTE, graded, correct partial knowledge exists, follows a human accessibility signature, and is separable from the scalar self-knowledge signal. We hypothesize this partial knowledge is (a) graded and correct at above-matched-chance rates such that only CORRECT fragments predict recognition/short-list success, (b) linearly decodable even though the full answer is not, and (c) carried by a representation separable (tested causally, not only by residual AUROC) from the scalar correctness/self-knowledge direction, such that constrained decoding conditioned on the decoded fragments recovers answers the model otherwise cannot produce without inflating fabrication on nonexistent-entity controls.
Related Work: Cognitive science establishes that in a TOT state humans reliably access correct fragments of an unrecallable target - first letter, syllable count, semantic features - and that feeling-of-knowing tracks the amount of CORRECT partial knowledge (Brown 1991/2011; Schwartz; the 2016 FoK-partial-knowledge study; 1975 decoding-failure account; 2008 multi-word-name study). In LLMs, prior interpretability work encodes only a SCALAR self-knowledge/correctness signal (No Answer Needed 2025; factual self-awareness directions 2025; LLMs Know More Than They Show 2024; answerability directions 2023; Do I Know This Entity 2024), and full-answer hidden-recoverability work (Inside-Out; Empty Shelves or Lost Keys) recovers the whole latent answer. The exact delta: scalar work predicts WHETHER the model will be right, not WHAT structured fragments of the specific unproduced target it holds; full-answer recovery is all-or-nothing, whereas we claim a multi-attribute, graded partial representation with a human accessibility signature and separability from the scalar axis - so it is not a repackaging of either. This is distinct from prior proposals (premature_lexicalization on committing to a wrong first token; familiarity_before_retrieval on a scalar coverage estimate): here the object is structured partial knowledge of the specific unproduced answer, and its assembly to recover hidden answers.
Abstract: Humans who cannot recall a word are often not simply ignorant of it: in a tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state they reliably retrieve correct fragments of the target - its first letter, its length, its semantic category - and feeling-of-knowing tracks how much correct partial knowledge they hold. We ask whether LLMs exhibit an analogous structured partial-knowledge state on failed factual queries. The phenomenon comes first: this reveals that 'the model does not know it' is too coarse a description of a latent knowledge state, with downstream value for abstention calibration, candidate generation for retrieval, and safer answer elicitation. Existing interpretability work encodes only a scalar 'will I be right' signal and treats failed recall as binary. We hypothesize instead that on failed queries the model holds graded, correct fragments of the specific unproduced target - decodable from intermediate activations even though the full answer is not, and carried by a representation separable from the scalar correctness direction. We credit only decoding above relation- and frequency-matched chance on held-out entities, and pre-register success-vs-leakage per attribute. We test three claims. (1) Fragmentary retrieval: linear probes recover partial attributes above matched chance, and their CORRECTNESS follows the human accessibility signature (only correct fragments predict recognition/short-list success). (2) Structure not scalar: the fragment directions are separable from the in-advance-correctness direction - tested causally via steering/ablation, not residual AUROC alone - so partial knowledge is multi-dimensional. (3) Assembly recovery: constrained decoding conditioned on decoded fragments (first letter + length + category) recovers correct answers the model otherwise fails to produce, with higher yield than free generation, temperature sampling, or a 'guess the first letter' re-prompt, while a pre-registered fabrication metric on nonexistent-entity controls bounds confident guessing. We report downstream utility (abstention/error reduction), not only recovery accuracy. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — Failed-recall dataset and fragmentary-retrieval decoding): Tests H2, that partial attributes of the specific unproduced target are linearly decodable even though the full answer is not. Data: constructed from PopQA (~14k), T-REx (LAMA subset ~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); for each model split into produced (correct free-generation) and failed (wrong/refused) sets matched by relation, answer frequency, and answer length; target 3,000 failed items with unambiguous partial attributes (semantic category, first letter/subword, length bucket, lexical neighbors); report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Trainable: linear probes on subject-token/last-token residual stream per attribute, L2-regularized, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV, held-out entities, label-shuffle control. Systems compared: probe accuracy on the failed set vs frequency/category-matched chance vs a produced-set upper bound. Decisive metric (before data), first: per-attribute decoding accuracy above matched chance on the failed set, and the fraction of failed items with >=1 correct decodable fragment. Convincing = first-letter and category probes exceed matched chance by >=15pp (CI excluding 0) and >=50% of failed items carry >=1 correct fragment. Negative = probes within 3pp of chance (no partial knowledge; H2 fails). Indecision band 3-15pp above chance: report weak, graded partial knowledge.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Human accessibility-signature test): Tests H1, that fragments are CORRECT at rates tracking the human accessibility signature (correct partial knowledge predicts recognition/short-list success; incorrect fragments do not). Data: the Exp 1 failed items. Model: same three frozen. Systems compared: (a) recognition test -- present a short list (true answer + distractors) and measure recognition; correlate recognition success with the number of CORRECT decoded fragments vs the number of INCORRECT fragments; (b) verbalized-fragment test -- prompt the model to guess first letter/category/length of the answer it could not produce, correlate verbalized-fragment correctness with probe-decoded-fragment correctness. Decisive metric (before data), first: increase in recognition accuracy per additional correct decoded fragment (logistic slope), and the contrast that incorrect fragments confer no such benefit. Convincing = positive slope for correct fragments (CI excluding 0) AND near-zero slope for incorrect fragments, plus verbalized-vs-probe fragment agreement above chance (kappa >=0.2). Negative = correct and incorrect fragments confer equal recognition benefit (fragments not diagnostic; H1's accessibility signature fails). Indecision band correct-fragment slope CI including 0 but point estimate positive: report weak accessibility signature.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Structure-vs-scalar dissociation): Tests the first half of H3, that partial-attribute directions are separable from the scalar correctness/self-knowledge signal. Data: Exp 1 activations. Model: same three frozen; recover the scalar in-advance-correctness/self-knowledge direction following existing methods (No-Answer-Needed / factual-self-awareness / Do-I-Know-This-Entity); residualize each partial-attribute probe on this scalar signal. Systems compared: partial-attribute decodability before vs after removing the scalar signal. Decisive metric (before data), first: residual per-attribute AUROC after removing the scalar direction. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 for >=2 attributes (partial knowledge is multi-dimensional, not one confidence axis). Negative = residual AUROC <=0.55 for all attributes (partial knowledge collapses to the scalar signal; H3's structure claim fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report a partial (graded) dissociation, weakening the strong 'structured' claim.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal steering/ablation of fragment directions): Tests that the decoded fragments are causal handles, supporting H3's assembly claim. Data: failed items with >=1 correct decodable fragment (from Exp 1), 1,000 held-out. Model: same three frozen; activation edits at the probe layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) amplify decoded fragment directions (first-letter, category) and measure the correct answer's probability; (b) reverse control ablating a fragment direction and confirming its decodability and recognition benefit drop; (c) content control (unrelated answers unchanged); random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): change in correct-answer log-probability / rank under fragment amplification vs random control. Convincing = correct-answer log-prob rises by >=0.5 nats (or rank improves by >=5 positions) over random control at a dose with perplexity within 5%, and ablation drops fragment decodability by >=15pp. Negative = <=0.1 nat change (fragments not causal). Indecision band 0.1-0.5 nats: partial causal support.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Assembly-recovery intervention): Tests the second half of H3, that assembling decoded fragments recovers answers the model otherwise cannot produce. Data: 1,000 held-out failed items; plus 300 nonexistent-entity controls (to measure fabrication). Model: same three frozen; a constrained-decoding pipeline that decodes first letter/subword + length + category from the failed-recall activations and constrains generation to matching answers over the model's own candidate distribution. Systems compared: constrained-assembly vs free generation, temperature/beam sampling, a 'guess the first letter then answer' re-prompt, and a random-constraint control. Decisive metric (before data), first: recovery rate of correct answers on held-out failed items MINUS false-answer rate on nonexistent-entity controls (recovered-per-unit-fabrication). Convincing = assembly recovers >=15pp more correct answers than the best baseline while false-answer rate on nonexistent controls rises <=5pp. Negative = <=3pp recovery gain, or fabrication rises >=15pp (assembly just induces confident guessing). Indecision band 3-15pp recovery with fabrication 5-15pp: report a capped-utility recovery.

Experiment 6 (H2/H3 — Cross-relation and cross-model transfer): Tests whether probes and the assembly pipeline generalize rather than being relation-specific. Data: probes/directions fit on a subset of relations (Exp 1) applied unchanged to held-out relations (800 failed items). Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred probes/pipeline vs in-relation-refit vs chance/random-constraint. Decisive metric (before data): transferred fragment-decoding accuracy above chance and transferred assembly-recovery as a fraction of in-relation-refit. Convincing = transferred fragment decoding >=10pp above chance AND assembly transfer >=60% of in-relation on >=2 models. Negative = transferred decoding <=3pp above chance (relation-specific encoding; the assembly pipeline does not generalize). Indecision band 3-10pp / 20-60%: partial transfer. Report Spearman rho between model scale and correct-fragments-per-failed-item (N=3 caveat).

Experiment 7 (H1 — Source and graded 'closeness-to-production' analysis): Tests H1's graded prediction, that failed items with more correct fragments are closer to production. Data: all Exp 1 failed items with per-item features (answer frequency, entity popularity, relation hops). Model: same three frozen. Systems compared: regression of per-item fragment correctness on frequency/popularity/hops; and a test that fragment count predicts 'closeness' (lower answer rank, higher recognition). Decisive metric (before data): correlation between number of correct fragments and closeness-to-production (answer rank / recognition), controlling for frequency. Convincing = correct-fragment count predicts lower answer rank and higher recognition with CI excluding 0, above frequency alone (Delta R^2 >=0.05). Negative = no residual predictive value (Delta R^2 <=0.01) (partial knowledge is not graded toward production; the weak-trace account fails). Indecision band 0.01-0.05: report a weak graded effect.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Above-chance fragment decoding could reflect probe exploitation of query-side correlations (e.g., relation type predicts category) rather than genuine partial knowledge of the specific target; frequency/category-matched chance baselines, held-out entities, subject-token vs query-token probe comparisons, and the correctness-specific accessibility signature (Exp 3, where only *correct* fragments confer recognition benefit) are the decisive controls.

Partial knowledge may collapse to the existing scalar self-knowledge signal; the residualization dissociation (Exp 4) is the key test, and a partial (graded) dissociation would weaken the strong 'structured' claim while remaining informative.

Assembly recovery could induce confident fabrication on genuinely-unknown items; nonexistent-entity controls and false-answer-rate specificity metrics (Exp 6) are essential and may cap practical utility.

First-letter/length fragments depend on tokenization and are noisiest for heavily subword-fragmented multi-token names; primary analysis restricts to answers with clean first-subword/length attributes and reports coverage.
The human accessibility parallel is motivational, not identity; recognition and verbalized-fragment tests are LLM-native operationalizations and are reported on their own terms.
Fragment directions may not transfer across relations if partial-knowledge encoding is relation-specific, limiting the generality of the assembly pipeline though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: retrieval_competition
Title: Retrieval Competition: How Interference Between Co-Activated Candidates Determines Whether Stored Knowledge Reaches the Answer
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM processes a factual query, it co-activates a *set* of competing candidate answers in the residual stream, and the final answer is decided by a winner-take-all competition whose outcome is largely insensitive to correctness. We hypothesize that (1) the geometry of this candidate set — number of competitors and the margin between the top competitor and the correct answer — is linearly readable at intermediate layers and predicts *which failure mode* occurs (interference-driven wrong answer vs. genuine ignorance), and (2) knowledge that is stored but not expressed typically loses this competition to a better-primed distractor, such that reweighting the competition (suppressing the winning distractor's direction) recovers the correct answer more selectively than amplifying the correct fact. Primary falsifiable claim (one sentence): candidate-set geometry - the number of viable competitors and the correct-vs-top-distractor margin - is linearly readable at intermediate layers and predicts whether a factual failure is interference-driven or ignorance-driven, a statistic prior competitor-suppression work (e.g. Forbidden Facts, logit-difference steering) never measured. We frame 'winner-take-all' as an empirical hypothesis about answer selection, not a universal mechanism, and treat selective distractor-suppression recovery as a secondary claim.
Related Work: A large literature shows internal states carry a knowledge/recall-strength signal (KEEN, 2024; SAPLMA, 2023; in-advance correctness probes, 2025; hallucination-risk probes, 2024; SCIURus shows uncertainty and factuality share circuits, 2025). Critically, 'LLMs Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know' (2025) shows associated hallucinations and true facts share the same recall geometry, implying internal signals track *retrieval activity* not *truth*. Inside-Out (2025) documents a 40% internal-vs-external hidden-knowledge gap. Knowledge-editing work (ROME, MEMIT) localizes facts to MLPs. None of these characterize retrieval as a *competition among multiple co-activated candidates* whose resolution — not storage — determines the answer, nor do they use the competitor-set geometry to predict failure *type* or to recover hidden knowledge by distractor suppression. My prior proposals concern single-fact routing gates and multiple format-bound copies of the *same* fact; this proposal is orthogonal: it concerns interference between *different* candidate facts. Delta in one line: prior work shows competition and suppresses specific answers (Forbidden Facts) or steers logit differences, but does not quantify competitor-set geometry, use it to classify failure TYPE, or recover out-competed knowledge by distractor subtraction; those are our additions. Operational definitions: a 'viable competitor' is an answer-type-consistent candidate above a support threshold in the tuned-lens readout; an 'interference-driven' failure = gold internally present while a specific wrong entity dominates; 'ignorance' = gold near-zero support at all layers; a 'recovered answer' = gold becomes greedy top-1 post-intervention. Downstream, the interference-vs-ignorance label enables a concrete action: route interference cases to distractor-suppression or retrieval and abstain on ignorance cases.
Abstract: Large language models often store a fact yet answer with a different, confidently wrong one. We propose that this is a symptom of retrieval as competition: a factual query co-activates a set of candidate answers in the residual stream, and the model resolves this set in a winner-take-all manner that is largely blind to correctness. Under this view, a stored fact fails to surface not because it is absent or ungated, but because it loses to a better-primed distractor (e.g., a more frequent entity, a lexically closer neighbor, or a co-occurring associate). We develop a method to read out the competitor set from intermediate layers by projecting the residual stream through the unembedding and identifying entity-typed candidates, then measuring competition geometry: the number of viable competitors and the logit margin between the top distractor and the correct answer. We test three claims: (1) competition geometry is linearly decodable and predicts whether a given failure is interference-driven (a specific distractor dominates) or genuine ignorance (the correct answer has near-zero internal support), distinguishing failure types that current confidence probes conflate; (2) hidden-knowledge failures (correct answer present internally but not generated) are disproportionately interference-driven; and (3) a targeted intervention that subtracts the winning distractor's direction recovers correct answers with higher specificity and less collateral damage than amplifying the correct-answer direction or ROME editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions, evaluating failure-type classification AUROC, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency. Confirming these claims reframes knowledge failures as resolution failures and yields a cheap, non-destructive way to surface out-competed knowledge. These labeling rules and thresholds are fixed in advance to avoid post-hoc taxonomy fitting, and we report an operational risk-coverage metric (net harmful-error reduction at matched coverage), not only AUROC, so the result speaks to selective-prediction practice and not only to diagnostics.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - a readable competitor set exists): Tests that factual queries co-activate a readable set of answer-type-consistent candidates with measurable competition geometry. Data: PopQA (14,282 questions, 16 relations), T-REx/LAMA (~34k, 41 relations), EntityQuestions (24 relations, ~176k); sample 10,000 single-token-first-entity facts stratified by relation and popularity, fewer than the pool because we restrict to single-token-first entities for clean vocabulary readout and cache per-layer projections. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; project the last-token residual at each layer through a tuned-lens (trained once, then frozen) restricted to a precomputed answer-type entity vocabulary per relation; seed 0. Systems compared: tuned-lens vs. raw logit-lens readout; the top-k competitor set vs. a shuffled-vocabulary null. Decisive metric: coverage = fraction of queries whose gold or a plausible distractor appears in the top-k answer-type set above a support threshold (first); supporting: number of viable competitors, top1-to-gold logit margin, candidate-distribution entropy, and the overtake layer. Convincing: >=70% coverage with the tuned-lens and geometry features that are non-degenerate (median >=2 competitors). Undecidable band: coverage 50-70% means readout is noisy - restrict later analyses to covered facts and report the restriction. Negative: <50% coverage, or no better than the shuffled-vocabulary null, means the competitor-set construct is not readable, blocking H2/H3.

Experiment 2 (H2 - competition geometry predicts which failure mode): Tests that geometry features separate interference-driven wrong answers from genuine ignorance. Data: failures from Experiment 1, hand-verifiable-labeled by rule into (a) interference (a specific wrong entity has high internal support and the gold answer is also internally present) vs (b) ignorance (gold has near-zero support at all layers); target 4,000 labeled failures. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; a trainable linear probe on the competition-geometry features predicts failure type, seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle control. Systems compared: geometry probe vs. a KEEN-style single-scalar confidence/correctness probe vs. chance. Decisive metric: AUROC of the geometry probe distinguishing interference from ignorance (first); supporting: the confidence-probe AUROC it must beat, and calibration. Convincing: geometry-probe AUROC >=0.75 and >=0.07 above the confidence probe - geometry carries failure-mode information a scalar confidence signal conflates. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.60-0.75 or within 0.07 of the confidence baseline means geometry helps but does not cleanly separate the modes - report a graded taxonomy. Negative: AUROC <=0.60 or no gain over the confidence probe falsifies the predictiveness half of H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - hidden knowledge loses to a better-primed distractor): Tests that stored-but-unexpressed facts are disproportionately interference-driven. Data: hidden-knowledge failures identified with an internal-vs-external gap protocol (gold internally supported but not generated) from Experiment 1's pool; target 2,500 hidden failures plus a matched baseline-failure set. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify each hidden failure as interference vs. ignorance using Experiment 2 labels; regress distractor properties (frequency, lexical similarity, subject co-occurrence) on winning. Systems compared: hidden failures vs. matched non-hidden failures (chi-square on interference rate); distractor-property regression vs. intercept-only. Decisive metric: difference in interference-driven proportion between hidden and baseline failures (first); supporting: regression coefficients on distractor frequency/similarity/co-occurrence. Convincing: hidden failures are interference-driven at a rate >=15 percentage points above baseline (chi-square p<0.001) and winning distractors are reliably higher-frequency/more-primed. Undecidable band: a 5-15 point gap is a real but modest association - report hidden knowledge as often, not usually, interference-driven, softening H3. Negative: <5 point gap means hidden failures are not distinctively competition-driven, falsifying the H3 mechanism.

Experiment 4 (H3 - suppressing the distractor beats amplifying the fact): Tests that reweighting the competition recovers hidden facts more selectively than boosting the correct direction or editing. Data: interference-driven hidden facts from Experiment 3, held out, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME comparator; at the competition layers, project out the winning distractor's unembedding-aligned direction, vs. (a) adding the gold-answer direction, (b) a ROME edit, (c) a random-direction control; scale swept, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: distractor-suppression vs. correct-amplification (matched to an equal logit shift) vs. second-best-distractor suppression vs. equal-norm random subtraction vs. contrastive decoding vs. logit-lens subtraction vs. ROME. Decisive metric: recovered-facts-per-unit-collateral = recovery rate / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated facts (first); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity change. Convincing: distractor-suppression recovers >=40% with <5% unrelated-accuracy drop and beats correct-amplification on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage over amplification means suppression is comparable, not clearly more selective - report parity. Negative: suppression recovered-per-collateral <=amplification, or recovery <20%, falsifies the selective-reweighting half of H3.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 - competition geometry is causal, not correlational): Tests that manipulating distractor support changes outcomes as the geometry predicts. Data: 1,000 correctly-answered facts (to induce errors) and 1,000 interference failures (to fix), from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; activation-patch the distractor's supporting subject/context signal into correct runs to induce interference errors on demand, and remove distractor support from failing runs; random-direction control. Systems compared: induced-error rate under distractor injection vs. random injection; fix rate under distractor removal vs. random removal. Decisive metric: induced-error rate from injecting distractor support (first); supporting: fix rate from removing it. Convincing: distractor injection induces errors in >=30% of correct cases (vs <=5% random) and removal fixes >=30% of failures - competition geometry is causally tied to the outcome. Undecidable band: 10-30% induced-error rate is weak causal control - report competition as contributory but not decisive. Negative: <10%, near the random control, means geometry is only correlational, undercutting H1/H2's causal reading.

Experiment 6 (H2 - geometry improves selective prediction): Tests that geometry features let the model abstain on ignorance while attempting recovery on interference. Data: the mixed failure set from Experiments 2-3 (target 6,000 failures) plus correct answers, held-out split. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; a selective-prediction policy over geometry features vs. a confidence-probe policy, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: geometry-based abstention+recovery vs. confidence-threshold abstention. Decisive metric: area under the risk-coverage curve (first, lower risk at equal coverage is better); supporting: recovery-attempt precision on interference cases. Convincing: geometry policy lowers risk at matched coverage by >=15% relative to the confidence baseline. Undecidable band: 5-15% improvement is a modest gain - report as incremental. Negative: <5% improvement means geometry adds no selective-prediction value beyond confidence.

Experiment 7 (H1-H3 generality - architecture-general competition): Tests that competitor sets, failure-mode prediction, and the hidden-knowledge link hold beyond one model. Data: reuse the Experiment 1 sampling (10,000 facts) per model. Model: repeat Experiments 1-4 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds/hyperparameters. Systems compared: Llama-3-8B vs. GPT-J-6B vs. Qwen2.5-7B on each decisive metric. Decisive metric: sign-consistency of the Experiment 2 AUROC gain, Experiment 3 interference-gap, and Experiment 4 suppression advantage across models (first); supporting: per-model coverage. Convincing: all three show geometry-probe AUROC >=0.70, a positive interference-gap, and a suppression advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: reversal in the majority means competition dynamics are model-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Vocabulary projection of the residual stream is noisy and can produce spurious 'candidates'; mitigated by tuned-lens, answer-type filtering, and causal patching validation rather than relying on logit-lens alone.
The interference-vs-ignorance dichotomy may be a continuum; a graded result would weaken the clean taxonomy but remain informative, and we report continuous competition metrics.

Distractor suppression could introduce new errors or degrade fluency if the subtracted direction overlaps with useful representations; strict specificity and perplexity controls are included and the intervention may prove impractical even if the analysis holds.
Correct answers may share directions with distractors (entity superposition), making clean subtraction impossible for some facts, limiting recovery coverage.
Multi-token entity answers complicate single-token logit-lens readout; we restrict primary analysis to single-token-first entities and report coverage.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: inheritance_failure
Title: Does a Canary Have Skin? Property-Inheritance Failures Are Caused by a Missing Category-Binding Operation in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM must decide whether a subordinate instance has a property that is stored at a superordinate category (e.g. 'does a canary have skin?', where 'has skin' is owned by 'animal'), it can fail EVEN when it independently stores both atomic facts (canary is-a animal; animals have skin). Our one crisp causal claim: such inheritance failures are caused by a missing category-binding operation - the property-owning category is present in the residual stream but is not composed into the instance representation - NOT by missing fact storage and NOT by similarity-based retrieval. As a signature we expect direct-query accuracy to fall with taxonomic distance to the property-owning category even after both atomic facts are verified stored; the decisive test is causal: activation-patching the category-binding from a same-instance run flips failures to successes, while patching semantically-similar-but-non-owning or norm-matched unrelated categories does not.
Related Work: A large literature dissociates recall from reasoning by layer/head/direction (Disentangling Recall and Reasoning 2025; Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning 2025; LiReFs 2025) and shows conceptual complexity is encoded at increasing depth (Concept Depth 2024; Hierarchical Deconstruction / DepthQA 2024). Clinical dissociation work (Knowledge-Reasoning Dissociation in Clinical NLI 2025) shows models possess facts but cannot compose them. The closest specific prior work is COMPS (Misra et al. 2023), which tests minimal-pair property inheritance and shows LMs favor properties on the more-similar of two concepts - i.e. it documents that inheritance is imperfect and similarity-driven, purely behaviorally. Our delta is explicitly mechanistic, not behavioral: (a) we hold atomic-fact storage FIXED via per-tuple verification, so a failure cannot be 'the model never learned it', which COMPS does not control; (b) we predict and causally localize a specific missing operation - a category-to-instance binding - via activation patching with matched semantic-similarity and norm-matched-unrelated controls, distinguishing a composition failure from COMPS's similarity account; (c) we ask whether the same binding direction transfers across taxonomic subtrees, testing whether it is a general composition operation rather than a per-pair statistic. NOVELTY LOCATION: the phenomenon (graded, distance-dependent inheritance failure) is largely KNOWN (Collins-Quillian 1969; COMPS 2023) and we claim only a cleaner storage-controlled measurement of it; the novelty is in the MECHANISM (a causally-isolated missing category-binding operation) and, secondarily, in the SETTING (storage-verified native taxonomic tuples with matched causal controls). We do not claim the behavior itself is new. This also differs from our prior proposals: consistency_seams (edit-time ripple), strategy_arbitration (retrieve-vs-assemble routing for two-hop chains), property_collapse (sibling-relation subspace confusion).
Abstract: Since Collins and Quillian (1969), conceptual knowledge has been modeled as a hierarchy where properties are stored economically at their most general applicable category and inherited by instances, and COMPS (2023) showed LMs inherit properties imperfectly and similarity-driven. We go beyond documenting this behavior and test its cause. Holding atomic-fact storage fixed - we keep only tuples where the model independently answers and internally encodes both the membership fact (instance is-a category) and the property fact (category has property) - we ask a single falsifiable question about how LLMs organize knowledge: are the remaining inheritance failures caused by a missing category-binding operation (the property-owning category is decodable in the residual stream but not composed into the instance representation), rather than by missing facts or by similarity-based retrieval? We predict (i) a behavioral signature: direct-query accuracy on inherited properties falls with taxonomic distance even on storage-verified tuples, and (ii, decisive) a causal signature: activation-patching the category-binding from a same-instance category-primed run flips failures to correct, whereas patching a semantically-similar non-owning category or a norm-matched unrelated category does not. The claim is falsified if storage-verified failures do not grade with distance, if the owning category is genuinely absent (not just uncomposed) on failures, or if the binding patch is no better than similarity/norm-matched controls. So what: if it holds, LM conceptual knowledge is stored compositionally and inheritance failures are a repairable binding step, not gaps in stored facts - so knowledge editors like ROME/MEMIT should target the binding, not re-write atomic facts, and a single reusable binding direction (which we test for cross-subtree and out-of-distribution transfer) would offer a cheap, general fix for a whole class of composition failures. This matters to practitioners because inherited/implied facts that a model 'knows' but fails to apply are a concrete reliability failure in retrieval and QA, and a mechanism-level fix is more auditable than fact-by-fact patching. We evaluate on GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and the Pythia suite, with one primary causal experiment and clearly-marked auxiliary generality checks.
Experiments: PRIMARY H1 precondition - Experiment 1 (storage-verified, curator-validated taxonomic probe): Establish the precondition that both atomic facts an inheritance query depends on are individually stored, and validate that the taxonomy labels are trustworthy, so later failures cannot be dismissed as missing knowledge or noisy ontology. Operational ownership criterion (stated before the main claim): a property is 'owned' by category C for instance I iff (a) the ConceptNet assertion HasA/CapableOf/HasProperty attaches the property to C, (b) C lies on I's WordNet hypernym path, and (c) NO node strictly between I and C carries the same assertion (nearest-owner uniqueness). Data: enumerate ~5,000 (instance, property, owning-category, distance in is-a hops 1-4) tuples from WordNet 3.0 (NLTK) x ConceptNet 5.7; filter by the ownership criterion to ~1,200 tuples. Curated validation: the user/annotators hand-check a random 150-tuple sample for ownership correctness; require >=85% agreement, and report the disagreement rate as a construct-validity bound. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; template 'Does a {instance} have {property}? Answer yes or no.' plus 3 paraphrases. Eligibility: keep tuples where BOTH atomic facts (membership query, property-at-category query) are answered correctly across >=3/4 templates AND are decodable by a logistic-regression content probe (seeds {0,1,2}, L2, 5-fold, label-shuffle null) from the last-token residual. Decisive metric: size and per-distance coverage of this 'inheritance-eligible' set. Convincing: >=400 eligible tuples with >=60 per distance and validation agreement >=85%. Indecision band: 250-400 eligible - under-powered. Below 250, or validation <85%, H1 is not testable on this model/dataset. Failure-analysis hook: log, for each dropped tuple, whether it failed the membership fact, the property fact, the probe, or paraphrase-consistency, so brittle/prompt-sensitive atomic facts are quantified rather than silently excluded.

PRIMARY H1 signature - Experiment 2 (graded taxonomic-distance failure on storage-verified tuples): Test that inheritance-query accuracy falls with taxonomic distance even when both atomic facts are stored. Data: the inheritance-eligible set (Exp 1). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; per-tuple direct-query accuracy and yes-token probability. Controls stated before the claim: (i) a matched control of non-inherited-but-true properties attached directly at the instance (distance 0); (ii) covariates - log instance frequency, log property frequency, log instance-property co-occurrence (from a large web-scale count proxy), query token length; (iii) cluster-robust SEs by owning-category. Decisive metric: OLS slope of per-tuple accuracy on distance with those covariates partialled out. Convincing: accuracy slope <= -0.05 per hop (95% CI excludes 0) for inherited properties while the distance-0 control slope CI includes 0. Indecision band: slope in (-0.05, -0.02). Negative (slope CI includes 0, or control shows the same slope) undercuts the graded-inheritance signature. Auxiliary (secondary, not load-bearing): report the logit-lens answer-onset layer vs distance and its Spearman rank correlation with the Collins-Quillian human latency ordering, framed only as a loose motivating analogue, not as a latency measurement.

PRIMARY H2 mechanism - Experiment 3 (owning category present but uncomposed on failures, beyond lexical baseline): Test that on failures the property-owning category is still internally represented rather than absent, and that this is not mere lexical residue of the prompt tokens. Data: eligible set split into model-correct ('success') and model-incorrect ('failure') inheritance queries. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; logistic-regression probe (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null) decoding owning-category identity from the INSTANCE-token and last-token residual streams per layer, trained on success cases, tested on held-out success and on failure cases. Critical control for the AUROC-interpretation concern: a lexical-baseline probe trained on the same surface tokens (bag-of-token embeddings of the prompt) - the residual-stream probe must beat this baseline for the category to count as internally-represented rather than read off input lexis; also compare instance-token vs last-token positions to show the category is bound at the instance, not just present as a prompt token. Decisive metric: peak-layer category-decoding AUROC on failures, and its margin over the lexical baseline. Convincing: failure AUROC >= 0.75, within 0.05 of success AUROC, and >= 0.10 above the lexical baseline. Indecision band: failure AUROC 0.60-0.75 or lexical margin 0.03-0.10 - partial/graded presence. Negative (failure AUROC <= 0.60, or no margin over lexical baseline) means the category is absent or merely lexical on failures, refuting the present-but-uncomposed claim.

PRIMARY (decisive) H2 mechanism - Experiment 4 (causal category-binding via activation patching with matched controls): The single decisive experiment - test that supplying the category-binding causally restores the inherited answer and that this is specific to the OWNING category. Data: matched same-instance pairs from the eligible set - a 'category-primed' run (prompt prepends 'A {instance} is a {category}.') and a 'bare-query' run. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; activation patching (TransformerLens) copying the residual stream at instance/last-token positions from primed into failing bare runs, swept over layers; reverse direction mean-ablates the binding in success runs. Systems compared (controls that isolate a binding vs generic context effect): (a) owning-category binding patch; (b) SEMANTICALLY-SIMILAR non-owning category patch (a sibling/cousin node at matched embedding similarity that does NOT own the property); (c) UNRELATED category patch with activation norm matched to (a); (d) random-position patch; (e) random-source patch. Decisive metric: net recovery = fraction of failures flipped correct by the owning-category patch minus the flip rate of the strongest control (b or c). Convincing: net recovery >= 25 percentage points at the best layer over the similarity/norm-matched controls, AND reverse ablation lowers success accuracy by >= 25 points, with random controls (d,e) < 5 points. Indecision band: net recovery 10-25 points - binding contributes but is not sufficient alone. Negative (< 10 points, or indistinguishable from the similarity/norm-matched controls) refutes the causal core: the effect is generic context injection, not a specific category-binding.

AUXILIARY H2 editing consequence - Experiment 5 (reusable binding direction vs editing atomic facts): Test the practitioner consequence - that a reusable low-rank binding direction restores inheritance more cleanly than editing either atomic fact. Data: eligible set, instance-disjoint train/test split; steering vector = mean residual difference (category-primed minus bare) over training instances, seeds {0,1,2}. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the injected direction (rank<=4). Systems compared: (a) binding-steering on held-out failures, (b) ROME edit of the membership fact, (c) ROME edit of the property-at-category fact, (d) random-direction control. Decisive metric: recovered-per-unit-collateral = recovery rate / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated held-out facts; secondary: specificity (accuracy change on non-inherited direct properties, guarding against over-attribution) and fluency (held-out perplexity delta). Convincing: steering recovery >= 30% with < 3-point drop on the 200 unrelated facts and a strictly better recovered-per-collateral ratio than both ROME edits. Indecision band: recovery 15-30% or collateral 3-6 points - parity, not superiority. Negative (no better than random, or worse collateral than ROME) bounds the editing claim.

AUXILIARY H2 generality - Experiment 6 (cross-subtree and out-of-distribution transfer of the binding direction): Test whether the binding is a general composition operation, not a per-category memorized patch, and whether it survives a taxonomy shift. Data: eligible tuples partitioned by WordNet subtree; ALSO an out-of-distribution held-out set built from a DIFFERENT ontology (Wikidata subclass-of + property statements) using the same ownership criterion, to test transfer beyond WordNet/ConceptNet. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared: within-subtree steering (upper bound), cross-subtree steering, Wikidata-OOD steering, random-direction control. Decisive metric: cross-subtree and OOD recovery relative to within-subtree recovery. Convincing: cross-subtree recovery >= 60% of within-subtree and OOD recovery clearly above random. Indecision band: 35-60% - partial generality. Negative (< 35% or at random) means the binding is category-specific, weakening the single-mechanism reading.

AUXILIARY H1/H2 generality - Experiment 7 (architecture replication and optional frontier sanity check): Test that the graded signature and its binding basis are not idiosyncratic to one model. Data: per-model eligible-set reconstruction (Exp 1 pipeline). Models: GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B, Pythia-6.9B, all frozen; re-run Exp 2-4 (distance slope, present-but-uncomposed decodability, patching recovery), seeds {0,1,2}. Optional low-cost frontier sanity check (behavioral only, no patching): query one API frontier model for the distance-accuracy curve on the eligible set to check the behavioral signature persists at scale. Decisive metric: sign/magnitude of the accuracy-vs-distance slope and patching net-recovery, replicated per open model. Convincing: negative distance slope (CI excludes 0) with matching present-but-uncomposed decodability and net patch recovery in >= 2 of 3 open models. Indecision band: replication in exactly 1 of 3. Negative (no replication) confines the claims to Llama-3-8B.

AUXILIARY H1 confound - Experiment 8 (composition vs surface co-occurrence, and scale): Test whether inheritance reflects genuine hierarchical composition rather than direct instance-property co-occurrence, and whether scale flattens the distance curve. Data: eligible set on the Pythia suite (open Pile pretraining corpus) enabling exact instance-property co-occurrence counts; Pythia 1.4B, 2.8B, 6.9B, frozen. Decisive metric: partial regression coefficient of inheritance-failure rate on taxonomic distance after controlling for log instance-property co-occurrence and property abstractness. Convincing: distance coefficient remains significant (CI excludes 0) with co-occurrence partialled out, and the distance slope magnitude decreases monotonically across the three scales. Indecision band: distance-coefficient CI half-width overlapping 0 by < 0.02 - co-occurrence and composition statistically entangled at this sample size. Negative (co-occurrence fully absorbs the distance effect) means the signature is surface statistics, refuting H1's hierarchical-storage claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Construct validity: WordNet/ConceptNet ownership is noisy; we mitigate with an explicit nearest-owner ownership criterion and a curator-validated 150-tuple sample (>=85% agreement required), and report the disagreement rate as an error bar on all downstream claims.

The graded distance effect could reflect surface co-occurrence rather than composition; the co-occurrence-partialled regression (Exp 8) and the similarity/norm-matched causal patching controls (Exp 4) are the decisive guards, and the main claim is only stated after these controls.

Decoding the owning category (Exp 3) could reflect residual lexical evidence of prompt tokens rather than a bound representation; the lexical-baseline probe and instance-vs-last-token comparison are required to license the 'present-but-uncomposed' reading.

The category-binding may be distributed/graded rather than a single injectable direction; activation patching (Exp 4), not the steering vector alone, is the decisive causal evidence, and graded recovery remains informative.

Atomic-fact storage verification risks overestimation from prompt leakage; conservative content-probe thresholds, paraphrase-consistency, and held-out verification mitigate this, and a per-tuple failure-analysis log quantifies brittle/prompt-sensitive atomic facts (Exp 1) rather than hiding them.
Binding injection could induce over-attribution (yes to non-inherited false properties); the non-inherited-property specificity control (Exp 5) is central and practical utility may be capped by this.
The answer-onset-layer latency analogue is only loosely comparable to human reaction time; we mark it auxiliary and treat the Collins-Quillian parallel as motivation, not identity.
Multi-token properties/instances complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first items with reported coverage.
Findings on 6-8B open models may not transfer to frontier-scale models; the optional behavioral-only frontier check (Exp 7) probes the signature but not the mechanism at scale.

Name: magnitude_prior_regression
Title: Regressing Toward the Typical: How a Compressed Magnitude Prior Distorts LLMs' Recall of Numeric Facts
Short Hypothesis: LLMs store numeric factual quantities (populations, distances, dates, masses, prices) but read them out through a query-independent compressed magnitude prior that pulls the answer toward the scale-typical value for that quantity type. Stated as one novel phenomenon: factual numeric recall exhibits regression-to-category-typicality that persists beyond corpus-frequency and tail-obscurity effects. The compressed/logarithmic magnitude representation itself is established prior art; our claim is the behavioral signature in FACTUAL RECALL, namely that many numeric-recall errors are not missing facts but prior-regression distortions - the correct magnitude is internally decodable, yet the emitted number is systematically shrunk toward the category's typical order of magnitude. We define the category-typical value operationally as the median log-value of authoritative ground truth within a quantity type, so the fit is not a tautology. We hypothesize (1) this regression is a gradable behavioral phenomenon whose signed distortion increases with the fact's log-distance from the category-typical magnitude, above frequency- and popularity-matched baselines; (2) the internally decodable magnitude is more accurate than the verbalized answer, which equals a shrunk-toward-prior transform of it; and (3) suppressing the compression prior (or steering toward the decoded internal magnitude) improves accuracy on atypical facts without editing any fact.
Related Work: Numeracy-probing work shows LLMs linearly encode log-magnitudes yet verbalize poorly ('LLMs Know More About Numbers than They Can Say', 2026), that number representations are sublinearly/logarithmically compressed like the human mental number line (Number Representations as Human Perception 2025; ALBERT numeracy 2024; Representational Geometry of Number 2026), and that digit-frequency (Benford) biases cause numerical hallucination (Benford's Curse 2025). Cognitive science documents systematic magnitude underestimation and log-to-linear shifts (Adults Underestimate Decimals 2022; Straightening Up 2011). The closest baseline family - which we separate from our contribution up front - is linear/log numeric encoding, the internal-vs-verbalized gap, Benford digit bias, and factual-recall benchmarks. All prior work studies magnitude encoding/verbalization of PRESENTED numbers or digit-generation bias; none isolate a prior-regression distortion of RECALLED factual quantities (the model shrinks a stored fact's magnitude toward its category-typical value), none test that the correct value is internally hidden and recoverable by suppressing the compression prior, and none rule this out against matched-frequency/tail-obscurity nulls. This is orthogonal to prior proposals (entity/attribute retrieval, gating, competition), transferring the human production-estimation regression bias into LLM numeric factual recall with a causal mechanism and a non-destructive fix.
Abstract: Large language models often produce a confidently wrong number when recalling a factual quantity - a city's population, a mountain's height, a country's GDP - with a magnitude that is off in a systematic direction. This is a special, MEASURABLE case of hallucination that matters for quantitative QA, retrieval QA, benchmark design, and any domain where numeric mistakes are costly. Prior interpretability work shows LLMs encode magnitude on a compressed, logarithmic-like internal scale and know more about numbers than they verbalize (established prior art); it does not connect this to errors in recalling real numeric facts. Our novel phenomenon is magnitude-prior regression: when recalling a numeric fact, the model reads the stored magnitude out through a query-independent compressed prior that pulls the answer toward the typical order of magnitude for that quantity type, so atypically large or small facts are systematically distorted even when the correct value is internally available - a structured bias, not random error or mere missing knowledge. We test three claims, defining each quantity type's 'typical' magnitude as the median log-value of authoritative ground truth. (1) Behavioral signature: recalled-number error is directional and grows with the fact's log-distance from typicality - large values underestimated, small overestimated - above frequency-, popularity-, and typicality-only nulls. (2) Internal-vs-verbalized gap: a linear magnitude probe recovers the fact's true magnitude more accurately than the verbalized answer, which aligns with a shrunk-toward-prior transform of the internal estimate (verbalized = k*internal + (1-k)*prior, k<1). (3) Causal recovery: suppressing the compression-prior direction, or steering readout toward the decoded internal magnitude, improves accuracy on a subset of atypical facts with high specificity, unlike a 'be precise' re-prompt or fact editing, and yields a diagnostic that separates 'missing' from 'distorting' a fact. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Numeric-fact dataset and directional-distortion dose-response): Tests H1, that recalled-number error is directional and grows with the fact's log-distance from the category-typical magnitude. Data: constructed from Wikidata (existing). Seven quantity types (city population, country population, mountain elevation, river length, country GDP, country area, celestial-body distance) with authoritative ground truth and wide within-category range; sample 1,500 facts per type (10,500) balanced across log-magnitude, each with 1 direct query plus 3 paraphrases; compute per-category typical magnitude (median log-value) and each fact's log-distance. This size gives >=150 facts per log-distance decile for stable slope estimates. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, frozen (bf16), greedy; record the verbalized number. Systems compared: observed signed error (log emitted - log true) vs an unbiased-noise null (zero-slope). Decisive metric (before data): per-category regression slope of signed error on log-distance-from-typical, controlling for entity popularity, answer digit-length, query length. Convincing = negative slope (large underestimated, small overestimated) with CI excluding 0 in >=5 of 7 categories. Negative = slope CI includes 0 in a majority (no regression-to-typical; H1 fails). Indecision band |slope| < 0.05 (log-units per log-distance-unit) with CI crossing 0: report as no reliable directional distortion for that category.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Internal magnitude probe vs verbalized answer): Tests H2, that the internally decodable magnitude is more accurate than the verbalized answer, which equals a shrunk-toward-prior transform of it. Data: Exp 1 facts, 80/20 split by entity. Model: same three frozen models; a linear log-magnitude probe on the subject-token/last-token residual stream at each layer, L2-regularized, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV; restrict to facts where the probe generalizes to held-out entities (report coverage). Systems compared: probe-decoded log-magnitude vs the model's verbalized log-magnitude, both against ground truth; and a fitted shrinkage model verbalized = k*internal + (1-k)*prior. Decisive metric (before data), first: mean absolute log-error of probe MINUS that of verbalized answer on held-out facts. Convincing = probe error lower by >=0.15 log-units (CI excluding 0) AND fitted shrinkage k<1 with CI excluding 1. Negative = probe no better than verbalized (difference CI includes 0), refuting the hidden-accurate-magnitude claim; H2 fails. Indecision band 0.00-0.15 log-units advantage: report a weak internal-vs-verbalized gap. Label-shuffle probe must be at chance.

Experiment 3 (H1 — Compression-prior localization): Tests the internal correlate behind H1's regression -- a separable category-typical prior direction. Data: Exp 1 activations, atypical vs typical facts contrasted within each category. Model: same three frozen; contrastive mean-difference direction plus logit-lens/tuned-lens over number tokens across layers; no weight training. Systems compared: a 'prior' probe (predicts category-typical value) residualized on the fact-magnitude probe (Exp 2) to test separability. Decisive metric (before data): residual AUROC/ R^2 of the prior signal after removing the fact-specific magnitude, best layer. Convincing = residual R^2 >=0.15 for the prior AND logit-lens shows monotone shrinkage of the number-token estimate toward the prior across the last third of layers. Negative = residual R^2 <=0.03 (no separable prior; the regression has no distinct locus). Indecision band 0.03-0.15: report an entangled prior, weakening the mechanistic localization but not the behavioral H1.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal suppression/steering of the prior): Tests H3's causal claim that suppressing the compression prior or steering toward the decoded internal magnitude improves accuracy on atypical facts without editing the fact. Data: 1,000 held-out atypical facts (top/bottom log-distance quartiles) not used in probe fitting. Model: same three frozen; activation edits at the Exp 3 layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) suppress the compression-prior direction; (b) steer toward the probe-decoded internal magnitude; (c) reverse control amplifying the prior; plus random-direction and content control (non-numeric answers unchanged). Decisive metric (before data): reduction in signed distortion (|log emitted - log true|) on atypical facts vs random control. Convincing = >=0.20 log-unit reduction over random at a dose keeping perplexity within 5%. Negative = <=0.03 log-unit change (no causal role; H3 fails). Indecision band 0.03-0.20 log-units: partial causal support. Reverse control must increase distortion by >=0.10 log-units to confirm directionality.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Recovery specificity and collateral cost): Tests that H3's recovery is specific to atypical facts and does not corrupt typical facts or unrelated behavior. Data: Exp 4 held-out atypical facts; 1,000 typical facts (near category median, already near-correct); 200 unrelated non-numeric facts (PopQA). Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our intervention vs a 'give the precise value / think carefully' re-prompt, auxiliary-probe finetuning per the numeracy literature (existing), ROME editing (existing, expected null since regression is systematic not per-fact), and random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: atypical-fact log-error reduction MINUS typical-fact log-error increase. Convincing = atypical reduction >=0.15 log-units while typical error rises <=0.03 log-units, unrelated-fact accuracy drops <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = typical error rises >=0.10 log-units or no net gain (over-correction). Indecision band typical increase 0.03-0.10 log-units: utility capped; report the trade-off curve.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Cross-category and cross-model transfer): Tests whether a single prior-suppression/magnitude-steering recipe generalizes. Data: direction fit on population facts (Exp 4) applied unchanged to elevation and GDP held-out atypical facts (800 each). Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction. Decisive metric (before data): transferred distortion-reduction as a fraction of in-domain-refit reduction. Convincing = >=60% of in-domain on >=2 categories and >=2 models. Negative = <=20% (category-specific prior; generality fails). Indecision band 20-60%: partial transfer. Report Spearman rho between model scale and regression-slope magnitude across the three models (rho <=-0.3 suggestive that larger models compress less; N=3 caveat).

Experiment 7 (H1 — Source analysis on an open-data model): Tests H1's mechanistic source -- that distortion is driven by the compressed prior, not tail-value obscurity. Data: OLMo-7B (existing open-data model); for 1,000 facts across categories compute the frequency distribution of each fact's magnitude in comparable corpus text and each fact's log-distance-from-typical. Model: OLMo-7B frozen; reuse Exp 1-2 pipeline. Systems compared: nested regression predicting distortion from log-distance-from-typical vs from raw corpus frequency of the true value. Decisive metric (before data): incremental variance (Delta R^2) explained by log-distance-from-typical over frequency-only. Convincing = Delta R^2 >=0.10 with the distance coefficient sign consistent with regression-to-typical. Negative = Delta R^2 <=0.02 (distortion is just tail obscurity, not a prior; the source claim fails). Indecision band 0.02-0.10: report the prior as a partial driver alongside obscurity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Numeric-recall errors could reflect genuinely missing facts (tail obscurity) rather than prior regression; the internal-probe recovery (Exp 3) and log-distance dose-response controlling for popularity (Exp 2) are the decisive separators, and coverage is reported for facts where the probe generalizes.
The compression-prior and fact-magnitude signals may be entangled; the causal suppression/steering tests (Exp 5), not probe accuracy alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Prior suppression could over-correct — introducing wild large values or degrading typical-fact accuracy; the typical-fact specificity control (Exp 6) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.

Multi-token number readout (large numbers span many tokens) complicates logit-lens and steering; primary analysis uses log-magnitude probes and order-of-magnitude accuracy metrics rather than exact-digit recovery, with reported coverage.

Directional distortion may be small relative to noise for some categories; per-category dose-response and the paired within-category design maximize power, and a modest but significant regression slope is still informative.
A single transferable intervention recipe may not exist if the prior is category-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Frequency proxies for magnitude distribution are only inspectable on open-data models; we validate the source claim on OLMo and treat closed-model proxies as approximate.
Findings on 7-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: stress_induced_retrieval_gating
Title: Stressed Out of an Answer: Transferring Stress-Induced Retrieval Impairment into LLM Factual Recall and Locating the Gate
Short Hypothesis: Primary claim (one falsifiable sentence): acute stress/urgency framing of a factual query causally installs a RETRIEVAL GATE over stored factual content — the correct answer stays internally decodable, but a query-independent 'stress' signal, computed before the answer, suppresses its expression. We operationalize 'stress' as affective urgency/threat framing held equal in token length and propositional content to matched controls, so it is dissociated from generic length, cognitive load, distraction, and salience. Borrowing the robust human finding that acute stress selectively impairs memory RETRIEVAL (sparing encoding/working memory and sparing neutral material), we infer retrieval-vs-encoding by contrasting parametric retrieval against an in-context lookup control (a working-memory analogue that stress should spare). Secondary predictions: (a) the human selectivity signature — retrieval of emotionally-arousing/high-stakes facts is impaired more than neutral facts; (b) suppressing the stress direction restores the hidden answer while preserving genuinely urgency-appropriate behavior and without harming calibration or refusal on non-stress queries. The contribution is anchored as mechanistic interpretability — locating and causally toggling the gate — not a re-documentation of stress-framing effects.
Related Work: StressPrompt (2024) shows LLMs mirror human stress-performance Yerkes-Dodson curves behaviorally and that stress prompts shift hidden states, but it is task-general (instruction-following, reasoning, EI) and does NOT isolate factual retrieval, hidden knowledge, a causal gate, or the selectivity signature. Human memory work (Kuhlmann et al. 2005; de Quervain; Schwabe & Wolf; 2020 systematic review) establishes that acute stress impairs RETRIEVAL specifically (not encoding/working memory) and selectively for emotionally-arousing material. Information Anxiety (2024) studies popularity-driven internal strain, not stress framing. Emotion-circuit work (Do LLMs Feel 2025; Emotion Inference 2025) localizes emotion representations but studies emotion expression/inference, not stress-gated factual recall. My prior proposals cover familiarity, difficulty, persona, and priming gates; none uses affective STRESS framing as the gating variable, tests the human retrieval-vs-encoding and arousal-selectivity dissociations, or shows stress-direction suppression recovers hidden facts. Primary novelty anchor (mechanistic interpretability): unlike StressPrompt and prompt-framing work — which measure task-general behavioral shifts and never isolate factual recall, hidden (still-decodable) knowledge, the arousal-selectivity/retrieval-vs-encoding dissociations, or a causal, suppressible gate — our contribution is to localize and causally toggle a stress retrieval-gate over stored facts.
Abstract: User-facing consequence first: urgent or safety-critical prompting ('a life depends on this — quickly!') can hide a correct fact an LLM actually stores, so the model can fail precisely when stakes are highest. In humans, acute stress reliably impairs memory retrieval—people fail to recall facts they demonstrably know, an effect that spares neutral material but hits emotionally-arousing content hardest, and that impairs retrieval while leaving encoding and working memory intact. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous, mechanistically-localizable effect in factual recall. We propose stress-induced retrieval gating: framing a factual query with stress/urgency cues ('URGENT—a life depends on this, quickly:') suppresses the model's expression of a fact it stores, because a query-independent stress signal computed early gates retrieval, while the correct answer remains internally decodable. We test three claims on factual queries wrapped in graded stress framings. (1) Behavioral transfer with the human selectivity signature: stress framing lowers recall of facts the model answers correctly under neutral framing, above matched baselines, and—mirroring human data—impairs retrieval of emotionally-arousing/high-stakes facts more than neutral facts, while a working-memory-style in-context lookup control is spared (retrieval-specific, not general degradation). (2) Localization and drivers: a linear stress probe is decodable before the answer, tracks surface stress cues rather than fact difficulty, and is separable (via residualization) from the fact-content signal; on stress failures the correct answer stays linearly decodable (hidden, not erased). (3) Causal, behavior-preserving recovery: activation-patching the stress representation from a neutral run, or subtracting the stress direction, restores stored facts with high specificity—preserving genuinely urgency-appropriate behavior (e.g., brevity)—and outperforming a 'stay calm' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA/T-REx plus a curated medical subset, evaluating stress dose-response, arousal selectivity, hidden-knowledge recovery, causal recovery, and specificity. If it holds, this motivates stress-robust evaluations, prompting guidelines for high-stakes queries, and activation-level recovery methods, and is relevant not only to interpretability but to LLM safety, evaluation, and deployment teams in domains such as emergency response, clinical triage, legal, and customer-support QA. H1 (the retrieval gate) is the primary claim; arousal selectivity, localization, and recovery are secondary analyses.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — stress-induced suppression of stored-fact expression): Tests whether stress/urgency framing lowers expression of a fact the model stores, beyond generic added-length distraction, with a graded dose-response. Data: PopQA (14,267 QA pairs) and EntityQuestions (~22k dev); per model, keep facts answered correctly under a plain neutral framing across 3 paraphrases, capped at 1,500 facts (fewer than the pool because 5 framings x paraphrases x per-layer caching multiplies cost); report per-model coverage. Each fact is rendered in 5 semantically-equivalent framings (neutral; mild urgency; high time-pressure; high-stakes/threat; social-evaluative), kept only if a GPT-4o judge plus a 100-item human spot-check agree the fact target and meaning are unchanged (>=90% agreement). Single-token-first answers only. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, all weights frozen, greedy decoding (temperature 0); no trained parameters here; each framing evaluated once (deterministic). Systems compared: each stress framing vs (a) the neutral baseline and (b) a matched-length neutral-filler control (same token count, no stress content). Decisive metric: stress-induced failure rate = fraction of neutral-correct facts that flip to wrong under a stress framing MINUS the matched-length-filler failure rate (paired McNemar); secondary: dose-response slope across the 5 ordered levels (mixed-effects logistic). Convincing: >=10 pp stress-minus-filler gap on the two strongest framings with a monotone or inverted-U dose-response, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: 3-10 pp gap, or a dose slope whose 95% CI includes 0 -> transfer weak, reported as partial with no strong claim. Negative (<3 pp, or filler matches stress) refutes behavioral transfer: stress framing does not suppress stored-fact expression beyond generic distraction.

Experiment 2 (H3 — arousal selectivity and retrieval-specificity signatures): Tests the human selectivity signature that stress impairs arousing/high-stakes facts more than neutral ones, and that the impairment is retrieval-specific (spares in-context lookup). Data: from the Exp-1 pool, form frequency-matched pairs (Wikidata pageview-decile matched) of arousing/high-stakes facts (death, disaster, medical entities) vs neutral facts, targeting ~600 matched pairs per model (capped for caching cost; report coverage). Retrieval-vs-lookup uses the same facts in two conditions: (i) parametric retrieval (answer from weights) and (ii) in-context lookup (the answer appears in the prompt and must be read out). Model: the same three frozen models, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: the stress x arousal cells, and the stress x (retrieval vs lookup) cells, each against its neutral counterpart. Decisive metric: the stress x arousal interaction (extra failure on arousing minus neutral under stress, in pp) and the stress x condition interaction (stress-induced failure on retrieval minus that on lookup, in pp). Convincing: arousal interaction >=5 pp AND stress harms retrieval >=8 pp more than lookup (lookup near-spared, <=3 pp), in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: arousal interaction 2-5 pp, or retrieval-minus-lookup 3-8 pp -> selectivity present but weak, reported as suggestive not confirmatory. Negative (arousal interaction <=2 pp, or stress harms lookup as much as retrieval) means the human selectivity/retrieval-specificity signature does NOT transfer and the effect is general degradation — an informative cross-species divergence, not support for the hypothesis.

Experiment 3 (H2 — hidden answer and stress-gate localization): Tests that during a stress failure the correct answer stays internally decodable and that a query-independent stress signal, computed before the answer, gates it. Data: stress-failure trials from Exp 1 (neutral-correct, stress-wrong), pooling framings to reach >=300 failures per model, plus their matched neutral runs; residual stream cached at subject and last-token positions across all layers (32 for Llama-3-8B, 28 for Qwen2.5-7B, 42 for Gemma-2-9B). Model: frozen; the only fitted objects are per-layer L2-logistic probes — a content probe (target = correct answer token) and a stress probe (target = ordinal stress level) — trained on 70% of facts and tested on the disjoint 30%, over 3 seeds (0/1/2), with a label-shuffled null. Systems compared: content-probe recovery on stress-failure trials vs the verbalized answer (~0% correct there) and vs the shuffle null; stress-probe output vs neutral-framing difficulty as competing drivers. Decisive metric: content-probe recovery accuracy of the correct answer on stress-failure trials; secondary: stress-probe peak AUROC and onset layer (must precede the answer position), standardized regression betas of the stress-probe output on surface-cue count vs difficulty, and residual separability (stress probe after residualizing out content). Convincing: recovery >=60% (>> verbalized and >> shuffle), stress-probe AUROC >=0.75 peaking before the answer token, surface-cue beta at least 2x the difficulty beta, and stress-after-content residual AUROC >=0.70. Undecidable band: recovery 40-60% or AUROC 0.60-0.75 -> signal present but weak/entangled, partial support. Negative (recovery at shuffle/chance, or stress-probe tracking difficulty more than surface cues) refutes the hidden-and-gated account: failures reflect erasure or genuine difficulty, not a stress gate.

Experiment 4 (H2 — causal stress gating by injection and patching): Tests that the stress signal, not fact content, causally gates retrieval. Data: 300 matched neutral/stress fact pairs per model, held out from the Exp-3 probe-training facts. Method: a stress steering vector = mean high-minus-low-stress activation difference at the Exp-3 onset layers (fitted on the training split, then frozen); activation patching of the stress representation from the neutral run into a stress-failure run; ablation of the top candidate stress attention heads. Model: three frozen models, temperature 0; interventions applied at a swept dose (scale in {0.5,1,2,4}x the vector norm), 3 seeds. Systems compared: (a) inject stress direction into a neutral run (induce failure), (b) patch neutral stress-state into a stress-failure run (restore), (c) content-only patch control, (d) random-direction control matched in norm, and (e) an orthogonal affect direction (positive-emotion/calm) matched in norm as a stronger causal-specificity control (an equally-strong but non-stress affect signal should NOT gate retrieval). Decisive metric: induced-failure rate from injection minus the random-direction control (pp), with its dose-response; secondary: restoration rate from patching vs the content-only patch. Convincing: injection raises failure >=15 pp over random-direction with a monotone dose-response, and patching restores >=50% while the content-only patch restores <10% — the stress signal, not content, gates. Undecidable band: injection 5-15 pp over control, or restoration 25-50% -> causal role partial, reported as suggestive. Negative (injection <=5 pp over random, or content-patch restores as well as stress-patch) means the stress signal is merely correlational, not the causal gate.

Experiment 5 (H4 — behavior-preserving recovery and cross-model generality): Tests that subtracting the stress direction restores hidden facts while preserving genuinely urgency-appropriate behavior, and that one vector generalizes.
