Data: held-out stress failures (>=400 per model, disjoint from fitting); specificity sets = 200 unrelated neutral facts, all stress-framed facts already answered correctly, and a non-stress calibration/refusal battery (calibration on answerable facts and appropriate refusals on unanswerable ones) to verify the fix does not distort calibration or refusal behavior on non-stress queries; a response-appropriateness set of framings that legitimately call for brevity/action, scored by a GPT-4o format classifier. Model: three frozen models; the low-rank mean-difference stress vector is fitted on a subset of relations and framings and applied to held-out relations and framings (the generality test); dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: stress-subtraction vs a 'stay calm / take a breath' re-prompt, stress-head ablation, ROME editing (expected null since the fact is stored), and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: recovery rate on held-out stress failures, reported jointly with collateral drop on the 200 unrelated + already-correct-stress facts and with format-appropriateness retention; secondary: held-out perplexity change. Convincing: recovery >=40% with <=2 pp collateral drop and >=90% format-appropriateness retained, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, and >=60% of the single-model recovery transferring to held-out relations and across all three models. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, or collateral 2-5 pp, or transfer 40-60% -> useful but capped/partial generality, reported as a utility ceiling. Negative (recovery <=20%, collateral >5 pp, or stripped legitimate urgency behavior) means no behavior-preserving recovery: the gate cannot be cleanly suppressed.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Stress framings add tokens/attention load, so the effect could be generic distraction rather than a stress-specific gate; matched-length neutral controls, the surface-cue driver regression (Exp 3), and especially the retrieval-vs-in-context-lookup dissociation (Exp 2, where stress should spare lookup) are the decisive separators.

LLMs might not reproduce the human arousal-selectivity or retrieval-specificity signatures (e.g., stress could impair uniformly or even help brief answers); a null/divergent pattern refutes the transfer but is itself an informative cross-species finding about LLM vs human memory.
The stress and fact-content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 4), not probe onset alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Recovery could remove legitimately urgency-appropriate behavior (brevity, action orientation) or degrade fluency; the response-appropriateness and correctly-answered-stress-framed specificity controls (Exp 5) are central and utility may be capped.

Verifying a fact is 'stored' during a stress failure risks probe overfitting; held-out probes, conservative thresholds, and neutral-framing recall as an extra check with reported coverage mitigate this.
A single transferable stress-suppression vector may not exist if gating is framing- or relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: anchor_selective_accessibility
Title: Anchored Recall: How an Irrelevant Anchor Contaminates Which Stored Facts an LLM Can Access
Short Hypothesis: Primary claim (one falsifiable sentence, one primary metric): anchoring in LLM factual recall is a selective-accessibility RETRIEVAL-CONTAMINATION effect, not mere output-distribution imitation — on an anchored trial that produces a wrong, anchor-shifted answer, the correct value the model otherwise recalls remains linearly decodable from intermediate activations (primary metric: probe recovery of the true value on anchored errors, far above the verbalized answer), i.e. the fact is hidden, not overwritten. 'Hidden knowledge' is tested as BOTH linear-probe decodability AND causal recoverability, kept as separate claims. Secondary predictions: (a) a transient anchor-accessibility signal, separable from fact content, scales with anchor magnitude/plausibility rather than only the model's un-anchored certainty; (b) suppressing that signal de-anchors the answer without editing facts, with high specificity and without harming legitimately-informative-anchor cases.
Related Work: Behavioral work now firmly establishes anchoring in LLMs (Anchors in the Machine 2025; CBEval 2024; AnchorBench 2026; anchoring meta-analysis 2023) and some mechanistic touches: Shapley attribution shows anchors reweight log-probs, authority-bias steering (Trust Me I'm an Expert 2026) subtracts a residual-stream bias vector, and Anchoring Depends on Confidence (2026) shows susceptibility tracks distributional certainty rather than accuracy. Numerical-attribute work (Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding 2025) shows irrelevant numeric context perturbs magnitude subspaces. Crucially, none test the classic human selective-accessibility account: that the anchor contaminates *which stored fact is retrieved* rather than only shifting the output distribution, none show the correct value remains internally recoverable during an anchored error (hidden knowledge), and none localize a transient anchor-accessibility signal that gates recall and can be suppressed to restore un-anchored recall. This is distinct from my magnitude_prior_regression proposal (a query-independent category-typical compression prior, no external anchor) and from context_priming_contamination (a semantic distractor entity, not a numeric comparison anchor). Primary novelty anchor: relative to Localizing-Anchoring-Pathways-style output-bias localization and the distributional-certainty account, our contribution is the human selective-accessibility framing — a hidden-knowledge probe plus a causal gate test that adjudicates anchor-property scaling against model-certainty — with strict controls for probe leakage, answer-format artifacts, and matched-confidence baselines, and an ablation showing the effect is absent for semantically-similar non-numeric distractors.
Abstract: User-facing consequence first: an irrelevant number placed before a factual query ('greater or less than 9,000,000?') does not merely skew an LLM's answer — it transiently hijacks which stored value the model can access, so numeric or clinical decision-support can be biased by context the user never intended as evidence. Large language models assimilate their answers toward irrelevant numeric anchors, a robust behavioral cognitive bias. But the leading human account of anchoring is not distributional imitation: it is selective accessibility, where comparing a target against an anchor makes anchor-consistent information more retrievable. We ask whether LLM anchoring is likewise a retrieval-contamination phenomenon in factual recall, and whether the model still holds the correct value it fails to report. We study anchored factual queries (e.g., 'Is the population of Riga greater or less than 9,000,000? Now, what is the population of Riga?') for facts the model answers accurately when un-anchored. We test three claims. (1) Retrieval contamination: on anchored trials that produce a wrong, anchor-shifted answer, a linear probe recovers the correct value from intermediate activations at rates far above the verbalized answer, showing the fact is hidden, not overwritten, and the emitted answer is an anchor-consistent competitor. (2) Accessibility locus and drivers: a transient anchor-accessibility signal, decodable before the answer and separable (via residualization) from the fact-content signal, predicts and scales with the anchor's magnitude and its plausibility, tracking selective-accessibility rather than only distributional certainty. (3) Causal recovery: suppressing the anchor-accessibility direction, or patching the pre-anchor representation, restores the un-anchored correct value with high specificity, whereas fact editing does not, and outperforms a 'ignore the previous number' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on numeric-fact sets from Wikidata, evaluating hidden-knowledge recovery, accessibility-signal prediction, causal recovery, and specificity, plus a safety transfer to clinical numeric facts. We pre-register one primary claim (retrieval contamination with a hidden correct value) and one primary metric (probe recovery on anchored errors), demoting the accessibility-signal and de-anchoring results to secondary analyses; the scope is numeric factual recall. Audiences include interpretability, robustness, and safety teams handling numeric/clinical facts.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — anchor-driven retrieval contamination with hidden correct value): Tests that an irrelevant anchor shifts the emitted value toward an anchor-consistent competitor while the correct value the model otherwise recalls stays internally decodable. Data: from Wikidata, single-numeric-answer facts (city population, elevation, area, founding year, drug dosage), restricted to facts the model answers within a tolerance band when un-anchored; target ~1,000 facts per model (capped; report coverage). Matched conditions per fact: no-anchor; high anchor; low anchor, introduced via the comparative pathway ('Is X greater or less than [anchor]? What is X?') at controlled log-distances, with both implausible/random and plausible anchors, plus a semantic (non-numeric) distractor condition matched for length/plausibility that is predicted NOT to induce assimilation (ruling out generic distraction). Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0; the only fitted object is a per-layer log-magnitude linear probe (held-out facts, 70%/30%, 3 seeds, shuffle null) reading the internal value on anchored-error trials. Systems compared: probe recovery of the true value on anchored-error trials vs the verbalized (anchor-shifted) value vs the un-anchored run. Decisive metric: probe recovery accuracy (within tolerance) of the true value on anchored errors; secondary: signed assimilation magnitude vs anchor log-distance (dose-response), and whether the emitted value aligns with an anchor-consistent competitor. Convincing: probe recovers the un-anchored value on >=60% of anchored errors (>> verbalized, comparable to the un-anchored run) with a monotone assimilation dose-response, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: recovery 40-60% -> value partly hidden, partly shifted internally, partial support. Negative (recovery near verbalized/chance) means anchoring is output-distribution imitation with no hidden correct value — refuting the selective-accessibility framing.

Experiment 2 (H2 — anchor-accessibility signal scales with anchor properties, not just certainty): Tests that a transient anchor-accessibility signal, separable from fact content, is decodable before the answer and scales with anchor magnitude/plausibility (selective accessibility) rather than only un-anchored distributional certainty. Data: anchored vs no-anchor runs for the Exp-1 facts; residual stream cached at subject/last-token across layers. Model: frozen; a per-layer L2 probe targets the accessibility signal, trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds; residualized against the fact-content/magnitude probe; shuffle null. Systems compared: accessibility signal regressed on anchor log-distance and plausibility vs the model's un-anchored distributional certainty (competing drivers). Decisive metric: standardized betas of anchor magnitude/plausibility vs un-anchored certainty in predicting the accessibility signal; secondary: per-layer AUROC of the signal predicting anchored error, onset before the answer, and residual separability from content. Convincing: anchor-property betas dominate the certainty beta (>=2x) and the signal predicts anchored error at AUROC >=0.72 after residualizing out content, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: anchor-to-certainty beta ratio 1-2x, or AUROC 0.60-0.72 -> the selective-accessibility and certainty accounts coincide, partial support. Negative (certainty dominates, or no separable signal) favors the distributional-certainty account over selective accessibility.

Experiment 3 (H2 — the accessibility signal causally gates recall): Tests that the accessibility signal causally produces assimilation. Data: 300 anchored-error and 300 no-anchor facts per model, held out from Exp-2 probe training. Method: patch the pre-anchor (no-anchor) representation into an anchored-error run; suppress the accessibility direction; inject the accessibility direction (or a synthetic anchor signal) into a no-anchor run; a content-only patch control. Model: frozen; interventions at Exp-2 layers, dose swept {0.5,1,2,4}x, 3 seeds. Systems compared: patch-restore, suppression, injection-induce, content-only patch, random-direction control. Decisive metric: induced-assimilation magnitude from injection vs the random-direction control (with dose-response); secondary: recovery rate of the un-anchored value from patching/suppression vs the content-only patch. Convincing: injection induces assimilation >=15 pp of the anchor gap over random-direction with monotone dose-response, and patch/suppression restores >=50% of un-anchored accuracy while the content-only patch does not, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: induced 5-15 pp, or recovery 25-50% -> partial causal role. Negative (induced <=5 pp over control, or content patch matches) means the accessibility signal is correlational, not the gate.

Experiment 4 (H3 — de-anchoring recovery with specificity and generality): Tests that suppressing the accessibility direction restores the un-anchored answer without editing facts and specifically. Data: held-out anchored queries (>=400 per model); specificity sets = no-anchor facts, cases where the anchor is legitimately informative, and 200 unrelated facts. Model: frozen; a low-rank anchor-accessibility steering vector fitted on a subset of relations/anchor types and applied to held-out ones and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: de-anchoring steering vs an 'ignore the previous number / answer independently' re-prompt, chain-of-thought, authority-bias-style residual steering, ROME editing (expected null), and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: reduction in assimilation / recovery of un-anchored accuracy, reported jointly with collateral change on no-anchor, informative-anchor, and 200-unrelated sets; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% assimilation reduction with <=2 pp collateral drop, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, transferring across relations and models. Undecidable band: 20-40% reduction, or collateral 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (<=20% reduction, collateral >5 pp, or harms legitimately-informative-anchor cases) means no clean de-anchoring.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Anchoring could be pure output-distribution imitation with no retrieval contamination; the hidden-knowledge probe (Exp 1) and the induce-on-demand causal test (Exp 3) are the decisive separators, and a null here would refute the selective-accessibility framing while remaining informative.

The anchor-accessibility and fact-content signals may be entangled, especially since both live in numeric-magnitude subspaces (per Multi-Attribute Confounding 2025); the causal patching/steering tests, not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Distinguishing selective accessibility from the distributional-certainty account (Owusu 2026) is subtle; the driver regression (Exp 2) that separates anchor-property scaling from un-anchored certainty is the key test, but the two may partly coincide.

De-anchoring could over-correct on cases where the anchor is legitimately relevant, or degrade fluency; the informative-anchor and no-anchor specificity controls (Exp 4) are central and utility may be capped.
Multi-token numeric readout complicates probing/logit-lens; primary analysis uses log-magnitude probes and tolerance-band accuracy rather than exact-digit recovery, with reported coverage.
A single transferable de-anchoring vector may not exist if accessibility is relation- or anchor-type-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: prefetch_slot_override
Title: Reserved but Wrong: How Early Plan-Slot Prefetching Overrides Fresh Retrieval of Facts Stated Later in an Answer
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM plans a multi-fact answer, it reserves 'slots' for facts it will state later and prefetches a coarse placeholder for each slot before the generation cursor reaches it. The minimal novelty claim in one sentence: this is a slot-specific stale-placeholder OVERRIDE mechanism, not generic long-context degradation or recency bias. We hypothesize a distinct failure mode - prefetch-slot override - in which a prematurely committed placeholder (a plausible but wrong entity, often the more typical/frequent one, decodable in the residual stream several tokens before the slot) overrides fresh, correct retrieval when the model reaches the slot, so the model states a fact it does not hold even though it would retrieve the correct value if that same fact were asked first or in isolation. The internal state constituting the 'placeholder' is the value linearly decodable at the pre-slot position that differs from the isolated-query answer; the mechanism is falsified if late-slot wrong answers track isolated-query retrieval failure equally (i.e., the model is simply ignorant), or if the effect is fully explained by matched-length long-generation degradation. We predict (1) the reserved-slot placeholder is decodable before the slot is generated, at a position distinct from where earlier facts are produced; (2) override errors concentrate on later slots where the placeholder was mis-prefetched while the correct value remains internally recoverable, above position- and frequency-matched baselines and a length-matched degradation baseline; and (3) suppressing the stale placeholder (not editing the fact) restores fresh retrieval with high specificity, without corrupting earlier correct slots.
Related Work: A growing body shows LLMs encode future-output attributes in advance: Emergent Response Planning (2025) probes future structure/content/behavior; ParaScopes (2025) decodes paragraph-scale plans; Future Lens (2023) recovers subsequent tokens from a single hidden state; chess look-ahead (Jenner et al. 2024) shows future targets are represented and moved backward in time. Separately, long-context factual degradation, recency/position bias, and attention dilution are documented and constitute the main alternative explanation we must rule out. All planning/lookahead work establishes that plan information is encoded and decodable and treats it as a capability; none ask whether an early reserved slot for a specific upcoming fact can be filled with the WRONG value that then overrides correct retrieval at generation time, none identify this as a factual-recall failure mode distinct from generic degradation, and none show a targeted intervention that suppresses the stale placeholder to recover the fact. Our controls are what separate the claim from position/length effects: the same fact, same model, isolated vs late-slot, permuted slot order, and matched cumulative context length. This is orthogonal to prior single-query proposals; here the object is a within-answer, position-dependent corruption caused by premature slot commitment during multi-fact generation.
Abstract: Large language models increasingly produce answers packed with multiple facts about a subject, and recent work shows they encode plans for their future output in advance. We ask whether this planning has a dark side for factual accuracy, with a concrete reliability consequence: a model can answer a fact correctly alone yet state it wrong when it appears later in the same response, so factual reliability of long-form synthesis depends on generation order, not just knowledge. We propose prefetch-slot override: when generating a multi-fact answer, the model reserves slots for facts it will state later and prefetches a coarse placeholder for each slot before the cursor arrives; when the placeholder is a plausible-but-wrong value (often the category-typical or more frequent entity), it overrides fresh retrieval at the slot. We distinguish this from generic long-context degradation with same-fact early-vs-late, permuted-order, and length-matched controls, and pre-register that if late-slot errors track isolated-query ignorance equally the claim collapses. We test three claims on templated multi-fact generation about entities, and additionally probe prevalence on a more realistic multi-fact biography-generation setting. (1) Prefetch decodability: the reserved slot's placeholder value is linearly decodable from the residual stream several tokens before the slot, at a position/layer distinct from where earlier facts are produced. (2) Override geometry: within-answer errors concentrate on later slots whose placeholder was mis-prefetched while the correct value remains internally recoverable (via probing and via querying the fact first), above position-, frequency-, and length-matched baselines. (3) Causal repair: suppressing the stale-placeholder direction, or patching the slot representation from an isolated-query run, restores the correct value with higher specificity and less collateral damage than fact editing or a 'double-check each fact' re-prompt, and we quantify the reduction in factual error rate in the generated answers, not only probing metrics. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — Multi-fact dataset and position-dependent override prevalence): Tests H2's behavioral core, that within-answer errors concentrate on later slots for the same fact that is answered correctly early or in isolation. Data: constructed from Wikidata (existing). Select 2,000 subjects each having >=4 single-token-first attributes under distinct relations (person: birth city, nationality, occupation, notable award; city: country, founding decade, mayor, region). For each subject build (i) a fixed-order K-slot multi-fact prompt, (ii) isolated single-fact queries, (iii) permuted-order versions placing each attribute early vs late. ~2,000 x (1 + 4 + 4) fits budget and yields >=1,500 paired early-vs-late items per attribute. To test prevalence beyond templated prompts, we add a realistic subset of 300 subjects for which the model free-generates a short multi-fact biography paragraph, scoring the same attributes for early-vs-late override to confirm the effect is not a template artifact. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared: accuracy of an attribute in an early slot vs a late slot vs isolation; a null where each fact is retrieved independently of position. Decisive metric (before data), first: increase in error rate from early/isolated to late slot for the SAME attribute (paired McNemar; mixed-effects logistic with slot-position x attribute), controlling for cumulative generation length. Convincing = late-slot error exceeds early/isolated by >=10pp with CI excluding 0 in >=3 relations, and late-slot wrong answers are disproportionately the category-typical/frequent entity. Negative = <=2pp position effect (no override; H2 fails). Indecision band 2-10pp: report weak position dependence.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Storage verification that the correct value is recoverable): Tests the 'hidden, not absent' half of H2. Data: override cases from Exp 1 (correct in isolation/early slot, wrong in a late slot). Model: same three frozen; a linear content probe on the residual stream at the pre-slot position, 80/20 split by fact, seeds {0,1,2}, label-shuffle control. Systems compared: (i) isolated/first-slot recall of the same fact, (ii) content-probe decoding of the correct value during the failing multi-fact run. Only cases passing both count as override (report coverage). Decisive metric (before data), first: content-probe recovery accuracy of the correct value at the pre-slot position minus the model's late-slot verbalized accuracy. Convincing = probe recovers the correct value at >=40pp above late-slot verbalized accuracy. Negative = probe within 10pp of verbalized (the fact is genuinely not retrieved; override reframed as ignorance). Indecision band 10-40pp: partial hidden storage; restrict downstream causal tests to high-confidence cases.

Experiment 3 (H1 — Ahead-of-time prefetch-placeholder decoding): Tests H1, that the reserved slot's placeholder is decodable several tokens before the slot is generated, at a position distinct from where earlier facts are produced. Data: Exp 1 multi-fact runs; probe train/test 80/20 by subject. Model: same three frozen; a linear probe decoding the value the model will emit at slot k, evaluated at offsets of 2/4/8 tokens before slot k while earlier facts are still being produced; seeds {0,1,2}, offset and layer by CV; label-shuffle and offset controls. Systems compared: override cases (does an early-decodable placeholder differ from the isolated-query answer?) vs correct cases; decoding at the pre-slot position vs at the earlier-fact positions. Decisive metric (before data), first: per-offset AUROC for decoding the emitted slot value ahead of time, and the fraction of override cases where a WRONG placeholder is decodable >=4 tokens early. Convincing = ahead-of-time AUROC >=0.70 at offset 4 AND >=50% of override cases show an early wrong placeholder that matches the later error. Negative = AUROC <=0.55 (no reserved placeholder; H1 fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report weak prefetching.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal repair by suppressing the stale placeholder): Tests H3, that suppressing the stale placeholder (or patching from an isolated-query run) restores fresh retrieval without editing the fact. Data: 1,000 held-out override cases (Exp 2). Model: same three frozen; activation edits at the pre-slot positions/layers from Exp 3, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) suppress the stale-placeholder direction (low-rank override-vs-correct difference); (b) patch the slot representation from an isolated-query run; (c) reverse control injecting a placeholder into an early slot; (d) content control (earlier correct slots unchanged); plus random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-slot recovery rate (emitted value flips to the isolated-query-correct value) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp over random at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=15pp override in early slots. Negative = <=5pp recovery (placeholder not causal; H3 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Repair specificity and collateral cost): Tests that H3's repair does not corrupt earlier correct slots or unrelated facts. Data: Exp 4 held-out override cases; the earlier correct slots in those same answers; 200 unrelated facts (PopQA). Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our suppression/patch vs a 'double-check each fact independently' re-prompt, re-querying each fact in isolation (upper bound), ROME editing (existing, expected null), random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: late-slot recovery rate MINUS accuracy drop on earlier correct slots (recovered-per-unit-collateral). Convincing = late-slot recovery >=25pp while earlier-slot accuracy drops <=3pp, unrelated accuracy drops <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = earlier-slot drop >=10pp or no net gain. Indecision band earlier-slot drop 3-10pp: utility capped; report trade-off.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Transfer, generality, and source): Tests whether a single suppression/patch recipe generalizes and whether override is driven by premature commitment to the category-typical value. Data: recipe fit on a subset of relations/positions (Exp 4) applied to held-out relations and positions (800 cases); plus a regression over all Exp 1 override rates on slot position, placeholder-vs-correct frequency gap, and inter-slot semantic relatedness. Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction; and the frequency-gap regressor vs position-only. Decisive metric (before data): (i) transferred recovery as a fraction of in-domain-refit; (ii) incremental Delta R^2 from the placeholder-vs-correct frequency gap over position-only. Convincing = transfer >=60% of in-domain on >=2 models AND frequency-gap Delta R^2 >=0.10 with positive sign (placeholder is the more frequent value). Negative = transfer <=20% OR frequency Delta R^2 <=0.02 (relation-specific and/or not frequency-driven). Indecision band: transfer 20-60% or Delta R^2 0.02-0.10 -> report partial generality/source. Report Spearman rho between model scale and override rate (N=3 caveat).
Risk Factors and Limitations: Position-dependent errors could arise from generic long-generation degradation or attention dilution rather than a specific stale-placeholder mechanism; the isolated-query control, permuted-order design (same fact early vs late), and the ahead-of-time placeholder decoding (Exp 4) are the decisive separators, and length controls are included.
The prefetched placeholder and the correct-value signal may be entangled; the causal patching/suppression tests (Exp 5), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Verifying a fact is 'stored' via isolated recall risks overestimation from format effects; conservative content-probe thresholds and first-slot recall as an additional check with reported coverage mitigate this.
Suppression could corrupt earlier correct slots or degrade fluency; the earlier-slot and unrelated-fact specificity controls (Exp 6) are central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.

Override may be rare relative to genuine ignorance for some attributes; the paired within-subject early-vs-late design maximizes power and a modest but significant position effect is still informative.
A single transferable intervention recipe may not exist if prefetching is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Ahead-of-time decoding is noisiest when slots are close together; primary analysis uses prompts with clear inter-slot separation and single-token-first answers, with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: retrieval_induced_suppression
Title: Retrieval-Induced Forgetting in LLMs: How Recalling Competing Facts Suppresses a Related Fact the Model Still Stores
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the classic retrieval-induced forgetting (RIF) effect from human memory, we hypothesize that when an LLM recalls some members of a shared category earlier in its output, it actively suppresses subsequent access to related-but-non-recalled members it otherwise stores. We separate two claims of differing strength: a primary BEHAVIORAL RIF signature, and a secondary, more speculative CAUSAL inhibition-direction claim. The strict RIF criterion (what would falsify it vs generic interference/priming): the target's accuracy drops after recalling CATEGORY-RELATED competitors but NOT after recalling unrelated facts, an equal-length filler, or length-matched decoding; if unrelated recall impairs equally it is generic interference, and if competitor recall HELPS it is priming - both refute RIF. We predict (1) this is a gradable behavioral phenomenon distinct from ordinary in-context interference, scaling with the semantic overlap and retrieval-effort of the earlier recall; (2) the correct answer remains linearly decodable during suppressed recall (hidden, not erased); and (3, secondary) an inhibitory 'recently-retrieved-competitor' direction is decodable and, only if it passes a specificity test (suppressing it restores the target without harming neighboring facts), suppressing it (not editing the fact) restores access. An operationally relevant effect is a >=8pp suppression that survives all matched controls.
Related Work: Human cognitive science establishes retrieval-induced forgetting (Anderson et al. 1994) and belief-inhibition-impairs-memory effects (De Neys & Franssens 2007; retrieval-induced impairment of analogical reasoning, 2019): actively retrieving some category members inhibits recall of related non-retrieved members. In LLMs, prior work studies reasoning-vs-retrieval competition (Reasoning or Retrieval? 2025; Knowledge-Neuron factual recall 2024), Toxic CoT where reasoning turns correct answers wrong via question-information loss in shallow layers (Focus on Your Question! 2024), and knowledge-conflict from externally injected context (Fakepedia). We position against the closest LLM baselines explicitly, one contrast per row: ordinary in-context interference / overwriting (co-activation at the query, not a post-retrieval after-effect); recency/forgetting (order effects, not category-specific inhibition); context priming (a distractor added to context, not the model's own prior retrieval act); versus our matched-control RIF test (impairment specific to related, competitively-retrieved items, after the model itself retrieved competitors). None transfer the RIF phenomenon - that the model's own earlier retrieval act leaves a lingering inhibitory trace that suppresses a related stored fact even after the competitors are no longer favored. This is a new behavioral phenomenon (RIF-in-LLMs) with a candidate causal locus and a non-destructive fix, orthogonal to prior query-internal competition and context-priming proposals.
Abstract: Human memory exhibits retrieval-induced forgetting (RIF): recalling some members of a category actively inhibits later recall of related, non-recalled members. We ask whether LLMs exhibit an analogous effect. The framing is a diagnostic of stored-knowledge suppression: an LLM may lose access to a stored fact simply because it just recalled related facts - not because the fact is absent or the prompt is hard - which matters for safety omissions (e.g., a correct but less-common treatment omitted after common ones are listed), memory debugging, and QA reliability. We propose retrieval-induced suppression and test it with a strict, pre-registered RIF criterion that separates it from generic interference and priming. (1) Behavioral signature (primary): for facts a model answers correctly in isolation, we first have it recall some competitors from the same category, then query a related non-recalled fact, and measure the accuracy drop relative to matched controls - recalling UNRELATED facts, and an equal-length filler - with output length, token budget, and answer position matched; suppression must appear only for category-related recall. We predict it scales with competitor-target semantic overlap and with retrieval effort. (2) Storage: a linear probe recovers the correct answer from intermediate activations during suppressed recall, pre-registered to guard against format leakage, showing the fact is hidden, not erased. (3) Mechanism (secondary): a linear 'recently-retrieved-competitor' inhibition signal is decodable and, subject to a specificity test, causally drives suppression; subtracting it restores access without broadly harming neighboring facts, outperforming a 'consider each item independently' re-prompt and fact editing. We report expected effect sizes and an operational threshold (>=8pp surviving all controls). Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, including a safe medical-fact replication.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — RIF dataset and suppression prevalence with matched controls): Tests H1's core behavioral claim, that recalling category competitors suppresses a related non-recalled stored fact beyond ordinary interference. Data: constructed from Wikidata (existing). Build category-structured sets (films directed by X, countries in region Y, works by author Z, drugs treating condition C); for each category designate practiced competitors Rp+, related-unpracticed targets Rp-, and unrelated-baseline items Nrp. Use 300 categories, ~2,000 Rp- targets the model answers correctly in isolation, single-token-first answers; report coverage. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared, output length matched: (a) suppression (recall Rp+ competitors, then query Rp-), (b) unrelated-recall control (recall Nrp, then query), (c) equal-length filler control. Decisive metric (before data), first: accuracy drop of Rp- targets in suppression vs the two controls (paired McNemar; mixed-effects logistic), the human RIF signature (Rp- < baseline, driven by category-related recall only). Convincing = suppression accuracy >=8pp below BOTH controls with CI excluding 0 in >=3 categories. Negative = suppression within 2pp of controls, or unrelated-recall drops equally (generic interference, not RIF; H1 fails). Indecision band 2-8pp: report weak RIF. A protective/opposite effect is recorded as an informative cross-species divergence.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Overlap and retrieval-effort dose-response): Tests H1's gradedness, that suppression rises with semantic overlap and competitive retrieval effort. Data: Exp 1 items, with (a) competitor-target overlap (entity-embedding similarity / taxonomic distance) and (b) retrieval effort (number of competitors recalled; easy high-frequency vs hard low-frequency competitors) varied. Model: same three frozen. Systems compared: suppression magnitude across overlap and effort levels; regression with overlap x effort. Decisive metric (before data): slope of suppression on overlap and on effort, plus the prediction that low-frequency targets suppress more. Convincing = both slopes positive with CI excluding 0, and effortful (low-frequency competitor) recall suppresses >=1.5x more than easy recall. Negative = both slopes' CI include 0 (suppression not graded by the RIF drivers; the RIF account weakens). Indecision band |standardized slope| < 0.1 with CI crossing 0: report as no reliable dose-response for that driver.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Hidden-knowledge probe): Tests H2, that the correct target stays linearly decodable during suppressed recall. Data: suppression cases from Exp 1; 80/20 split by fact; label-shuffle control. Model: same three frozen; linear answer probe on subject-token/last-token residual stream, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV. Systems compared: probe recovery in the suppression condition vs the model's verbalized accuracy there vs the isolation-condition probe (upper bound). Decisive metric (before data), first: probe recovery minus verbalized accuracy on suppression cases. Convincing = probe recovers at >=40pp above verbalized and within 10pp of the isolation probe (hidden, not erased). Negative = probe within 10pp of verbalized (target genuinely lost; H2 fails). Indecision band 10-40pp: partial hidden knowledge, report as graded.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Inhibition-signal localization): Tests the internal correlate underpinning H3 -- a separable 'recently-retrieved-competitor' inhibition direction. Data: Exp 1 activations at the target query, suppression vs unrelated-recall contrast. Model: same three frozen; contrastive mean-difference inhibition direction per layer; target-content probe for residualization; no weight training. Systems compared: inhibition direction residualized on target-content (it should track presence/overlap of recalled competitors, not the specific target). Decisive metric (before data): residual decodability (AUROC) of the inhibition signal after removing target-content, best layer, and whether its magnitude correlates with attention over the earlier-recalled tokens. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 and positive correlation with competitor-attention. Negative = residual AUROC <=0.55 (no separable inhibition signal; H3's locus fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report an entangled, graded inhibition signal.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Causal recovery): Tests H3's causal claim, that suppressing the inhibition direction restores access. Data: 1,000 held-out suppression cases. Model: same three frozen; activation edits at Exp 4 layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) suppress the inhibition direction; (b) patch the target-query residual stream from an unrelated-recall run; (c) reverse control injecting the inhibition direction into an unrelated-recall run; (d) content control (unrelated facts unchanged); plus random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-target recovery rate (matches the isolation-condition answer) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp over random at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=15pp suppression. Negative = <=5pp recovery (inhibition not causal; H3 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Recovery specificity and collateral cost): Tests that H3's recovery is specific. Data: Exp 5 held-out cases; the recalled Rp+ competitors; Rp- targets already correct under suppression; 200 unrelated facts. Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our suppression vs a 'consider each item independently / ignore earlier answers' re-prompt, fresh-context re-query (upper bound), ROME editing (existing, expected null), random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: target recovery rate MINUS accuracy drop on Rp+ competitors and already-correct Rp- (recovered-per-unit-collateral). Convincing = recovery >=25pp while Rp+/already-correct accuracy drops <=3pp, unrelated <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = collateral drop >=10pp or no net gain. Indecision band 3-10pp collateral: utility capped; report trade-off.

Experiment 7 (H3 — Transfer, generality, and safety): Tests whether a single inhibition-suppression vector generalizes and whether RIF causes higher-stakes omissions. Data: vector fit on a subset of categories (Exp 5) applied to held-out categories (800 cases); plus a clinical replication of Exp 1-2 on a curated safe medical subset (after recalling several common treatments, does the model suppress a correct less-common but critical treatment/contraindication?), 600 items from an existing medical QA source. Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction; clinical suppression vs general-knowledge suppression. Decisive metric (before data): (i) transferred recovery as a fraction of in-domain-refit; (ii) clinical suppression prevalence. Convincing = transfer >=60% of in-domain on >=2 models AND clinical suppression >=8pp (at least as large as general). Negative = transfer <=20% OR clinical suppression <=2pp. Indecision band: transfer 20-60% or clinical 2-8pp -> partial. Report Spearman rho between model scale and RIF magnitude (N=3 caveat).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The suppression could be ordinary in-context interference or generic long-output degradation rather than a genuine RIF after-effect; the matched unrelated-recall and equal-length filler controls (Exp 2), the overlap dose-response (Exp 3), and the RIF-specific prediction that only *category-related* non-recalled items are impaired are the decisive separators.

A key RIF prediction (impairment specific to related, competitively-retrieved items) may not hold in LLMs; a null or opposite result (recalling competitors *helps* via priming) would refute the transfer but is itself an informative finding about how LLM memory differs from human memory.
Verifying the target is 'stored' via isolation recall risks overestimation from format effects; conservative content-probe thresholds and fresh-context re-query with reported coverage mitigate this.
The inhibition and target-content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 6), not probe accuracy alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

The recovery intervention could re-corrupt the recalled competitors or degrade fluency; the Rp+/Rp-/unrelated specificity controls (Exp 7) are central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
A single transferable inhibition-suppression vector may not exist if RIF is category-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: parametric_binding_capacity
Title: Who Did What? A Working-Memory Binding-Error Signature in LLMs' Simultaneous Recall of Multiple Entities
Short Hypothesis: Primary claim (one falsifiable sentence): when an LLM must recall parametrically-stored attributes of several distinctly-named entities at once, its errors are dominated by BINDING errors — correctly retrieving the pool of attributes but MISASSIGNING them across the co-queried entities (swapping A's attribute onto B) — rather than by attribute loss or out-of-set intrusion, and this swap dominance grows with the number of co-queried entities (a set-size effect). Swap, intrusion, and omission are pre-registered mutually-exclusive labels, and a swap must be the correct answer for a specific co-queried entity (controlling output-ordering and copying). This is framed explicitly as a new problem setting plus error signature (parametric multi-entity recall), not a new general theory of binding. Secondary predictions: (a) on swaps the correct attributes are still decodable (binding failure, not retrieval failure); (b) an entity-attribute binding-attention pathway carries the assignment and its degradation causally produces swaps; (c) strengthening that binding non-destructively reduces swaps — claimed only if the intervention isolates binding from retrieval and output-format effects.
Related Work: Human WM research shows capacity limits specifically impair temporary bindings, not items: increasing set size raises binding errors (confusing which attribute belongs to which list item) while item memory is spared (Oberauer 2019 'WM Capacity Limits Memory for Bindings'; the Interference Model 2012/2023). In LLMs, PI-LLM / 'Unable to Forget' (2025) study proactive interference over IN-CONTEXT streamed key-value updates (the attributes are given in the prompt and later overwritten), and n-back capacity work (2023-2024) shows attention-entropy-driven capacity limits on in-context tasks. All existing LLM work provides the to-be-bound information in context; none study whether recalling PARAMETRICALLY-STORED attributes of multiple entities simultaneously produces the human binding-error signature (misassignment, not loss), whether it scales with the number of co-queried entities, or whether a specific attention binding pathway causally produces the swaps. This is also distinct from my prior proposals: retrieval_competition concerns candidate competition for a single entity; context_priming_contamination and homograph_entity_fusion concern bleed from a different or same-named entity; here the object is cross-entity attribute MISBINDING among several correctly-stored, distinctly-named entities held in working memory at once. Primary novelty anchor: a new problem setting (simultaneous recall of separately-stored attributes of distinctly-named entities) and a human-WM-style swap-over-intrusion error signature — distinct from in-context binding benchmarks (PI-LLM, MultiBind) where the to-be-bound information is given in the prompt; the causal binding-attention account is a secondary mechanistic contribution.
Abstract: User-facing consequence first: asked about several known entities in one shot ('give the birth country of Curie, Einstein, and Turing'), an LLM increasingly reports the right facts attached to the wrong entities as the list grows — a swap failure directly relevant to multi-entity QA, agent state-tracking, and knowledge retrieval. A hallmark of human working memory is that its capacity limit does not erase items but corrupts their bindings: as more items are held, people increasingly confuse which attribute goes with which item, while rarely intruding attributes that were never in the set. We ask whether large language models exhibit this binding-error signature when recalling parametrically-stored facts about several entities simultaneously. We construct queries that ask for one attribute of each of k co-mentioned entities (e.g., 'Give the birth country of Marie Curie, Albert Einstein, and Alan Turing'), where the model reliably recalls each attribute in isolation. We predict three things. (1) Behavioral signature: as k grows, accuracy declines and the errors are dominated by cross-entity binding errors—the model outputs an attribute that is correct for a DIFFERENT co-queried entity (a swap) far more than it outputs an attribute belonging to no queried entity (an extra-list intrusion) or omits it, mirroring the human within-set binding-error pattern, above frequency- and length-matched baselines. (2) Mechanism: a swap is a binding failure, not a retrieval failure—the correct attribute pool is present (all correct attributes are decodable / appear somewhere in the output) but the entity-to-attribute assignment is scrambled; an attention pathway that binds each attribute to its subject token carries the assignment, and its degradation (measured by attention dispersion across the co-queried subjects, echoing n-back attention-entropy findings) predicts swaps. (3) Causal, non-destructive recovery: strengthening the entity-attribute binding attention (or patching the binding representation from a single-entity run) reduces swaps and recovers correct assignments with high specificity, outperforming a 'answer one at a time' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on entity-attribute sets from PopQA/T-REx, evaluating set-size dose-response, error-type decomposition, attention-dispersion prediction, causal recovery, and specificity. If confirmed, swap-dominant binding failures are a concrete diagnostic target for multi-entity reasoning and agent reliability. We state plainly that the primary contribution is a behavioral phenotype (H1: swap dominance and set-size scaling), with the retrieval-intact and causal-binding-pathway results as secondary mechanistic analyses.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — set-size dose-response on simultaneous recall): Tests that recall accuracy declines as the number of co-queried entities grows, beyond added prompt length. Data: PopQA (14,267) and T-REx; select entities with single-token-first attributes under a shared relation (person->birth country, city->country, element->group). For each set size k in {1,2,3,4,6,8}, build queries listing k distinct, differently-named entities, including only entities the model answers correctly at k=1; match sets on popularity and total prompt length across k; target ~400 sets per k per model (capped for compute; report coverage). Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, all weights frozen, temperature 0; no trained parameters. Systems compared: accuracy across k vs a length-matched filler control (the k=1 target padded with equal-length non-entity filler), separating set size from length. Decisive metric: per-entity accuracy slope vs k (mixed-effects logistic, controlling length and per-entity difficulty); secondary: accuracy gap between the k-entity set and the length-matched filler at each k. Convincing: a significant monotone accuracy decline with k that exceeds the filler control by >=8 pp at k>=4, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: decline present but the set-vs-filler gap is 3-8 pp -> length partly confounds, partial support. Negative (no decline, or set matches filler) means simultaneous recall shows no capacity-limited set-size effect.

Experiment 2 (H1 — binding-error dominance): Tests that errors at k>1 are dominated by cross-entity swaps (misassignment) rather than out-of-set intrusions or omissions. Data: the erroneous responses from Exp 1 at k>1; each error labeled SWAP (attribute correct for a different co-queried entity), EXTRA-LIST INTRUSION (belongs to no queried entity), or OMISSION/other, with randomized entity order to control copying, and split by whether co-queried entities are semantically similar vs dissimilar (testing that swaps are not driven by content similarity alone). Model: the same three frozen models, temperature 0. Systems compared: the swap rate vs the extra-list-intrusion rate as a function of k, against a random-substitution null (where swaps and intrusions would scale with set composition alone). Decisive metric: swap-to-intrusion ratio and its growth with k; secondary: absolute swap rate. Convincing: swaps significantly exceed intrusions (ratio >=2:1) and the ratio rises with k while intrusions stay near baseline, in >=2 of 3 models — the within-set-confusion signature. Undecidable band: ratio 1.2-2:1, or flat in k -> binding signature weak, partial support. Negative (intrusions >= swaps, or ratio <=1.2:1) refutes the binding-error transfer: errors are dominated by out-of-set intrusion or loss, an informative cross-species divergence.

Experiment 3 (H1 — retrieval intact, assignment scrambled): Tests that a swap is a binding failure, not a retrieval failure — the correct attributes are retrieved but misassigned. Data: swap-error trials from Exp 2; for each, check whether the emitted set is a permutation of the set's correct attributes, and probe each subject's position. Model: frozen; a per-layer L2-logistic content probe (target = that subject's correct attribute), trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds with a shuffle null. Systems compared: (i) rate at which the output is a permutation of the correct answers vs chance permutation; (ii) per-subject probe recovery on swap trials vs the verbalized (misassigned) answer. Decisive metric: per-subject probe recovery of the correct attribute on swap trials; secondary: permutation-of-correct-answers rate above chance. Convincing: probe recovers each subject's correct attribute at >=60% on swap trials (>> verbalized), and outputs are permutations of the correct set above chance, in >=2 of 3 models — establishing binding failure. Undecidable band: recovery 40-60% -> partly retrieved, partly lost, mixed mechanism. Negative (recovery near shuffle, outputs not permutations) means swaps are retrieval failures (attribute absent), not binding failures — refuting the mechanism.

Experiment 4 (H3 — attention binding pathway causally produces swaps): Tests that an entity-attribute binding attention pathway carries the assignment and that its degradation causally produces swaps. Data: the k>1 sets from Exp 1-2; identify heads whose answer-position attention concentrates on the corresponding subject token (candidate binding heads); 300 held-out sets for intervention. Model: frozen; measure binding-attention dispersion = entropy of the answer position's attention over co-queried subjects; interventions sharpen (upweight own-subject, downweight others) or blur (raise entropy) this attention, and patch the binding representation from a k=1 run; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: dispersion as a swap predictor (held-out AUROC); sharpen (reduce swaps) vs blur (induce swaps) vs random-attention-edit control vs content control. Decisive metric: swap-rate change from sharpening vs the random-edit control (pp), with induce/reduce symmetry; secondary: held-out AUROC of dispersion predicting swaps, and whether dispersion rises with k. Convincing: dispersion predicts swaps at AUROC >=0.70, sharpening cuts swaps >=10 pp and blurring induces >=10 pp over random-edit, while the content control does neither, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.58-0.70 or swap change 3-10 pp over control -> partial causal role. Negative (AUROC <=0.58 and swap change <=3 pp over control) means no causal binding-attention pathway; misbinding arises elsewhere.

Experiment 5 (H4 — binding-strengthening recovery with specificity): Tests that strengthening the binding reduces swaps and recovers assignments without editing facts and with high specificity. Data: held-out multi-entity queries (>=400 per model); specificity sets = single-entity (k=1) queries and entities already correctly assigned; monitor for new extra-list intrusions. Model: frozen; the best binding-strengthening intervention from Exp 4 applied with dose control across k and across the three models; 3 seeds. Systems compared: binding-strengthening vs an 'answer one entity at a time' re-prompt and vs splitting into k separate queries (upper bound), and a random-attention-edit control. Decisive metric: swap reduction and per-entity accuracy gain at each k, reported jointly with collateral drop on single-entity and already-correct sets and any new intrusions; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: swap reduction >=10 pp and accuracy gain >=8 pp at k>=4 with <=2 pp collateral drop and no new intrusions, beating the re-prompt, and transferring across relations and the three models. Undecidable band: gain 3-8 pp, or collateral 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (gain <=3 pp, collateral >5 pp, or new intrusions) means binding cannot be strengthened non-destructively.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Multi-entity queries add output-formatting demands that could cause errors unrelated to binding; the equal-length filler control (Exp 1), the swap-vs-intrusion diagnostic (Exp 2, which is specific to within-set confusion), and the attribute-pool-present test (Exp 3) are the decisive separators.

Swaps could reflect output-ordering/copying artifacts rather than genuine misbinding; randomizing entity order, comparing free-order vs fixed-order outputs, and requiring the swap to be the correct answer for a specific co-queried entity mitigate this.

The binding-attention signal and correct-attribute content may be entangled; the causal patching/attention tests (Exp 4), not attention-dispersion correlation alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Binding-strengthening could over-focus attention and harm cases needing cross-entity context, or degrade fluency; the single-entity and already-correct specificity controls (Exp 5) are central and utility may be capped.

LLMs may not reproduce the human dominance of swaps over intrusions (errors could be mostly out-of-set intrusions instead); a divergent pattern would refute the human-binding transfer but is itself an informative cross-species finding.
A single transferable binding-strengthening recipe may not exist if binding is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token attributes complicate assignment scoring and readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first attributes with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: prototype_pressure_override
Title: The Penguin Problem: How a Typicality-Gradient Prior Overrides Stored Atypical Facts About Category Members
Short Hypothesis: Primary claim (one falsifiable sentence): LLMs store a graded category-prototype signal that competes with instance-specific recall, producing prototype-pressure override — for an atypical category member the model asserts the prototype-consistent (but false-for-this-instance) attribute ('a penguin can fly') even though it correctly STORES the atypical fact, and override frequency rises monotonically with the instance's atypicality (distance from the category prototype). Storage is verified before the analysis (correct under isolating phrasing across paraphrases/formats AND content-probe-decodable) so override is separated from ignorance, and ambiguous attributes are filtered out. Secondary predictions: (a) on override the correct atypical attribute stays linearly decodable (hidden, not lost) while a prototype-strength signal — separable from instance content, meaning it decodes above a shuffle null after residualizing out content and tracks typicality rather than the queried answer — predicts and causally drives the error; (b) suppressing the prototype direction restores the atypical fact without flipping correct typical-member answers. The central novelty is the real-member factual-override phenomenon plus the hidden-knowledge dissociation; the transferable suppression vector is framed as exploratory.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs exhibit graded typicality effects (Do LMs learn typicality judgments from text 2021; How Well Do DL Models Capture the Typicality Effect 2024; Cross-Language Typicality 2025), that property inheritance in LMs is jointly driven by taxonomy and similarity and these are entangled in internal subspaces (Characterizing Similarity in Property Inferences 2024; Property Induction Framework 2022), and that categorical/hierarchical concepts are encoded as linear polytopes with orthogonal parent-child geometry (Geometry of Categorical and Hierarchical Concepts 2024). Human graded-membership theory (Typicality/Graded Membership/Vagueness 2007; HyperLex 2016) motivates the phenomenon. Crucially, all existing LLM work asks whether models *reproduce* graded typicality or generalize novel properties along taxonomy/similarity; none isolate a *factual-recall failure* in which a typicality-gradient prior *overrides a genuinely stored atypical attribute* of a real category member (the 'penguin flies' error), none show the correct atypical value stays internally decodable during the override, and none demonstrate a causal prototype-suppression fix. This is distinct from my property_collapse (sibling-relation confusion sharing a subspace) and inheritance_failure (composition of a superordinate property into an instance): here the object is the graded prototype signal itself overriding a correctly-stored, category-violating attribute, and the failure axis is instance atypicality. Primary novelty anchor: not prototype/typicality geometry itself (well established), but its reframing as a factual-recall OVERRIDE of a genuinely-stored, category-violating attribute on real members, with a hidden-knowledge dissociation and a causal prototype-suppression test; low-rank suppression is a diagnostic/repair consequence of the mechanism claim, not itself the novelty.
Abstract: User-facing consequence first: some LLM factual errors about exceptions ('a penguin can fly', 'a whale lives on land') are not missing knowledge but prototype pressure overriding a fact the model actually stores — a distinct, potentially repairable class of hidden-knowledge failures relevant wherever exceptions matter for factuality and trustworthiness. Humans and LLMs both represent category members on a typicality gradient—a robin is a more central bird than a penguin. We ask whether this graded prototype structure produces a systematic factual-recall failure. We propose prototype-pressure override: when asked about an attribute of an atypical category member, an LLM asserts the prototype-consistent value ('a penguin can fly') even though it correctly stores the atypical fact, because a graded prototype signal competes with and overrides instance-specific recall. We test three claims on category-attribute queries over real entities with known typical and atypical members. (1) Behavioral signature: for attributes the model recalls correctly under an isolating phrasing, prototype-consistent errors on atypical members rise monotonically with the instance's atypicality (its distance from the category prototype, estimated from the model's own typicality gradient and from human norms), above frequency-matched baselines. (2) Hidden fact and locus: on override errors a linear probe recovers the correct atypical attribute from intermediate activations at rates far above the verbalized answer (hidden, not lost), and a prototype-strength signal—decodable before the answer and separable (via residualization) from the instance-content signal—predicts override. (3) Causal recovery: suppressing the prototype direction, or patching the instance representation from an isolating run, restores the correct atypical attribute with high specificity—preserving correct recall on typical members—whereas fact editing does not, and it outperforms a 'be precise about this specific case' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, evaluating atypicality dose-response, hidden-fact recovery, causal recovery, and specificity. We narrow the primary claim to behavioral override plus the hidden-knowledge dissociation (H1-H2), framing general prototype-suppression transfer as exploratory, and we report whether the failure occurs at nontrivial rates beyond curated category-property pairs. Attributes are ambiguity-filtered and prompts include naturalistic phrasings alongside templated yes/no forms.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — atypicality dose-response of prototype-pressure override): Tests that prototype-consistent errors on atypical category members rise monotonically with the instance's atypicality, on facts the model verifiably stores (separating override from ignorance). Data: curated categories with a shared characteristic property true for typical members but false for specific atypical members with authoritative ground truth (birds+can-fly: robin=yes, penguin/ostrich/kiwi=no; mammals+live-on-land: whale/dolphin=no; fruits+sweet: lemon=no; fish+has-scales: shark/catfish=no; reptiles+lays-eggs: some vipers=no); target ~800 (member, property) items per model spanning the typicality gradient (capped; report coverage). Storage verification (embedded): keep only atypical items the model answers correctly under an isolating phrasing AND whose correct answer a content probe decodes — the 'override-candidate' set — so any prototype-pressure error is not ignorance. Atypicality estimated two ways: the model's own typicality gradient and human norms where available. Attributes with ambiguous truth (e.g., senses of 'sweet', 'scales', 'lays eggs') are filtered by requiring an authoritative source plus >=90% agreement of a GPT-4o judge and a human spot-check; queries use both templated yes/no (single-token-first) and one naturalistic paraphrase to check the override is not a template artifact. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0. Systems compared: prototype-consistent error rate vs atypicality (mixed-effects logistic controlling popularity, property frequency, length), with a typical-member control (should be answered correctly). Decisive metric: the override-rate-vs-atypicality slope; secondary: correlation with human typicality norms. Convincing: a significant positive monotone slope with error rate >=15 pp higher for the most atypical decile than the least, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: slope positive but the extreme-decile gap is 5-15 pp -> weak effect, partial support. Negative (flat slope) refutes the atypicality-graded override claim.

Experiment 2 (H2 — hidden atypical fact and prototype-strength signal): Tests that during override the correct atypical attribute stays decodable and a separable prototype-strength signal predicts the error. Data: override errors from Exp 1 and their isolating-phrasing runs; residual stream cached at subject/last-token across layers. Model: frozen; per-layer L2-logistic probes — a content probe (target = correct atypical answer) and a prototype-strength probe (target = the member's category-prototype similarity/typicality) — trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds; the prototype probe residualized against content; shuffle null. Systems compared: content-probe recovery on override errors vs verbalized (~0) and vs the isolating run; prototype-strength signal as an override predictor after residualizing out content; alignment with the category concept vector. Decisive metric: content-probe recovery of the correct atypical answer on override errors; secondary: per-layer AUROC of the prototype-strength signal predicting override after residualization, and its regression on atypicality vs true difficulty. Convincing: content recovery >=60% (>> verbalized, comparable to the isolating run) AND prototype-strength AUROC >=0.72 after residualization, tracking typicality not the queried answer, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: recovery 40-60% or AUROC 0.60-0.72 -> partly hidden/entangled, partial support. Negative (recovery near verbalized, or no separable prototype signal) refutes the hidden-fact and separable-prototype claims.

Experiment 3 (H2 — the prototype signal causally drives override): Tests that the prototype-strength signal causally produces the override. Data: 300 override cases and 300 typical-member items per model, held out from Exp-2 probe training. Method: suppress the prototype-strength direction (low-rank difference between prototype-dominant and instance-dominant states) on override cases; patch the instance representation from an isolating run into an override run; inject the prototype direction into an isolating run to induce override (dose-response with atypicality); a content control. Model: frozen; interventions at Exp-2 layers, dose swept {0.5,1,2,4}x, 3 seeds. Systems compared: suppression, instance-patch, prototype-injection-induce, content control, random-direction control. Decisive metric: correct-atypical-answer expression rate from suppression/instance-patch vs the random-direction/content controls; secondary: induced-override rate from prototype injection with atypicality dose-response. Convincing: suppression/patch expresses the correct atypical answer on >=50% of override cases while injection induces >=15 pp override over random-direction with monotone dose-response, and the content control does neither, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: expression 25-50%, or induced 5-15 pp -> partial causal role. Negative (expression <=25% and induced <=5 pp over control, or content control matches) means the prototype signal is correlational.

Experiment 4 (H3 — prototype-suppression recovery preserving typical members, with generality): Tests that suppressing the prototype direction restores atypical facts without flipping correct typical-member answers, and generalizes. Data: held-out override cases (>=400 per model); specificity sets = typical members (prototype-consistent answer is correct and must not flip to a false negative), already-correct atypical items, and 200 unrelated facts. Model: frozen; a low-rank prototype-suppression vector fitted on a subset of categories (e.g., birds+can-fly) and applied to held-out categories (e.g., mammals+live-on-land) and across the three models; dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: prototype-suppression vs a 'consider this specific case carefully' re-prompt, ROME editing (expected null since the fact is stored), and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: atypical-fact recovery rate, reported jointly with typical-member accuracy change (must not drop) and collateral on already-correct and 200-unrelated sets; secondary: held-out perplexity. Convincing: recovery >=40% with <=2 pp typical-member accuracy drop and <=2 pp other collateral, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, transferring across categories and models. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, or typical-member drop 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (recovery <=20%, or typical-member accuracy drops >5 pp) means the prototype cannot be suppressed non-destructively.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Prototype-consistent errors could reflect genuine ignorance of the atypical fact rather than override; the storage-verification step (Exp 1) and the isolating-phrasing recovery are the decisive separators, with conservative content-probe thresholds and reported coverage.

The prototype-strength and instance-content signals may be entangled (typicality and category concept share subspaces, per Property Inferences 2024 and the polytope geometry); the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 3), not probe separability alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Suppressing the prototype direction could over-correct—flipping correct prototype-consistent answers on typical members to false negatives, or degrading fluency; the typical-member specificity control (Exp 4) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.

Atypicality is estimated (from the model's own gradient and human norms) and imperfect; we use multiple operationalizations and report their consistency, and the dose-response is robust to monotone atypicality proxies.

Override may be modest relative to genuine ignorance for very obscure atypical members; the popularity-matched baseline and paired within-category design (typical vs atypical members) maximize power, and a significant monotonic effect is still informative.
A single transferable prototype-suppression vector may not exist if the prior is category-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Yes/no verification framing is prompt-sensitive; we use multiple paraphrases and restrict to single-token-first answers, reporting robustness and coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: ordinal_access_chain
Title: Recited but Not Indexed: Why LLMs Know a Sequence Yet Fail to Retrieve Its Nth Element
Short Hypothesis: Primary claim (the paper's main contribution): the representational format of memorized real-world ordered knowledge is dissociable — a neighbor-CHAIN signal (predicting adjacent elements) and a running-POSITION/INDEX signal are separately decodable, and the index signal is selectively weak/absent during positional-query failures, so 'what is the Nth element' fails while 'what comes after Y' succeeds even though the Nth element is internally recoverable. The behavioral gap (positional << neighbor accuracy, worse mid-sequence) is treated as an incremental, expected phenomenon; the genuine contributions are (i) the chain-vs-index representational dissociation and (ii) causal recovery by patching/injecting a running-position signal from a recitation run (with reverse ablation impairing positional access). Falsification: if the index signal is equally strong during failures, or chain and index are inseparable, or recovery fails, the chain-over-index account is refuted. We separate this storage-format failure from generic counting/arithmetic incompetence via a counting-competence baseline (same-N positional queries over an in-context-provided list, where counting must work) and the neighbor-vs-positional contrast on the same elements.
Related Work: Beyond Memorization (2024) shows LLMs access parametric memory sequentially but struggle with RANDOM access, mitigating via recitation and training-time sentence permutation on SYNTHETIC data; it offers no inference-time mechanistic locus, no test on real-world ordered knowledge, and no steering fix. Your-Context-Is-Not-an-Array (2024) locates in-CONTEXT random-access failure in attention on algorithmic tasks, not parametric ordered knowledge. Serial-position / temporal-bias / SORT / listwise-ranking work (2022-2025) all concern IN-CONTEXT ordering, positional bias, or episodic order recall, not positional access to sequences stored in weights. Structure-Development-in-List-Sorting (2025) studies training-time head specialization on synthetic sorting. Crucially, none isolate ordinal-access-by-position as a distinct parametric-recall failure on real ordered knowledge, none contrast a neighbor-chain vs position-index representation causally, and none show a non-destructive intervention that recovers the Nth element. This is orthogonal to all my prior single-fact retrieval/gating proposals; here the object is the internal representational format of ordered knowledge (chain vs index) and how query type gates access. Primary novelty anchor: not the sequential-easy/random-hard behavioral gap (established by Beyond Memorization on synthetic data with training-time mitigation), but an inference-time representational dissociation (chain vs index) on REAL memorized ordered knowledge plus a causal position-injection fix — distinct from in-context lost-in-the-middle/positional-bias work and from the Reversal Curse.
Abstract: User-facing consequence first: an LLM can flawlessly recite the order of US presidents yet fail 'who was the 14th president', so correct recitation does NOT imply indexable access — a representational-access failure (not missing knowledge) that harms chronology QA, rankings, taxonomies, and multi-hop retrieval over ordered facts. Large language models memorize ordered sequences from pretraining: the order of US presidents, the alphabet, chart rankings, the periodic-table order, a book's chapter order. Prior work shows LLMs can recite memorized content sequentially but struggle to access it randomly, mitigating this only at training time on synthetic data. We propose an inference-time mechanistic account for real ordered knowledge: LLMs store sequences as a neighbor-linked chain accessible by traversal, not as position-indexed slots, so positional queries fail while neighbor queries succeed. We call this ordinal-access failure, and predict it is not a storage failure: the Nth element is internally recoverable even when the model cannot answer 'what is the Nth element'. We test three claims on curated ordered-knowledge sets. (1) Behavioral signature: for sequences the model can fully recite and whose neighbor relations it answers correctly, direct positional queries ('what is the Nth X?') fail at rates far above neighbor queries, and failure grows with position N and with mid-sequence location, above frequency-matched baselines. (2) Chain-vs-index dissociation: a linear probe recovers a neighbor-chain signal (predicting adjacent elements) and, separately, a running-position/index signal; whether a query is answered by chain traversal vs index lookup is decodable, and on positional failures the correct element remains decodable while the position-index signal is weak/absent. (3) Causal recovery: patching a 'running-position' representation from a recitation run into a direct-positional-query run, or injecting a decoded position-index direction, recovers the Nth element with high specificity, whereas fact editing does not, and outperforms a 'recite then answer' re-prompt. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, evaluating positional-vs-neighbor accuracy, position dose-response, hidden-element recovery, causal recovery, and specificity. This matters even where tools/retrieval exist, because parametric ordered recall still underlies many reasoning steps and benchmark items, and it argues for access-aware knowledge probing. We include at least one non-canonical, user-relevant sequence family and a counting-competence baseline. The representational dissociation and causal recovery are the primary claims; the behavioral gap and dose-response are secondary.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — ordinal-access failure with hidden Nth element): Tests that direct positional queries fail where neighbor queries succeed on the same elements, and that the Nth element is nonetheless internally recoverable.
