Data: sequences with authoritative order from Wikidata/reference sources — ordinal succession (US presidents, monarchs, Olympic hosts by year), canonical fixed orders (alphabet, months, periodic-table order, planets), ranked lists (chart-topping songs, champions by year); restrict to sequences the model recites in full correctly and to single-token-first answers; target ~200 sequences with ~3,000 elements per model (capped; report coverage). Three query forms per element: NEIGHBOR, POSITIONAL, FULL RECITATION. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen, temperature 0; the only fitted object is a per-layer L2-logistic probe (held-out sequences, 70%/30%, 3 seeds, shuffle null) reading the Nth element on positional-failure trials. Systems compared: POSITIONAL accuracy vs NEIGHBOR accuracy on the same neighbor-correct elements (paired McNemar); probe recovery vs verbalized on positional failures. Decisive metric: positional-minus-neighbor accuracy gap on the same elements; secondary: probe recovery of the correct Nth element on positional failures vs verbalized. Convincing: positional accuracy >=15 pp below neighbor accuracy AND probe recovers the Nth element on >=60% of positional failures (>> verbalized), in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: gap 5-15 pp, or recovery 40-60% -> weak/partly-hidden, partial support. Negative (gap <5 pp, or recovery near verbalized) refutes the ordinal-access-failure and hidden-element claims.

Experiment 2 (H3 — position and mid-sequence dose-response): Tests that positional-query failure grows with N and is worst mid-sequence (longest chain traversal). Data: the positional-query results from Exp 1, indexed by position N and distance from both endpoints; controls for element popularity and sequence length. Model: the same three frozen models, temperature 0. Systems compared: positional accuracy as a function of N and mid-sequence location vs a null where accuracy is independent of position (mixed-effects logistic); plus a counting-competence baseline in which the same 'Nth element' query is answered over an in-context-PROVIDED list (so pure counting must succeed), isolating storage-format failure from arithmetic/counting incompetence. Decisive metric: the accuracy-vs-position curve shape — a significant decline with N and a U-shape (endpoints easy, middle hard) after controlling popularity/length; secondary: mid-sequence-minus-endpoint accuracy gap. Convincing: a significant monotone N effect and a mid-sequence dip >=15 pp below endpoints, robust to popularity controls, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: dip 5-15 pp, or an N effect present only without popularity control -> traversal-cost account weak, partial support. Negative (flat accuracy in N/position) means access is not traversal-cost-limited — evidence against the chain account.

Experiment 3 (H2 — chain-vs-index representational dissociation): Tests that a neighbor-chain signal and a running-position/index signal are separately decodable and that the index signal is weak/absent during positional failures. Data: residual stream from recitation, neighbor, and positional runs over the Exp-1 sequences. Model: frozen; two per-layer probes — a neighbor-chain probe (predict the adjacent element / adjacency) and a running-position/index probe (predict the current element's ordinal position during recitation) — trained 70%/30% over 3 seeds, residualized against each other, shuffle nulls. Systems compared: index-signal strength during recitation/neighbor success vs during positional failures. Decisive metric: index-probe accuracy during positional-query failures vs during recitation (the diagnostic drop); secondary: per-layer AUROC of each probe and their residual non-redundancy. Convincing: both probes decode above shuffle and non-redundantly, and the index signal is >=20 pp weaker during positional failures than during recitation, in >=2 of 3 models. Undecidable band: index drop 8-20 pp -> partial dissociation. Negative (index signal equally strong in both, or chain and index inseparable) weakens the chain-vs-index account; a genuine absence of any index signal is itself informative about a chain-only format.

Experiment 4 (H4 — recovery of the Nth element by injecting a running-position signal): Tests that patching a running-position representation from recitation, or injecting a decoded index direction scaled to N, recovers the Nth element without editing facts and specifically. Data: held-out positional-query failures (>=400 per model); specificity sets = neighbor queries, already-correct positional queries, and 200 unrelated non-sequence facts. Model: frozen; the running-position vector and index direction from Exp 3 (fitted on train sequences) applied to held-out sequences and across the three models; also an ablation of the index signal during recitation (should remove positional access); dose swept, 3 seeds. Systems compared: recitation-patch / index-injection vs a 'recite then answer' re-prompt (upper bound), chain-of-thought counting, ROME editing (expected null), and a random-direction control. Decisive metric: correct-Nth-element recovery rate, reported jointly with collateral change on neighbor, already-correct, and 200-unrelated sets; secondary: whether index-ablation during recitation removes positional access (reverse causal check), and held-out perplexity. Convincing: recovery >=40% with <=2 pp collateral drop, ablation removing positional access, beating the re-prompt by >=15 pp, transferring across sequence types and models. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, or collateral 2-5 pp -> capped utility. Negative (recovery <=20%, collateral >5 pp, or ablation has no effect) means position access cannot be causally injected — refuting the recovery claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Positional-query failure could reflect arithmetic/counting incompetence (the model cannot map N to a step count) rather than a chain-vs-index storage format; the hidden-element probe (Exp 1) and the recitation-patching recovery (Exp 4) separate storage-format failure from counting failure, and the neighbor-vs-positional contrast on the same elements controls for element knowledge.

The neighbor-chain and position-index signals may be entangled or the position signal may be genuinely absent (no index representation at all); the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 4), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and a graded result remains informative. A genuine absence of any position-index signal is itself an informative finding about the chain-only format.
Recitation itself may be imperfect or the model may recite a wrong order, confounding storage verification; we restrict to sequences with verified-correct full recitation and report coverage.

Position injection could over-correct (produce a plausible but wrong element at the target position) or degrade fluency; the neighbor-query and already-correct specificity controls (Exp 4) are central and utility may be capped.
Endpoint elements (first/last) may be trivially accessible for reasons unrelated to indexing (salience/frequency), inflating the U-shape; popularity controls and mid-sequence focus mitigate this.
A single transferable position-injection recipe may not exist if position encoding is sequence-type-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token elements complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: scalar_incoherence
Title: Ordered but Incoherent: When LLMs Answer Comparisons Pairwise Instead of From a Shared Scalar, Breaking Transitivity
Short Hypothesis: LLMs can store a coherent scalar for an entity attribute in a linear subspace, yet many comparative-recall queries are decided not by reading that scalar but by an ad-hoc pairwise 'who-is-bigger' shortcut driven by local lexical/frequency cues. We state the central claim causally, as a theorem-like prediction: shortcut-decided comparisons are the mechanistic CAUSE of transitivity violations (A>B, B>C, yet C>=A), because pairwise decisions need not cohere into a global order whereas scalar-decided comparisons are guaranteed transitive. A comparison is operationally 'shortcut-decided' when the model's answer diverges from the sign of its own scalar-subspace projection, or is confidently emitted at near-zero true scalar margin. We hypothesize (1) whether a comparison is scalar- vs shortcut-decided is decodable and gradable via the alignment between the answer and the scalar-subspace projection; (2) transitivity violations concentrate on shortcut-decided, small-margin triples above frequency- and margin-matched baselines AND above a fitted scalar-noise null; and (3) forcing the answer to be read from the shared scalar subspace (patching/steering the answer position toward the isolated scalar projections) restores a global transitivity index and improves comparison accuracy without editing any stored attribute value.
Related Work: The Geometry of Numerical Reasoning (2024) shows LLMs extract numeric attributes into linear subspaces and that causal intervention there alters comparison answers; Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding (2025) shows attributes share overlapping subspaces perturbed by irrelevant context. BERT IS-A transitivity (2022) and NLI/veridicality transitivity work show behavioral transitivity failure but offer no mechanism. Relational-reasoning-and-inductive-bias (2025) studies transitive inference via in-weights vs in-context circuits on synthetic ordinals, not stored real-world attributes; rationality/transitivity-axiom benchmarks (2025) are purely behavioral. Recent pairwise-comparison papers document that LLMs answer comparisons via local heuristics, but they treat the shortcut as a behavioral curiosity. We separate clearly what is prior art from our delta. Prior art: (a) numeric attributes live in linear/monotonic scalar subspaces, and (b) comparisons can be answered heuristically. What is new here: (1) that transitivity is the diagnostic OBSERVABLE of the shortcut - a global-coherence signature no single-comparison probe can reveal, so it is not a rebranding of pairwise-comparison work; (2) an operational scalar-vs-shortcut arbitration criterion; (3) the causal claim that shortcut decisions PRODUCE intransitivity, tested against a scalar-noise null; and (4) a non-destructive repair that restores global order by forcing scalar reading. This reframes comparative-recall failure as a scalar-vs-pairwise arbitration problem, orthogonal to prior single-fact and set-level proposals.
Abstract: Large language models can answer 'Was Einstein born before Curie?' and encode entity attributes like birth year in linear subspaces, yet they violate transitivity: told nothing false, they will affirm A>B and B>C but deny A>C. This matters wherever an assistant is trusted to rank or compare - dates, quantities, priorities - because intransitive comparisons make its factual ordering incoherent and unauditable. Prior mechanistic work assumes comparisons are read from a single shared scalar subspace, which would guarantee transitivity, so it cannot explain the violations; the linear scalar subspace and the existence of heuristic shortcuts are established prior art. Our new claim is causal: comparative recall is often decided by an ad-hoc pairwise 'who-is-bigger' shortcut driven by local lexical/frequency cues, and because pairwise decisions need not cohere, this shortcut is the mechanistic cause of transitivity violations. We test three claims on comparative queries over ordered attributes (birth/death year, latitude, elevation, population, physical size). (1) Dissociability: a probe over the attribute's scalar subspace predicts the correct comparison, while a separable, residualized 'pairwise-shortcut' signal predicts the model's answer beyond the scalar; each comparison is operationally labelled scalar- vs shortcut-decided. (2) Violation geometry: transitivity-violating triples concentrate on shortcut-decided, small-true-margin comparisons above frequency-, popularity-, and margin-matched baselines and above a fitted scalar-noise null, and the shortcut flag predicts held-out violations. (3) Causal repair: patching the answer to be read from the shared scalar subspace, or suppressing the pairwise-shortcut direction, restores a global transitivity index (measured over many triples, not cherry-picked cycles) and improves comparison accuracy with high specificity, whereas editing individual attribute values does not; we also report how often the repair changes user-visible comparison answers. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluating probe separability, violation prevalence, causal recovery, and specificity, and positioning transitivity as a new auditing signal for factual-comparison reliability.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — Ordered-attribute dataset and transitivity-violation prevalence): Tests the premise behind H2, that transitivity violations exist above what a single stored scalar with noise would produce. Data: constructed from Wikidata (existing knowledge base, >1M entities carry the target scalars) plus the existing THINGS/size-norm set for commonsense physical size. Across five attributes (birth year, death year, latitude, elevation, city population) we sample 2,000 entities each (10,000) spread evenly over each attribute's magnitude range, and form 3,000 known-order triples per attribute (15,000 triples = 45,000 pairwise yes/no queries); this many gives >=200 triples per margin bin for stable estimates and is capped there by inference cost. Each query uses one fixed template plus 3 paraphrases. Model: Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, weights frozen (bf16, single 80GB GPU), greedy decoding, no trainable parameters. Systems compared: observed cyclic-violation rate per triple vs a fitted single-scalar null (each pairwise answer sampled from one per-entity latent scalar with per-pair logistic noise fit to the data). Decisive metric (stated before data): excess cyclic-violation rate over the null, per attribute, with 95% bootstrap CI. Convincing = >=5 percentage-point (pp) excess with CI excluding 0 in >=3 of 5 attributes. Negative (<=1pp excess) = violations are explained by scalar-storage noise and H2's premise fails. Indecision band 1-5pp: report as inconclusive for that attribute and do NOT advance the shortcut interpretation there.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Scalar-subspace vs pairwise-shortcut probes): Tests H1's claim that whether a comparison is scalar- or shortcut-decided is decodable via two separable signals. Data: the 45,000 pairwise queries from Exp 1, split 80/20 by entity (no entity in both train and test). Model: same three frozen models; two trainable linear probes on the last-token residual stream at each layer -- (a) a PLS/linear scalar-subspace probe fit to each entity's ground-truth scalar, giving a scalar-difference prediction, and (b) a logistic 'answer probe' predicting the model's actual yes/no. L2-regularized, trained with seeds {0,1,2}, layer chosen by 5-fold CV on train only. Systems compared: scalar-difference sign vs true order; answer-probe vs model answer; and, by residualizing the answer probe on the scalar projection, the residual predictivity of the model's answer. Decisive metric (before data): residual AUROC of the answer probe after removing the scalar projection, best layer, test set. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 (a competing shortcut carries answer information beyond the scalar). Negative = <=0.55 (answer fully explained by the scalar; no separable shortcut, H1 fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report a graded, weak shortcut and do not claim clean dissociability. Label-shuffle control must sit at 0.50.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Violation geometry: concentration on shortcut-decided, small-margin triples): Tests H2's specific geometry claim. Data: the Exp 1 triples, each pairwise comparison tagged with (a) scalar margin = |difference of scalar projections| from Exp 2 and (b) answer-vs-scalar alignment; shortcut-decided = answer diverges from scalar prediction or margin near zero with a confident answer. Model: same frozen three; the Exp 2 probes reused (no new training). Systems compared: violation rate on shortcut-decided small-margin triples vs frequency- and margin-matched scalar-decided triples; a mixed-effects logistic regression predicts held-out violations from margin, shortcut-flag, entity co-occurrence frequency, and lexical similarity. Decisive metric (before data): odds ratio for the shortcut-flag predicting violations, controlling for frequency and margin, on held-out triples. Convincing = OR >=2.0 with CI excluding 1 and held-out AUROC >=0.65. Negative = OR CI includes 1 (violations not tied to shortcut decisions; H2 fails). Indecision band OR 1.3-2.0: report weak concentration, insufficient to attribute violations to the shortcut.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal repair by forcing scalar reading): Tests H3's core causal claim that forcing the answer to be read from the shared scalar subspace restores transitivity without editing any stored value. Data: 1,000 held-out shortcut-decided violating triples (from Exp 3), never used in probe training. Model: same frozen three; interventions are activation edits, no weight training. Systems compared, all at matched edit norm: (a) patch the comparison-answer position with the injected scalar projections of both entities computed in isolation; (b) suppress the learned pairwise-shortcut direction (low-rank difference of shortcut- vs scalar-decided matched states); (c) reverse control -- amplify the shortcut direction to induce violations; plus random-direction and no-op controls. Dose alpha swept over {0,0.5,1,2,4}x the direction norm. Decisive metric (before data): per-triple transitivity-restoration rate (fraction of violating triples made consistent) for (a)/(b) vs random-direction control. Convincing = >=30pp absolute gain over random control at a dose that keeps held-out perplexity within 5%. Negative = <=5pp gain (forcing scalar reading does not restore coherence; H3 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: report partial causal support. Reverse control must raise violations by >=10pp to confirm directionality.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Repair specificity and collateral cost): Tests that H3's repair is specific -- it restores coherence without editing stored values or harming unrelated behavior. Data: the Exp 4 held-out triples, plus 1,000 scalar-decided comparisons the model already answers correctly, plus 200 unrelated non-comparison facts sampled from PopQA (existing, ~14k questions). Model: same frozen three, best intervention and dose from Exp 4. Systems compared: our scalar-reading/shortcut-suppression vs a 'recall each value first, then compare' re-prompt, ROME editing of individual attribute values (existing method, expected null since values are not wrong), and random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), reported first: net transitivity-violation reduction MINUS accuracy drop on already-correct scalar-decided comparisons (recovered-per-unit-collateral). Convincing = violation reduction >=20pp while scalar-decided accuracy drops <=3pp and unrelated-fact accuracy drops <=2pp and perplexity rises <=5%. Negative = collateral drop >=10pp or no net gain. Indecision band: scalar-decided drop 3-10pp -> utility is capped; report the trade-off curve rather than a clean repair. ROME expected to give <=5pp violation reduction, confirming the failure is not per-value.

Experiment 6 (H1/H3 — Cross-attribute and cross-model transfer): Tests whether the H1 signals and H3 repair generalize rather than being attribute- or model-specific. Data: probes/directions fit on birth-year comparisons (from Exp 2/4) applied unchanged to elevation and city-population held-out triples (1,000 each). Model: repeat on all three frozen models. Systems compared: transferred direction vs an attribute-matched direction refit in-domain vs random-direction. Decisive metric (before data): transitivity-restoration rate of the transferred direction as a fraction of the in-domain-refit rate. Convincing = transferred achieves >=60% of in-domain rate on >=2 attributes and >=2 models. Negative = <=20% (repair is attribute-specific; practical generality fails, though the per-attribute science stands). Indecision band 20-60%: report partial transfer. Also report whether larger models show fewer violations (Spearman rho between parameter count and violation rate across the three models), with rho <=-0.3 taken as suggestive only given N=3.

Experiment 7 (H2 — Source analysis: lexical/frequency drivers of the shortcut): Tests the mechanistic source behind H2 -- that shortcut reliance is driven by local lexical/frequency 'who-is-bigger' cues rather than scalar retrieval. Data: all Exp 1 comparisons with per-pair features: scalar margin, entity-pair co-occurrence frequency (from an open web-corpus n-gram count), attribute type, lexical similarity. Model: frozen three, reusing Exp 2 shortcut-flags; no new training. Systems compared: nested regressions predicting shortcut reliance and violation rate with vs without the frequency/lexical features. Decisive metric (before data): incremental variance explained (Delta R^2) by frequency/lexical cues over margin-and-attribute-only, on held-out comparisons. Convincing = Delta R^2 >=0.10 with the frequency coefficient sign positive (more co-occurrence -> more shortcut) across >=2 models. Negative = Delta R^2 <=0.02 (shortcut not lexically driven; the source claim is unsupported though the behavioral/causal claims may stand). Indecision band 0.02-0.10: report frequency as a partial driver.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The scalar subspace and the model's answer may be so tightly coupled that a separable 'shortcut' signal is not identifiable; the residualization (Exp 3) and the causal induction of violations (Exp 5c) are the decisive tests, and a graded result remains informative.

Transitivity violations could reflect genuine scalar-storage noise rather than a distinct shortcut; the margin-matched null (Exp 2) and shortcut-vs-scalar arbitration measure (Exp 4) are designed to separate these, but the distinction may be partly a continuum.
Forcing scalar-based reading could degrade cases where the pairwise answer was actually correct, or hurt fluency; the scalar-decided specificity control (Exp 6) is central and utility may be capped.

Fitting a reliable scalar subspace requires enough entities per attribute and is noisiest for physical-size/commonsense attributes; we report which attributes admit reliable subspaces and restrict primary analysis accordingly.
A single transferable repair recipe may not exist if the shortcut is attribute-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Comparison answers depend on template phrasing (larger vs smaller framing); we use paraphrases and report robustness, since framing itself may modulate shortcut reliance.
Findings on 7-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: format_bound_knowledge
Title: Format-Bound Knowledge: Why LLMs Store the Same Fact in Multiple Query-Specific Copies and Fail to Transfer Between Them
Short Hypothesis: The same factual knowledge is stored not once but as several redundant, format-specific representations tied to the surface form of the query that taught it (e.g., cloze vs. question vs. comparative vs. procedural use). Retrieval failures often arise from a 'format mismatch': a query in one format cannot access a fact whose representation is bound to another format. We hypothesize these format-specific copies are (a) causally dissociable via activation patching, (b) linearly identifiable as distinct residual-stream directions for the same fact, and (c) that a single learned 'format-bridge' steering vector can transfer access across formats without weight editing. Primary falsifiable claim: within a single model, formats induce causally separable fact representations - patching a fact signal from a success format into a failure format restores access above a matched null. Secondary claims: (i) a single low-rank format-bridge vector transfers access across facts of a format pair, and (ii) format-boundedness traces to format-skewed pretraining exposure. The 'distinct linear directions' result is treated as a corroborating empirical signature, not the core claim; the account falsifies if format effects vanish after controlling for query difficulty/encoding or if patching transfers while probes do not separate. We say 'format-bound copies' as shorthand for causally separable access pathways, not a commitment to discrete storage over a shared store with format-specific access.
Related Work: Prior work localizes facts to mid-layer MLPs (ROME, Knowledge Neurons) and separates recall from reasoning circuits by layer/head (Disentangling Recall and Reasoning, 2025; LiReFs, 2025; Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning, 2025). Procedural-vs-declarative studies (Meta-Cognitive Analysis, 2024; Procedural Knowledge Drives Reasoning, 2024) and SynthWorlds (2025) show declarative and procedural knowledge behave differently but treat each fact as a single store accessed differently. Knowledge-neuron work on multi-hop recall (2024) and RL-improves-traversal (2025) note query representations diverge while fact representations stay similar. None ask whether a *single fact is stored as multiple format-bound copies* whose non-interchangeability causes retrieval failure, nor demonstrate a format-bridge intervention. We reframe the storage/retrieval debate: instead of 'one store, many queries,' we test 'many format-specific stores of the same fact,' a distinct and testable structural claim. In one sentence, our delta: unlike paraphrase-consistency and cross-lingual steering (the closest methodological baseline, compared against directly), we test whether formats induce causally separable fact representations within a single model, and we benchmark explicitly against the one-store-many-queries null. Who should care: interpretability, robustness, and knowledge-editing researchers, for whom format-boundedness implies format-aware evaluation suites and interventions rather than treating knowledge as a single invariant store.
Abstract: Large language models frequently answer a fact correctly when it is phrased one way but fail when it is phrased another, even without any reasoning steps. Standard accounts treat each fact as a single stored association accessed by different queries. We propose an alternative structural hypothesis: LLMs store the same fact as multiple redundant, format-specific representations, each bound to the surface form under which the fact was most often encountered (cloze completions, direct questions, comparative judgments, and procedural usage). Retrieval failures then arise from format mismatch: a query in one format activates a pathway to a copy that is missing or weak, while another copy holds the fact intact. We test this with a controlled multi-format probe set: for each fact we build four semantically equivalent query formats and identify facts answered correctly in some formats but not others. Using activation patching across formats and linear probing of the residual stream, we test whether (1) format-specific representations are causally dissociable, (2) the same fact yields distinct, format-predictive linear directions, and (3) patching or steering activations from a successful format into a failing one restores access. We further learn a single low-rank 'format-bridge' steering vector per format pair and test cross-fact, cross-format transfer, comparing recovery rate, specificity, and fluency against ROME weight editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B. Confirming the hypothesis would replace the 'one fact, many queries' picture with a 'many format-bound copies' account, unifying puzzling paraphrase-sensitivity and internal-vs-external knowledge gaps and yielding a cheap non-destructive way to unlock format-inaccessible knowledge. Phenomenon value is distinct from application value: even if the bridge vector is simple, format-bound access would change how the field builds factual-QA evaluation suites and editing-generalization tests (which must probe multiple formats) and would explain paraphrase-sensitivity without invoking missing knowledge. We keep the structural claim conservative - reporting a graded rather than discrete-copy geometry if the evidence warrants - and separate the bridge contribution, which stays useful even if the strong copy hypothesis weakens.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - multi-format fact set with per-format correctness): Builds the substrate for the one-store-vs-many-copies test by rendering each fact in four formats and recording per-format correctness. Data: facts from PopQA (14,282 questions, 16 relations), the T-REx slice of LAMA (~34k triples, 41 relations), and EntityQuestions (24 relations, ~176k questions); we sample 8,000 facts stratified by relation and popularity decile, fewer than the full pool because each fact is expanded into 4 formats (32,000 items) and re-scored on 3 models. Each fact is rendered as (a) cloze completion, (b) direct WH-question, (c) true/false verification, (d) comparative multiple-choice; format equivalence is filtered by a GPT-4o meaning-preservation judgment plus a 200-item human spot-check (kept if judge agreement >=0.9 and human agreement >=0.85). Split 70/30 fact-disjoint into analysis/test. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; greedy decoding, per-format correctness logged, seed 0 for generation. Systems compared: the four formats against each other, per fact. Decisive metric: per-format accuracy and the coverage of facts correct in >=1 format (first); supporting: pairwise format-agreement rates. Convincing: >=60% of facts are correct in at least one format and formats disagree on >=20% of facts, giving a usable format-bound pool. Undecidable band: format-disagreement of 10-20% is a thin substrate - proceed but flag low power for H1-H4. Negative: <10% disagreement means formats behave interchangeably, undercutting the format-boundedness premise before any mechanism test.

Experiment 2 (H1 - format-mismatch prevalence: one store vs. many copies): Tests whether a single format-independent store explains the data or whether a real fact-by-format interaction remains. Data: the 32,000 (fact, format) correctness records from Experiment 1's analysis split. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; the model here is the data source, and the statistical model is a logistic regression predicting correctness from per-fact difficulty, per-format bias, answer-space entropy, query length, and answer training-frequency, versus an augmented model adding a fact-by-format interaction (so a significant interaction cannot be explained by matched difficulty, answer entropy, or frequency); 3 cross-validation folds. Systems compared: null single-store logistic model vs. interaction model, likelihood-ratio tested. Decisive metric: fraction of facts correct in some-but-not-all formats (the format-bound set) that survives the null, i.e. the interaction's Delta pseudo-R^2 over the null (first); supporting: likelihood-ratio p-value and the raw format-bound fraction. Convincing: format-bound fraction >=20% with interaction Delta R^2 >=0.10 and LR p<0.001 - inconsistent with a single format-independent store. Undecidable band: Delta R^2 0.03-0.10 signals a graded rather than discrete-copy picture - we would report format-boundedness as a continuum, weakening the strong copy claim. Negative: Delta R^2 <0.03 (interaction not significant) means one noisy store fits the data, falsifying H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 - format-specific copies are causally dissociable via patching): Tests whether the fact signal that succeeds in format S can be transplanted to restore a failing format F. Data: matched pairs (same fact, success format S, failure format F) from the format-bound set, target 1,500 pairs (fewer than the full set because patching is one forward pass per component per pair). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; activation patching of residual-stream, MLP, and attention-head activations from S into F at subject and last-token positions across all layers; random-source-run null. Systems compared: S-into-F patches vs. random-source patches, per component/layer. Decisive metric: fraction of F failures flipped to correct by patching from S (first); supporting: which layers/components carry the transferable signal. Convincing: >=35% of failures flip under S-patching vs <=10% under the random control, localized to a coherent layer band - copies are causally linked and transplantable. Undecidable band: 15-35% flip rate means copies are partially linked - report partial dissociability. Negative: <15% flip, near the random control, means the format representations are missing or fully independent, so no single transferable fact signal exists.

Experiment 4 (H3 - distinct linear fact directions per format): Tests whether the fact-carrying direction shifts systematically with format. Data: residual-stream activations for the format-bound facts across their four formats (analysis split, ~6,000 facts x 4). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; trainable linear probes decode (a) fact identity and (b) query format from the last-token residual stream, with held-out facts and label-shuffle controls, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: cosine similarity of the fact-direction across formats for format-bound vs. format-robust facts; probe on real vs. shuffled labels. Decisive metric: mean cross-format cosine similarity of the decoded fact direction for format-bound facts (first, lower = more copy-like); supporting: format-classifier AUROC and fact-decode accuracy. Convincing: format-bound facts show cross-format fact-direction cosine <=0.5 while format-robust facts stay >=0.8, and the format classifier reaches AUROC >=0.85 - distinct, linearly identifiable copies. Undecidable band: cosine 0.5-0.8 for format-bound facts indicates overlapping-but-shifted directions - report a graded geometry. Negative: cosine >0.8 (indistinguishable from format-robust facts) or shuffle-level probes means there are no distinct format-specific directions, falsifying H3.

Experiment 5 (H4 - a single format-bridge steering vector transfers access without weight editing): Tests whether one low-rank vector per ordered format pair restores access in the failing format. Data: for each ordered pair S->F, a training split of (success-in-S, failure-in-F) states and a fact-disjoint held-out set of failing-F queries; target 600 held-out failures per major pair. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; the bridge is the mean activation difference between S-success and F-failure states, rank<=8, added at the Experiment 3 best layer; alpha swept 1-6, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: bridge vector vs. a random-direction control vs. no intervention. Decisive metric: recovered-facts-per-unit-collateral = recovery rate / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated facts (first); supporting: raw recovery rate, held-out perplexity change, and cross-fact/cross-format transfer of one vector. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% unrelated-accuracy drop and <2% perplexity rise, and one vector transfers to held-out facts of the same pair at >=25% recovery. Undecidable band: recovery 20-40%, or transfer only within-fact, means bridges are largely fact-specific - report limited but real transfer. Negative: recovery <20% or no better than the random control means no single bridge vector transfers access, falsifying H4.

Experiment 6 (H4 - bridge vs. weight editing): Tests whether the training-free bridge matches or beats weight editing on selectivity and cost. Data: the held-out failing-F queries from Experiment 5 (target 600 per pair). Model: Llama-3-8B; ROME and MEMIT edit the failing format's fact (weights modified) vs. the frozen-weight bridge; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: bridge vs. ROME vs. MEMIT. Decisive metric: recovered-facts-per-unit-collateral (first); supporting: wall-clock/compute per recovered fact and perplexity change. Convincing: bridge matches or exceeds ROME/MEMIT recovered-per-collateral at >=5x lower compute per fact. Undecidable band: bridge within +/-20% of editing on recovered-per-collateral - report parity, a still-useful training-free alternative. Negative: bridge recovered-per-collateral <0.8x editing means weight editing is the better lever, limiting H4's practical claim though leaving the mechanism intact.

Experiment 7 (H1 origin - format-boundedness traces to format-skewed pretraining exposure): Tests whether a fact's format-boundedness correlates with the format distribution of its supporting pretraining occurrences. Data: format-bound vs. format-robust facts scored on a model with searchable pretraining data; occurrences retrieved by pretraining-data search over the Pile/C4 shards, target 2,000 facts with >=5 retrievable supporting passages each. Model: Pythia-1.4B (open training data), frozen; format of each occurrence auto-labeled (cloze/QA/comparative/procedural) by pattern + classifier. Systems compared: format-entropy of a fact's occurrences for format-bound vs. format-robust facts. Decisive metric: regression coefficient (and AUROC) of occurrence format-skew predicting a fact's format-boundedness (first); supporting: partial correlation controlling for total occurrence count. Convincing: format-skew predicts format-boundedness at AUROC >=0.65 after controlling for frequency. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.55-0.65 is a weak trend - report as suggestive of a training-exposure origin. Negative: AUROC <=0.55 means exposure skew does not explain boundedness on this model, and we note it may still differ on the 6-8B models.

Experiment 8 (H1-H4 generality - architecture-general format-boundedness): Tests that prevalence, dissociability, distinct directions, and the bridge hold beyond one model. Data: reuse the Experiment 1 pipeline (8,000 facts x 4 formats) per model. Model: repeat Experiments 2-5 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds/hyperparameters. Systems compared: Llama-3-8B vs. GPT-J-6B vs. Qwen2.5-7B on each decisive metric. Decisive metric: sign-consistency across models of the Experiment 2 interaction Delta R^2, Experiment 3 flip rate, and Experiment 5 recovery (first); supporting: per-model format-bound fraction. Convincing: all three models show significant format-fact interaction, S-into-F flip >=25%, and bridge recovery >=25%. Undecidable band: the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope the claim to those architectures. Negative: reversal in the majority of models means format-boundedness is model-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Format 'equivalence' is imperfect; comparative/verification formats may impose extra task demands beyond retrieval, confounding format-boundedness with task difficulty. Mitigated by regression controls and by focusing patching on subject-token fact signals rather than answer formatting.
The 'one store vs many copies' distinction may be a continuum rather than discrete copies; a graded result would still be informative but weakens the strong hypothesis.

Linear probe format-signatures could reflect query encoding rather than distinct fact copies; the patching experiment (which manipulates fact-carrying activations, not query tokens) is the decisive causal test.
A single format-bridge vector may not transfer across facts if bridges are fact-specific, limiting practical utility though still scientifically informative.
Steering could induce confident hallucination on facts not actually stored in any format; strict specificity controls are required.
Pretraining-origin analysis is only feasible on small open-data models and may not generalize to the 6-8B evaluation models.

Name: property_collapse
Title: Property Collapse: When Shared Relational Subspaces Cause LLMs to Retrieve the Right Property but the Wrong Attribute
Short Hypothesis: LLMs organize relational knowledge around coarse-grained shared 'properties' (e.g., a country-of-X subspace serving country-of-capital, country-of-food, country-of-birthplace). We hypothesize a distinct, previously uncharacterized failure mode—property collapse—in which the model correctly retrieves the shared property value but fails to preserve the fine-grained relation-specific distinction, producing a confidently wrong attribute drawn from a sibling relation that shares the property. We predict (1) errors concentrate on relations that share a property with a competing relation, (2) the shared-property subspace is causally responsible (patching it transfers answers across sibling relations while patching the residual relation-specific component does not), and (3) a targeted 'relation-disambiguation' steering vector that sharpens the relation-specific component recovers correct attributes more selectively than weight editing. Primary falsifiable claim: property-collapse errors (right shared property, wrong sibling attribute) concentrate on relations sharing a property with a competing sibling, above frequency- and similarity-matched baselines, and are causally localized to the shared-property subspace - patching it transfers answers across siblings while patching the relation-specific residual does not. Definitions: a 'property group' = relations sharing a coarse value type; a 'sibling relation' = another relation in the group; a 'collapse error' = the emitted answer is a valid sibling attribute of the same subject; 'residual weakness' = a low-magnitude relation-specific LRE component; 'recovery' = the gold attribute becomes top-1. The disambiguation steering vector is derived from the relation-specific residual alone. This lives in the LRE-amenable sibling-relation setting on T-REx/PopQA, not general factual retrieval.
Related Work: Hernandez et al. (2023) show relation decoding is often linear (LRE); Chen et al. (2025, 'Structure of Relation Decoding Linear Operators') show these decoders are property-centric—shared across semantically-close relations rather than relation-specific—explaining limited relation-wise generalization. 'On Relation-Specific Neurons' (2025) reports neuron versatility and interference (deactivating one relation's neurons changes another's recall). 'Does Knowledge Localization Hold True?' (2024) shows entity and relation knowledge are stored separately. Non-linear relational composition (2025) shows generalization scales with entity semantic similarity. All of these characterize that relational structure is shared/property-based, but none identify property collapse as a concrete, predictable failure mode of factual answering, none causally decompose retrieval into a shared-property component and a relation-specific component to localize the failure, and none propose sharpening the relation-specific component as a non-destructive fix. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (expression gating, format-bound copies, candidate competition, route arbitration, pre-retrieval familiarity): here the object is the shared geometry of relation decoders and the relation-confusion errors it produces. Delta over Chen et al. 2025 at the right level of abstraction: they show relation decoders are property-centric (a geometry result); we turn that geometry into a falsifiable failure distribution (where errors concentrate), a causal shared-vs-residual decomposition (which component carries the collapse), and a residual-sharpening non-destructive fix - none of which follow from the geometry alone, and all distinct from neuron-level sibling interference, which reports cross-relation neuron overlap but not a predictable answering error. Practically, the collapse diagnostic flags exactly the sibling-competition cases where an edit is most likely to leak to a sibling relation, which is its most actionable downstream value for editing safety.
Abstract: Recent interpretability work shows large language models decode relational facts using linear operators that are not relation-specific but property-centric: a single 'country-of-X' subspace, for example, is reused across country-of-capital, country-of-food, and country-of-birthplace. We ask whether this shared organization creates a predictable failure mode. We propose property collapse: when answering a query, the model reliably retrieves the shared coarse property (the right country) but fails to preserve the fine-grained relation-specific distinction, yielding a confident attribute belonging to a sibling relation that shares the property. Under this account, some knowledge failures are not storage or gating failures but binding failures within a collapsed shared subspace. We test three claims. (1) Prevalence: factual errors concentrate on relations that share a property with a competing relation, and the wrong answers are disproportionately valid attributes of a sibling relation for the same subject, above frequency- and similarity-matched baselines. (2) Causal decomposition: using linear relational embeddings we split each relation's decoder into a shared-property component (common across sibling relations) and a relation-specific residual; activation patching shows the shared component transfers answers across siblings while the residual carries the disambiguating signal, and property-collapse errors correspond to a weak relation-specific residual. (3) Intervention: a low-rank relation-disambiguation steering vector that amplifies the residual component recovers correct attributes with higher specificity and less collateral damage than ROME editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on LRE relation sets and T-REx/PopQA, evaluating error-type prevalence, causal transfer, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency. We fix all thresholds in advance from a pilot rather than post-hoc, ablate the LRE-based decomposition against simpler baselines (PCA and class-conditional probes), and control for entity frequency, subject ambiguity, and co-occurrence so the concentration claim is not confounded. We do not overstate real-world reach: the effect is claimed within LRE-amenable sibling relations, and its value is a concrete reliability/editing diagnostic rather than a broad capability result.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - sibling-relation groups with per-subject ground truth): Builds relation groups sharing a coarse property and subjects participating in multiple siblings, so sibling attributes are known ground truth. Data: the LRE relation set (~47 relations) plus T-REx/LAMA and PopQA; group relations by shared property (e.g. country-of-capital, country-of-food, country-of-birthplace share country-of-X) following a property-centric taxonomy; build subject sets in >=1 sibling group, target 8 sibling groups covering 4,000 subjects with all sibling attributes labeled from Wikidata, fewer because we require multi-relation participation and single-token-first attributes. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; per-subject sibling attributes recorded; seed 0. Systems compared: within-group relations. Decisive metric: coverage = subjects with >=2 sibling attributes both single-token and Wikidata-verified (first); supporting: per-group sibling overlap. Convincing: >=8 groups and >=3,000 usable subjects, enough for per-group statistics. Undecidable band: 1,500-3,000 usable subjects is thin - report reduced power. Negative: <1,500 usable subjects means the sibling structure is too sparse to test property collapse here.

Experiment 2 (H1 - property-collapse errors over-represent on high-sibling-overlap relations): Tests that errors concentrate where a sibling relation competes. Data: model errors on the sibling-group queries from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify each error as (a) property-collapse (answer is a valid sibling attribute of the same subject - right property, wrong relation), (b) property error (wrong property value), (c) generic. Systems compared: property-collapse rate on high- vs. low-sibling-overlap relations, against a null matched on answer frequency and entity/relation lexical similarity (logistic regression / chi-square). Decisive metric: odds ratio of property-collapse errors with sibling overlap, above the matched null (first); supporting: per-group collapse rates. Convincing: sibling overlap raises property-collapse odds by >=2x over the matched null (p<0.001). Undecidable band: odds ratio 1.3-2x means a real but modest concentration - report property collapse as a minor, localized mode. Negative: odds ratio <=1.3x or null-indistinguishable means collapse is not driven by sibling competition, falsifying H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 - decoder decomposes into shared-property and relation-specific components): Estimates per-relation linear relational embeddings (LREs) and splits each into a shared-property subspace and a relation-specific residual. Data: few-shot prompts to estimate an LRE per relation in the 8 groups. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; align/average sibling LRE operators to get the shared low-rank subspace, subtract to get the relation-specific residual; restrict to linearly-decodable relations. Systems compared: full LRE vs. shared-only vs. residual-only decoding, plus an ablation against simpler decompositions - PCA of sibling decoders and class-conditional probes - to show the LRE shared/residual split is not an artifact of one method. Decisive metric: decoding accuracy retained by each component alone (first); supporting: rank of the shared subspace. Convincing: the shared component alone retains >=60% of sibling-common decoding while the residual carries the relation-specific distinction (residual-only distinguishes siblings at >=0.6 accuracy) - a meaningful decomposition. Undecidable band: shared component retaining 40-60% indicates entangled components - defer to the causal test (Experiment 4) rather than relying on the decomposition. Negative: neither component isolates its role (both near full or near chance) means the decomposition is not meaningful, weakening H2's operationalization.

Experiment 4 (H2 - the shared-property subspace is causally responsible): Tests that patching the shared component transfers answers across siblings while patching the residual does not. Data: matched subjects appearing in relation A and sibling B, target 1,500 pairs. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch the shared-property component of A into a run of B (should collapse B toward A), (b) patch only the relation-specific residual (should flip to the correct relation-specific attribute); random-component control. Systems compared: shared-component patch vs. residual patch vs. random. Decisive metric: fraction of cases where the shared-component patch flips B toward A's answer minus the fraction where the residual patch does (first, the causal signature of property collapse); supporting: residual-patch disambiguation rate. Convincing: shared-component patches flip >=40% of cases while residual patches flip <=10% toward A (and residual patches instead restore the correct attribute >=30%) - the shared subspace carries the collapse. Undecidable band: a shared-minus-residual flip gap of 10-25 points means partial localization - report weak causal support. Negative: no gap, or residual patches transferring as much as shared, means the shared subspace is not the locus, falsifying H2.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 - weak relation-specific residual predicts collapse): Tests that collapse errors have a systematically weaker relation-specific residual than correct answers. Data: property-collapse errors vs. correct answers on the same relations, target 3,000 each. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; measure the magnitude/alignment of the relation-specific residual in the subject representation via LRE projection; label-shuffle control. Systems compared: residual-strength features for collapse vs. correct, real vs. shuffled labels. Decisive metric: AUROC of residual-strength predicting collapse (first); supporting: effect size of the residual-magnitude difference. Convincing: AUROC >=0.70 with collapse cases showing reliably weaker residual signal. Undecidable band: AUROC 0.58-0.70 is a weak association - report as suggestive. Negative: AUROC <=0.58 or shuffle-level means residual strength does not predict collapse, weakening H1/H2's account.

Experiment 6 (H3 - relation-disambiguation steering recovers attributes more selectively than editing): Tests that sharpening the relation-specific residual recovers correct attributes without breaking siblings. Data: held-out collapse errors, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; a rank<=8 per-group vector amplifying the queried relation's residual (from calibrated-vs-collapsed matched-state differences), alpha swept; random-direction control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: disambiguation steering vs. ROME vs. MEMIT vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated facts and on sibling relations (first, sibling accuracy guards against over-sharpening); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% drop on unrelated and sibling facts, beating ROME/MEMIT on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage, or 5-10% sibling degradation, is parity/marginal - report as comparable with a sibling-cost caveat. Negative: recovery <20%, or sibling accuracy dropping >10%, falsifies the selective-recovery half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 - one disambiguation vector generalizes within a property group): Tests transfer rather than relation-pair-specific fixes. Data: train the vector on one relation pair per group, apply to held-out sibling pairs. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; single vector per group applied unchanged, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: cross-pair transfer vs. within-pair oracle. Decisive metric: cross-pair recovery rate (first); supporting: gap to oracle. Convincing: cross-pair recovery >=25% and within 0.5x of oracle. Undecidable band: 10-25% recovery or below 0.3x oracle means largely pair-specific - report limited transfer. Negative: <10% cross-pair recovery means no general shared-subspace-sharpening signal, limiting H3.

Experiment 8 (H1-H3 generality - architecture-general property collapse): Tests that concentration, causal locus, and steering hold beyond one model. Data: reuse the Experiment 1 sibling-group set (4,000 subjects) per model. Model: repeat Experiments 2-6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds/hyperparameters. Systems compared: Llama-3-8B vs. GPT-J-6B vs. Qwen2.5-7B on each decisive metric. Decisive metric: sign-consistency of the Experiment 2 odds ratio, Experiment 4 shared-minus-residual gap, and Experiment 6 steering advantage (first); supporting: per-model coverage. Convincing: all three show collapse odds >=1.5x, a positive shared-minus-residual gap, and steering advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: reversal in the majority means property collapse is model-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Property collapse may be rare relative to generic errors, making the effect small; the frequency/similarity-matched baseline is essential and a modest but significant effect would still be informative.
LRE decoders are only linear for ~half of relations (Hernandez et al.); analysis is restricted to linearly-decodable relation groups, limiting coverage, which we report explicitly.

The shared/residual decomposition is a modeling choice; if the shared and residual components are entangled, the causal patching test (Exp 4) rather than the decomposition itself is the decisive evidence.

Wrong answers matching a sibling attribute could arise from generic co-occurrence rather than true property collapse; per-subject ground-truth sibling attributes and residual-strength causal tests mitigate but may not fully eliminate this confound.

Disambiguation steering could corrupt sibling-relation recall (over-sharpening); we explicitly measure sibling accuracy pre/post as a specificity control, and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
A single transferable disambiguation vector may not exist if collapse is relation-pair-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token attributes complicate LRE readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first attributes with reported coverage.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: late_polarity_binding
Title: Content First, Polarity Last: Why LLMs Retrieve the Fact but Ignore Whether the Query Denied It
Short Hypothesis: In factual queries, LLMs first form a polarity-blind subject-attribute content representation, and the query's polarity (affirmation vs. negation) is bound to it later by a separate, weaker signal. We make three scoped, falsifiable claims. (i) Timing: a polarity-invariant content direction becomes decodable several layers before a query-polarity direction is applied to the answer. (ii) Causality: patching the late polarity signal from a correct-polarity run into a negation-override run flips the answer to the correct polarity while leaving content unchanged, and ablating it induces spurious negation, whereas patching content does neither. (iii) Intervention: low-rank steering of this late polarity direction recovers stored true-negation answers with less collateral damage than fact editing while preserving affirmative recall. The novel object is the causal timing of polarity binding and the isolated polarity direction, not a new theory of why negation fails.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows a 'belief conflict': LLMs answer polar negative questions correctly but generate positively-biased text about negative commonsense (Say What You Mean, 2023), attributing this to reporting bias and statistical shortcuts; negated-LAMA studies (Understanding by Understanding Not, 2021; Kassner & Schutze) show models complete negated cloze the same as affirmative. Strong-hallucinations-from-negation (2024) treats negation theoretically as a latent operation and proposes a fix without localizing a mechanism. Closest is recent (2026) mechanistic work on negation that already argues negation failure comes from later overshadowing rather than absent negation ability; we adopt that framing but our delta is concrete and testable: (a) an onset-ordering result (content decodable several layers before query polarity is applied), (b) a patching asymmetry (polarity-patch flips answer polarity with content held fixed, while content-patch does not fix polarity), and (c) a recovery-specific low-rank steering that fixes override with less collateral than fact editing (ROME/MEMIT) and beats prompt-reformatting/CoT/logit-bias baselines. INLP (2020) shows negation leaves a linear imprint; entity-recognition (Do I Know This Entity, 2024) and answerability directions (2023) concern coverage/self-knowledge, not query polarity. Novelty here lives in the mechanism and the intervention (causal timing of polarity binding, an isolated polarity direction, and a targeted fix), not in the phenomenon itself. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (gating, format copies, entity competition, route arbitration, familiarity, property collapse, lexicalization, overregularization, temporal anchors, consistency seams, inheritance, say-vs-use): here the object is the *polarity* of the query and its late binding to polarity-blind content.
Abstract: Large language models often affirm a fact even when the query negates it, and generate positively-biased statements about things they can correctly deny in yes/no form—the 'belief conflict.' A recent mechanistic account attributes this to later overshadowing rather than missing negation ability; we sharpen that into a specific, falsifiable decomposition of negation failures and a targeted fix. We propose factual retrieval is two-stage: the model forms a polarity-blind subject-attribute content representation early, then a separate, later, weaker signal binds the query's polarity (affirm vs. negate). We test three scoped claims. (1) Timing: a content probe (polarity-invariant object recall) and a polarity probe (affirmative vs. negative frame) are separable residual-stream directions whose onset layers differ, content emerging first. (2) Causality: patching the late polarity signal from a correct-polarity run into a negation-override run flips answer polarity with content unchanged; ablating it induces spurious negation; content-patching fixes neither—with predefined sites, windows, and success criteria. (3) Intervention: low-rank steering of the late polarity direction recovers correct-polarity answers with more specificity and less collateral than ROME/MEMIT fact editing and than prompt-reformatting, CoT, and logit-bias baselines, while preserving affirmative recall. So what: if true, negation robustness should be evaluated and repaired as a late binding stage rather than as missing knowledge—giving interpretability a decomposition and editing/mitigation a cheaper, more specific lever for safety-critical denial/refusal and factual QA under negated prompts; if false (no onset ordering, no patching asymmetry, or steering no better than baselines), negation failure is better modeled as absent or entangled knowledge and effort should return to fact-level editing and data curation. We guard the central risk—that the 'polarity direction' is merely answer confidence, negation lexical cueing, or subject frequency—with explicit confound controls, and treat probe-onset ordering as suggestive only, letting the causal patching test decide. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on negated-LAMA, T-REx/PopQA, and negative-commonsense (CSK-PN).
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — polarity-paired dataset and true-polarity baseline): Build minimally-contrasting affirmative/negative pairs and establish, per fact, the model's 'true' polarity knowledge so override can later be separated from ignorance. Data: adapted from LAMA/T-REx and PopQA (factual) plus CSK-PN negative-commonsense assertions; for each fact build an affirmative cloze/question, its negation, and a matched polar-QA form ('True or false: ...'). Restrict to single-token-first answers and single negation cues; target ~2,500 pairs across >=8 relations/domains after filtering; report exact counts at each filter stage. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): fraction of facts where the polar-QA form is answered correctly for BOTH the affirmative and the negated statement (the 'polarity-aware' eligible set), computed with conservative confidence thresholds and a paraphrase-consistency check to guard against prompt leakage. Convincing: >= 1,500 eligible pairs. Indecision band: 1,000-1,500 eligible — reduced power, reported. Negative (< 1,000 eligible, or polar-QA at chance) means the model does not store the negations and H1-H3 are untestable on this model; the pipeline stops here rather than proceeding on facts the model does not know.

Experiment 2 (H1 — content decodable before polarity, with confound controls): Test that polarity-invariant content is decodable earlier than the query's polarity, and that the polarity signal is not merely a confound. Data: eligible pairs from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a content probe (predict the object, across both polarities) and a polarity probe (affirmative vs. negative) via logistic regression on subject-token and last-token residuals at every layer (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null, tuned-lens matched-capacity control, and a random-onset null). Confound controls (decisive for the polarity probe's validity): the polarity probe must survive (a) regressing out answer/option confidence, (b) matching negation lexical cues across classes (paraphrased negation surface forms, cloze vs. polar-QA), and (c) controlling subject/entity frequency—report probe AUROC before and after each control. Decisive metric (first): onset-layer difference = (layer where polarity probe first exceeds 0.7 AUROC after controls) minus (layer where content probe first exceeds 0.7 AUROC), bootstrap 95% CI; secondary, residualized unique AUROC of each probe. Convincing: onset difference >= 4 layers (polarity later), CI excludes 0, both probes non-redundant after residualization AND the polarity probe retains AUROC >= 0.65 after all confound controls. Indecision band: onset difference 1-4 layers, or polarity AUROC 0.55-0.65 after controls — weak ordering; timing rests on the causal test (Experiment 3). Negative (difference CI includes 0/reversed, or polarity probe collapses to a confound) refutes the ordering in H1.

Experiment 3 (H1 — causal two-stage timing via patching, sites and criteria predefined): Test causally that the failure is late/weak polarity application, not missing content. Data: matched correct-polarity and override runs from the eligible set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Predefined protocol: activation site = residual stream at the last query token; patching window = the polarity-onset layers identified in Experiment 2 (report the exact layer indices); success = the model's argmax answer changing to the correct polarity while the decoded content token is unchanged. Conditions: (a) polarity-patch from a correct-polarity run into an override run; (b) polarity-ablation in a correct affirmative run (reverse control) expected to induce spurious negation; (c) content-patch alone, expected not to fix polarity; (d) random-position and random-run patches. Decisive metric (first): net polarity-correction rate = fraction of overrides flipped to correct polarity by the polarity patch minus the random-patch rate. Convincing: net correction >= 25 points, reverse ablation drops affirmative accuracy >= 25 points, and content-patch and random < 5 points. Indecision band: net correction 10-25 points — polarity contributes but is not solely decisive. Negative (< 10 points, or content-patch fixes it) refutes the late-polarity causal account.

Experiment 4 (H2 — negation-override concentrates where positive content is primed): Classify and predict override errors, and separate positive-content dominance from reporting bias. Data: negated/negative queries from the eligible set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; classify each response as (a) negation-override (affirmative-content answer given, but polar-QA shows true polarity is known), (b) genuine ignorance (polar-QA also wrong), (c) correct. Predictor: override probability as a function of positive-content priming (affirmative-form answer confidence and subject-attribute association strength) vs. a null logistic model controlling answer frequency and lexical similarity. Auxiliary source analysis: add, as regressors, an affirmative-vs-negative pretraining-frequency asymmetry (Pile co-occurrence counts) and syntactic distance of the negation cue to the answer, to gauge how much override is positive-content dominance vs. reporting bias. Decisive metric (first): partial coefficient of content-priming on override (log-odds, CI), and out-of-sample AUROC of the Experiment-2 content-vs-polarity signal imbalance predicting override on held-out items. Convincing: priming coefficient CI excludes 0 and held-out AUROC >= 0.70. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.70 — weak prediction. Negative (coefficient CI includes 0, AUROC ~0.5) means override is not driven by positive-content dominance, refuting H2.

Experiment 5 (H3 — polarity steering recovery vs. fact-editing and prompting baselines): Test that boosting the late polarity signal fixes override while preserving affirmative recall, and that it beats cheap alternatives. Data: eligible set, instance-disjoint train/test; polarity steering vector = mean residual difference (correct-polarity minus override) at the Experiment-3 sites, seeds {0,1,2}, rank <= 4. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the injected direction. Systems compared: polarity-steering, content-direction manipulation, ROME/MEMIT fact edit, random-direction control, AND three non-mechanistic baselines—prompt reformatting, chain-of-thought prompting, and logit bias on the negation. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = override-recovery rate divided by accuracy drop on a held-out set of correctly-answered affirmative queries (the critical over-negation control); secondary, accuracy on 200 unrelated affirmative facts and fluency (held-out perplexity delta). Convincing: recovery >= 30% with < 3-point drop on correct affirmatives and on the 200 facts, beating all comparators (including the prompting baselines) on recovered-per-collateral. Indecision band: recovery 15-30% or collateral 3-6 points, or only parity with a prompting baseline — over-negation/utility caps; reported. Negative (no better than random or a prompting baseline, or affirmative accuracy collapses) refutes H3.

Experiment 6 (H1/H3 — transfer and architecture generality; auxiliary): Test whether late polarity binding and its fix generalize beyond one model/relation, with claims explicitly conditioned on replication. Data: pairs partitioned by relation and by factual-vs-commonsense domain; polarity vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out relations/domains. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B (architecturally distinct), frozen; re-run Experiments 2-5, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation override-recovery relative to within-relation, plus replication of the content-before-polarity onset ordering and patching asymmetry per model. Convincing: cross-relation recovery >= 50% of within-relation AND onset ordering plus patching asymmetry replicate in >= 2 of 3 models (i.e., at least one non-Llama architecture). Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-relation 30-50% — model/relation-dependent; generality claims are withdrawn to the replicating model(s). Negative (no transfer/replication) confines H1-H3 to Llama-3-8B. Also report whether larger models bind polarity earlier (lower override rate).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'polarity direction' could be a confound—answer confidence, negation lexical cueing, or subject/entity frequency—rather than a genuine polarity signal; Experiment 2's before/after-control AUROCs and the causal patching in Experiment 3 (not probe onset alone) are the load-bearing tests, and if the direction fails the controls the central claim collapses.

The content and polarity signals may be entangled rather than cleanly separable; a graded/partial dissociation would weaken the strong two-stage claim while remaining informative, and the causal patch is decisive over the probe onset.

Negation-override may be conflated with genuine ignorance; the polar-QA control (establishing the model knows the true polarity) is essential, and strong-prompt leakage could overestimate knowledge—we use conservative thresholds, paraphrase-consistency, and report per-filter counts.

Polarity steering could over-negate—making the model deny true affirmative facts; the correctly-answered-affirmative specificity control (Exp 5) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds; the fix may also only match, not beat, a prompting baseline.
Probe-onset timing could be a probe-difficulty artifact; tuned-lens, matched-capacity, random-onset nulls, and causal patching mitigate this but cannot fully exclude it.

A single transferable polarity vector may not exist if polarity handling is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative; generality claims are conditioned on replication in >= 2 architectures.

Cloze-form negation ('is not ___') is under-determined; we prioritize verification/polar and single-answer negation formats, restrict to single-token-first answers and single negation cues, and report format- and coverage-specific results.
Findings on 6-8B open models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: premature_lexicalization
Title: Right Concept, Wrong Word: Premature Lexical Commitment as a Distinct Knowledge-Retrieval Failure in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When answering factual queries, LLMs internally select the correct target entity as an abstract, token-agnostic concept representation, but the final answer is produced through a separate, later lexicalization step that maps concept to first output token. We hypothesize a distinct failure mode—premature lexicalization—in which the model commits to a high-prior or low-perplexity first token before the concept representation is fully resolved, causing it to emit a lexically-adjacent wrong entity (one sharing the committed first token/subword) even though the correct concept was internally selected. We predict (1) the concept selection and lexical commitment are dissociable and decodable at different layers, (2) a substantial fraction of factual errors are 'right-concept-wrong-word' cases where the correct entity is decodable as a concept but is out-competed at the lexicalization stage by a first-token-sharing distractor, and (3) delaying/re-weighting the lexical commitment (suppressing the prematurely-committed first token direction) recovers the correct entity more selectively than weight editing. Primary falsifiable claim: there is a distinct error class - right concept, wrong word - where the token-agnostic concept probe recovers the correct entity yet the output is a first-token-sharing distractor, and suppressing the prematurely-committed first-token direction fixes it while patching the concept representation does not (Exp 4). The two-stage concept->lexeme mechanism is established prior art; our novelty is this error class plus the causal first-token intervention, not the mechanism itself. 'Right concept' is labeled by held-out-alias/paraphrase invariance chosen to be independent of surface lexical overlap, and premature-lexicalization is a precise binary label (concept-correct AND emitted answer shares the early-committed first token/subword with a distractor).
Related Work: A large body of work studies layer-wise commitment: 'Guess-then-Refine' (2025) shows early layers propose high-frequency tokens later refined; Iterative Inference / commitment-depth studies (2024–2026) track when models lock in answers; 'How LLMs Use Their Depth' (2025) shows first tokens of multi-token facts need more depth. Geva et al. (2023) describe attribute extraction via attention over an enriched subject. Concept-vs-language separation has been studied for multilingual models (language-agnostic concept spaces) but not for the concept-vs-lexeme distinction within a single language for factual recall. Confidence Regulation / entropy neurons (2024) and token-frequency effects on recall are documented. None of these identify premature lexicalization—a specific dissociation between token-agnostic concept selection and first-token lexical commitment—as a concrete, predictable factual-error mode, nor propose suppressing a prematurely-committed first-token direction as a non-destructive fix. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (expression gating, format-bound copies, candidate competition among entities, route arbitration, pre-retrieval familiarity, property collapse): here the failure is not choosing the wrong entity but choosing the wrong *word* for a correctly-chosen entity, driven by first-token statistics. What is new vs established, stated plainly: guess-then-refine, depth-of-commitment, and concept-vs-language separation already establish the two-stage geometry; we contribute the within-language factual error class and a targeted first-token intervention. That intervention is distinguished from contrastive decoding, reranking, and generic logit suppression by being concept-conditioned and causally validated (it must fix premature-lexicalization but not wrong-concept errors), and it is inference-time and cheap, compatible with production decoding.
Abstract: Large language models sometimes produce a factual answer that is close to but not the correct entity—e.g., a name that shares a first syllable or subword with the right one. We propose that some of these errors reflect a distinct, overlooked mechanism: premature lexicalization. Under this view, factual recall proceeds in two stages—selecting the target entity as a token-agnostic concept, then lexicalizing that concept into output tokens—and errors arise when the model commits to a high-prior first token before the concept is fully resolved, emitting a lexically-adjacent wrong entity while the correct concept was internally selected. We test three claims. (1) Dissociability: a concept probe (predicting the correct entity in a token-agnostic representation, e.g., via aliases/paraphrastic descriptions) and a lexical probe (predicting the committed first output token) are separable and become decodable at different layers, with concept selection preceding or coexisting with a later lexical-commitment surge. (2) Prevalence: 'right-concept-wrong-word' errors—where the correct entity is decodable as a concept yet the output is a first-token-sharing distractor—form an identifiable fraction of factual errors, concentrated where the correct entity's first token is high-perplexity/rare and a distractor shares a common first token, above frequency-matched baselines. (3) Intervention: suppressing the prematurely-committed distractor first-token direction (or re-scoring the first token conditioned on the concept representation) recovers correct entities with higher specificity and less collateral damage than ROME editing. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B on PopQA, T-REx, and EntityQuestions, evaluating probe separability, layer-onset ordering, error-type prevalence, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency. We report a user-facing metric (exact-match improvement and calibration, not only internal recovery), quantify prevalence on standard factual-QA rather than only curated entity sets, and benchmark against simple decoding baselines - first-token reranking, logit bias, constrained decoding, and nearest-neighbor token substitution - with an ablation ruling out trivial tokenizer/prefix artifacts and ordinary wrong-entity mistakes. Thresholds for 'concept precedes lexical commitment' are fixed in advance.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 - concept and lexical signals are decodable at different layers): Tests that a token-agnostic concept representation becomes decodable before the first-token lexical commitment. Data: PopQA (14,282), T-REx/LAMA (~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); sample 9,000 facts whose answer entity has >=2 attested aliases/paraphrastic descriptions, fewer than the pool because alias sets are needed for the concept probe. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; two trainable per-layer probes on the last-token residual - a concept probe (target: a shared concept ID invariant across aliases, trained on one surface form and tested on held-out aliases) and a lexical probe (target: the emitted first token); seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle and alias-shuffle controls. Systems compared: concept vs. lexical onset layers, bootstrap CIs. Decisive metric: onset-layer difference (first-layer at AUROC>=0.7) between concept and the lexical-commitment surge (first, concept should precede); supporting: per-layer accuracy/AUROC. Convincing: concept onset precedes lexical commitment by >=3 layers with non-overlapping CIs, both above shuffle. Undecidable band: a 1-3 layer gap or overlapping CIs cannot separate timing from probe difficulty - defer precedence to the causal test (Experiment 4). Negative: lexical onset at/before concept, or concept at alias-shuffle level, falsifies H1.
