Experiment 2 (H1 - concept and lexical directions carry non-redundant information): Tests they are not collinear. Data: the residual activations from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; cross-linear-predictability and residualization of the two directions, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: concept predicting the correct entity before vs. after removing first-token-predictive variance. Decisive metric: retained concept->entity accuracy after residualizing out lexical variance (first); supporting: direction cosine similarity. Convincing: concept still predicts the correct entity at >=0.7 relative accuracy after residualization and cosine <=0.5. Undecidable band: retained accuracy 0.5-0.7 or cosine 0.5-0.75 indicates partial entanglement - report graded separability. Negative: retained accuracy <=0.5 or cosine >0.75 means the two collapse to one signal, falsifying the two-stage claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 - right-concept-wrong-word errors are a substantial, statistically distinct share): Tests that many errors are concept-correct but lexically out-competed by a first-token-sharing distractor. Data: model errors on Experiment 1 facts. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify errors into (a) premature-lexicalization (concept probe recovers the correct entity but the emitted answer shares the early committed first token/subword with a distractor), (b) genuine wrong-concept, (c) other. Systems compared: type-(a) rate when the correct entity's first token is rare and a competitor shares a common first token, against a null controlling for entity frequency and overall lexical similarity (logistic regression / chi-square). Decisive metric: fraction of errors that are premature-lexicalization, above the matched null (first); supporting: odds ratio with the rare-correct-token / shared-distractor-token condition. Convincing: >=20% of errors are premature-lexicalization, >=10 points above the null, with the predicted first-token-statistics dependence. Undecidable band: 8-20% above a null gap <10 points means the mode is real but minor - narrow H2 to a secondary mode. Negative: <8% or null-indistinguishable means the failure is not distinct from wrong-concept errors, falsifying H2.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 - the failure lives in lexicalization, not concept selection): Causally dissociates the two stages. Data: premature-lexicalization failures (target 1,200) plus wrong-concept failures (target 1,200) from Experiment 3. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch the concept representation from a correct run into a premature-lexicalization failure (should NOT fix it if the failure is lexical), (b) suppress the distractor's first-token direction at the commitment layers (should fix it), (c) amplify the concept direction alone; random-direction control. Systems compared: concept-patch vs. first-token-suppression vs. concept-amplification vs. random, on the two failure types. Decisive metric: fix-rate gap = first-token-suppression fix rate minus concept-patch fix rate on premature-lexicalization failures (first, the causal signature); supporting: the reverse pattern on wrong-concept failures. Convincing: on premature-lexicalization failures, first-token suppression fixes >=35% while concept patching fixes <=10% (gap >=25 points), and the pattern reverses for wrong-concept failures. Undecidable band: a 10-25 point gap means partial localization - report weak causal support. Negative: no gap, or concept patching fixing as much as suppression, means the failure is not lexicalization-stage, falsifying the H1/H2 mechanism.

Experiment 5 (H1 - lexical commitment can precede concept resolution): Tests that for these errors the committed first token overtakes early and before the concept is resolved. Data: the premature-lexicalization vs. correct-answer cases from Experiments 3-4. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; tuned-lens locates the layer where the eventual first token overtakes competitors and where the concept probe first recovers the correct entity. Systems compared: concept-correct layer vs. lexical-commitment layer, and committed-token early prior for error vs. correct cases. Decisive metric: fraction of premature-lexicalization errors with concept-correct-layer <= lexical-commitment-layer AND an anomalously early/high first-token prior (first); supporting: distribution of the layer gap. Convincing: >=60% of these errors satisfy both conditions vs a correct-answer base rate <=30%. Undecidable band: 40-60% means the timing signature is inconsistent - report as partial. Negative: <40%, near the correct-case base rate, means premature commitment is not the signature, falsifying H1's timing prediction.

Experiment 6 (H3 - re-weighting lexical commitment recovers the entity more selectively than editing): Tests suppression / concept-conditioned re-ranking against weight editing. Data: held-out premature-lexicalization failures, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; (a) suppress the committed distractor first-token direction at commitment layers, (b) re-score the first token by projecting the concept representation to constrain candidates; random-direction control; alpha swept; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: suppression / concept-conditioned re-ranking vs. simple decoding baselines - first-token reranking, logit bias, constrained decoding, nearest-neighbor token substitution - vs. ROME vs. MEMIT vs. random, reporting exact-match and calibration alongside recovered-per-collateral. Decisive metric: recovered-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on 200 unrelated facts (first); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% collateral, beating ROME/MEMIT on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage is parity - report as comparable. Negative: recovery <20% or no advantage falsifies the selectivity half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 generality - one recipe transfers across relations and models): Tests transfer and architecture-generality. Data: train the suppression/re-ranking identification on one relation subset, apply to held-out relations; reuse the Experiment 1 pool per model. Model: single recipe on Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 1, 3, 4, 6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds. Systems compared: cross-relation transfer vs. within-relation oracle; three models per decisive metric. Decisive metric: cross-relation recovery rate and cross-model sign-consistency of the Experiment 3 concentration and Experiment 6 advantage (first); supporting: per-model onset gaps. Convincing: cross-relation recovery >=25% and all three models show the concentration and a recovery advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: transfer 10-25% or the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: <10% transfer or majority model reversal means the mechanism is fact/model-specific.

Experiment 8 (H2 - the failure is driven by first-token statistics): Tests that premature-lexicalization rate rises with adverse first-token statistics. Data: per-fact premature-lexicalization outcomes over the 9,000 facts. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; regress error rate on correct-answer first-token frequency, first-token overlap with high-frequency distractors, and answer token length. Systems compared: first-token-statistics regressors vs. an entity-frequency-only baseline. Decisive metric: partial R^2 of the first-token features beyond entity frequency (first); supporting: sign and magnitude of each coefficient. Convincing: first-token features add partial R^2 >=0.10 with the predicted signs (rare correct first token, common shared distractor token, longer answers all raise the rate). Undecidable band: partial R^2 0.03-0.10 is a weak trend - report as suggestive. Negative: partial R^2 <0.03 means first-token statistics do not drive the failure, falsifying the core mechanistic claim of H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Defining a truly token-agnostic 'concept' probe is hard; alias-based invariance is imperfect and may leak surface information. We use held-out aliases and paraphrastic descriptions and report coverage; the causal patching test (Exp 4) is the decisive evidence rather than probe onset alone.

Premature-lexicalization errors may be rare relative to genuine wrong-concept errors, yielding a small effect; the frequency/similarity-matched baseline is essential and a modest significant effect remains informative.

Concept and lexical stages may be entangled (not cleanly two-stage), weakening the strong dissociation claim; graded results would still be scientifically informative and we report continuous measures.

Suppressing a first-token direction could degrade fluency or introduce new errors when the direction overlaps useful features; strict specificity and perplexity controls are included and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
Analysis focuses on entities where first-token distinctions are meaningful; single-token answers and heavily subword-fragmented names complicate readout, and we report coverage restrictions.
A single transferable intervention recipe may not exist if the failure is fact-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: self_commitment_lock_in
Title: Believing Its Own Words: How an LLM's Earlier Self-Generated Answer Overrides Correct Knowledge It Still Holds
Short Hypothesis: Within a multi-turn interaction, an LLM treats its own previously generated answer as privileged evidence and lets it override subsequent factual recall: once the model has committed to a (possibly wrong) claim earlier in the conversation, it re-produces that claim on a later, logically independent query even when it stores the correct answer and would produce it in a fresh context. The novel claim is a factual-recall-specific self-authorship effect: holding the wrong content and its position in context constant, reproduction is stronger when the content is attributed to the model itself than when identical content is attributed to the user or a neutral third party. We hypothesize this self-commitment lock-in is (1) a gradable behavioral phenomenon distinct from generic in-context copying/entrainment, driven specifically by the answer being self-generated rather than merely present in context; (2) associated with an attention pathway from the prior-answer tokens into the current-query answer readout that is stronger for self-authored than externally-authored content; and (3) reducible by ablating that pathway or subtracting a learned self-commitment direction, restoring the correct answer without editing any stored fact. Claims (2) and (3) are stated as hypotheses to be adjudicated by the ablation/patching evidence, not assumed.
Related Work: The novelty here is a new SETTING (multi-turn factual recall) plus a new CONTROL (authorship of otherwise-identical committed content) plus a new INTERVENTION (self-commitment-direction suppression), not the claim of a wholly new internal mechanism. Prior-work map: (a) Contextual Entrainment (Llama See, Llama Do, 2025) showed LMs upweight any token present in context via 'entrainment heads' but treats all context tokens alike; residual delta: we hold the wrong content and its position constant and vary only authorship, isolating a self-authored increment above generic entrainment. (b) Sycophancy / self-preference work, incl. 2508.02087 (self-generated content is more persuasive to the model than externally-provided content) and BrokenMath (models defend their own prior wrong solutions); these show self-authored content is favored in preference/agreement or open-ended reasoning. Residual delta: our held-constant variable is authorship of a matched factual assertion and our measured outcome is corruption of specific, independently-verifiable factual recall of knowledge the model demonstrably still stores (checked by fresh-query and probe), rather than stated preference, agreement, or proof-defense. (c) Conversation-dynamics work (Linear representations change over a conversation, 2026) studies representational drift of high-level concept directions like factuality, not corruption of a specific fact by the model's own prior answer. (d) When-Do-LLMs-Admit-Mistakes (2025) studies retraction of a stated belief (the reverse direction). (e) Fakepedia / knowledge-conflict work injects EXTERNAL counterfactual context and does not isolate self-authorship. None of these hold content/position fixed while varying authorship, and none test whether correct-but-overridden knowledge is recoverable by intervening on a self-authorship signal. This transfers the human phenomena of self-generated-commitment bias and self-shared retrieval-induced forgetting into LLM multi-turn factual recall; it is orthogonal to my prior single-turn proposals (gating, format copies, competition, arbitration, familiarity, polarity, procedures, priming).
Abstract: Large language models increasingly operate over multi-turn conversations, where their own earlier outputs become part of the context for later queries. We ask whether a model treats its own prior answer as privileged evidence that overrides its stored knowledge. We propose self-commitment lock-in: once an LLM has produced a (possibly incorrect) factual claim earlier in a conversation, it re-produces that claim on a later, logically independent query even when it stores the correct answer and would give it in a fresh context. We first document the phenomenon behaviorally. For facts the model answers correctly in isolation, we engineer conversations in which the model is first led to commit to a wrong value (via a leading sub-question), then later asked the fact directly, and measure how often it now returns its own earlier wrong value. The decisive, falsifiable control is authorship: we compare identical wrong content, in an identical context position, attributed to (a) the model's own prior turn, (b) the user, and (c) a neutral third party, and additionally control surface framing, politeness, and discourse structure across conditions. The core claim is falsified if, after these controls, self-authored content is reproduced no more than externally-authored content (a self-authorship lift whose CI includes zero) -- i.e., lock-in is ordinary in-context copying. We predict instead that lock-in is strongest when the content is self-authored, scales with the committed answer's assertiveness and recency, and concentrates on low-frequency facts, above matched baselines. We then test a Location + Causal Intervention account, stated as hypotheses adjudicated by the causal evidence: a probe should recover a self-authorship signal at the prior-answer tokens (reported as recoverability, with a probe-failure analysis, not as proof of a discrete 'belief'); attention analysis and activation patching should reveal a pathway carrying this signal into the current-query readout, stronger for self- than externally-authored content; and ablating that pathway or subtracting a learned self-commitment direction should recover the correct answer with high specificity and without editing any fact. So what: if the effect is large, multi-turn chat systems, tool-using agents, long-horizon assistants, and safety audits must treat a model's own prior outputs as a distinct, discountable evidence source rather than trusted context, and self-commitment suppression offers a knowledge-preserving fix; if it is absent, the field can treat the risk as ordinary entrainment and design context handling accordingly. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, evaluating lock-in prevalence, authorship dose-response, probe recoverability, causal recovery, and specificity. Thresholds below are pre-registered and justified by matched null/baseline comparisons rather than absolute cutoffs.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 -- fact and two-stage conversation construction): Build conversations where the model first commits to a wrong value and is later re-queried, over facts it answers correctly fresh. Data: adapted from PopQA/T-REx/EntityQuestions; select facts (subject, relation, correct a) the model answers correctly single-turn, then build a Stage-1 leading exchange that induces the model to assert a specific wrong a_false (verified it was actually produced) and a Stage-2 direct query. Restrict to single-token-first answers; target ~2,500 facts across >=8 relations; report coverage. Human audit of Stage-1 induction quality: two annotators rate a 150-item sample for whether a_false was genuinely asserted (not hedged/refused) and record a failure-mode taxonomy (refusal, partial assertion, off-target value, format break); report inter-rater agreement. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen. Decisive metric (first): fraction of facts BOTH answered correctly fresh AND successfully induced to a_false in Stage 1 (the eligible set). Thresholds are set relative to design power: convincing >= 1,500 eligible (adequate power for an 8-point lift at the planned n); indecision band 1,000-1,500 (reduced power, reported); below 1,000 the design is under-powered. Negative (few facts can be induced, or fresh accuracy is low) means the premise cannot be set up and H1-H3 are untestable here.

Experiment 2 (H0 -- authorship-controlled conditions with framing/discourse controls): Create matched conditions that hold the wrong content a_false and its position constant while varying its author, isolating authorship from mere presence in context AND from surface framing. Data: eligible facts. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; conditions: (a) self-authored (model produced a_false in Stage 1), (b) user-authored (user asserted a_false), (c) third-party-authored (a quoted neutral source asserts a_false), (d) no-commitment control (Stage 1 present, a_false never stated). Beyond matching the a_false string and position across (a)-(c), we match assertiveness/politeness wording, turn count, and discourse structure via templated paraphrase sets, and include a swapped-attribution sanity condition (self-authored text relabeled as user-authored) to catch pure framing effects. Decisive metric (first): audit that all conditions are well-formed and that a_false text/position AND framing features (politeness, assertiveness, length) are matched across (a)-(c) (manual audit of a 100-item sample on a fixed rubric). Convincing >= 95% matched; indecision 85-95% (minor leakage; fix templates and re-audit); negative (< 85%) means authorship is confounded with content/position/framing and must be rebuilt before any lock-in claim.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- self-commitment lock-in exceeds generic entrainment and mirrors self- vs external framing): Test that Stage-2 reproduction of a_false is driven specifically by self-authorship, above any in-context mention and above the first-person/third-person framing effect from prior sycophancy work. Data: eligible facts across the four conditions. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen. Systems compared: self-authored vs user-authored vs third-party vs no-commitment, plus the swapped-attribution sanity condition, paired per fact against a generic-entrainment null that treats all in-context mentions of a_false identically (logistic regression author x fact; paired McNemar). Decisive metric (first): self-authorship lift = P(Stage-2 = a_false | self-authored) minus P(Stage-2 = a_false | user-authored), paired, CI; secondary, dose-response on Stage-1 assertiveness (hedged vs confident), recency (turns), and target popularity. Pre-registered thresholds (justified as the smallest effect that would change practitioner guidance and exceeds expected annotation noise): convincing lift >= 8 percentage points with CI excluding 0 and a monotone assertiveness dose-response; indecision 3-8 points (weak self-authorship increment atop generic entrainment; report as suggestive); negative (lift CI includes 0, or effect vanishes under swapped-attribution) refutes H1 -- lock-in is ordinary in-context copying, not self-commitment.

Experiment 4 (H0 -- storage verification: knowledge overridden, not lost): Confirm that in lock-in cases the correct answer a is still recoverable, separating lock-in from genuine belief change. Data: self-authored lock-in cases from Experiment 3. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; verify a via (i) a fresh single-turn query and (ii) a logistic-regression content probe decoding a from the Stage-2 residual stream (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null). We treat the probe as evidence of superficial RECOVERABILITY of a, not proof of an accessible internal 'belief'; we add a probe-failure analysis (calibration, where decoding fails vs the fresh-query result, sensitivity to layer/seed) and require fresh-query agreement as the stronger criterion. Decisive metric (first): fraction of lock-in cases where a is BOTH answered correctly fresh AND probe-decodable during Stage 2 (verified-recoverable). Convincing >= 60%; indecision 40-60% (a substantial minority reflect belief change; restrict downstream analysis to the verified subset and report shrinkage); negative (< 40%) means most 'lock-in' is genuine belief updating, undercutting the hidden-knowledge premise.

Experiment 5 (H2 -- a self-authored commitment signal is decodable): Test that a signal distinguishing self- from externally-authored identical content exists at the relevant positions. Data: verified-recoverable lock-in cases and matched externally-authored cases. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a logistic-regression probe (seeds {0,1,2}, label-shuffle null) at the prior-answer (a_false) token positions and the Stage-2 answer position to distinguish self- from externally-authored content. This is a decodability/association test, not a causal one; causality is decided in Experiment 6. Decisive metric (first): peak-layer AUROC distinguishing self- from externally-authored identical content, and cosine alignment of the query-position signal with a_false's unembedding. Thresholds justified against the label-shuffle and random-direction nulls: convincing AUROC >= 0.75 with unembedding alignment above the random-direction null; indecision 0.60-0.75 (weak/partial signal; the causal test is then decisive); negative (AUROC <= 0.60) means self-authorship is not separately encoded at these sites, weakening H2.

Experiment 6 (H2/H3 -- causal test of a self-commitment attention pathway): Test whether specific attention heads carry the self-authored commitment into the Stage-2 answer; the mechanism claim is made ONLY conditional on this causal evidence. Data: verified-recoverable lock-in cases. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; (a) identify Stage-2 answer-position heads attending to the prior-answer tokens and compare their attention weight for self- vs externally-authored content; (b) ablate their attention to the prior-answer tokens; (c) activation-patch the Stage-2 answer-position residual from a no-commitment run into a lock-in run and measure recovery of a; (d) reverse control -- inject the self-commitment signal into a no-commitment run to test whether lock-in is induced. Systems compared: candidate-head ablation vs random-head ablation vs no-commitment patch vs random-position patch. Decisive metric (first): lock-in reduction from ablating the candidate heads' attention to prior-answer tokens, net of random-head ablation. Thresholds justified as clearly exceeding the random-control ceiling: convincing net reduction >= 50% relative, no-commitment patch recovers a >= 25 points net, reverse injection induces lock-in >= 25 points, candidate heads attend more to self- than externally-authored content, and random controls < 5 points; indecision net reduction 20-50% relative (attention is one of several routes); negative (ablation ~ random) refutes the attention-pathway account and the mechanism claim is withdrawn.

Experiment 7 (H3 -- suppression restores the correct answer without editing any fact): Test that subtracting the self-commitment direction fixes lock-in cleanly. Data: verified-recoverable cases, fact-disjoint train/test; steering vector = mean residual difference (lock-in minus no-commitment matched states), seeds {0,1,2}, rank<=4, subtracted at the layers identified in Experiment 6. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the subtracted direction. Systems compared: self-commitment subtraction, entrainment-head ablation (Experiment 6b), 'reconsider independently' re-prompt, ROME edit (expected not to help -- no fact is wrong), random-direction control. Decisive metric (first): recovered-per-unit-collateral = correct-answer recovery rate divided by the accuracy drop on cases where the prior commitment was CORRECT (over-correction control); secondary, accuracy on 200 unrelated facts and fluency (perplexity delta). Thresholds justified against the re-prompt and random baselines: convincing recovery >= 30% with < 3-point drop on correct-prior-commitment cases and on the 200 facts, beating the re-prompt baseline on recovered-per-collateral; indecision recovery 15-30% or collateral 3-6 points (partial; report parity with re-prompting); negative (no better than random/re-prompt, or harms correct-prior cases) refutes H3.

Experiment 8 (H1/H3 -- AUXILIARY: transfer, generality, and safety): Auxiliary; not required for the core single-model claim. Test generality across relations and models and whether lock-in produces higher-stakes errors. Data: eligible facts partitioned by relation; suppression vector trained on a subset, applied to held-out relations. Models: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; re-run Experiments 3-7, seeds {0,1,2}. Safety transfer: replicate Experiments 2-3 on a curated safe subset of clinical facts (~400 items, publicly documented and non-actionable), where a benign early wrong commitment about a drug indication corrupts a later independent answer. Decisive metric (first): cross-relation recovery relative to within-relation, replication of the self-authorship lift (Experiment 3) per model, and the self-authorship lift in the clinical setting. Convincing: cross-relation recovery >= 50% of within-relation, lift replicates (CI excludes 0) in >= 2 of 3 models, clinical lift CI excludes 0; indecision: replication in 1 model, cross-relation 30-50%, or clinical lift 3-8 points (model/relation/domain-specific; report scope); negative (no transfer/replication, no clinical lift) confines H1-H3 to one model and general-knowledge prompts. Also report whether larger models lock in more.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The self-vs-external authorship conditions differ in surface framing, so the effect could be a framing/politeness/discourse artifact rather than genuine self-commitment; matched-content-and-framing controls, the generic-entrainment null (Exp 3), the swapped-attribution sanity condition, and the constant-text/position manipulation are essential, and a residual self-authorship lift after all controls is the decisive behavioral evidence.

Novelty is a new setting + control + intervention, not a claim of a wholly new internal circuit; closest prior work (self-preference/sycophancy, e.g. 2508.02087, BrokenMath) already shows self-authored content is favored, so the contribution rests on the factual-recall outcome and the authorship-held-constant control rather than on the mechanism being unprecedented.

Lock-in could reflect genuine belief updating rather than overridden-but-stored knowledge; the storage-verification step (Exp 4) with conservative thresholds and a probe-failure analysis separates the two, but the probe measures superficial recoverability, not a guaranteed accessible 'belief', so fresh-query agreement is treated as the stronger criterion and strong-prompt leakage may overestimate storage.

The self-commitment signal and correct-answer recall may be entangled; the causal patching/ablation tests (Exp 6), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and the mechanism claim is withdrawn if ablation matches random controls; graded results remain informative.

Suppression could over-correct (discard legitimately relevant prior context) or degrade fluency; the correct-prior-commitment and unrelated-fact specificity controls are central and utility may be capped.

Lock-in may overlap with contextual entrainment; the authorship contrast is designed to separate them, but partial overlap would weaken the 'distinct-from-entrainment' claim while remaining informative.
A single transferable suppression vector may not exist if lock-in is relation-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B open models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: schema_overregularization
Title: Overregularization in LLMs: When a Stored Exception Loses to a Generalizable Rule It Contradicts
Short Hypothesis: LLMs store both broad generalizable rules/schemata (e.g., 'the plural of X is X+s', 'a country's capital is its largest city', 'company founders are CEOs') and specific exception facts that violate those rules. We hypothesize a distinct, predictable failure mode—overregularization—in which the model retrieves and produces the rule-consistent answer even when it internally stores the correct exception, because the rule pathway and the exception pathway compete and the rule wins on ambiguous or low-frequency exceptions. We predict (1) rule application and exception recall are causally dissociable pathways decodable at different depths, (2) overregularization errors concentrate on low-frequency exceptions where the rule is strong, above matched baselines, and (3) suppressing the rule pathway (not amplifying the fact) selectively recovers the stored exception with high specificity, whereas ROME-style fact editing does not address the root cause. Primary falsifiable claim: for exceptions the model demonstrably stores, suppressing a rule direction recovers the stored exception substantially more than amplifying the exception-content direction, while the same rule suppression degrades correct answers on true regulars (the positive control proving we manipulated the rule pathway). We test whether this rule direction is distinct from the known reasoning-vs-memorization switch direction (e.g. LiReFs); if it is not, we report overregularization as a mechanistic application of that direction to a new, concrete cross-domain failure class rather than a new mechanism. 'Stored exception' is defined strictly and falsifiably: recoverable by two orthogonal probes AND under a different prompt family AND robust across paraphrases; ambiguous multi-token items are excluded.
Related Work: Prior work shows reasoning/generalization and memorization occupy separable-but-interacting circuits and layers (Disentangling Recall and Reasoning, 2025; Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning, 2025; Demystifying LLM Layers, 2025), that memorization builds on and coexists with generalization mechanisms with intermediate reasoning outputs computed even when a memorized label is emitted (Reason to Rote, 2025), and that a single linear direction mediates a reasoning-vs-memorization switch (LiReFs, 2025). Declarative statements causally shape generalization (Tell, don't show, 2023). All of these characterize that rule/generalization and fact/memorization mechanisms co-exist, but none identify overregularization—the rule pathway overriding a correctly-stored exception—as a concrete, predictable factual-answering failure, none causally localize the failure to rule-vs-exception competition, and none propose rule-pathway suppression as a non-destructive fix. This is also orthogonal to my prior proposals (expression gating, format-bound copies, entity-candidate competition, retrieve-vs-assemble route arbitration, pre-retrieval familiarity, property collapse, premature lexicalization): here the competition is between a productive rule and a fact that violates it, mirroring the classic human overregularization phenomenon (e.g., 'goed' for 'went'). Delta from LiReFs-style switch-direction work stated exactly: they identify a single reasoning-vs-memorization direction; we ask whether a rule-application pathway causally overrides a correctly-stored exception, measure a new quantity (rule-suppression recovery minus content-amplification recovery, with a regulars-degradation control), and identify a new failure class - overregularization - that the switch direction alone does not predict. We test our rule direction against the LiReFs direction directly; a null there downgrades the claim to an application, not a discovery.
Abstract: Large language models generalize from productive rules and schemata—regular plurals, default relational patterns, statistical regularities—while also storing specific facts that violate those rules. We propose that this dual organization creates a distinct, overlooked failure mode we call overregularization: when a query targets an exception, the model produces the rule-consistent answer even though it internally stores the correct exception, because a rule-application pathway competes with and overrides an exception-recall pathway. Under this account, some knowledge failures are neither storage nor gating failures but rule-vs-exception arbitration failures, directly paralleling human overregularization ('goed' for 'went'). We build controlled rule/exception item sets across three domains—morphology (irregular inflection), factual relations with statistical defaults (e.g., capital≠largest-city, founder≠CEO), and numeric/temporal regularities—and identify exceptions that the model stores (recoverable under strong prompting or by a linear content probe) yet answers with the rule-consistent value. We test three claims. (1) Dissociability: a rule-strength probe (predicting the rule-consistent output) and an exception-content probe (predicting the correct stored exception) are separable and decodable at different layers, with rule signals emerging early. (2) Prevalence: overregularization errors concentrate on low-frequency exceptions with high rule support, above frequency- and similarity-matched baselines, and the wrong answers are disproportionately the exact rule-predicted value. (3) Intervention: suppressing the rule pathway (via a learned low-rank rule direction) recovers the stored exception with higher specificity and less collateral damage than amplifying the fact or ROME editing, and preserves correct rule application on true regulars. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluating probe separability, layer-onset ordering, error-type prevalence, causal transfer, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency. To keep the phenomenon from reading as a curiosity, we quantify prevalence at scale and, where possible, on commonly used factual-QA/editing items rather than only linguistically curated sets, with matched controls (low-frequency rule-consistent facts, high-frequency exceptions, random-label baselines) and pre-registered metrics. The application story is concrete: when a query targets a stored exception, suppressing the generic rule - rather than editing the fact - can restore correctness without harming rule application on regulars; we state plainly whether this changes diagnosis, evaluation, or editing practice, and we do not claim a new mechanism unless the rule direction beats prior switch directions under controlled comparison.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 - rule/exception items with rule-predicted and true values): Builds controlled items where a productive rule and a stored exception diverge. Data: constructed from three domains - (a) morphology: regular vs. irregular inflections (plurals, past tense) from a standard English inflection list (~2,000 irregulars available; use 1,500); (b) factual defaults with documented exceptions - capital-vs-largest-city, founder-vs-CEO, author-vs-most-famous-work - built from Wikidata (target 3,000 exception items where rule-predicted != correct); (c) numeric/temporal regularities (e.g. month-length exceptions). Per item we record the rule-predicted answer, the correct answer, and an exception flag; fewer than all candidates because each needs verified rule-vs-exception divergence. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; seed 0. Systems compared: rule-predicted vs. true value per item. Decisive metric: coverage = verified exception items with single-token-first answers across the three domains (first); supporting: per-domain counts. Convincing: >=3,500 verified exception items spanning all three domains. Undecidable band: 1,500-3,500 items is thin - report reduced power. Negative: <1,500 usable exceptions means the phenomenon cannot be tested at scale here.

Experiment 2 (H1/H2 - exceptions are actually stored): Confirms the model stores each exception, so overregularization is a retrieval-not-storage failure. Data: the exception items from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; storage confirmed by (i) strong retrieval prompts / few-shot demonstrations and (ii) a trainable linear content probe decoding the correct answer from the residual stream, seeds 0/1/2, conservative thresholds. Systems compared: strong-prompt recovery and content-probe recovery vs. a label-shuffle control. Decisive metric: fraction of exceptions with positive storage evidence by both criteria (first, defines the stored-exception set); supporting: content-probe AUROC. Convincing: >=50% of exceptions pass both criteria, giving a solid stored-exception set. Undecidable band: 30-50% pass means the stored set is modest and strong-prompt leakage is a risk - report conservative coverage. Negative: <30% pass, or content probe at shuffle level, means few exceptions are genuinely stored, so overregularization cannot be distinguished from ignorance.

Experiment 3 (H1 - rule and exception signals decodable at different depths): Tests that the rule signal is decodable earlier than the exception content. Data: the stored-exception set from Experiment 2. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; two trainable per-layer probes - a rule-strength probe (target: the rule-predicted token / a scalar rule-applicability score) and an exception-content probe (target: the correct answer); onset-layer test with bootstrap CIs, residualization orthogonality check, seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle controls. Systems compared: rule vs. exception onset layers. Decisive metric: onset-layer difference (first-layer at AUROC>=0.7), rule expected earlier (first); supporting: post-residualization retained predictiveness of each. Convincing: rule onset precedes exception onset by >=3 layers with non-overlapping CIs, and each retains predictiveness after residualizing out the other (retained AUROC >=0.70). Undecidable band: a 1-3 layer gap or overlapping CIs cannot establish depth separation - defer to the causal test (Experiment 5). Negative: exception onset at/before rule, or the two collapsing under residualization, falsifies H1.

Experiment 4 (H2 - overregularization concentrates on low-frequency exceptions with strong rules): Tests the prevalence pattern. Data: errors on the stored-exception set. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify errors into (a) overregularization (emitted answer equals the exact rule-predicted value while the exception is stored), (b) other, (c) correct. Systems compared: overregularization rate vs. exception frequency and rule support, against a null controlling for exception-answer frequency and lexical similarity to the rule-predicted answer (logistic regression / chi-square). Decisive metric: odds ratio linking low exception frequency + high rule support to overregularization, above the matched null (first); supporting: per-domain rates. Convincing: odds ratio >=2x over the null (p<0.001) - overregularization concentrates as predicted. Undecidable band: odds ratio 1.3-2x is a modest but real concentration - report as a localized minor mode. Negative: <=1.3x or null-indistinguishable falsifies H2's concentration claim.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - rule suppression, not fact amplification, is the effective lever): Causally dissociates weak exception recall from an overriding rule pathway. Data: overregularization failures (target 1,500) plus true regulars (target 1,000 as a positive control). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch the exception-content representation from a correct run into a failure, (b) suppress the rule direction (from Experiment 3) at rule-onset layers, (c) amplify the exception-content direction alone; positive control: rule suppression on true regulars must degrade their correct rule-based answers; random-direction control. Systems compared: content-patch vs. rule-suppression vs. content-amplification vs. random, plus the regulars control. Decisive metric: exception recovery under rule-suppression minus recovery under content-amplification (first, the causal signature that the rule pathway is the lever); supporting: degradation of true regulars under rule suppression (must be substantial). Convincing: rule suppression recovers >=35% of exceptions while content amplification recovers <=15% (gap >=20 points), AND rule suppression degrades true regulars by >=30% (confirming the rule pathway was manipulated). Undecidable band: a 10-20 point recovery gap, or <15% regulars degradation, means the rule pathway is only partly the lever - report weak causal support. Negative: no gap (amplification works as well), or no regulars degradation, means we did not isolate an overriding rule pathway, falsifying H1/H3's mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H3 - rule-suppression steering recovers exceptions selectively; editing does not address the cause): Tests a training-free rule-suppression vector against fact editing. Data: held-out overregularization failures, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; a rank<=8 rule vector (mean difference of rule-dominant vs. exception-dominant matched states) subtracted, alpha swept; random-direction control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: rule-suppression vs. exception-direction amplification vs. ROME/MEMIT editing of the exception vs. suppression along the known LiReFs reasoning-vs-memorization direction (to test whether our rule direction is genuinely distinct) vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-exceptions-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on (i) 200 unrelated facts and (ii) held-out true regulars (first, regulars must stay correct); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% drop on unrelated facts and true regulars, beating ROME/MEMIT on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage, or 5-10% regulars degradation, is parity/marginal - report with a caveat. Negative: recovery <20%, or regulars degrading >10%, falsifies the selective-recovery half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 generality - one rule-suppression vector transfers across families and models): Tests transfer and architecture-generality. Data: train on one domain/rule family, apply to held-out ones; reuse the Experiment 1 items per model. Model: single vector on Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 2-6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds. Systems compared: cross-family transfer vs. within-family oracle; three models per decisive metric. Decisive metric: cross-family recovery rate and cross-model sign-consistency of the Experiment 4 concentration and Experiment 6 advantage (first); supporting: per-model onset gaps. Convincing: cross-family recovery >=25% and all three models show concentration and a recovery advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: transfer 10-25% or the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: <10% transfer or majority model reversal means the mechanism is family/model-specific.

Experiment 8 (H2 - the failure is driven by rule strength versus exception weakness): Tests the source of overregularization. Data: per-item overregularization outcomes across domains. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; regress overregularization rate on exception-answer frequency, rule productivity (fraction of the family following the rule), and the frequency ratio between rule-predicted and true answers. Systems compared: rule-strength regressors vs. an exception-frequency-only baseline. Decisive metric: partial R^2 of rule productivity + frequency ratio beyond exception frequency (first); supporting: coefficient signs. Convincing: rule-strength features add partial R^2 >=0.10 with the predicted signs (higher productivity and higher rule:exception frequency ratio raise the rate). Undecidable band: partial R^2 0.03-0.10 is a weak trend - report as suggestive. Negative: partial R^2 <0.03 means rule strength does not drive the failure, falsifying the core mechanistic claim of H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Cleanly separating 'rule' from 'exception' representations may be hard when they are entangled (superposition); the causal patching and rule-suppression tests (Exp 5–6), rather than probe onset alone, are the decisive evidence, and graded results would still be informative.
Overregularization errors may be rare relative to generic errors; the frequency/similarity-matched baseline is essential and a modest but significant, well-localized effect remains publishable.
Establishing that an exception is truly 'stored' risks overestimation from strong-prompt leakage; we use conservative content-probe thresholds and held-out verification and report coverage limits.

Rule suppression could break correct rule application on genuine regulars or degrade fluency; the true-regulars specificity control (Exp 5c/6) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
A single transferable rule-suppression vector may not exist if rules are family-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate probe/logit-lens readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: persona_knowledge_suppression
Title: In Character, Out of Knowledge: How a Low-Competence Persona Suppresses Facts the Model Still Stores
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM adopts a low-competence or non-expert persona ('answer as a young child', 'as a medieval peasant', 'as someone who failed science'), it fails factual queries it answers correctly in the default assistant voice. The exact falsifiable delta is that persona failures are EXPRESSION-GATING, not storage loss, and that competence is SEPARABLE from style: the fact remains stored (linearly decodable during the failure), and a persona-competence signal computed early in the network - distinct from the persona's stylistic behavior and from genuine fact difficulty - causally gates its expression. It would count as failure of this novelty if probes only recover residual semantics rather than the answer-specific token, or if the intervention that reopens knowledge also destroys the persona's style. We hypothesize (1) the correct answer remains answer-specifically decodable from intermediate activations during persona failures (hidden, not erased); (2) a persona-competence direction, separable from fact-content and from generic refusal, predicts and causally drives suppression and scales with implied incompetence rather than fact difficulty; and (3) suppressing this direction (not editing the fact) reopens the hidden knowledge while leaving the persona's stylistic behavior intact. We treat the existence of a single transferable competence vector as a hypothesis to test, not an assumption.
Related Work: Prior behavioral work shows low-knowledge personas (child, toddler, layperson) reduce factual accuracy (Prompting Science Report 4, 2025; LLMs downplay cognitive abilities, 2024), that persona assignment triggers abstentions and stereotype-driven errors (Bias Runs Deep, 2023), and that inquiry personas alter QA accuracy and cause hallucinated limitations/refusals (Who's Asking?, 2025). Mechanistic work localizes persona information to early MLP layers and identity-token positions (Dissecting Persona-Driven Reasoning, 2025; Localizing Persona Representations, 2025) and builds role/steering vectors (Role Vectors, 2025; SRPS, 2025). Split Personality Training (2026) uses a second persona to read latent knowledge for auditing; entity-cell work (Friends and Grandmothers in Silico, 2026) causally toggles stored facts. Our contribution narrows away from the KNOWN result 'low-knowledge personas hurt accuracy' and toward two specific claims prior work does not establish, one row per claim: (i) Prompting Science Report 4 / Who's Asking? document the accuracy drop but not that the fact stays answer-specifically decodable during failure; (ii) persona-vector papers build steering directions but do not show a competence direction that causally GATES stored knowledge separably from style; (iii) none demonstrate a style-preserving, non-destructive recovery. This is orthogonal to prior single-turn retrieval/gating proposals: here the gating variable is the persona's implied competence, and the object is knowledge suppressed by role-play.
Abstract: Large language models will happily role-play as a young child, a medieval peasant, or someone who failed high-school science - and when asked a factual question in such a low-competence persona, they often get it wrong even though the same model answers correctly as the default assistant. The user-visible consequence comes first: persona and role-play prompts can HIDE correct answers, so evaluations run under such prompts may underestimate a model's actual knowledge, and auditing under deceptive or role-play prompts (including medical and safety settings) can miss facts the model holds. Prior work documents that low-knowledge personas degrade accuracy but treats this as a capability change. We propose instead a knowledge-suppression failure: the fact remains stored and answer-specifically recoverable, but a persona-competence signal computed early in the network causally gates its expression, separably from style. We test three claims on factual queries wrapped in personas of graded implied competence (expert, default, layperson, child, incompetent-character) with competence-neutral style controls. (1) Hidden knowledge: on persona-induced failures, a linear probe recovers the correct answer far above verbalized accuracy, above matched baselines, demonstrating answer-specific decodability rather than mere semantic proximity. (2) Localization and drivers: a persona-competence direction, decodable early and residualized-separable from fact-content and generic refusal, predicts suppression and scales with implied incompetence rather than fact difficulty. (3) Causal, style-preserving recovery: suppressing the competence direction (or patching it from a default-voice run) reopens hidden facts while the persona's style is retained (judged by a persona classifier), outperforming a 'be accurate' reminder and fact editing, with minimum-viable success criteria stated per experiment so partial support is still reportable. This anchors impact to persona reliability, more reliable knowledge evaluation, and non-finetuning recovery, not a general safety breakthrough. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B on PopQA, T-REx, and a medical-fact subset.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — Persona-graded dataset and suppression scaling with implied competence): Tests the behavioral premise of H2, that a persona-competence signal (not mere style) drives suppression that scales with implied incompetence. Data: constructed from PopQA (~14k), T-REx (LAMA subset ~34k), EntityQuestions (~176k); select 2,500 facts the model answers correctly in the default voice, wrapped in a fixed template under five competence conditions (matched expert, default, layperson, young child, in-character incompetent) plus two competence-neutral style controls (cheerful, formal). Single-token-first answers only; report coverage. 2,500 x 7 = 17,500 prompts fits budget and gives tight per-condition estimates. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared: accuracy across competence conditions vs the style-only controls; ordinal (mixed-effects logistic) regression of accuracy on implied competence. Decisive metric (before data), first: accuracy drop from default to the incompetent persona, and the monotonic ordinal slope across competence, vs a null where persona only adds output-format noise (style-control accuracy). Convincing = incompetent-persona drop >=15pp AND monotonic ordinal slope CI excluding 0 AND style controls drop <=3pp (tracks competence, not style). Negative = drop <=3pp or style controls drop as much (no competence-specific suppression; premise fails). Indecision band 3-15pp drop: report weak suppression.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Hidden-knowledge probe): Tests H1, that the correct answer stays linearly decodable during persona failures. Data: persona-suppression cases from Exp 1 (correct under default, wrong under a low-competence persona); 80/20 split by fact; label-shuffle control. Model: same three frozen; a linear answer probe on the subject-token/last-token residual stream, L2-regularized, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV on held-out facts. Systems compared: probe recovery accuracy under the low-competence persona vs the model's verbalized accuracy there vs the default-voice probe (upper bound). Decisive metric (before data), first: probe recovery accuracy minus verbalized accuracy on suppression cases. Convincing = probe recovers the correct answer at >=40pp above verbalized accuracy and within 10pp of the default-voice probe (fact hidden, not erased). Negative = probe within 10pp of verbalized accuracy (fact truly gone; H1 fails). Indecision band 10-40pp above verbalized: partial hidden knowledge; report as graded. Shuffle probe must be at chance.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Persona-competence direction: localization and driver): Tests H2's localization and that the direction tracks implied competence, not fact difficulty. Data: Exp 1 activations across competence conditions. Model: same three frozen; contrastive mean-difference persona-competence direction per layer; a fact-content probe for residualization; no weight training. Systems compared: the competence direction's activation regressed on implied competence vs on true fact difficulty (baseline default-voice confidence); competence direction residualized on the fact-content signal. Decisive metric (before data): standardized regression coefficient on implied competence minus that on fact difficulty, plus residual decodability of competence after removing content. Convincing = competence coefficient >=2x the difficulty coefficient AND residual competence AUROC >=0.70, at an early MLP/identity-token layer as prior persona-localization predicts. Negative = difficulty coefficient >= competence coefficient, or residual AUROC <=0.55 (no separable competence signal; H2 localization fails). Indecision band residual AUROC 0.55-0.70: report an entangled, graded competence signal.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Causal drive of suppression): Tests H2's causal claim that the competence direction drives suppression. Data: 1,000 held-out suppression cases (Exp 1). Model: same three frozen; activation edits at Exp 3 layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) suppress the competence direction; (b) patch the competence representation from a default-voice run; (c) reverse control injecting the low-competence direction into a default run; (d) content control (fact-content signal unchanged); plus random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-fact recovery rate (correct answer, matching the default-voice answer) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp over random at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=15pp suppression in default runs. Negative = <=5pp recovery (direction not causal; H2 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Style-preserving recovery and specificity): Tests H3, that suppressing the direction reopens knowledge while leaving persona style intact and unrelated behavior unharmed. Data: Exp 4 held-out suppression cases; 1,000 facts the persona already answers correctly; 200 unrelated facts. Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our suppression vs a 'be accurate regardless of persona' reminder, dropping the persona entirely (which trivially recovers knowledge but destroys style), ROME editing (existing, expected null), random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: recovery rate AT constant persona-style retention -- style retention judged by a persona classifier / GPT-4o rating that the output is still in character. Convincing = recovery >=25pp while style-retention drops <=5pp vs the persona baseline, already-correct accuracy drops <=3pp, unrelated accuracy drops <=2pp, perplexity <=5%. Negative = recovery forces style-retention drop >=20pp (knowledge and style inseparable) or no recovery. Indecision band style-drop 5-20pp: dissociation is partial; report the recovery-vs-style trade-off.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Cross-persona and cross-model transfer): Tests whether a single competence-suppression vector generalizes. Data: vector fit on a subset of personas/relations (Exp 4) applied unchanged to held-out personas and relations (800 cases). Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction. Decisive metric (before data): transferred recovery as a fraction of in-domain-refit. Convincing = >=60% of in-domain on >=2 personas and >=2 models. Negative = <=20% (persona-specific; generality fails). Indecision band 20-60%: partial transfer. Report Spearman rho between model scale and suppression magnitude across the three models (rho <=-0.3 suggestive that larger models suppress less; N=3 caveat).

Experiment 7 (H1/H2 — Safety-domain transfer): Tests whether H1 hidden-knowledge and H2 competence-driven suppression appear in a higher-stakes domain. Data: a curated medical/clinical factual-recall subset (drug indications, symptom-disease facts) drawn from an existing medical QA set (e.g. MedQA/DrugBank-derived), 800 facts the model answers correctly in the default voice, wrapped in low-competence inquiry personas ('I'm just a worried parent with no medical background'). Model: same three frozen. Systems compared: replicate Exp 1 prevalence and Exp 2 hidden-knowledge probe and Exp 4 causal drive on this subset vs the general-knowledge result. Decisive metric (before data): suppression prevalence and hidden-knowledge gap in the medical subset. Convincing = suppression prevalence >=15pp and hidden-knowledge gap >=40pp, i.e. at least as large as general knowledge, demonstrating higher-stakes hidden failures. Negative = medical prevalence <=3pp (suppression does not transfer to this domain). Indecision band 3-15pp: report domain-attenuated suppression.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Persona-induced errors could reflect genuine strategy change (the model deliberately 'dumbs down') rather than knowledge suppression; the hidden-knowledge probe (Exp 3) and the causal, style-preserving recovery (Exp 6) are the decisive separators—if recovering the fact necessarily breaks the persona, the gating claim is weakened but still informative.
The persona-competence and fact-content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 5), not probe accuracy alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Style preservation and knowledge recovery may trade off (suppressing the competence direction could also erase persona style); the persona-classifier metric (Exp 6) quantifies this and utility may be capped if the two cannot be dissociated.

Suppression prevalence may be modest for some persona/relation combinations; the ordinal competence gradient and paired within-fact design maximize power, and a significant monotonic effect is still informative.
A single transferable competence-suppression vector may not exist if suppression is persona-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
The style-vs-competence control persona may imperfectly isolate competence from other persona attributes; multiple control personas and regression on implied competence mitigate this.
Multi-token answers complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7–9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.

Name: conditional_suppression_effect
Title: Suppressed by an Aside: Transferring the Human Conditional-Suppression Effect into LLMs and Locating the Premise-Gating Mechanism
Short Hypothesis: LLMs exhibit the classic human conditional-reasoning suppression effect: adding a logically-irrelevant additional-condition premise to a valid modus ponens / modus tollens argument suppresses endorsement of the deductively valid conclusion, whereas adding an alternative-condition premise selectively suppresses the invalid inferences (denial-of-antecedent / affirmation-of-consequent) - the double dissociation observed in humans. We scope the novelty to the MECHANISTIC delta, not to first behavioral transfer: prior LLM work already reports conditional fallacies and partial additional-vs-alternative effects, but none (i) probe a hidden state for a still-decodable valid conclusion, (ii) causally localize a premise-gating direction, or (iii) show a specificity-preserving intervention. 'Suppression' is operationally the drop in endorsement of a specific inference form caused by a non-defeating added premise, in ABSTRACT (letter) items that isolate logical form from world knowledge, distinguishing it from generic fallacy or ambiguity. We hypothesize this is not a competence failure but a premise-gating failure: the model still derives the valid conclusion internally (it is linearly decodable), a distinct premise-gating signal triggered by the extra premise gates its expression, and suppressing that signal restores the valid inference without editing the rule while preserving legitimate defeasibility. We test behavioral transfer, internal decodability, and causal editing as three separable claims, not bundling one as implying the others.
Related Work: Human cognitive science established the suppression effect (Byrne 1989; Bonnefon; Quelhas & Johnson-Laird 2016; Suppression of Inferences From Counterfactual Conditionals 2020): a valid modus ponens is suppressed by an additional premise while invalid inferences are suppressed by an alternative premise - a precise double dissociation. In LLMs, mechanistic work on fact-vs-counterfactual competition (Ortu et al. 2024; Fakepedia 2023) and RULEBREAKERS (2024) shows models over-rigidly apply logic and mis-integrate world knowledge, and semantic-vs-symbolic reasoning work (2023) shows reliance on surface semantics; some conditional-reasoning papers already observe partial additional-vs-alternative behavior. The exact delta versus each: those papers characterize behavioral inconsistency, but none show a hidden-state probe recovering a decodable valid conclusion when it is behaviorally withheld, none causally localize a premise-gating direction that is engaged in BOTH arms of the dissociation, and none demonstrate an intervention that restores valid inferences while preserving genuine defeasibility. This is orthogonal to prior factual/entity-retrieval proposals; here the object is defeasible conditional inference and how an incidental premise gates a correctly-computed logical conclusion.
Abstract: Since Byrne (1989), cognitive science has documented the suppression effect: people who correctly infer 'she got wet' from 'if she watered the plants she got wet' and 'she watered the plants' stop endorsing that valid modus ponens once an additional premise ('if the sprinkler was on she got wet') is added - even though it does not logically defeat the inference - while an alternative premise instead suppresses the invalid inferences. The broader stake is evaluation of reasoning systems: this is a hidden-competence-vs-expression split, where a model may compute the valid conclusion yet withhold it, so reasoning benchmarks can misattribute expression failures to missing competence, and prompt-sensitivity diagnostics and targeted reliability interventions follow if the split is real. We first document the behavior on controlled conditional-reasoning items (MP, MT, DA, AC) in ABSTRACT and everyday forms, pre-registering the primary interaction - additional premise suppresses MP/MT, alternative premise suppresses DA/AC, in abstract items with matched premise-length and plausibility controls - and testing its plausibility and scale dose-response. We then test a mechanistic hypothesis: the valid conclusion is still internally derived (linearly decodable) even when withheld, and a distinct premise-gating signal, separable from conclusion content, causally suppresses its expression. Activation patching from a baseline (no-extra-premise) run and subtraction of a learned premise-gating direction restore the valid conclusion with high specificity, while injecting the direction induces suppression on demand; a negative-control set where suppression is logically WARRANTED confirms the intervention preserves genuine defeasibility rather than globally restoring affirmations. Behavioral transfer, internal decodability, and causal editing are reported as separate claims. Any clinical/procedural arm is reported descriptively, not as a safety claim. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Suppression dataset and additional-vs-alternative double dissociation): Tests H1's behavioral core, the human double dissociation (additional-condition premise suppresses valid inferences; alternative-condition premise suppresses invalid inferences). Data: constructed by adapting the classic Byrne/Quelhas conditional-reasoning paradigm (existing stimuli, tens of items) into 1,200 controlled items: each base 'if A then C' yields four inference probes (modus ponens, modus tollens valid; denial-of-antecedent, affirmation-of-consequent invalid) x three versions (baseline; +additional-condition; +alternative-condition), in both everyday-semantics and abstract/letter forms; endorsement via a fixed yes/no/uncertain template plus 3 paraphrases. 1,200 items x 4 x 3 x 2 forms fits budget and gives >=100 items per cell. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared: endorsement across premise-type x inference-type vs a null where any added premise adds uniform noise. Decisive metric (before data), first: the premise-type x inference-type interaction (additional suppresses valid; alternative suppresses invalid) in a mixed-effects logistic regression, in the ABSTRACT form (isolating logic from world knowledge). Convincing = interaction CI excluding 0 in >=2 models AND additional-premise drop on valid inferences >=15pp. Negative = no interaction (uniform or no suppression; H1 fails as a human-signature). Indecision band interaction present only in everyday but not abstract form: report as semantics-driven, not a form-level suppression effect.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Plausibility and scale dose-response): Tests H1's gradedness, that suppression scales with the added premise's plausibility. Data: Exp 1 items with the added premise's plausibility/salience varied over 4 levels (rated by an existing plausibility norm / GPT-4o). Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B (and, where an intra-family size series is affordable, two sizes of one family), frozen. Systems compared: suppression magnitude across plausibility levels; and across model scale. Decisive metric (before data): slope of suppression on premise plausibility. Convincing = positive slope with CI excluding 0 in >=2 models, mirroring the human graded effect. Negative = flat slope (suppression not plausibility-graded; the human-likeness claim weakens). Indecision band |standardized slope| < 0.1 with CI crossing 0: report as no reliable dose-response. Scale effect reported as Spearman rho between size and suppression (N small; suggestive only), distinguishing 'more human-like defeasibility' from 'over-rigid logic'.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Hidden-conclusion probe): Tests the first half of H2, that the valid conclusion is still internally derived when behaviorally withheld. Data: suppression cases from Exp 1 (valid inference endorsed at baseline, withheld under the additional premise); 80/20 split by item; label-shuffle control. Model: same three frozen; a linear probe on the conclusion-position/last-token residual stream decoding whether valid conclusion C is derived; seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV. Systems compared: probe recovery under suppression vs verbalized endorsement vs the baseline run (upper bound). Decisive metric (before data), first: probe recovery of the valid conclusion minus verbalized endorsement on suppression cases. Convincing = probe recovers at >=40pp above verbalized and within 10pp of baseline (derived but expression-gated). Negative = probe within 10pp of verbalized (the model did not derive C; H2 fails). Indecision band 10-40pp: partial internal derivation, report as graded.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Premise-gating signal localization): Tests the second half of H2, a separable premise-gating direction that mirrors the behavioral dissociation. Data: Exp 1 activations, additional-premise (suppressing) vs baseline contrast. Model: same three frozen; contrastive mean-difference gating direction per layer; conclusion-content probe for residualization; no weight training. Systems compared: gating direction residualized on conclusion-content (should track added-premise presence/plausibility, not the specific conclusion); and whether the same direction is engaged by additional premises for valid inferences AND by alternative premises for invalid inferences (mechanistic counterpart of Exp 1). Decisive metric (before data): residual AUROC of the gating signal after removing conclusion-content, and its cross-engagement across the dissociation. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 and the direction engaged in both dissociation arms. Negative = residual AUROC <=0.55 (no separable gating signal; H2 localization fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report entangled gating.

Experiment 5 (H2/H3 — Causal intervention): Tests H2's causal drive and H3's restoration. Data: 1,000 held-out suppression cases. Model: same three frozen; activation edits at Exp 4 layers, dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}; no weight training. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) patch the conclusion-position residual stream from a baseline (no-extra-premise) run; (b) subtract the learned gating direction; (c) reverse control injecting the gating direction into a baseline run; (d) content control (unrelated inferences unchanged); plus random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-item recovery of the valid conclusion (matches baseline endorsement) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp over random at a dose with perplexity within 5%, AND reverse control induces >=15pp suppression. Negative = <=5pp recovery (gating not causal; H2/H3 causal link fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Recovery specificity: preserving legitimate defeasibility): Tests H3's key specificity requirement, that reopening valid inferences does not indiscriminately restore inferences that SHOULD be suppressed. Data: Exp 5 held-out suppression cases; a genuinely-defeasible set where the added premise is a TRUE blocking condition that should reduce confidence (300 items); 200 unrelated reasoning/factual items. Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose. Systems compared: our intervention vs a 'reason strictly from the premises' re-prompt, chain-of-thought, random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: valid-inference recovery rate MINUS inappropriate restoration on genuinely-defeasible items (recovered-per-unit-over-restoration). Convincing = valid recovery >=25pp while genuinely-defeasible confidence is restored <=5pp, unrelated accuracy unchanged (<=2pp), perplexity <=5%. Negative = genuinely-defeasible items restored >=20pp (we broke legitimate defeasibility) or no valid recovery. Indecision band 5-20pp over-restoration: utility capped; report the selectivity trade-off.

Experiment 7 (H3 — Transfer, generality, and optional safety): Tests whether a single gating-suppression vector generalizes across inference forms and domains. Data: vector fit on a subset of forms/domains (Exp 5) applied to held-out forms and item domains (600 cases); optional safety replication of Exp 1-2 on curated clinical/procedural conditional rules ('if symptom X and no contraindication, give treatment T'), 400 safe items. Model: all three frozen. Systems compared: transferred vs in-domain-refit vs random-direction; clinical suppression vs general. Decisive metric (before data): transferred recovery as a fraction of in-domain-refit; plus clinical suppression prevalence. Convincing = transfer >=60% of in-domain on >=2 models (architecture-general mechanism). Negative = transfer <=20% (inference-form-specific; generality fails). Indecision band 20-60%: partial transfer. Clinical arm reported descriptively: suppression >=15pp there flags a higher-stakes error mode.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The behavioral suppression could be a genuine, appropriate defeasibility response rather than an unwanted gating of a valid inference; the abstract-form items (isolating logical form from world knowledge) and the additional-vs-alternative double-dissociation test (Exp 2) are the decisive separators - only the human-signature selectivity distinguishes suppression-effect from rational defeasance.

LLMs might not reproduce the human double dissociation at all (e.g. suppress uniformly or over-rigidly apply logic per RULEBREAKERS); a null or divergent pattern is itself an informative cross-species comparison, though it would weaken the 'human-like suppression' framing.
The premise-gating and conclusion-content signals may be entangled; the causal patching/injection tests (Exp 6), not probe decoding alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

The recovery intervention could indiscriminately restore inferences that *should* be suppressed (breaking legitimate defeasibility) or degrade fluency; the genuine-defeasibility specificity control (Exp 7) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
Endorsement is prompt-sensitive (yes/no/uncertain framing, phrasing); we use multiple paraphrases and report robustness, since framing itself may modulate suppression.
A single transferable gating vector may not exist if suppression is inference-form-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.
